d: Love in all its forms: romantic, familial, and the Confucian ethic of universal benevolence.

e: eight; the luckiest number and the eight trigrams
d: Eight is the most coveted number in modern China through its near-homophony with 发 fā (to prosper), and the classical foundation of the eight trigrams that structure the Yijing.
Sunlight on a single point. The character that names the color of mourning, the color of clarity, the empty plate, and the speech that hides nothing.
百姓, the hundred surnames, is classical Chinese for the common people, because the full range of ordinary family names stands in for everyone who is not nobility.

e: full, satisfied, to eat one's fill
d: The food radical 饣 wraps the sound of 包 (bāo), so the glyph itself is a stomach packed full like a dumpling.

e: to report, to announce; newspaper; to repay
d: A hand cuffing a kneeling criminal once meant sentencing; today the same glyph carries newspapers, reports, and the moral arithmetic of repayment.
Two people standing back-to-back: the direction of cold and turning away that became the name of China's capital.
A tree with its root marked: the character for where a thing comes from. From root grows origin, the fundamental, one's own, the principal sum, and the bound volume you hold in your hand.
Bamboo over hair: the bamboo-handled writing brush drawn as a character. From the implement grow the act of writing, the strokes that build a glyph, and a measure word for sums and deals.
A character rooted in the image of a blade that divides without exception: certainty as the sharpness that leaves no room for maybe.
The character at the heart of the I Ching, the dynastic cycle, and the modern vocabulary of reform: change as the one constant.

e: surface, to express, a table, a watch
d: The garment radical worn on the outside: 表 runs from the outer surface of things to showing feeling, the chart on a page, and the watch on a wrist.

e: illness, disease, to fall ill, fault
d: A person sweating on a sickbed with the phonetic 丙 inside: the radical 疒 frames every Chinese word for being unwell.
The most used character in Mandarin, and the foundation of every denial, refusal, and negation.

The right-side city-mound radical marks an administrative division. From that grows the whole family of parts and wholes: a section of something, a government ministry, a military unit, and the measure word counted out for films, machines, and phones.
A sprout breaking ground, the first sign of growth. From that image grow two threads: talent as raw promise, and the adverb 才 that marks something later, harder, or smaller than expected.
Plants gathered to be eaten. From the picked greens grows a whole table: the vegetable, the cooked dish, the regional cuisine, and the slangy put-down for anyone weak at a task.
A field of grass under the morning sun: the grass radical over 早 zǎo (early) gives the plant its sound, and from the meadow grow the senses of herb, straw, and a hasty rough draft.
The character that gave the world its word for tea: a grass over wood over man, a plant that shaped civilization, and the locus of China's richest material culture.
One altar character, two civilizations: read shàn it yields thrones and sacrifices to earth; read chán it transliterates Sanskrit dhyāna and founds Zen.

e: to produce, give birth, property, output
d: From birth to bounty: a character that spans biological generation and industrial output, linking the miracle of birth to the logic of production and wealth.
A long banner of cloth that came to mean what endures: the constant and the lasting, the ordinary and the common, and the things that happen again and again.

e: to sing, to chant, to call out
d: A mouth beside the sun-doubled 昌: the radical names the act of singing while 昌 carries only the sound.

e: dynasty, imperial court, to face toward; (zhāo) morning
d: The sun rising among grasses with the moon still in the sky. From that dawn scene grow two readings: zhāo, the morning and its youthful vigor, and cháo, the court that met at daybreak, the dynasty it served, and the preposition toward.

A halberd standing guard over a finished task. From that image grows the whole field of completion: to become, to succeed, to accomplish, the ready-made and the mature, and even the colloquial yes that settles a matter.
A rampart of earth raised around a settlement: the character where the wall and the city it protects are one and the same word.
To eat, and the extraordinary range of Chinese life encoded in a single food verb.

e: to exit, to emerge, to produce
d: 出 is two plants growing upward out of the earth: emergence itself written as a glyph, from physical exits to publication to standing out from the crowd.

e: to pierce, to bore through, to wear, to put on
d: A tooth gnawing through the roof of a cave: one image for boring a hole and for the body slipping into clothing.

e: to pass on, transmit, spread; (zhuan) a biography, a commentary
d: The person radical carrying something onward: one figure handing a thing to the next. From that image grow the senses of 传, read chuan when it means to pass down, transmit, and spread, and read zhuan when it names a biography or a classical commentary.
A pictophonetic built on 舟 (boat): the hull carries the meaning while the right side supplies the sound, covering every craft from sampan to ocean liner.

e: spring, springtime, vitality, the stir of desire
d: Sun pressing up through young shoots: the season of growth, and the oldest Chinese metaphor for life-force and erotic longing.

e: word, term, diction, the sung lyric
d: Speech beside a phonetic 司: the unit we call a word, the wording a speaker chooses, and the classical lyric form that grew up beside regulated verse to be sung to set tune-patterns.
A metal character whose oldest sense was inlay and grinding; from crossed, interlocking lines it slid to things crossing wrongly, the modern sense of error.

e: to hit, to strike; the most versatile verb in Mandarin
d: To hit, and a hundred extensions: make a call, play a sport, pack a bag, get an injection. The most productive light verb in Chinese.
Big, great, large: a person with arms wide open, the original measure of magnitude.

e: generation, era, to substitute, on behalf of
d: The person radical carrying the sense of succession: one figure standing in the place of another. From that single image grow the four faces of 代: to replace or act for someone, to do a thing on their behalf, the generation that succeeds the one before, and the era or dynasty in which a life is set.
A pictophonetic egg: the 虫 radical for small creatures sits under a sound element, and in slang it turns people into scoundrels.

e: to be, just at, ought; (dàng) appropriate, to treat as
d: A high-frequency polyphone with two readings. As dāng it means to serve as, to be at a given time or place, and ought to; as dàng it means appropriate, to treat something as, and to pawn. The tone tells you which sense is in play.
As a resultative complement suffix, 到 converts any action verb into a claim of completion: 听到 means not just hearing but hearing that arrived, perception proven by contact.
The character that opens the Dàodéjīng and names Daoism: way, path, principle, and the measure word for rivers and light.
Virtue not as rule-following but as accumulated moral power: what radiates from a person whose conduct has been straight long enough to become second nature.
Heaven above, earth below: the second power of the cosmos, and the root of every word about place, ground, and belonging.
A fire radical 火 fused with the sound 丁, naming everything from oil lamps to the red light that stops traffic.

e: low; to lower; to bow down
d: A person stooping: the phonetic 氐 gives the sound while the human radical supplies the posture, and together they built one of the most culturally loaded words in modern Chinese.
Bamboo over younger-brother, an image of things laid out in sequence. From it grows the prefix that turns a count into an order, plus the older senses of examination rank and grand residence.
From a single dot of ink the character spreads into points and decimals, into the hours of the clock, into ordering food and lighting a flame, and into the small quantity that softens a sentence.
Lightning descending from a rain cloud, a character that jumped from describing the weather to naming the force that defines modern civilization.

e: (diào) to transfer, tune, accent; (tiáo) to adjust, to blend, to mediate
d: A high-frequency polyphone with two readings. As diào it means to transfer, a melody or key, a tone, an accent; as tiáo it means to adjust, to blend, to mediate. The reading tells you whether 调 is moving things or harmonizing them.
A settling element coming to rest under a roof. From that image of a thing made still and fixed in place grows the whole field of 定: to decide, to set, the fixed and stable, the certain and sure.
The sun rising behind a tree, and the direction that anchored China's cosmological, political, and poetic imagination.

e: to understand, to know, to grasp
d: A heart-radical verb where comprehension is felt, not just decoded: to truly get something is to take it in inwardly.

e: to move, to act, to stir
d: Force applied to a thing sets it in motion. From that one idea grow the words for sport and activity, for the stirred heart, for the drive that pushes a machine or a life forward, and for the verb itself.
Reading as the act of voicing what is written: the everyday verb for studying, declaiming a text, and (figuratively) interpreting a person, a situation, or a sign.
An arrow set beside a ritual bean-pot measures the short distance, so 短 builds its meaning of brevity from a comparison of two small lengths.

e: team, group, band, military unit; measure word for groups
d: A crowd of people 人 packed against an earthen mound 阝, the image that gives 队 its sense of a formed-up team or column.
Two evenings stacked: the character that encodes abundance, comparison, and the most common question about quantity in Mandarin.

A pictograph of a beard, borrowed early as one of the busiest function words in literary Chinese. 而 links clause to clause as and, but, or yet, ties manner to verb, and frames set phrases like 而且 and 而已.
The pictograph of an ear that anchors Chinese words for listening, fame, and the furred handles on bronze vessels.
The number two encodes the foundational split that drives all of Chinese cosmology: yin and yang, the two forces from which everything else unfolds.

e: to send out, to develop, hair
d: One simplified glyph that swallowed two traditional characters. 发 carries the fa reading of sending, emitting, and developing (traditional 發) and the fa reading of hair on the head (traditional 髮).
Water against the level mark. From that image of fair, flowing measure grows the whole field of 法: the law and the court, the method and the way of doing a thing, and the Buddhist Dharma itself.
One glyph that runs from the literal square to the cardinal directions, to the place a thing sits, to the method by which it is done. The geometry of orientation and approach.
A door radical leaning over the phonetic 方: the side-chamber under a roof that grew into every word for house, room, and the family branches that fill them.

e: to fly, to dart; high, swift
d: A single bird caught mid-flap, one outstretched wing and the rising line of its body, frozen at the instant it leaves the ground.
Two wings spreading in opposite directions: from that image of opposition grows the great negator. Not and non-, the line between right and wrong, and the un- prefix that turns a word against itself.
A knife splitting a thing in two. From the cut grows everything that comes in parts: the minute on the clock, the point on a test, the cent in your pocket, and the act of separating itself.
The character that moves crops, carries seeds, and became the Chinese word for cultural character itself.

e: to seal, envelope, to confer (a fief)
d: A handful of earth heaped over a boundary mound, sealed by hand: 封 ties envelopes, granaries, and feudal grants to the same gesture of closing something off.

e: husband, a grown man, laborer; the literary particle fú
d: A grown man pictured with a hairpin marking adulthood: the husband and the married couple (丈夫 夫妻 夫人 夫妇), the adult man and laborer (农夫 渔夫 大夫), skill and effort (功夫 工夫), and the classical literary particle 夫 fú that opens a sentence.
The character that carried an entire worldview across the Silk Road: etymology, Buddhism, the 佛-family of compounds.
The most recognized Chinese character in the world: fortune, blessing, and the art of the upside-down 福.
A hand gripping a stone axe: the tool of the one who heads the household, drawn as the figure of the father himself.
A full wine jar tucked under a roof: the picture of a household storehouse packed to its rafters with plenty.

e: to alter, to change, to correct, to reform
d: A hand raises a stick over a kneeling child: 改 is change enforced by correction, not drift, which is why it leans toward fixing what is wrong.
Feeling, perception, gratitude, and the cosmology of sympathetic resonance.
A tall palace gate rising above the ground, and the character that anchors Chinese words for excellence, happiness, and examination pressure simultaneously.

e: to tell, to announce, to report
d: A mouth aimed upward: the character for delivering words to authority, and the root of advertising, accusations, and warnings.

e: elder brother, a familiar term for an older young man
d: Two 可 stacked into one glyph; the doubled phonetic came to carry the warmest word in the family, elder brother.

e: song, lyrics; to sing, to chant
d: The radical 欠 (an open, exhaling mouth) drives the meaning of song, while 哥 supplies the gē sound.

The general-purpose measure word that counts almost anything, and the root of individual. From the bamboo-stalk tally grew the everyday classifier 一个 and the words for individual, personality, and build.

e: even more; to change; night watch
d: A character that split across two readings: the comparative pulse of spoken Mandarin and the sonic clock of premodern China.
Three strokes encoding heaven, earth, and the human craft connecting them: the root character for all labor, skill, and making in Chinese.

e: public, fair, common, a duke, male
d: A line dividing away the private self. From that image grow everything held in common, every fair dealing, the metric measures, and the elder male: public, impartial, official, and a duke.
Merit earned through effort: from meritorious service and success to the patient skill the Chinese call gongfu, and even work in physics.
A pictophonetic glyph where the beast radical 犭supplies the meaning and 句 lends only the sound, naming the most domesticated of animals.

The mouth radical holding what ten generations have spoken down the years: 古 is what is old because it has been handed on. From that single image grow the senses of antiquity (古代 古老 远古), the classical and the antique (古典 古文 古董 古迹 考古), and the quaint or unconventional (古怪 古板).
故 binds five senses into one glyph: cause, the old and former, deliberateness, the literary "hence," and the deceased. The thread is a settled cause behind what is done or what has passed.

e: to close, to concern, the frontier pass
d: The bolt that closes a gate, the mountain pass that controls a frontier, and the relation that ties two people together. One character holds all three.

e: to observe, view, outlook, Daoist temple
d: The eye that looks and the mind that judges. From watching a thing closely grow two families of meaning: to observe and to view, and the settled outlook through which a person sees the world. A second reading, guàn, names the Daoist temple.

e: a public building, hall, shop, establishment
d: A food-radical building: the eating-house that grew into the library, the museum, and the embassy.
A radical and a word: the cliff-shelter that became the prefix for everything expansive, from Guangzhou to Guangdong to radio broadcasts.
A pictograph of a spirit with an oversized head: the disembodied soul of the unvenerated dead, a folk-religion category distinct from deity, demon, and ancestor.
A walled enclosure protecting its people: the Chinese concept of nationhood written in a single character.
A child-radical fused with the earthly branch 亥: 子 carries the meaning, 亥 lends the rising sound hái.
Water plus the phonetic 每: the sea, the ocean, and by extension any vastness. From 大海 and 海洋 to the coastal city 上海, the navy 海军, and the crowd that becomes a 人海.

e: to harm, injury, calamity, to fear
d: Under the roof a mouth and a blade build the sense of injury done; the same glyph also means to fear, as in 害怕.

e: the Han river, dynasty, people, and a man
d: A river that named a dynasty, and a dynasty that named a people. From the water of 汉水 grew 汉族 the Han ethnicity, 汉语 and 汉字 the Chinese language and script, and 好汉, the brave fellow.
Good, well, to like, and the tone split that doubles its expressive range.

e: to drink; (hè) to shout, to cry out
d: A mouth radical paired with the phonetic 曷, splitting cleanly into the everyday hē you drink with and the older hè you shout with.
A lid closing down over the mouth of a vessel. From that image of two parts meeting and fitting grows the whole field of joining, suiting, closing, and adding up into a whole.
禾 (grain) beside 口 (mouth): 和 is both Mandarin's everyday "and" and the Confucian ideal of harmony without uniformity.
河 began as the personal name of one river, the Yellow River, before it widened to mean any river at all.
Black on the surface, but the live sense is moral: the black market, the underworld, the hacker. The color that names everything that operates out of sight.

很 is the word for very, but its strangest job is doing nothing: Chinese needs a degree adverb before a plain adjective, and 很 fills that slot so quietly that 我很好 means simply I am fine, not I am very well.

e: red, the color of luck and celebration
d: The cultural keystone color: weddings, New Year, the red envelope, and a century of revolutionary politics all run through this one character.

One simplified character collapsed two completely separate traditional forms: 後 (a trailing foot in motion) and 后 (a commanding mouth), binding the spatial sense of behind with the imperial sense of empress in a single glyph.
A person standing watch beside the road. From the figure of one who waits and watches grows the everyday word for when (时候), the act of awaiting (等候), and the long rhythm of the weather (气候).
A water radical against the phonetic 胡, naming every still inland water from West Lake to the jianghu of wandering swordsmen.

A plant caught in its transformed, blooming state: the flower, the act of spending money or time, and the patterned, fancy, or blurred. One glyph that runs from the garden to the wallet to the dazzled eye.

e: to change, to transform, to melt
d: The character of transformation itself: melting, digesting, civilizing, and the productive -ize suffix that builds half of modern technical Chinese.

e: to draw, a painting, a stroke
d: A hand with a brush drawing the boundaries of a field. From that image grows the whole world of pictures: to paint, a painting, and the single stroke of a character.
Speech beside a tongue: the everyday character for spoken words. From it grow talking and conversation, the telephone, a dialect or standard language, and the topics and sayings people pass around.

e: bad, rotten, spoiled; to break down
d: A picto-phonetic built from 土 earth and 不 not: spoiled soil that yields nothing, extended to anything gone bad or broken.
A breath of open delight: the hand and the open mouth that make laughter. From this glyph come joy and merriment, to like and to welcome, and the lively, high-spirited mood.

e: to change, to exchange, to swap, to trade
d: A hand verb: every kind of swap, from changing money to changing trains, runs through one moving palm.

e: yellow, gold, the imperial color; to fall through
d: The color of loess soil and the emperor, of the mother river and the egg yolk, and the one color slang that means a plan has collapsed.

e: to return, to turn back, a time
d: Two squares nested like a coiling eddy. The character for coming back: returning home, turning around, replying, and counting the times a thing happens.

e: to live, to be alive, lively, work
d: Water gives the verb its life: a stream over a tongue, the flow that means being alive, and from there everything that moves, breathes, and gets done.
Three flames rising: the character for fire and one of the most productive radicals in Chinese.
The simplified 鸡 swaps a chicken-coop hand 又 in where the traditional 雞 kept the sound-bearer 奚 beside the bird.
A heart pressed from above: 急 stacks a phonetic element over 心, so the glyph itself feels the squeeze of urgency.

e: oneself, self, the sixth Heavenly Stem
d: A picture of a coiled, bending thread borrowed long ago to mean the self. From it grows everything turned inward: oneself, the private view, self-restraint, and the sixth of the ten Heavenly Stems.

e: to remember, to record, a mark
d: Speech set beside the self: the act of fixing something so it will not be lost. From that image grow three senses: to remember, to write down, and the mark left behind.
House, family, school of thought, nation (国家): the fractal of belonging.
A person standing beside 介 jiè: the worth a thing takes on only once two people sit down to trade for it.
Sunlight in the crack between two doors: the character for the space between things. From that gap grow time, the middle ground, the human world, and the room you count one by one.

e: simple, brief, terse; a bamboo writing slip
d: Before paper, a letter was a strip of bamboo; from that narrow slip 简 grew into the words for simple, brief, and a short note.

e: to see, to meet, to appear
d: An eye on legs. The character that built Chinese verbs of seeing, meeting, opinion, and the moment a thing first comes into view.
The measure word for matters, garments, and gifts, and the character behind documents, parts, and cases.
Corner, horn, angle: the character that opens this site's name (角落書屋).
The everyday word for foot, and by extension the base of any standing thing: a mountain, a wall, a script. The flesh-and-bone counterpart to literary 足.

A hand with a rod beside a child at the lesson. From that scene of instruction grows a wide field: to teach and educate, to teach a skill in the spoken jiao reading, and the teaching that became the word for religion.

e: to connect, to join, to receive, to meet
d: The hand that joins: 接 puts a wrist behind every link, every catch, and every arrival you go out to greet.
The walk radical 行 splits open into a crossroads, and the jade-tablet phonetic 圭 sits inside, marking the place where roads cross and people pass.

A bamboo joint, the segment between the knots. From that node grows everything that comes in sections: the joint of a limb, the chapter of a book, the festival that knots the calendar, and the restraint that keeps a thing within bounds.

e: to tie, to unite, to conclude, to bear fruit
d: A knot tied in silk thread. From that image grows everything that binds and resolves: the knot you tie, the union of two people, the conclusion that settles a matter, and the fruit a plant ties onto its branch.
A woman radical fused to the sound-lender 且, 姐 names the elder sister and stretches to cover every miss and young lady in modern address.

e: to untie, to solve, to explain, to dissolve
d: The character for cutting apart and undoing: untying and liberating, solving and explaining, dissolving and relieving. A polyphone read jiě, jiè, and xiè, pictured as a hand prying an ox horn from the ox.

e: to borrow, to lend, to make use of
d: One glyph carries both halves of a loan: 借 means borrow and lend at once, the direction settled only by context.
Nuggets of gold beneath the earth, and one of the Five Phases that governs autumn, the west, and sharpness.
Thread drawn taut over the silk radical; the same word carries a tight knot, a tense nerve, an urgent deadline, and a tight wallet.
Walking toward something as close as a hatchet strike, and the character that covers both spatial proximity and the specific historical era Chinese scholars call the modern period.

e: to enter, to advance, to take in
d: A foot on the road and a bird that only ever walks forward. From that image grows everything that moves ahead and moves in: to enter, to advance, to progress, to carry out, and to take goods in.

e: classic, scripture, to pass through, warp threads
d: The lengthwise warp threads strung on a loom, the structural through-lines that hold a fabric together. From that image grow the canonical classic, the act of passing through, and the running of an enterprise.

e: nine; the imperial number and the highest of the yang
d: Nine is the largest single digit and the highest yang number, reserved for the emperor and the heavens: nine dragons, nine gates, the Nine-Five supreme position, the ninth heaven.
The antonym of 新, and much more than it. 旧 carries both the weight of cherished tradition and the stigma of backwardness, depending entirely on who is speaking.

e: to rescue, to save, to relieve
d: A hand wields a stick to pull someone out of danger; the phonetic 求 once meant a desperate plea for help.

e: sentence, phrase, a unit of speech
d: A wrapping line drawn over a mouth: speech bundled into a single unit. From that image grows the sentence, the line of verse, and the measure word that counts the remarks we say.

e: to open, to start, to operate
d: Two hands lifting the bar across a closed gate. From that single image flow most of modern life: opening a door, starting a meeting, driving a car, writing a check, blooming.

e: to look, to watch, to read, to visit
d: 看 = hand above eye, shielding from the sun to see in the distance: visual attention with effort, encoded in a gesture everyone has made.
A two-stroke mouth character whose ancient sense of affirming breath became the pivot of permission, capability, and worth in classical and modern Chinese.
A cave with the work of hollowing inside it. The character that names the open sky, the empty room, the wasted afternoon, and the Buddhist śūnyatā at the heart of Chan.
A simple rectangle for an open mouth: one of the most productive radicals in the script, present in hundreds of characters for speaking, eating, and openings.
The grass radical over 古 names a bitter herb on the tongue, then stretches to every flavor of hardship and effort.

e: to stride; to span; to bestride
d: The character of the long stride: a foot-radical verb that reaches from "step over a threshold" to "span an era" to the modern policy vocabulary of cross-border, cross-industry, cross-cultural everything.
快 joins 忄 (heart) to 夬 (a decisive cut): speed and joy are the same image, a heart running without drag.
A tree boxed inside four walls and unable to grow: the picture of being hemmed in, the source of both hardship and sleepiness.

e: to come, to arrive, toward the speaker
d: Oracle bone wheat plant turned direction-word: 来 pulls everything toward the speaker, including time itself.
A stooped elder with long hair: age as wisdom, seniority as moral authority, and the Daoist sage who wrote the Daodejing.

A picture of a wooden frame strung with silk and a drum, an early musical instrument. The simplified 乐 carries two readings: yuè for music, the original sense, and lè for joy, the happiness that music gives.
Rain over fields struck by lightning: the ancient pictograph of thunder that became a deity, a Yijing trigram, and a metaphor for decisive force.

e: to leave, to be apart, away from
d: Once the name of a netted mythical bird, 离 was borrowed so long ago for to part that almost no speaker recalls its feathers.
The character that encodes Confucian social order: the ceremonial forms that bind family, society, and cosmos into one coherent whole.
From field stacked on earth, 里 named the bounded cultivated interior of a settlement and became the unit of distance that measured the realm's interior reach.

The veins running through a piece of jade, the lines a carver follows when cutting. From that grain grows everything ordered: the inner pattern of things, principle and reason, and the work of putting a matter in order.
A picture of a plough or a flexed sinew, the image of bodily exertion. From that one shape grows everything pushed by force: raw strength, the capacity to do, and the effort poured into a task.
One simplified glyph that absorbed two traditional characters: 歷 (to pass through, history) and 曆 (calendar). The word that holds both lived experience and reckoned time.
Carts moving in a line: a character that joins things in space, in sequence, and in emphasis, from 连接 to the famous 连...都 construction.
The flesh-radical face that doubles as a ledger of dignity: in Chinese you can lose it, save it, or tear it apart.

e: to practice, to train, to refine, skilled
d: Before it meant drilling and rehearsal, 练 was a verb for boiling raw silk soft, the repetition of treatment that hardens into skill.

e: two (of); a pair; the tael, the other word for two
d: 两 is the two used before measure words, the two of quantity and pairing, as opposed to 二 the two of counting and order, a distinction that is one of the first real puzzles a learner meets.
商量 shangliang, to discuss, is literally to measure something out together: the act of weighing it between two minds before anyone decides.

e: zero; raindrops, the fractional remainder, and the late invention of nothing
d: Zero began as falling raindrops and the leftover odd remainder, taking on the meaning of mathematical nothing only late, the placeholder that Chinese numerals long managed without.

e: six; the six directions; a smooth and lucky number
d: Six closes space into the six directions (the four compass points plus up and down) and, through its near-homophony with 流 liú (to flow), became a number for things going smoothly.
China's most powerful mythic creature: benevolent, not fearsome; the emperor's emblem and the Chinese people's self-described totem.
The walked road, where 道 is the navigated way: 路 is the surface beneath the foot, the route the messenger takes, the journey of a life measured in distance.

e: to discuss, a theory or treatise
d: Reasoned speech put in order: the verb for discussing, debating, and commenting, and the noun for a theory, a view, or a treatise. Also Lun in the title of the Analects.

e: to fall, to settle, to land
d: Falling, settling, and the beauty of things arriving at their place.
A three-stroke pictograph of a horse in profile that hides the mane, legs, and tail of its towering ancestor 馬.
Pace becomes a moral register: 慢 màn carries the same heart radical as 快, and extends from physical slowness into social neglect and arrogance.
A large sheep carrying horns: beauty as abundance, sacrifice, and the pleasure of the highest good.
A picture of a two-leaf gate. From the swinging doors grow the gateway, the household behind them, the school or trade you enter, and the measure word for whole courses of study.

A pictograph of a face inside its outline that opened outward into surfaces, sides, and aspects, became a measure word for flat things, and in simplified script swallowed the separate character for flour and noodles.
The common people as a collective subject: the populace, the citizen, the folk and the nation, and the civilian set against the military. From 人民 the people to 民族 ethnic nation to 民主 democracy.
名 is 夕 dusk plus 口 mouth: darkness falls, you cannot see who approaches, so you call out a name. Identity asserted through speech.
Sun and moon combined: brightness, clarity, dawn, and understanding.
A mouth speaking an order: 令 above, 口 inside. The character that holds together three of the heaviest words in Chinese: life, destiny, and the command from above.
A tree seen whole: trunk, branches, roots. The pictograph that became a radical, a wuxing element, and the building block of 林, 森, 本, and 末.

e: eye; to look at; section heading
d: The pictograph of an eye that became the Chinese radical for everything seen, watched, and classified.
The direction that Chinese buildings face and emperors receive guests: warmth, productivity, and the seat of imperial ritual power.
The everyday second-person pronoun whose formal twin 您 embeds 心 (heart) directly into the character: address with warmth.
A person carrying a harvest of grain: year as the cycle of agricultural labor, and the heart of the Chinese New Year tradition.

e: to recite, to keep in mind, to miss
d: 念 holds the present moment 今 over the heart 心: to keep something in mind, to recite aloud, to long for what is absent. The 念 of 念佛 recitation, 想念 longing, and the single thought-moment of Buddhist psychology.
A four-stroke pictograph of an ox head seen straight on, the horns still visible; in modern slang it means impressively good.
A character compressed from a graph that showed working the fields at the time of the stars, the whole cycle of growing crops.
A kneeling figure with crossed arms: one of the most productive radicals in the script, present in characters for family relationships, feelings, and cultural concepts.

e: to run; to flee; to operate
d: The everyday verb of running: a foot-radical character whose semantic range stretches from "the legs in motion" to "running an errand" to "the engine is running" to a small but productive family of escape-and-flee compounds.

e: friend, companion; of the same group
d: Two strings of cowrie shells hung side by side, an old unit of value, borrowed early for companions of equal standing who keep close company.

e: bank note, ticket, vote, a slip of paper
d: Flames rising over an altar where spirit money burned: 票 carries the smoke of an offering into the modern banknote, the ticket stub, and the ballot.
Three mouths stacked: a character about multiplicity, evaluation, and the discerning assessment of quality, from product grades to moral character.

A pictograph of something level and balanced. From that flat surface grows a wide field of meaning: the even and the smooth, the equal and the fair, the calm and the peaceful, and the plain and ordinary.

e: seven; the rhythm of mourning, festival, and the soul
d: Seven measures the cycles of death and renewal in Chinese culture: the seven-day periods of mourning, the seventh-night lovers' festival, and the seven emotions of the heart.
A winnowing basket that became the pronoun holding classical Chinese together: the silent 'its' behind thousands of literary phrases.
From weather to anger to the cosmic force underlying TCM and martial arts.
Thousand is the order of magnitude where a precise count gives way to poetic vastness: a thousand miles, a thousand autumns, ten thousand changes, the number that means simply too many to count.
Chinese places the past in front (前) and the future behind: the known faces you while the unknown approaches from behind, the inverse of the English spatial metaphor for time.
Money: the character that drives markets, proverbs, and the Chinese conversation about wealth.
Water beside the color of new growth. The character that names limpid water, distinct speech, a clean reputation, a settled account, and a cool quiet evening.
The heart radical beside the phonetic 青: the movements of the heart. From that one image grows feeling and mood, affection and love, and the wider sense of a situation or state of affairs.

e: to go, to leave, to depart, to remove
d: The character that marks every departure, from leaving the house to the euphemism for death. 去 is the verb of things moving away.
Enter, and find the jade flawless. From that image of unblemished jade grows everything whole and complete: the entire set, the intact and unbroken, and the adverb that sweeps up all of it at once.

A character that once meant to burn and was borrowed for the abstract sense so, correct, this-is-how-it-is. Today it builds the connectives 然后 and 然而, the conjunctions 当然 and 虽然, and rides as a -ly suffix on words like 忽然 and 突然.
The four dots of flame beneath 执 carry physical heat into the heat of crowds, fervor, and whatever is trending.
Two strokes, barely changed since the oracle bones, write 人 rén; add 二 and you get 仁, Confucian benevolence.

e: humaneness, the kernel of human relation
d: The character that anchors Confucian ethics: 亻 + 二, the self in relation to another. Etymology, the virtue-cluster compounds, and the seed-kernel sense that links moral and botanical 仁.
The act of recognition: knowing something for what it is, owning up to it, and the small set of compounds that turn this on the world, on others, and on oneself.
The oldest pictograph in the script: a circle with a dot for the sun, now a radical in hundreds of characters related to time, light, and warmth.
A roof over a valley: the space that holds. To contain, to tolerate, the face one shows, and the easy in rongyi.

e: meat, flesh, the pulp of fruit
d: A pictograph of a meat slab with its marbling drawn inside; squeezed onto the left of a character it becomes 月, the flesh-moon of the body radicals.
A woman speaking and a mouth complying: from following a command grew the great comparison-and-condition word. 如 is how Chinese says like, as, for example, and if.
Three is the number of completion in Chinese cosmology (Heaven, Earth, Human), and the numeral that generates the ten thousand things in Daoist thought.
A kneeling figure beneath a person: color as visible manifestation, and the character that links aesthetics to desire.
Three peaks rising from the earth: the oldest pictograph and the axis of Chinese sacred geography.
The character at the heart of Mencius argument that human nature is originally good: the moral sprouts waiting to be cultivated.

e: above, up, to go up, to mount
d: The most productive spatial primitive in Chinese. 上 starts as a notch above a line and ends up meaning everything from logging on to getting addicted.
Small with a stroke removed: the character for scarcity that doubles as the word for youth when read in falling tone.

e: society, an association, the god of the soil
d: The altar radical beside the earth: a shrine to the god of the soil and the community that gathered around it. From that image grow society itself, the many kinds of association and agency, and the ancient soil-and-grain spirits that once stood for the state.
The character that names both the gods of Chinese folk religion and the focused attention of the human mind, because in Chinese thought they belong to the same category of phenomenon.
A sprouting plant: life emerging from the earth. The most generative radical in Chinese.

A chime-stone struck before a listening ear. From that image grow the everyday word for sound and voice, the tone of speech, and the wider sense of making something known: a declaration, a reputation, a name.
十 is written as a cross (a vertical stroke cutting through a horizontal one), the point where all four cardinal directions meet, making ten the numeral of total completion.
The sun moving: time as something visible, measurable, and morally weighted.

A roof over a house full of goods. From that image of a full dwelling grows everything substantial: the real and the true, the solid and sturdy, the actual practice that gets things done, and the ripened fruit.

A pictograph traditionally read as three tens joined together, the span of thirty years that makes one generation. From that root grow the four faces of 世: the generation that succeeds the one before, the lifetime or the life to come, the era stacked from many lives, and the wider world of human society in which all of it unfolds.

The character for an affair, a matter, a thing that happens. From an ancient pictograph of a hand holding the implements of office, it became Chinese for everything abstract that occupies us: business, jobs, incidents, and the everyday "no problem."
The copula, the cleft construction, classical 是非 right-and-wrong.
A five-fingered hand drawn from life: one of the most productive radicals in the script, present in hundreds of action characters.

e: head, first, chief, a measure word for songs and poems
d: A drawn head, with hair above an eye, and from it the senses of first, foremost, chief, leader, and the classifier you count songs and poems with. 首 is its own radical.
Book, writing, calligraphy: the character that holds civilization together.
The first of the five elements, the radical that runs through hundreds of compounds, and the Daoist image of how to act in the world.

e: to speak, to say, to explain
d: To speak, say, explain, and persuade: the character at the center of all communication.
The field of the mind above the heart: thinking as cultivation, longing as thought turned inward.
A figure kneeling beside a corpse. The character behind the strongest verb of finality in Chinese, the bedrock of every taboo, and the intensifier that turns 累 into 累死了.

e: four; the four directions; the homophone of death
d: Four organizes the Chinese world into quarters, the four directions, four seas, four seasons, yet its near-homophony with 死 sǐ (death) makes it the most avoided number in modern China.

e: to see off, to send, to give
d: A figure waving 关 at someone whose feet 辶 are already carrying them away: 送 is farewell built into the road itself.
他 was gender-neutral for a millennium until 她 was coined in 1917 to solve a translation problem that Classical Chinese had never needed to solve.
它 began as a picture of a snake and once meant other; in the twentieth century it was reassigned to the non-human third person, completing the homophonous 他/她/它 triad that exists only in writing.
她 is the youngest character in everyday Chinese, invented in 1917 to translate "she," and the cause of one of the loudest grammatical fights in modern Chinese letters.
The character 大 (big) with one extra dot, pushing big past its limit into too-much. From that excess grow the everyday too, the highest and grandest, the sun, and the supreme pole of Taiji.
The head-radical character behind every exam question and discussion topic. From the leaf or head of a thing grows the question to solve, the theme to discuss, and the act of inscribing a poem.
The person beside the root: the body as a person's base. From the physical body grow substance and system, the whole as against the part, and the act of grasping a thing by living through it.
Heaven as moral authority, weather, time, and the ground of 天命 the Mandate of Heaven.

e: to listen, to hear, to obey
d: The simplified 听 = mouth + axe, but the traditional 聽 encodes whole-body Confucian listening: ear, eye, heart, and upright virtue arrayed together in a single glyph.

e: to go through; to connect; general; fluent
d: The walk-movement radical drives a path through every obstacle, giving 通 a single character that covers passage, communication, expertise, and the ordinary general state of things.
Voices joined under one cover: the character for sameness and shared ground. From it grow the words for being alike, doing things together, and the people who share your role, your class, your cause.
The head, and from it the top of a hill, the end of a street, the start of a thing, the chief of a group, and the toneless tag on a hundred everyday nouns. The simplified 头 stands for traditional 頭.

e: map, diagram, to plan, to seek
d: A character for diagrams, maps, intentions, and plots: anything that represents the world at one remove, or seeks to reshape it.
A mound of soil with a base: the earth phase of the Five Elements, and the root of hundreds of characters for land, construction, and cultural belonging.

A diviner reading the shells at the wrong hour, off the normal schedule. From that image grows everything beyond the boundary: the outside, the outer surface, the foreign land, and the relatives on the mother's side.
完 means both whole and finished, and the bridge between them is intact completeness; its most important job is as a result complement, the 完 that ends 吃完, 做完, and 看完.
万 is the Chinese hyperbole unit. Where English reaches for millions, Chinese reaches for 万 to express the immeasurable, because the written number 10,000 originally meant scorpion.
Three horizontals joined by one vertical: the ruler who connects heaven, earth, and humanity. Also the most common Chinese surname, and a radical that is secretly 玉 (jade) in disguise.

e: to gaze afar, to hope, reputation
d: A person on a mound looking into the distance, with the moon above: from that raised gaze grow three senses. To gaze and look afar (眺望, 望远镜, 张望), to hope and expect (希望, 期望, 盼望, 失望), and reputation or prestige (名望, 威望, 声望). As a coverb it can even mean toward, like 朝 or 向.
A kneeling figure pinned beneath a cliff overhang spells danger, where the same overhang also carries the sound.

e: to do; to act; for; because of
d: In oracle bone script 为 is a hand leading an elephant, and it sits at the center of Daoist 无为 non-action.
A tattooed figure: writing as marks on the body, culture as the accumulated markings of civilization.

e: to ask, to inquire, to ask after
d: A mouth at the gate, asking. From that image grow the everyday verb to ask, the noun for a question or problem, the warm act of asking after someone, and the stern act of holding to account.
The character for 'I' began as a toothed bronze halberd: the assertive grip of a weapon became the grammatical mark of a self.
Room, dwelling, and the human need for shelter: the character at home.

A dancer with arms outstretched, holding nothing. The character behind every Chinese negation of having, every Daoist non-doing, and the philosophical pole that pairs with 有 to frame the whole cosmos.

e: five; the organizing number of correlative cosmology
d: Five is the center plus the four directions, the number that completes the Chinese cosmos: five phases, five colors, five tones, five flavors, five viscera, all keyed to one master grid.

The foot radical 止 carrying a dagger-axe 戈: the soldier on the march, and the older reading that to wield arms well is finally to halt them. From 武力 armed force to 武术 martial arts to 威武 powerful and dignified, the character holds the whole world of strength wielded with discipline.
An ox under a phonetic, once the word for varicolored cattle, that broadened into the whole world of things: every object, all matter, the myriad creatures, and even a person as a figure.
A bird settling into its nest at sunset: the direction that gave Chinese the word for "things" when it paired with east.

A festive drum sounding above an open mouth: the sound of joy and the smiling mouth that answers it. From this image grow the words for liking, delight, and every happy occasion, above all the wedding.

A hand holding silk threads. From that image of holding strands together come the great connecting words of modern Chinese: the system, the relationship, the link, the university department, and the colloquial act of tying a knot.

e: below, down, to descend, to issue
d: The mirror image of 上: a notch below the line that governs everything from going downstairs to issuing imperial decrees.
The luster of jade coming into view. From that glint of something becoming visible grows the whole vocabulary of appearing, of the present moment, and of what is ready and on hand.

An eye examining a tree. From that act of looking grow two readings: level-tone xiang, the mutual that binds two sides face to face, and falling-tone xiang, the appearance you look at, the looking itself, and the minister who looks over the realm.
Grain stacked over a mouth of sweetness: 香 is the smell of ripe rice, and the word still means both perfume and a hot meal worth eating.

e: to think, to want, to miss
d: 想 = 相 (mutual, facing) + 心 (heart): the heart turned toward something, carrying the full range from thought to desire to longing in a single gesture.

e: direction, toward, to face, all along
d: A window opening in a wall, facing one way. From that image grows the whole field of orientation: the direction a thing points, the preposition toward a target, the inclination of a heart, and the sense of all along, up to now.
Three minimal strokes that became the Confucian axis of moral character: the 小人 (petty person) and the 君子 (exemplary person) are the two poles every learner of classical Chinese must know.

e: to laugh, to smile, to mock
d: Bamboo over a bending person: a form that has split scholars since the Song over whether laughter or rustling reeds came first.
写 simplified from 寫, which shows a magpie under a roof: the bird that mimics and transmits, giving its voice to the written mark.
The radical at the root of all feeling, and the Chinese conception of thought itself.
Chopping fresh wood with an axe: the character whose compounds span New Year greetings, fresh produce, marriage, and the great question of what counts as modern.
A person standing by their word: one of the most visually transparent characters in the language, and the virtue that holds every contract, conversation, and relationship together.
Born of the sun radical and a sprout, 星 names the stars, the planets, the week, movie fame, and the spark that starts prairie fires.

e: to walk, to act, a row, a trade
d: One of the great polyphonic characters: xíng "to walk; to act; conduct" and háng "row; profession; firm." A pictograph of a four-way crossroads, the place where walking and the world are organized.

e: shape, form, to appear, to compare
d: The character for visible form: shape and figure, the body as form, the act of taking shape and being described, and the lay of a situation. A pictophonetic compound built on the pattern-strokes radical 彡.

The heart radical carrying the sense of innate nature: what a thing is born to be. From that core grow the four faces of 性: a persons disposition or character, sex and gender, the property or quality of a thing, and the productive abstract suffix that turns adjectives into -ness and -ity nouns.
Hands guiding a child beneath a roof: the character for learning as both action and institution.
Rain over a sweeping hand: snow is the precipitation you can hold. The same character means dazzling white and, by a buried metaphor, to wipe clean an old grievance.
The root of every word about words: the mouth open, the tongue moving, the speech rising.
The everyday word for eye, and by extension any small opening, any moment of looking, any judgment made through sight. The body-part counterpart to literary 目.
A sunlit mound: the simplified 阳 sets a hill beside the sun. From that bright south slope grow the sun itself, the active masculine half of the cosmos, and the place names that face the light.
A word once rooted in wood that grew into the language of appearance and kind: how a thing looks, what type it is, the sample held up as a model, and the everyday this-way and how of manner words.
Want, need, must, and will: the grammar engine disguised as a single character.
A pictograph that lost its original image entirely and became one of the most load-bearing particles in classical Chinese: the gavel at the end of every verdict.

A notched rack for hanging bells and chimes, then the work hung upon it. From that frame grows the whole field of doing: the trade one practices, the industry one builds, the cause one devotes a life to, the coursework one masters, and in Buddhist thought the karma one accrues.
The simplest mark a brush can make carries the heaviest philosophical weight in Chinese civilization: 道生一，一生二，the Dao generates One, and One generates everything.

e: by means of; using; because; in order to
d: A classical Chinese preposition and conjunction so versatile that it anchors half the grammar of formal Chinese: the word that turns one thing into the means, standard, or cause of another.
The Confucian virtue of doing what is morally right, and the simplification that erased a sheep, a self, and the entire picture of what righteous form looks like.

e: meaning, intention, the wish of the mind
d: Sound over heart: 意 is what the heart means before it is spoken. From that image grows meaning and significance, intention and willingness, and the notions of attention, satisfaction, and the unexpected.

e: cause, reason, because of, to follow
d: A person resting inside an enclosure, the mat one lies on. From that image of lying-upon comes the basis one builds on, then the cause behind an effect and the because that links the two.

e: the shaded slope, the lunar, the covert
d: The shadow half of the cosmos and the everyday word for an overcast day. From the dark side of a hill grew the lunar calendar, the hidden plot, and time itself as light and shade.
A mouth with a sound marked inside it. From that image grow the words for sound and music, for the way a syllable is pronounced, and for tidings carried from afar.

e: ought, should; (yìng) to respond, to answer, to handle
d: A high-frequency polyphone with two readings. As yīng it means ought to or should; as yìng it means to respond, to answer, to adapt, and to handle. The tone tells you whether the sense is obligation or response.
用 began as a pictograph of a bucket or bell (a vessel put to work) and became the character that Zhuangzi inverted in his doctrine of 无用之用: the use of uselessness.
Possession, existence, and the have/be distinction that reshapes grammar.
A right hand raised to a mouth: the hand that feeds and speaks, whose authority in Chinese extended to favoring, protecting, and placing the highest things to the right of the seat.

e: at, in, to, than (the classical preposition)
d: The workhorse preposition of formal Chinese. 于 marks where, when, toward whom, and against what a thing is measured, and it is bound into a long list of everyday disyllables like 由于, 终于, and 等于.
The oracle bone shows rain falling from the sky: one of the most transparent pictographs in the script, and the radical that organizes all Chinese weather.
Speech radical plus the phonetic 吾 (I, me): the character for language carries the self within it, encoding the idea that language is the medium through which the self speaks to the world.
Three jade discs on a cord, one dot away from 王 (wáng, king): the stone Confucius said was virtue made visible.
Long robes trailing as you walk away: distance encoded in motion, and the ambivalence of far-off places in Chinese thought.
A crescent moon in profile, and one of the most poetically charged characters in Chinese literature.
The character of crossing-and-exceeding: a foot-radical verb that travels from "stride over a barrier" to "the more, the more" to a Chinese state name and a national poetic gesture.
The simplified 云 is older than the traditional 雲, a rare case where the modern form recovers the ancient one.
The adverb that sequences and repeats: again, one more time, and the subtle art of "and then."

e: to be at, located, in progress
d: The character that locates: a seedling rooted in earth, expanded into location, preposition, and progressive aspect.

e: to stand, to halt, a station, a stop
d: A person planted upright on the ground, holding their place: from the body that will not move grows the station, the stop, and the website you log on to.
A person with flowing long hair. One character, two readings: cháng (long) and zhǎng (to grow, elder), the richest dual-reading in Mandarin.
Truth not as accuracy but as authenticity: the unadorned thing itself, prized in Daoist self-cultivation and in everyday emphasis.

e: upright, correct, exactly, in the midst of
d: A foot halting squarely on the target line. From that image grows everything straight and correct: the upright, the standard, the exact moment, and the ongoing right-now.

e: of, going, this: the classical connective
d: The most-written character in classical Chinese: a possessive particle, pronoun, and verb fossilized into pure grammar.
知 = arrow + mouth: knowledge as the swift, target-hitting utterance, and in Wang Yangming, the act of knowing is inseparable from the act of doing.
The Confucian virtue of knowing what is right to do; separately, the Buddhist prajñā that sees through the nature of things altogether.

e: middle, China, to hit the mark
d: An arrow piercing through the center of a target: the character that names China as the Middle Kingdom and encodes the Confucian virtue of equilibrium.
A figure bearing a heavy load. From that weight grows everything that carries gravity: the heavy, the important, the grave. Read again as chóng, the same load comes back, layered and repeated.
A lamp flame steady on its stand: the central light that grew into the master of a household, the main thing among many, the one who decides, and the Lord of a faith.

A picture of a swaddled infant that grew into one of the busiest characters in the language: a child and a son, the honorific for a Master, the empty noun-suffix on a thousand words, and the seed of a thing.
The character that names itself, and the whole system of 汉字.
A picture of a nose, the thing an ancient speaker pointed at to mean me. From that gesture grows the self, the source a thing comes from, and the sense of a thing acting of its own accord.

e: to walk, to go, to leave
d: A figure in motion with feet below: the basic verb of movement that Chinese uses where English uses dozens of different words.
The foot that became the word for sufficiency, and the radical anchoring every character involving legs, running, and roads.
最 is the single word that pushes any adjective to its limit: the -est of English, the most of comparison, the marker that turns 好 into 最好 and 后 into 最后.
A left hand holding a carpenter's square: the assisting hand at the ruler, and by extension the word for unorthodox, heterodox, and everything that deviates from the orthodox path.

e: to do, to make, to compose
d: A person setting something in motion. From the act of beginning grows the whole vocabulary of doing, making, and composing: the job you work, the work you create, and the role you act out.

e: to do, to make, to act as
d: 做 is the everyday verb for doing and making, a late character built to carry the work that 作 had grown too literary to do, and the two still split the labor between them.

阿弥陀佛 is the Buddha of Infinite Light and Life who presides over the Western Pure Land, and his name is itself the central practice: to recite 南无阿弥陀佛 is the simple path of Pure Land devotion, open to everyone.

e: prajñā; the Buddhist wisdom that sees emptiness
d: 般若 is the specific Buddhist wisdom that perceives the emptiness of self and phenomena: not knowledge, not cleverness, but the realization that dissolves clinging at its root.
The everyday word for help, both verb and noun, and how it differs from the lighter 帮 and the separable 帮忙 (to do a favor).
Compare and qualify: the word that measures differences and hedges claims in everyday Mandarin.
Notes, jottings, and the Chinese literary tradition of the brush-record.
必须 is the strongest of the everyday modal verbs of obligation: a non-negotiable requirement that the speaker presents as not-up-for-discussion.
From wild forest leaf to civilizational ritual: how tea became China's quintessential art of presence.
The vessels, tools, and objects of the tea table: from the Yixing purple clay teapot to the fairness pitcher, each implement with a name, a function, and an aesthetic logic.
The standard Chinese word for product: what production yields and commerce moves. From factory floor to digital marketplace, 产品 names the output of organized human effort.
The thread passed down through generations: and the concept that sits at the center of every Chinese debate about modernity, identity, and what to keep.
The most important holiday in the Chinese calendar: customs, foods, taboos, the reunion dinner, and the cultural weight of the Spring Festival.
Two Sanskrit terms fused into one Chinese compound: the wish that beings be happy and the wish that they be free from suffering: both directions of the same opening movement.
The compound at the center of Chinese moral philosophy: the Way and its virtue, inseparable and mutually defining.
East-west as the word for 'stuff': a window into directional cosmology.
Chinese builds its "how much" by welding many to few, part of a system where opposites fuse into the scale between them.
方向 is the compass-word that holds together physical heading, life direction, political orientation, and the deeply Chinese sense that getting your bearings: 辨方向, is the first move in any undertaking.
Geomancy, qi flow, and the cosmological logic of favorable siting.
The wind of culture and the ways of the people: how 风俗 differs from 习惯 and why the distinction matters.
Happiness as elevation: spirits that rise. The everyday glad word, and how it divides the territory with 开心, 快乐, and 幸福.
Tea prepared with skill and time: the Southern Chinese brewing method that defines serious tea culture, built on small vessels, multiple short steeps, and total attention.
The everyday word for work, both the activity and the job itself, and how it differs from 上班 (to go to work), 职业 (occupation), and 事业 (career).
Mastery earned through time: martial arts is the paradigm case, but the word covers any deeply cultivated skill.
Old affairs made into meaning: how the Chinese word for story encodes a philosophy of the past as the source of truth.
The untranslatable social fabric: relational leverage, it matters.
A compound of the two most culturally loaded characters in Chinese: country and family, that encodes the Confucian political imagination in two syllables.
The world's oldest continuously used writing system: how Chinese characters work, why they look the way they do, and the categories every learner needs to know.
The title the First Emperor invented in 221 BCE by welding together 皇 (august sage-king) and 帝 (high god), and how it differs from 王 king, 君 sovereign, and 天子 the Son of Heaven.
The outsider world of wanderers, martial artists, and street wisdom.
The classical Chinese word for the nation: not a territory but a landscape; not a state but a living geography that dynasties rose and fell to possess.
China's ancient agricultural calendar: 24 precise moments that mark the turning of the year, still shaping food, medicine, and daily life.
China's preeminent performing art: a total synthesis of song, stylized speech, acrobatic movement, and martial performance that evolved in Beijing during the Qing dynasty.
The everyday verb for giving an opinion or impression, and how it differs from the more formal 认为 and from 想 (to want / to think over).
The Confucian moral ideal that replaced aristocratic birth with cultivated virtue as the basis of social authority: anyone who does the work of 仁义礼智信 qualifies.
China ran the world's longest experiment in testing, thirteen centuries of imperial exams, and the vocabulary still sits every June for the gaokao.
The polite manners owed to guests: and the gentle dance of refusal, insistence, and ritual modesty that runs through every Chinese social interaction.

e: to leap across, to span, to transcend
d: The compound that lets the Chinese language span gaps: physical, historical, technological, generational. The verb of choice when "越长城" is read figuratively.
The cosmic blueprint Confucius spent his life trying to restore: and why manners are a civilizational technology.

The everyday word for politeness: what 礼 (ritual propriety) becomes when it is shrunk down to the scale of ordinary social life. Polite forms, polite faces, and the precise way modern Chinese distinguishes 礼貌 from 客气, 礼节, and the older 礼 itself.
The character for historian shows a hand holding a brush over a vessel: in ancient China, the scribe who held the brush held power.
The good heart-mind: the Chinese word for conscience carries a philosophical claim that moral knowledge is a natural endowment, not an acquired rule.
轮回 renders Sanskrit saṃsāra as 'wheel' plus 'return': the karmic cycle carrying beings through six realms until liberation.

The Analects: a thin book of recorded conversations and sayings that became the most quoted text in East Asian civilization, the entry point to Confucian thought, and the textbook of imperial education for two thousand years.
Giving, losing, and saving face: the social grammar of dignity.
Understanding as illumination: sun-and-moon brightness plus plain white. The clarity verb, and its siblings 懂, 知道, and 了解.
Fate, destiny, and the tension between cosmic order and human will.

e: Nirvana; the extinction of craving and the end of rebirth
d: 涅槃 is the Buddhist soteriological terminus: the extinction of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the cessation of the karmic cycle that they fuel.
The everyday word for friend, and the rich web of relationship terms (好朋友, 男朋友, 交朋友) built around it.
菩萨 is the being who stands at the threshold of complete enlightenment and turns back: choosing to remain within the cycle of existence until every sentient being can be liberated alongside them.
The common speech: how China standardized its national language, what Mandarin actually is, and how it relates to Cantonese, Shanghainese, and the Chinese dialects.
The everyday adverb for "actually, in fact," used to correct an impression or reveal the real situation, and how it differs from 实际上, 事实上, and 本来.
Cultivating the vital breath: China's ancient practice of aligning body, breath, and mind.
谦虚 is both a Confucian virtue and a social practice: in Chinese interaction, it functions as a required performative register, not just an internal attitude.

e: heaven and earth; the two primary trigrams
d: The first two hexagrams of the Yijing encode the entire cosmos: Qian is pure creative yang, Kun is pure receptive yin, and between them all change unfolds.
The everyday sequence word for "then, after that," the 先…然后… frame for ordering steps, its overuse as a spoken filler, and how it differs from 接着, 后来, and 于是.

e: the human world; the mortal realm
d: The world of people: where karma plays out, where flowers fade in April, and where the only beings who can hear the Dharma are born.
Human life: not biological existence, but the arc of a life lived: its meaning, its seasons, its reckoning.
The supreme Confucian virtue: the quality of genuine care for other people that holds civilization together.
To recognize the 真 of a thing and engage with it on its own terms: the everyday word for taking work, study, and other people seriously rather than going through motions.

The paired word that names the Chinese landscape: not "scenery" in the Western sense, but a cosmological pairing of the still and the flowing that became the central subject of a thousand years of painting and poetry.
Mountains and waters as a cosmological pair -- the genre that made ink the equal of philosophy.
The word for society that China borrowed from Japan, which had borrowed the characters from China: a compound forged at the altar of the earth.
The word for body doubles as the word for health, asking about it is a greeting, and its second character got luckier in simplification than any other.
The generic term for any deity in the Chinese religious world: and, in classical philosophy, the luminous intelligence that distinguishes the divine from the merely powerful.
The foundational act of economic life: and, in China's Marxist political vocabulary, the act from which all social relations flow. Life gives rise to production; production sustains life.
A chime-stone struck beside an ear: the word for sound welds raw noise to patterned tone, and Chinese theory kept the two distinct.

Poetry stood at the center of Chinese civilization for two thousand years: the primary medium for expressing emotion, demonstrating education, and participating in the social life of the literati class.
The word for a historical era or age, built from 时 (time) and 代 (generation), and how it differs from 时期 a period, 年代 a decade, 时候 a moment, and 现代 modern times.
The everyday word for a point in time, and the indispensable 的时候 ("when") pattern that every learner needs.
Time: the compound that anchors all temporal expression in Mandarin.
The art where writing becomes a performance of character: and why the Chinese brush is a philosophical instrument.
The term Silk Road was coined by a German geographer in 1877: the Chinese themselves had no single name for the trade network that defined their contact with the world for a millennium.
The foundational dyad of Chinese cosmology, pairing Heaven and Earth as the two poles of the created order within which all human life unfolds.
The political and cosmological concept that legitimized three thousand years of Chinese dynasty: heaven's appointment of the rightful ruler.

e: Heaven and humanity as one: the unity of cosmic and human order
d: The organizing claim of Chinese cosmology: Heaven and humanity are not separate domains, and human flourishing depends on alignment with the natural order.
The pre-nation-state Chinese political imagination: the civilized world.
The word that names the organizing project of this entire site: and a concept that Chinese thought built from the ground up differently than the West did.

文明 names both a state of cultivated life (literacy, ritual, the refined arts) and the global concept of civilization. The two meanings share a single Chinese word, and the doubling is the whole story.
One word for both "question" and "problem", and the everyday phrases (没问题, 有问题, 出问题) built from it.

e: non-action; acting in accord with nature
d: 无为 is the Daoist elimination of forced, ego-driven action: the master principle behind effortless effectiveness, sage governance, and Zhuangzi's cook whose knife stays forever sharp.
The art of stopping weapons: how China systematized combat into a living philosophy of the body.
The everyday word for hope, both the verb and the noun, and how it differs from 想 (to want), 愿意 (to be willing), 盼望 (to long for), and 期待 (to look forward to).
The everyday verb for liking, and how it differs from loving (爱), enjoying (喜爱), and being willing (愿意).
The word for the modern era, built from 现 (present, manifest) and 代 (generation, age), how Chinese history slices time into 古代 / 近代 / 现代 / 当代, and how 现代 differs from 现在 now.
The everyday word for now, where it sits in a Chinese sentence, and how it differs from 目前 (at present), 此刻 (this very moment), and 如今 (nowadays).
Confucius took a word that meant "commoner" and turned it into the permanent opposite of the gentleman: the small-hearted schemer of every office.
An elder supported by a child's hands: the cardinal Confucian virtue that placed care for parents at the foundation of all moral life.
The everyday word for "certainly, definitely," covering both confident prediction and firm resolve, the 一定要 (must) pattern, and how it differs from 肯定, 必须, and 一定会.
The everyday word for a little while, how it marks both a short duration and the near future, and how it differs from the verb-softener 一下 and from 等会儿.
The everyday word for "together," the 跟…一起 frame for joint action, the "in one place" sense, the "altogether" use of 一起, and how it differs from 一块儿, 一同, and 一共.
The healing courtyard: how an arrow wound, a wine jar, and the institutional suffix 院 assembled the word for hospital.
Doing what is right because it is right: 义 as the enacted path of Confucian ethics, the constant that gives 仁 its direction.
Meaning, interest, charm, and the gift-giving idiom 意思意思.
The binary engine of all classical Chinese thought.
Music and joy share a single character, a soulmate is "the one who knows your tone," and the zither smashed for a dead friend still echoes.
Buddhist karmic fate: 500 years of cultivation to share a boat with a stranger, a thousand to share a pillow.
A series of fortification systems built across multiple dynasties, whose most visible sections are Ming-era brick: not the continuous ancient rampart of popular imagination.
The primary progressive marker in Mandarin -- placed before a verb to signal an action caught in mid-motion, exactly now, still in progress.
The everyday verb for knowing a fact, and how it differs from 认识 (to be acquainted with) and 了解 (to understand deeply).
智慧 brings together Confucian moral discernment and Buddhist prajna under one compound: two traditions, one word, different objects of knowing.

Two characters older than the country they now name. 中 (center) and 国 (state) joined three thousand years ago to mean "the central states"; the modern country took the phrase for itself only in the 19th century.
Brush and ink as philosophy: Chinese painting aims to capture the spirit of a subject and express the painter's inner cultivation rather than represent what the eye sees.
中文 names both the written script and the spoken language: the most common term among learners, but it sits alongside 汉语, 普通话, and 汉字 in a system of names that carries real distinctions.
Two thousand years of systematic medical thought: qi, yin-yang, the Five Elements, acupuncture, and the living tradition that treats the person, not the disease.
The adverb for "finally, at last," used when something long-awaited or hard-won comes to pass, where it sits in a sentence, and how it differs from 最后, 总算, and 到底.
Laozi placed 自然 at the center of his cosmology: the Way models itself on what is so of itself: no outside force required.
祖先 sits at the center of Chinese religious life: ancestor veneration is a living practice through which families maintain active, reciprocal continuity with the dead.

e: imam — the Chinese Muslim term for mosque leader and scholar
d: From Persian ākhund (scholar, teacher). 阿訇 āhōng is the standard Chinese Muslim term for the mosque's imam and religious authority, combining the functions of prayer leader, teacher, legal counselor, and community elder.

e: love it so much you cannot put it down
d: Lit: love-not-release-hand. The standard phrase for something you cannot stop using, reading, or holding: so beloved that your hand refuses to let go. Used for books, gadgets, food, art. 这本小说写得太好了，让人爱不释手 "This novel is so well-written; you can't put it down."

p: ài měi zhī xīn, rén jiē yǒu zhī
e: the love of beauty is universal — everyone has a heart for beauty
d: Classical proverb affirming the universality of aesthetic appreciation. Often used to gently excuse vanity or the appreciation of beautiful people and things.

Literally "to love but be unable to aid," used when you sympathize and would gladly help, but cannot. A gracious, slightly rueful way to decline: 我也想帮你，可惜爱莫能助 ("I'd like to help, but sadly it's beyond me"). The 助 again is the aid of 帮助.

e: love me, love my dog — love extends to all connected with the beloved
d: Lit: love-house reach-crow. If you love the house, you even love the crow on the roof. Love spreads to everything associated with the beloved, even people or things that would otherwise seem unremarkable.

e: to walk calmly in place of riding: to be content with a simple, unhurried life
d: Lit: walk at ease, treat it as a carriage. Here 当 takes the dàng reading, "to treat as." From a Warring-States anecdote: to stroll on foot and reckon it as good as riding, content without luxury.

e: to live in peace and be content in one's work: a settled, secure life
d: Lit: peaceful-dwelling, joyful-work. 安居 is to live securely, 乐业 to take pleasure in one's occupation. The classic image of social well-being: a people housed, employed, and at ease. Often invoked as the aim of good governance.

e: Allah — God in Chinese Muslim usage
d: The standard Chinese transliteration of Arabic Allāh. Chinese-speaking Muslims also use 真主 Zhēnzhǔ (True Lord , a theologically informed Chinese rendering, placing Islamic monotheism in dialogue with Confucian cosmology).

e: to follow the proper sequence: to do things step by step in due order
d: Lit: according-to-section, settle-into-rank. Originally a writer's image of arranging material into its right divisions and lines; now it means to proceed methodically by the established order, neither rushing nor skipping steps. Here 部 keeps its old sense of an ordered division.

e: arrogant and rude; haughty and without manners
d: Lit: arrogant-rude-without-courtesy. The social-failure sense of 慢 crystallized into a four-character indictment.

p: bā xiān guò hǎi, gè xiǎn shén tōng
e: "the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each showing their powers" — everyone uses their own talents
d: The Eight Immortals, crossing the sea, each rely on a different magical skill rather than a single method. The saying describes a group facing a shared task in which every member contributes through their own distinct ability, and is used to praise resourceful, varied teamwork.

e: to seize the moment; to grasp the opportunity at the right time
d: 把握 bǎwò (grip; certainty; grasp) + 时机 shíjī (the right moment). A common exhortation in business, speech, and motivational contexts. Also used as a noun: 有把握 yǒu bǎwò = "to be confident, certain" (lit. to have a grip on it). 没有把握 = "not sure, not confident."

e: hair gone hoary white: aged, in advanced old age
d: Lit: white-hair-grey-grey. A vivid picture of a head of grizzled white hair, used affectionately or respectfully of the elderly. Again the fà reading, since the phrase is literally about hair.

e: a hundred shots, a hundred hits — unerring accuracy
d: 百 (hundred) + 发 fā (to shoot, release) + 百 + 中 zhòng (to hit the mark). A perfect score: every arrow finds its target. From archery contexts in the Warring States period, now applied to any domain where one's predictions, arguments, or shots unfailingly land.

e: a hundred feelings converging — a complex rush of mixed emotions all at once
d: Lit: hundred-feelings-intersect-gather. For when emotions are too tangled and complex to name individually. 百 = figurative "many."

e: a hundred schools contend — free intellectual debate; a golden age of ideas
d: Lit: "hundred schools contend and cry out." The standard Chinese phrase for the Warring States philosophical explosion. Still used today for any period of open intellectual competition.

p: bǎi wén bù rú yī jiàn
e: hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once
d: From the Han Shu (Book of Han), attributed to general Zhao Chongguo (赵充国), who when asked by Emperor Xuan to estimate how many troops would be needed for a campaign said: "Hearing about a situation a hundred times is not as good as seeing it once.

e: unbowed after a hundred setbacks — perseverance through repeated failure
d: 百 (hundred) + 折 zhé (to break, to bend; a setback) + 不 (not) + 挠 náo (to scratch; to give way, to yield). Literally: a hundred snappings, yet never yielding. The material image is bamboo or a sword repeatedly bent but not permanently deformed.

e: to ruin the family's good name: to disgrace one's household
d: 败坏 (to corrupt, ruin) acting on 门风, a family's reputation and moral tradition. Said of conduct shameful enough to stain the whole family, a phrase out of old domestic and clan morality.
Brandishing an axe at Lu Ban's door: the idiom for presuming to display skill before someone who has mastered it.

e: half the Analects suffices to govern all under heaven — the centrality of the classics in governance
d: Attributed to the Song statesman 赵普 Zhào Pǔ, who supposedly told an emperor that he governed with only half his knowledge of the Analects and had the other half in reserve.

e: half understanding, half not: imperfectly grasped
d: A colloquial set phrase built on the 半A不A frame (half-A, not-A). It marks shaky comprehension, the state of catching the gist of a lecture or a foreign language without truly mastering it.

e: "half a catty, eight taels" — six of one, half a dozen of the other; much the same
