d: A piece of classical economics still quoted in policy debates: when a bumper harvest crashes prices, the farmer who grew it earns less, not more.

e: bone and flesh joined together: bound by blood kinship
d: The image is that bone and flesh cannot be pulled apart. Used for the inseparable bond between family members, and figuratively for a homeland and its people.

e: to confine oneself to old ways: to be complacent and refuse to progress
d: Literally "wall yourself in with your old footsteps." 封 here is the self-imposed boundary. A common criticism of stagnant institutions or people who resist new ideas.

e: to deliberately mystify: to make something seem more obscure or profound than it is
d: 故 (deliberately) + 弄 (nòng, to play with, to manipulate) + 玄 (xuán, mysterious, dark, profound) + 虚 (xū, empty, unreal). To purposely dress something up as mysterious in order to confuse or impress, when in fact there is little substance behind it.

e: attend to this and lose that — unable to manage everything at once
d: 顾 gù (to attend to; to look after) + 此 cǐ (this) + 失 shī (to lose) + 彼 bǐ (that; the other). Fix your attention on one thing and something else slips away. Describes resource constraints, divided attention, and the predicament of managing competing priorities.

e: when the melon is ripe, the stem falls — things happen at the right natural moment
d: Lit: melon-ripe-stem-fall. Things should not be forced; they will happen naturally when conditions are right. The Daoist principle of naturalness encoded in a harvest image.

e: "wipe the eyes and look again" — to see someone with new respect after they've changed
d: 刮目 (to wipe / rub the eyes) + 相看 (to look at each other; to regard). Clear your eyes and look again at the person in front of you , because they are no longer who you thought they were.

e: "relationship close and tight" — closely connected; intimately related
d: A descriptive fixed phrase rather than a classical 成语, but widely used as a set expression in formal Chinese writing and speech. 这两家公司的关系密切，共享很多资源。"These two companies are closely connected and share many resources." The closeness can be personal, institutional, or strategic.

e: corrupt officials drive the people to revolt
d: The phrase that captures the whole moral logic of Water Margin: rebellion springs not from the people's wickedness but from the oppression of corrupt officials who leave them no other choice.

e: open, upright, and honest — nothing to hide
d: Lit: light-bright-correct-great. Used to describe someone who acts with complete transparency and moral integrity. 他做事光明正大 "He does things openly and uprightly."

e: time flies like an arrow — the days pass with frightening speed
d: 光阴 guāngyīn (time, light-and-shadow) + 似 sì (resembles) + 箭 jiàn (arrow). Time shoots past like a loosed arrow, gone before you can grasp it. Usually paired with its twin 日月如梭 (the sun and moon shuttle by like a weaver's shuttle). 光阴似箭，日月如梭，一晃十年就过去了。

e: bring glory to the clan and illuminate the ancestors
d: 光 (illuminate) + 宗 (clan lineage) + 耀 (cause to shine) + 祖 (ancestors). The foundational aspiration of Chinese family-oriented ambition: achievement is owed to and shared with those who came before. Used sincerely in formal contexts; with ironic distance among younger generations.

e: to return to the root and settle the bottom: in the final analysis, when all is said and done
d: Lit: return-root-conclude-bottom. Used to introduce the fundamental point after stripping away the surface: 归根结底，还是钱的问题 "in the end, it still comes down to money." Here 结 carries the settling sense.

e: the country is prosperous and the people are at peace
d: The classical blessing for a nation: 泰 tài (great peace) + 民安 (the people are secure). Used in toasts, New Year wishes, and political rhetoric. The Confucian ideal of good governance.

e: cross the river, then tear down the bridge
d: A vivid picture of ingratitude: discarding the very means or person that got you across once you are safely over. A sharp accusation in modern speech.

e: to roar with laughter: a full belly laugh
d: 哈哈 is the sound of laughter itself, 大笑 a big laugh. The everyday, vivid way to say someone burst out laughing. Common in narration and casual speech alike.

e: the sea does not surge — peaceful passage; a stable, unchallenged realm
d: Lit: sea-not-raise-waves. A classical phrase for the ideal of peaceful sea passage , exactly what Mazu provides. Used in Mazu temple inscriptions and ritual prayers.

e: till the seas run dry and the rocks crumble: forever, unchanging
d: Lit: sea-dry stone-rot. A vow of eternal constancy, used in oaths of love and loyalty: even when the impossible happens and the ocean dries up, the feeling will not change.

e: the sea is wide and the sky is open: boundless; (of talk) freewheeling and unconstrained
d: Lit: sea-wide sky-empty. It paints limitless space, hence both a feeling of total freedom and a way to describe rambling, anything-goes conversation: 海阔天空地聊 "to chat about everything under the sun."

e: sea-sized capacity: a vast tolerance or a huge amount
d: 海 hǎi (sea) + 量 liàng (capacity). A capacity as large as the sea. Traditionally a generous compliment for someone of great tolerance, whether a magnanimous temperament (大人有海量, your honor is broad-minded) or a formidable drinking capacity at the table.

e: a horse that harms the herd: one bad apple
d: From the Zhuāngzǐ, where the Yellow Emperor is told to govern by removing whatever harms the herd. Now the person who spoils a group or organization.

e: to hold pungency and swallow bitterness: to endure every hardship
d: 茹 (rú) means to eat. Almost always said of parents, especially mothers, who suffer silently for years to raise their children.

e: losing your own way while trying to imitate another's — ending up with neither
d: From the Zhuangzi (秋水 chapter). The problem: imitation so total that it erases the imitator's original competence. Used for people who pursue a foreign or fashionable style so completely that they lose their own footing.
The archetypal image of examination preparation: the scholar sitting through winter nights by a cold window, studying by lamplight, without heat or comfort.

e: to sweat the oxen and fill the rafters: a vast number of books
d: Coined by the Tang writer Liǔ Zōngyuán. So many volumes that hauling them makes the oxen sweat and stacking them fills the house to the roofbeams. Praise for a great library or prolific output.

e: without the slightest problem; absolutely fine
d: A stronger, more emphatic version of 没问题, using 毫无 ("not the slightest"). It asserts that something is completely fine or certain, with no doubt or difficulty whatever. Common in confident assurances and formal contexts.

e: a wise fellow avoids a loss he can plainly see coming
d: Lit: a good-fellow does not eat the loss before his eyes. Folk wisdom that real courage includes the sense to step back from a fight you cannot win, rather than charging in for pride.

e: good times don't last — a beautiful scene cannot endure
d: Lit: good-scenery-not-long. An expression of Buddhist impermanence and Chinese realism about fortune. Used when pleasant circumstances are ending or were brief.

e: the Song of Good and Done — the vanity of worldly craving
d: The song sung by a tattered Daoist near the start of the novel, teaching that all the things people chase (rank, gold, lovers, children) end in nothing, and that 好 (good) and 了 (finished with, let go of) are ultimately the same.

e: good things take time — good outcomes require much grinding and effort
d: Lit: good-things-much-grinding. Used to console someone experiencing delays or obstacles on the path to something valuable. The consolation: friction is the price of worth.

e: take good care of yourself; do well for yourself
d: A formal farewell or parting injunction: "do well in your own conduct." Can be warm (a mentor to a student) or pointed (a warning to behave). Context determines whether it is affectionate or admonishing.

e: to drink the northwest wind: have nothing to eat, go hungry
d: A vivid colloquial idiom: with no food, all you can swallow is the cold wind. Said wryly of poverty or a failed livelihood, "我们都去喝西北风了".

e: in keeping with feeling and reason: fair and reasonable
d: Lit: accords-with-feeling, accords-with-reason. Said of a decision or request that satisfies both human sentiment and good sense, so no one can fault it. The doubled 合 stresses that it fits on every count.

e: vertical alliance and horizontal linkage — coalition against a dominant power, or accommodation with it
d: The two grand strategic options of the Warring States endgame. Used today in geopolitics, business competition, and organizational dynamics to describe the choice between forming a coalition against a dominant player and making separate deals with it.

e: which way to turn; what course to take
d: Literally "where to go, what to follow", the weighing of a hard choice between paths. A more literary cousin of 怎么办, asking not just "what to do" but "which direction to commit to". Here 何 is the classical "how / what" that 怎么 replaced in everyday speech.

e: to soften one's light and share the dust: to blend in and live among ordinary people
d: From the Daoist classics: to dim one's brilliance and mix with the common crowd rather than stand apart. A vision of how the wise move within society, joining its dust instead of towering over it. The ideal of fitting unobtrusively into the social whole.

e: harmony brings wealth — a gentle manner attracts prosperity
d: 和气 héqi (harmony of manner; friendliness) + 生 shēng (to generate) + 财 cái (wealth). The principle that amicable dealings create the trust and goodwill that sustain business. Posted in shops across the Chinese-speaking world.

e: the lioness of Hedong roars: a fierce, jealous wife
d: From a Song poem by Su Shi teasing his friend Chen Jichang (Chen Zao), whose wife's temper made him quail. 河东 (Hedong) names her clan's home east of the Yellow River. Still used, half teasing, for a domineering spouse.

e: the river runs clear and the sea is calm: peace under good rule
d: Since the Yellow River is famously muddy, its running clear is a near-impossible omen of a sage age. Paired with a calm sea, it stands for an era of order and prosperity. Formal, literary register.

e: a crane standing among chickens: head and shoulders above the rest
d: The tall white crane towering over a yard of squat fowl. Said of a person whose talent or bearing makes them stand out from an ordinary crowd.

e: red-red fire-fire — flourishing, booming, and full of warmth
d: A doubled, emphatic form of 红火. The image is a scene so prosperous and lively it seems to glow like fire.

e: red cheeks, thin fate — a beautiful woman is destined for a hard or short life
d: 红颜 hóngyán (rosy cheeks, a beautiful woman) + 薄命 bómìng (thin or meager fate). A fatalistic literary trope: great beauty seems to attract misfortune, and the most celebrated beauties of history met tragic ends. 自古红颜多薄命。

e: the Feast at Hong Gate — a banquet set as a trap
d: The Shiji's most famous set-piece: the banquet at which Xiang Yu's faction plotted to kill the future Han founder Liu Bang, where the sword-dance of 项庄 (项庄舞剑) masked an assassination attempt and Liu Bang escaped by a hair.

e: "the worry of looking back" — concern for what you leave behind; anxiety about what is happening at the rear
d: 后 (behind; the rear) + 顾 (to look back; to attend to) + 之 (classical possessive particle) + 忧 (worry; anxiety).

e: "the latecomer occupies the top" — the newcomer surpasses those who came first
d: 后来 (later arrival) + 居上 (occupies the upper position). From the Shǐjì (史记), the court historian Sima Qian. A newly promoted official sitting above older ministers in court: the latecomer had outranked his seniors.

e: "the young are to be feared" — the next generation will surpass those before them
d: From the Analects of Confucius (论语·子罕): 后生可畏，焉知来者之不如今也？(The young are to be feared , how do we know the ones still to come will not surpass those of today?) 后生 = those born later, the younger generation. 可畏 = worthy of awe, of apprehension.

e: profound virtue bears all things; great moral force sustains everything it carries
d: 厚 hòu (thick; deep; generous; substantial) + 德 dé (virtue; moral force) + 载 zài (to carry; to bear; to support) + 物 wù (things; the ten thousand things; all beings).

e: to favor the past over the present: to esteem antiquity and slight the modern
d: Literally "thick toward the ancient, thin toward the present." Criticizes the habit of prizing everything old while dismissing the contemporary. Its mirror is 厚今薄古, valuing the present over the past. A pointed term in debates over tradition and modernity.

e: fox-friends and dog-companions: a bad crowd
d: Lit: fox-friends, dog-friends. 狐 fox and 狗 dog stand for the sly and the low. The phrase scorns worthless drinking companions and hangers-on, the kind of friends who lead you nowhere good. A parent's word of warning.

e: lake light and mountain hues: beautiful lake-and-mountain scenery
d: A set phrase praising scenic landscape, the stock compliment paid to West Lake and its kin.

e: the Humen Opium Destruction — Lin Zexu's burning of British opium in 1839
d: Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of 1,200 tons of British-owned opium at Humen (虎门), Guangdong, in June 1839. The act that triggered the First Opium War. Commemorated as a patriotic symbol in Chinese history education. The date (June 26) is marked as China's National Anti-Drug Day (中国禁毒日).

e: flowers in full bloom, moon perfectly round — a moment of perfection and happiness
d: The classic wedding blessing and New Year wish. Flowers (spring beauty) + full moon (reunion, completeness) = the ideal of a happy, complete life. Often inscribed on wedding gifts and red envelopes.

e: flowers red, willows green — a riot of bright spring color
d: 花 huā (flowers) + 红 hóng (red) + 柳 liǔ (willow) + 绿 lǜ (green). A set image of late spring at its most colorful: red blossoms against green willows. By extension it describes anything gaudy and brightly multicolored, sometimes with a faint hint of being overdone. 公园里花红柳绿，游人如织。

e: the year of the flowery cycle — age sixty
flower streets and willow lanes: the pleasure quarters
d: A classical euphemism for the red-light district, where 花 (flower) and 柳 (willow) stand for courtesans. Literary and old-fashioned; appears in Ming and Qing fiction.

e: when the flower blooms, the Buddha is seen — sudden illumination after patient waiting
d: Originally a Pure Land image (the lotus flower opening in the Pure Land to reveal the practitioner reborn there, seeing Amitābha), adopted by Chan as a metaphor for sudden enlightenment: the moment when all the conditions are right and understanding blooms.

e: flowery words and clever speech: sweet, deceptive talk
d: Lit: flowery-words-clever-speech. Honeyed, ornamented talk meant to flatter or deceive. Here 花 carries its "showy, dressed-up" sense, words made pretty to mislead rather than to tell the truth.

e: to turn danger into safety: to avert a crisis; to come through unscathed
d: 化 huà = to transform, 险 xiǎn = danger, peril, 为 wéi = into, 夷 yí = level ground, flatness, safety. Lit: "transform the perilous into the level." Describes turning a dangerous, threatening situation into a safe one, often through skill, calm, or good fortune. 在关键时刻，他冷静地化险为夷。

e: "turn the whole into pieces" — to break something large into small scattered parts
d: 化 (to transform) + 整 (the whole) + 为 (into) + 零 (the scattered pieces). To disperse one large thing into many small ones: a big force split into small units that move unseen, a large task divided into manageable bits, a lump sum paid in installments.

e: to draw a cake to ease hunger: to comfort oneself with empty fantasy
d: Lit: draw-cake-fill-hunger. A painted cake feeds no one. The idiom mocks any plan or promise that satisfies in imagination only, offering the picture of a thing in place of the thing itself.

p: huà hǔ bù chéng fǎn lèi quǎn
e: tried to paint a tiger, ended up with a dog
d: Colloquial proverb for the same failure: aiming high, imitating without understanding, producing something worse than the original and worse than doing nothing.

e: drawing a dragon and dotting the eye — the small finishing touch that brings the whole alive
d: From a Tang anecdote: the painter Zhang Sengyou painted dragons but refused to add eyes; when pressed, he dotted the eyes of two , and they immediately flew off the wall. The dot is what brings the form to life. Used today for the small but decisive move that makes a piece of work click.
He finished first, so he kept drawing, and lost the prize. The idiom for ruining a good thing by overdoing it.

e: the talk does not meet: the conversation does not click
d: Lit: words-not-matching-the-moment. Said when two people simply cannot find common ground in conversation. The fuller saying 话不投机半句多 adds that "when talk does not click, even half a sentence is too much."

e: there are words within the words: a remark carries a hidden meaning
d: Lit: inside-the-words-there-are-words. Said when someone speaks with an implied second meaning, hinting at more than the surface remark admits.

e: to harbor talent yet meet no chance: gifted but unrecognized
d: Lit: cradle-talent-not-encounter. The lament of the able person who never finds a ruler, patron, or era that will use their gifts. A recurring theme in classical poetry, where the unemployed scholar mourns his wasted ability.

e: bad people and bad deeds: wrongdoers and their misdeeds
d: A set four-character phrase pairing 坏人 with 坏事, often in the formula 与坏人坏事作斗争, "to struggle against wrongdoers and wrongdoing." Carries a formal, almost official register.

e: wild with joy: overjoyed, beside oneself with delight
d: Lit: joy-Heaven-glad-Earth, joy that fills the whole sky and ground. Said of someone bursting with happiness at good news, a reunion, or a festival. 一家人欢天喜地过新年 "the family rang in the New Year overjoyed."

e: elated and inspired: filled with joy and high spirits
d: Lit: joyful-glad-drum-dance, so cheered that one beats the drum and dances. Used of a group lifted and energized by good news or a great event, joy that rouses people to action.

e: eunuch domination of state power — when palace servants usurp the emperor's authority
d: A recurring theme in Chinese historiography across multiple dynasties, but reaching its most extreme form in the late Ming. 专权 (monopolize power) is always pejorative. The phrase is invoked whenever insiders with access but no mandate accumulate power.

e: a friend made in times of hardship — a friend in adversity
d: A friendship forged through shared difficulty, prized in Chinese culture as the truest kind. 患难 huànnàn means hardship and danger; 交 jiāo here is the noun "friendship, bond." The related proverb is 患难见真情 ("adversity reveals true feeling"): you learn who your real friends are when times are hard.

e: "completely transformed to something new" — completely renewed; a total makeover
d: 焕然 (huànrán, resplendently bright; the appearance of something that has been renovated or refreshed) + 一新 (completely new). The appearance of something that has undergone a total transformation: 装修完工后，房间焕然一新 (after the renovation was complete, the room was completely transformed).

The emperor's kin and the families connected to the throne by marriage, the privileged inner circle of the imperial house. Now used, often with a sardonic edge, for anyone who enjoys protection or privilege through family connections to power.

e: suddenly, greatly awakened — the flash of realization
d: 恍然 (in a flash) + 大悟 (great awakening, 悟 being the enlightenment verb of Chan Buddhism and the Monkey King's name 悟空). The eureka moment: the detective's final chapter, the student when the proof clicks. Chinese lets you borrow the vocabulary of enlightenment for algebra.

e: turn your head and there is the shore: it is never too late to repent
d: Lit: turn-the-head-is-shore. From the Buddhist 苦海无边，回头是岸 ("the sea of suffering is boundless; turn back and the shore is there"). To stop a wrong course and come back is itself salvation.

e: to turn the heart and shift the will: to change one's mind, to relent
d: Lit: turn-heart-shift-intent. Said of someone who softens, reconsiders, or comes back to a relationship or decision they had set aside.

e: painting both sound and color: vivid and lifelike (of a description)
d: Lit: paint-sound-paint-color. Of telling or describing something so vividly that the listener seems to hear and see it. High praise for a gripping, animated account.

e: seamlessly whole as if formed by nature: without a trace of artifice
d: Lit: wholly-so-Heaven-made. Praises a work of art or writing so unified that it seems made by nature rather than by human hands, with no visible seams or effort. 浑然 means "in one undivided whole."

e: alive and bouncing about: brimming with health and energy
d: Lit: alive-leaping-wildly-jumping. The image of a fish on the deck or a healthy child who cannot keep still. Used for someone bursting with vitality, often after recovering from illness.

p: huó dào lǎo, xué dào lǎo
e: live until old, learn until old — lifelong learning
d: The most common proverb for lifelong learning: you learn for as long as you live. An encouragement to keep studying at any age, and a gentle reminder that no one has ever learned enough to stop. Equivalent in spirit to the English "you're never too old to learn."

e: vivid and lifelike: so vivid it seems to come alive before you
d: Lit: alive-spirit-alive-appearing, with 活 doubled for emphasis. Describes a story, performance, or portrait so vivid and animated that the thing depicted seems present in the room. High praise for vividness.

e: to add oil to the fire — to make a bad situation worse
d: Lit: fire-above-add-oil. The Chinese equivalent of "adding fuel to the fire." 你别火上加油了 "Don't make things worse." The equivalent English idiom "add fuel to the fire" has exactly the same logic.

e: fiery golden eyes — seeing through deception
d: The Monkey King's eyes, hardened in the furnace of the Daoist god Laojun, that let him see through every demon's disguise to the true form beneath. The chengyu now means sharp, penetrating discernment, the ability to see through falsehood and recognise the real nature of a person or situation.

e: genuine goods at a fair price: the real thing, no fakery
d: Lit: goods-genuine-price-real. A merchant's pledge that the wares are authentic and honestly priced. By extension it certifies anything as the genuine article, not a counterfeit or an exaggeration.

e: to pick bones out of an egg: to nitpick, to find fault where there is none
d: A vivid colloquial saying: an egg has no bones, so hunting for one means inventing flaws. Used of a critic or boss who complains about everything.

e: the hen flies off and the eggs break: to lose everything, ending up empty-handed
d: A botched scheme where both the chicken and its eggs are lost. Said when an attempt to grab more leaves you with nothing at all.

e: chickens fly and dogs leap: utter chaos and uproar
d: A farmyard thrown into panic, hens flapping and dogs bolting. Describes a household or scene in total disorder. Lively and colloquial.

e: chicken feathers and garlic skins: trivial, petty matters
d: The kitchen sweepings nobody bothers with. Used to dismiss a quarrel or complaint as not worth the fuss: 别为这点鸡毛蒜皮的事吵架.

e: errors accumulated until they harden into accepted norm
d: Lit: accumulate-wrong-become-right. When a mistake or deviation is repeated so long it calcifies into convention. Applied in linguistics (describing language change), ethics, and institutional analysis. A cautionary concept: not all norms are correct simply because they persist.

From the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian): repeated criticism, even if each instance is minor, accumulates into something that can destroy a person entirely. This is the specific personal consequence that Pang Cong feared, and that happened to him.

e: accumulate goodness, achieve virtue — individual good acts build character over time
d: From Xunzi (荀子): 积土成山…积善成德，而神明自得，圣心备焉。 "Pile earth to make a mountain; accumulate goodness to achieve virtue, and the divine intelligence arrives of itself, the sage's mind becomes complete." Virtue on this account is a slow deposit, not a bolt of insight.

e: accumulate the few and it becomes the many
d: The thrift-and-study chengyu: small savings, daily vocabulary reviews, and minor improvements compound. The financial-app era has given it a second life in savings-product marketing, and teachers deploy it against the student who dismisses ten minutes of practice as pointless.

e: to pass the exam and make a name: to win rank and renown at once
d: Lit: reach-rank-become-famous. The double prize of the imperial scholar, to place in the examination and so earn lasting reputation. The dream that drove generations of candidates to the 科举.

e: eager for quick merit and near-term gain: shortsighted opportunism
d: Lit: anxious-merit-near-profit. A criticism of those who chase immediate results and quick profit at the expense of long-term, sustainable success. The opposite of the 功夫 ethic of patient, foundational effort.

e: urgent as a shooting star — desperately urgent
d: Lit: urgent-like-shooting-star-fire. A shooting star (流星) appears briefly and is gone: something that needs to be acted on instantly before the moment passes. Used in military dispatches and urgent appeals.

e: wisdom born from urgency — a bright idea in a crisis; thinking fast under pressure
d: 急 jí (urgent; pressed; crisis) + 中 zhōng (within; in the midst of) + 生 shēng (to be born; to arise) + 智 zhì (wisdom; clever idea). The intelligence that surfaces specifically when there is no time to think: the flash of insight that saves a situation.

p: jǐ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén
e: do not impose on others what you yourself do not want — the Silver Rule
d: Analects 15.24. Confucius called this 恕 shù (reciprocity, forgiveness), the negative formulation of the Golden Rule. One of the most famous sentences in Chinese. Appears in the UN Declaration of Human Rights as a cross-cultural parallel. 己 = oneself; 施 = to impose/apply; 于人 = onto others.

p: jǐ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén.
e: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
d: Appears twice in the Analects (12.2, 15.24) as the Confucian formulation of the negative Golden Rule. Called the doctrine of 恕 shù (sympathetic understanding). This formulation was inscribed on the UNESCO building in Paris as one of humanity's foundational ethical principles.

e: the memory is still fresh: as vivid as if it just happened
d: Lit: memory-still-new. Said of an event or scene one recalls so clearly that time seems not to have dulled it. 至今记忆犹新 "to this day it remains fresh in my mind."

p: jì shēng yú, hé shēng liàng?
e: Since you bore Zhou Yu, why also bear Zhuge Liang?
d: The dying lament attributed to the Wu commander 周瑜 Zhou Yu, repeatedly outmatched by his rival Zhuge Liang.

e: an everyday home meal: a common, unremarkable occurrence
d: Lit: home-ordinary-simple-meal. Literally plain home cooking, used figuratively for anything that happens so routinely it is no big deal: 加班对他来说是家常便饭 "working late is routine for him."

e: home with only four walls — extreme poverty; owning nothing
d: Lit: home-merely-four-walls. 徒 = only; merely; bare. The household contains nothing but the four walls themselves. Used in literature to describe destitution. Often contrasted with 家财万贯 jiācái wànguàn (immense family wealth). A stock phrase for total financial ruin.

e: known to every household — a household name; universally known
d: Lit: family-understood-household-known. 喻 = understood; 晓 = known; aware. Every family understands it; every household knows it. 这首歌已经家喻户晓了。(This song is now known to everyone.) The go-to phrase for "universally famous" in Chinese.

e: worth a string of cities: of immense value
d: From the Warring States tale of the 和氏璧 jade, which King Zhao of Qin offered fifteen cities to obtain. To be worth 连城 is to command a value beyond ordinary reckoning.

Literally "firm and settled, not shifting", steadfast in resolve, never wavering. The 定 ("settled, fixed") at its heart is the same 定 in 一定; here it describes a will that has fixed on its course. The deepest form of the resolve 一定要 voices.

e: the gap admits not a hair: a situation of extreme danger or urgency
d: Lit: the-gap-does-not-allow-a-hair. The interval is so narrow not even a single hair could fit, so the margin for error is none at all. Here 间 takes the jiān reading for the gap itself.

e: love all under Heaven impartially — the Mohist manifesto in four characters
d: 兼 jiān (jointly; all together) + 爱 ài (love) + 天下 tiānxià (all under Heaven; the world). The compressed statement of Mozi's central ethical position: love extended equally to every person without gradation by family, state, or social proximity.

e: to study and refine through relentless, focused effort
d: From the Zhanguo Ce account of Su Qin reading until he was exhausted, jabbing his own thigh with an awl to stay awake. 练 carries the sense of working material over and over until it is honed.

e: simple, clear, and gripping the essentials: succinct and pointed
d: 简 simple, 明 clear, 扼要 to grip the crux. Common in formal evaluation of summaries and briefings, marking a text that wastes no words.

e: to see someone dying and not save them
d: The harshest social indictment in the 救 family: standing by while another perishes. Used today to condemn indifference, whether a bystander ignoring an accident or an institution refusing aid.

e: to be laughed at: forgive my poor effort
d: Lit: be-seen laughed-at. A set humble phrase: 让您见笑了 ("I've let you laugh at me") deflects praise for one's own work or skill. Polite, slightly formal register.

e: see righteousness and act with courage — to step up when others need help
d: 见 jiàn (to see; to perceive) + 义 yì (righteous action; what is right) + 勇 yǒng (courage; bravery) + 为 wéi (to do; to act). From the Analects (论语): 见义不为，无勇也 , "To see what is right and not do it is a want of courage" (Confucius, 2.24).

e: a wandering swindler, a roving con artist
d: The 江湖 of itinerant healers and fortune-tellers turned into a label for a charlatan who works the crowds.

e: Jiang's talent is exhausted — creative powers have run dry; the burnt-out genius
d: From the Southern Qi dynasty writer Jiang Yan (江淹), famed for his prose, who stopped producing good work later in life. Legend says he dreamed that a man demanded his writing brush back; after that, his talent was gone. 他感觉自己江郎才尽了。

e: rivers and mountains like a painting; the land is breathtakingly beautiful
d: From Su Shi's 念奴娇·赤壁怀古 (Remembering Chibi, to the tune of Nian Nu Jiao), written in 1082 at the site of the famous Three Kingdoms battle. 江山如画，一时多少豪杰 (the rivers and mountains like a painting , how many heroes in that one moment).

e: the rivers, mountains, and altars of soil and grain: the whole realm, the state
d: Literally "rivers and mountains, the altars of soil and grain." 江山 the land and 社稷 the altars together name the entire country a ruler holds in trust. A grand, classical phrase for the state as a whole, the territory and the legitimacy that come with it.

p: jiāngshān yì gǎi, běnxìng nán yí
e: easy to change the landscape, hard to change one's nature; a leopard can't change its spots
d: The full proverb. 易 yì (easy) + 改 gǎi (to change; to alter) / 难 nán (difficult) + 移 yí (to shift; to move; to transplant). The contrast is between the external world , rivers and mountains, the landscape of history , and the internal: 本性, innate character, the temperament you were born with.

p: jiāng shān yì gǎi běn xìng nán yí
e: territory is easy to change; fundamental nature is hard to move — a leopard cannot change its spots
d: Classic proverb about human nature used in resignation or rueful acknowledgment. 他就是这样的人，江山易改本性难移。(He's just that kind of person; a leopard can't change its spots.) Often invoked by someone who has tried to change another person and given up.

e: to take the mistake and run with it: to leave a wrong thing as it is
d: Lit: take-the-error-go-with-the-error. Rather than undo a mistake already made, one accepts it and proceeds on that footing, often because correcting it would cost more than living with it.

e: heads together, ears joined: to whisper privately
d: Two people lean in until one mouth nearly touches the other's ear. The image of leaning close to murmur in secret, often disapproving when done during a meeting or class.

e: feet planted on solid ground: down-to-earth, steady and practical
d: Lit: feet-tread-solid-ground. High praise for someone who works steadily and realistically rather than chasing empty schemes. The 实 here is the solid earth underfoot.

p: jiào wǒ rúhé bù xiǎng tā
e: "How could I not think of her" — Liu Bannong's 1920 poem, set to music by Zhao Yuanren
d: Not classical, but the most famous early appearance of 她 in print. The poem is addressed to "her", variously read as a lover, the homeland (Liu was abroad in Britain when he wrote it), or both. The song became one of the defining works of early modern Chinese music.

e: teaching and learning grow each other: the teacher learns by teaching
d: Lit: teach-learn-mutually-grow. From the Liji (Record of Rites). Teaching exposes what the teacher does not yet understand, so instructing others deepens one's own knowledge; the two advance together.

e: all are greatly delighted — everyone ends up happy
d: Originally the closing formula of Buddhist sutras, where the assembly rejoices at the teaching and departs; now the phrase for win-win endings, amicable settlements, and comedies. It is also the standard Chinese title of Shakespeare's As You Like It, a translation with better provenance than most.

e: one after another: coming in quick succession
d: Literally "joining the second, linking the third," counting events as they pile up. Describes things happening in rapid, repeated succession, most often a run of incidents or problems: 接二连三地出事 (one mishap after another).

e: linked and unbroken: continuous, without interruption
d: 接连 doubles the sense of joining; 不断 says the chain never breaks. Describes rain, applause, or news that keeps coming.

e: to raise a pole and rise up — to start a popular rebellion
d: 揭 (raise, lift) + 竿 (pole, bamboo staff) + 而起 (and rise up). The idiom originates in the Qin dynasty collapse (221–206 BCE), when the rebel leader Chen Sheng reportedly rallied followers with nothing but a raised pole: no weapons, no banners, no organization, just the act of standing up.

e: street talk and lane discussion: common gossip, popular chatter
d: The talk of the town, idle public discussion of an affair. Carries a faintly dismissive tone, the chatter of ordinary streets as opposed to considered opinion.

e: street corners and lane ends: all about town, on everyone's lips
d: Names the public places where people gather and gossip. Often used of news or rumor that has spread everywhere: 这件事在街头巷尾传开了, the story spread to every corner of town.

e: "rising section by section" — steady, continuous increase
d: 节 jié = section; segment; node. Each node advances the rise. Used for prices, temperatures, performance metrics, or any quantity that climbs steadily over time. Common in economic and news reporting.

e: a branch sprouts from the joint: new complications arise unexpectedly
d: Lit: joint-outside-grow-branch. A side branch springs from the node of a stalk where none was wanted. Said when an already settled matter throws up fresh, unwelcome problems.

e: to scrimp on clothes and food: to live frugally and pinch every penny
d: Lit: economize-clothing-cut-back-food. To deny oneself even basics in order to save, said of those who tighten the belt hard, often to support a family or reach a goal.

e: to knot grass and carry rings: to repay a kindness, even after death
d: Lit: tie-grass-hold-ring. From two old tales of gratitude: a ghost knotted grass to trip an enemy and save his benefactor, and a magpie brought jade rings to repay a rescuer. Together they stand for never forgetting a debt of kindness.
A common modern four-character set phrase for the strong bond between sisters or close female friends. Frequent in titles, toasts, and warm descriptions of female friendship.

e: borrow a knife to kill a man: destroy a rival by another's hand
d: The third of the Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六计). You stay clean while a third party does the deed; still vivid in business and political commentary today.

e: borrow the wind to sail the boat: turn outside conditions to your own ends
d: A close cousin of 顺水推船, stressing the borrowed force: you let someone else's momentum carry your own plan forward.

e: use the past to satirize the present
d: A classic mode of Chinese writing: cloak criticism of present rulers in a story about an ancient dynasty. Long the safest way to speak truth to power.

e: to offer flowers borrowed from another — presenting something that isn't yours
d: Used with self-deprecating humor when giving a gift that wasn't originally yours , passing along a recommendation, re-gifting, or presenting another person's work as an offering. The image: lacking flowers of your own to offer at the Buddhist altar, you borrow someone else's.

e: seize on a topic to make a wider point: use a pretext to vent
d: Literally "borrow the subject to elaborate." Common for someone who turns a small matter into a platform for a bigger grievance.

p: jīn guó bù ràng xū méi
e: "the woman's headdress yields nothing to the man's beard" — a woman who is the equal of any man
d: 巾帼 jīnguó , a woman's hair ornament, by metonymy "woman." 须眉 xūméi: beard and brows, by metonymy "man." Used in praise of female generals (Mulan, Hua Mulan; Liang Hongyu), athletes, and accomplished women.

e: heroine — a woman of exceptional courage and achievement
d: Lit: kerchief-hood hero. 巾帼 jīnguó is the traditional women's headdress, used by extension to mean women collectively. A 巾帼英雄 is a female hero, a woman who has achieved what is extraordinary even by the standards of men. Hua Mulan 花木兰 is the archetype. Used to praise exceptional women in any field.

e: the present cannot compare with the past
d: Literally "today is not what the past compared to," meaning things have changed greatly, usually for the better, so that now far surpasses before. 今 (now) versus 昔 (former times). A common way to mark dramatic progress or transformation.

e: one's name inscribed on the golden list — exam success
d: The 金榜 was the yellow placard of palace-exam graduates posted outside the examination compound. Classical culture counted it among life's four great joys, alongside the wedding night, rain after drought, and meeting an old friend far from home. Today it captions every gaokao congratulations post.

e: to keep a beauty in a golden house — to keep a mistress in luxury
d: From a Han dynasty story: Emperor Wu as a child said he would build a golden house for the girl Ah Jiao (阿娇) if she became his wife. Now means to keep a mistress in a secret dwelling. A literary idiom that appears in Tang poetry and classical fiction.

p: jīn wú zú chì, rén wú wán rén
e: no gold is pure, no person is perfect
d: Pure 24-karat gold is too soft to be durable; impurity is what makes gold useful. The proverb uses this fact to excuse human flaws: perfection is neither achievable nor desirable. Used to express tolerance of others' shortcomings.

e: words of gold and jade — invaluable advice
d: Lit: gold-jade-fine-words. Used to praise someone's counsel or wisdom. "Your words are truly 金玉良言" = "That is genuinely valuable advice." The pairing of gold and jade 金玉 represents the two most precious materials.

e: do what you can as a human, then accept Heaven's decree
d: The natural paired response to 事与愿违. Where 事与愿违 names the gap between intention and outcome, this phrase names the correct attitude toward that gap: maximum effort, then acceptance of what lies beyond one's control. The two phrases together describe the full Confucian-Daoist response to adversity.

e: utterly good and utterly beautiful — perfection achieved
d: Confucius used this phrase to evaluate music: the highest praise for something that excels in both moral virtue and aesthetic form. Used today for flawless work, ideal relationships, and perfect events.

e: tight gongs and dense drums: intense, busy preparation
d: From the loud, crowded percussion that builds before an opera's climax. Modern usage describes a project being driven forward at full, urgent pace behind the scenes.
The pivotal moment when everything hangs in the balance. Common in news and narrative for the turning point of a crisis or contest.

e: "adding flowers on top of brocade" — making something excellent even better
d: Brocade (锦 jǐn) is already the finest silk, already decorated with woven patterns. Adding flowers on top of it is a gift that was not needed but is delightful. Contrasted with 雪中送炭 (sending coal in the snow), helping someone in genuine need. 锦上添花 is the luxury gesture; 雪中送炭 is the necessary one.

p: jìn zhū zhě chì, jìn mò zhě hēi
e: those near red become red; those near ink become black — environment shapes character
d: Two parallel 者 constructions: 近朱者 = the one(s) near vermilion / 近墨者 = the one(s) near ink. The argument is that proximity to good or bad influences changes a person's nature, just as a white object held near ink absorbs its color.

p: jìn zhū zhě chì, jìn mò zhě hēi
e: near vermilion turns red, near ink turns black — you become like the company you keep
d: 近 jìn (close to) + 朱 zhū (vermilion) + 者 zhě (one who) + 赤 chì (red); 近 + 墨 mò (ink) + 者 + 黑 (black). Whoever stays near red dye turns red; whoever stays near ink turns black. A classic statement that environment and company shape character, attributed to the Jin-dynasty writer Fu Xuan 傅玄.

e: hard to advance and hard to retreat: caught in a dilemma
d: Lit: advance-retreat-both-hard. To be stuck where neither going forward nor falling back will do, the classic no-win bind. The 进 / 退 pairing makes the trap vivid.

e: to endure long without fading: standing the test of time
d: Lit: pass-through long, not declining. Said of a song, a brand, a custom, or a reputation that stays popular and vigorous over many years rather than fading away.

e: the startled spirit has not yet settled: still shaken after a fright
d: Lit: startled-soul-not-yet-settled. Describes someone whose nerves are still rattled in the aftermath of a shock or narrow escape, the heart not yet returned to rest.

e: "startling heaven, shaking earth" — earth-shaking; of tremendous power or significance
d: 惊 jīng (to startle; to alarm) + 动 dòng (to move; to shake). When something is so significant that heaven is startled and earth trembles, the hyperbole names genuine magnitude. Used for historic events, monumental achievements, and powerful works. 他们完成了一项惊天动地的壮举。

e: diligent and careful in one's work
d: A phrase of high praise for someone who does their work with constant care and seriousness, never cutting corners. 兢兢 conveys cautious diligence; 业业 the steady attention to one's 业 (work, duties). Common in performance reviews and tributes, the model of the conscientious worker.

e: to unite with wholehearted sincerity: to stand together in good faith
d: Lit: pure-sincere-unite. A call for a group to bond in genuine, undivided solidarity rather than in mere appearance. 结 here is the uniting sense, the bond made fast among people.

e: serve the country with utmost loyalty — the supreme patriotic commitment
d: The four characters said to have been tattooed on Yue Fei's back by his mother (精忠 = utmost loyalty; 报国 = repay/serve the country). Whether the tattooing story is historical or legendary, the phrase became the supreme expression of Chinese patriotic loyalty.

e: to revere ancestors and honor the lineage
d: A set phrase expressing the core ethic of ancestor veneration: to show reverence (敬 jìng) to direct ancestors (祖) and to honor the lineage (宗) as a whole. Used in ritual speeches, genealogy prefaces, and New Year ancestral hall ceremonies.

e: the Jingkang Humiliation — national shame that demands redemption
d: The capture of the Song imperial family by the Jurchen Jin dynasty in 1127 CE. Invoked by Yue Fei and every subsequent patriot as the wound that must be avenged. Still appears in modern Chinese political rhetoric when national pride or territorial integrity is at stake.

e: the eighty-one tribulations — a long sequence of trials that must all be passed
d: From 西游记: the pilgrims must survive exactly eighty-one ordeals (九九, "nine nines," a number of completeness) before the scriptures can be won.

e: "one hair from nine oxen" — a trifling amount; a drop in the bucket
d: 九牛 (nine oxen) and 一毛 (a single hair). A lone hair plucked from nine whole oxen is utterly negligible against the mass it comes from. The phrase comes from Sima Qian, who wrote that his own death would weigh on the world no more than one hair lost from nine oxen.

e: "nine deaths, one life" — a narrow escape from death; surviving against all odds
d: 九死 (nine chances of death) against 一生 (one chance of life). To come through a danger in which the odds of dying were nine to one, a hair's-breadth survival. Used of soldiers, explorers, and patients who pull through against overwhelming odds: 九死一生，终于活了下来.

e: "beyond the ninth heaven and the clouds" — utterly out of mind; flung far away
d: 九霄 (the ninefold heaven, the top of the sky) plus 云外 (beyond the clouds). To cast something to the ninth heaven and past the clouds is to banish it completely from thought: 把承诺忘到九霄云外 (to forget a promise entirely).

e: long illness makes the patient a doctor
d: Chronic experience becomes expertise. Said of patients who know their condition better than junior doctors, and by extension of anyone whose long exposure to a problem has made them its reluctant expert: the veteran user who knows the software's bugs better than the developers.

e: "the old departs, the new arrives" — natural renewal and change
d: 旧 jiù (old; worn; the previous) + 去 qù (departs) + 新 xīn (new) + 来 lái (arrives). The cycle of replacement: what has aged goes away, what is fresh comes in. Used for seasons (winter's cold 去, spring 来), generations, technologies, fashions.

e: to bring up an old matter again: to reopen a settled affair
d: Lit: old-matter-again-raise. The chóng reading, again. Said when someone dredges up a past issue better left closed.

e: to relieve suffering and rescue from peril
d: A Buddhist phrase, the standing epithet of the bodhisattva 观音 (Guānyīn), 救苦救难 (one who relieves the suffering and saves from calamity). Now also figurative for any savior figure.

e: save the dying, aid the wounded
d: 救 (save) the 死 (dying), 扶 (support) the 伤 (wounded). The classic motto of medicine and the Red Cross spirit, naming the doctor's and rescuer's duty in four characters.

e: to use local materials; to make do with what is immediately available
d: Lit: just-ground-take-materials. 就地 = "right here on the spot" (from 就 = to approach what is near). 取材 = to gather materials. The idiom celebrates resourcefulness , using what is immediately at hand rather than waiting for something better. The 就 captures the "readiness without delay" quality.

e: dwelling in safety, think of danger: stay alert in good times
d: From the Zuǒ Zhuàn. The classic counsel of prudent statecraft: when secure, prepare for the threat that has not yet come. A staple of formal and editorial Chinese.

e: to hold a chess piece without setting it down: to hesitate and waver
d: Lit: raise-chesspiece-not-settle. The image of a player holding a piece in the air, unable to commit to a move. Said of anyone caught in indecision who cannot fix on a choice.

e: world-famous: renowned throughout the whole world
d: Lit: the whole world has heard the name. 举世 means the entire world taken together, 闻名 means to be known by name. Said of a person, place, or work whose fame reaches everywhere, as in the Great Wall or a celebrated master.

p: jǔ tóu sān chǐ yǒu shénmíng
e: three feet above your head there are divine spirits — you are always watched
d: A foundational folk-religion moral warning: the gods are always observing human conduct; no action goes unseen. Functionally identical to the Western "God is watching." Used to caution against wrongdoing, especially in private. The full proverb: 举头三尺有神明，不畏人知畏己知。

e: to argue strongly on principle: to stand on reason and contend hard for it
d: Lit: rely-on-principle-strongly-contend. To take one's stand on what is right and fight for it in argument, not backing down so long as reason is on your side.

e: the exemplary person is not a vessel
d: Confucius says the junzi is not a utensil: not defined by function, not limited to one use. The Analects' argument against reducing a person to their usefulness.

e: the friendship of noble people: plain as water, lasting and unselfish
d: Lit: noble-person's friendship. From the saying 君子之交淡如水, "the friendship of the noble is bland as water," meaning a true bond needs no flattery or gifts and so never sours.

e: to enlighten the people; to awaken popular wisdom and intelligence
d: 开启 kāiqǐ (to open; to initiate; to unlock) + 民 mín (the people; the populace) + 智 zhì (wisdom; intelligence; discernment).

e: "to split open heaven and cleave earth" — to create the world; a groundbreaking, unprecedented achievement
d: From the Pangu myth (盘古 Pángǔ). In the beginning, all was 混沌 hùndùn: undifferentiated chaos. Pangu broke it open. The light, clear elements rose and became Heaven; the heavy, turbid elements sank and became Earth. Pangu stood between them for 18,000 years until the separation was permanent.

e: the Glorious Era of Kaiyuan — the High Tang at its zenith
d: The reign-era name 开元 (713–741 CE) under Emperor Xuanzong gave its name to the period of Tang's greatest cultural and economic flourishing. Population reached approximately 50 million; the examination system produced its greatest talents; Chang'an was at its most cosmopolitan.

e: open up the source and restrain the flow: increase income and curb spending
d: Lit: open-source-restrain-flow. The classic principle of sound finance: widen what comes in while narrowing what goes out. Applied to household budgets, companies, and the state alike.

e: the flourishing era of Kangxi and Qianlong — the Qing golden age
d: The compound reign-name shorthand 康乾 (Kangxi-Qianlong) with 盛世 (flourishing era, golden age).
The system of selecting officials by competitive written examination, which the Sui began and later dynasties developed into the central institution of Chinese government.

e: worthy of song and worthy of tears — so moving as to deserve both celebration and mourning
d: 可 + 歌 (to sing) + 可 + 泣 (to weep). Used for heroic, sacrificial stories: deeds of such weight they call for both elegy and lament. 革命先烈的事迹可歌可泣。(The deeds of the revolutionary martyrs are worthy of song and tears.) High formal register.

e: can be seen but not reached — within sight but out of grasp
d: 可望 (can be hoped for/seen) + 不可即 (cannot be approached). Used for goals, dreams, and people that seem close but remain permanently out of reach. Often carries a wistful rather than bitter tone.

e: overcome the self, return to rites — the Confucian definition of humaneness
d: From Analects 12.1: 克己复礼为仁. "To overcome the self and return to rites is to achieve 仁." One of the foundational statements of Confucian ethics. The phrase is quoted whenever the relationship between self-discipline and social form is under discussion.

e: Carving the Boat to Find the Sword
d: He marked the boat where his sword fell into the river. When the boat reached the shore, he dived where the mark was.

e: the Empty Fort Strategy — bluffing strength from weakness
d: Zhuge Liang, holding an undefended town against a vastly superior army, flings the gates open and sits calmly playing the zither on the wall. The enemy commander, certain so bold a display must conceal an ambush, retreats.

e: "empty before, cut off behind" — unprecedented and unrepeated; without equal in all of history
d: 空 kōng (empty; void) + 前 (before; the past) + 绝 jué (cut off; without) + 后 (after; the future). Nothing like it has existed in the past (the front is empty of precedent) and nothing like it will exist in the future (the back is cut off from repetition).

e: the mouth says yes but the heart says no — saying one thing while thinking another
d: Lit: mouth-yes-heart-no. The classic expression for hypocrisy or false agreement: when outward words and inner feelings are opposites. Used for people who agree to your face while disagreeing inside, or who say what they think you want to hear rather than what they actually believe.

e: bitterness ends, sweetness comes: hardship gives way to better days
d: 苦 (bitter) and 甘 (sweet) frame a full turn of fortune. The standard consolation offered to anyone enduring a long hard stretch; the reward is built into the saying.

e: bitter mouth, grandmotherly heart: to urge earnestly and patiently
d: Describes someone who repeats hard advice tirelessly out of genuine care, the way an old woman nags her grandchild for their own good.

e: "to span seas and cross oceans" — to travel vast distances
d: A modern four-character compound that pairs 跨 and 越 in parallel slots: exactly the kind of construction Chinese loves. Used for international trade, transcontinental travel, or any long voyage. Not classical, but stylistically formal enough to appear in policy speeches and ceremonial writing.

e: "to mount one's horse and lift one's blade" — to ride out armed and ready
d: A four-character battle-formula common in classical novels and modern wuxia. The image is a general or knight-errant hoisting himself astride his horse with weapon drawn: the moment of departure for combat.

e: "crossing fiscal years" — spanning more than one annual cycle
d: Bureaucratic and accounting vocabulary, not classical, but ubiquitous in modern policy and business documents. 跨年度项目 (a project spanning fiscal years), 跨年度预算 (multi-year budget). Useful as a tag of how 跨 has migrated from the body's stride into the calendar's accounting.

e: whip a fast horse — press on faster when already moving well
d: Lit: fast-horse-add-whip. The image is of a courier or cavalry rider who is already galloping but spurs the horse harder anyway. Metaphorically: when momentum is good, don't coast. Used to encourage continued effort or accelerated progress, often in workplace or project contexts.

e: a cornered beast still fights: desperate last-ditch resistance
d: From the Zuǒ Zhuàn. A trapped animal will fight on even with no hope, so the phrase warns that a cornered opponent is dangerous. Used of enemies making a final stand.

e: to learn through hardship and act through effort
d: From the Zhōngyōng (Doctrine of the Mean). Knowledge won the hard way, by struggle, and conduct sustained by force of will. Praises perseverance over native talent.

e: to have enough time; to make it in time
d: A potential complement construction: 来 (come/arrive) + 得 + 及 (reach in time). The negative 来不及 is one of the highest-frequency colloquial expressions. 来不及了！ "There's no time!" Both forms exemplify the potential complement use of 得/不.

e: of unknown origin: provenance unclear, background not established
d: 来历 láilì = origin, background, where something or someone came from (历 here is the path-walked-through that produced the present state); 不明 bù míng = not clear. Said of a person whose background cannot be verified, or an object whose provenance is suspect. It carries a note of suspicion.

e: "coming and going as one pleases" — complete freedom of movement; unhindered
d: 来去 (coming and going, the full freedom of movement) + 自如 (naturally; freely; as one wishes). The ideal of total freedom: moving in any direction without restriction or obstacle.

e: the days to come are still long — there is still much time ahead
d: 来日 = the coming days, the future (days that come toward us). 方长 = just beginning to be long. A comfort phrase: things not accomplished now can still be done; relationships not deepened yet have time. 我们来日方长，不必着急 "We still have plenty of time ahead , no need to rush."

e: turn no one away; welcome all comers; refuse nothing that comes
d: 来者 = those who come + 不拒 = do not refuse. Originally a statement of generous hospitality or all-accepting policy. Used in commercial contexts (a shop that accepts all customers), in descriptions of a person with an open-door policy, and ironically for someone who takes on too much work.

e: faking the yu-pipe to fill out the ensemble — an impostor padding the numbers
d: From the Han Feizi: King Xuan of Qi kept a 300-piece yu-pipe ensemble, and Mr. Nanguo, who could not play a note, mimed along on a full salary. The king died; his successor preferred solos; Nanguo fled overnight.

e: to wolf down food — to eat ravenously like a wolf and tiger
d: Lit: wolf-swallow tiger-gulp. Vivid image of eating without manners or restraint. Used humorously for someone who is very hungry or eating too fast.

e: wolf's heart, dog's lungs: cruel and ungrateful
d: A vivid curse for someone heartless who repays kindness with betrayal. The wolf and dog organs stand for savagery and baseness. Strong, accusatory register.

e: to drift across rivers and lakes: to roam without a fixed home
d: The romantic image of the wanderer with no settled address, common in martial-arts fiction and travel writing.

e: to exhaust the people and drain the treasury
d: The chengyu that names exactly what brought the Sui down: undertaking projects so costly in labour and money that they ruin both the population and the state's finances.

e: old but growing ever stronger — vigorous in old age
d: Lit: old-yet-increasingly-vigorous. From the Book of the Later Han: the general Ma Yuan said, "A man of ambition grows more vigorous as he grows old; a hero grows stronger with age." Used to praise an older person who retains energy, capability, and drive. A compliment, never ironic.

e: to rehash old ideas: to bring out a tired theme again
d: Lit: to pluck the old tune once more. A dismissive phrase for repeating a stale argument or worn-out idea as if it were new. Here 调 takes the diào reading, "a tune, a melody."

e: an old horse knows the road — experience guides better than intelligence
d: From the Han Feizi: Duke Huan of Qi was lost in the mountains; an advisor suggested releasing an old war horse, which led the army home by the familiar road. Used to justify consulting experienced people rather than relying on theory or intelligence alone. One of the most famous 老 idioms.

e: "appropriate for old and young alike" — suitable for everyone
d: 老 (old) + 少 shào (young) + 皆 (all, both) + 宜 (appropriate, fitting). The old-young pair covers the full lifespan: if something suits both extremes, it suits everyone.

e: an old scholar's stock talk: a hackneyed, oft-repeated remark
d: Lit: old-scholar-often-says. A truism so worn from repetition that it carries little weight, the Chinese equivalent of a tired platitude.

e: so happy as to forget Shu: too content to think of home
d: Lit: happy-not-miss-Shu. From the deposed ruler of the kingdom of Shu, who, kept in comfort by his conquerors, said he no longer missed his homeland. Now said of anyone so absorbed in present pleasure that they forget where they came from.

e: joy at its extreme gives birth to sorrow
d: From the Records of the Grand Historian: the wit Chunyu Kun warned King Wei of Qi, over wine, that drinking to the limit ends in disorder and joy at its limit turns to grief (酒极则乱，乐极则悲).

e: joy lies within it — to find genuine pleasure in what one is doing
d: 乐 lè (joy; pleasure) + 在 zài (to be located at; exists in) + 其中 qízhōng (within it; therein). Describes the absorption of someone who has found true satisfaction in their work or activity.

e: thunder and lightning together — a violent storm; used of chaotic, intense situations
d: Lit: thunder-lightning-together-intensify. Describes a fierce storm where both thunder (雷 léi) and lightning (电 diàn) are striking simultaneously. Used metaphorically for any situation of simultaneous, intense upheaval: a chaotic meeting, an emotional confrontation, a turbulent period.

e: as fierce as thunder, as swift as wind — to act with decisive, energetic speed
d: Lit: thunder-fierce-wind-moving. 厉 means severe, sharp, intense; 行 means to move, to act. The phrase describes a person or policy that executes with the speed and force of a storm: no hesitation, no dragging of feet. Used to praise decisive leadership or swift implementation.

p: léi shēng dà, yǔ diǎn xiǎo
e: thunder loud, raindrops small — all noise, no substance
d: A folk proverb elevated to proverbial status. The contrast is between the dramatic announcement and the meager follow-through: the thunder promised a deluge, but only a few drops fell.

e: detached palaces and separate lodges: the many residences a ruler kept beyond the main palace
d: A classical 成语 for the scattered country retreats and travelling-lodges of an emperor or great house. Here 馆 carries its oldest sense, the official lodge where the powerful stayed on the road.

e: to depart from the classics and rebel against the Way: heterodox, unorthodox
d: From the Confucian frame: to stray from the canonical texts (经) and turn against orthodox doctrine (道). Modern usage is broad, describing any rebel who breaks with convention, sometimes admiringly.

e: to stray ten thousand li from the topic: to wander hopelessly off subject
d: Lit: leave-topic-ten-thousand-li. The 万里 (ten thousand li) is hyperbole for an enormous distance, so the phrase describes talk or writing that has drifted so far it has lost the thread entirely.

Literally "to leave the village and turn one's back on the well", to go far from home, often driven by hardship. The 井 (well) stands for the home community that gathered around shared water. Here 离 is the verb of parting at its most poignant, leaving the place one belongs to.

e: ritual collapses, music decays — the breakdown of the social order
d: The Spring and Autumn diagnosis of what had gone wrong with Zhou civilization. Vassal lords using the eight-row ritual dance (八佾 bā yì) reserved for the Son of Heaven was the specific provocation that opens the Analects' third chapter, with Confucius saying "If this can be endured, what cannot?" Use…

e: rites value reciprocity — one courtesy deserves another; give and take
d: From the 礼记 Lǐjì (Record of Rites): 礼尚往来，往而不来，非礼也；来而不往，亦非礼也. "礼 values mutual exchange; to offer without receiving back is not 礼; to receive without offering back is also not 礼." The principle of reciprocity as the governing logic of social life.

e: "to honor the worthy and condescend to the lower-ranked" — a leader's courteous treatment of those beneath them
d: Originally describing rulers and high officials who treated talented commoners and lower-ranked scholars with genuine respect , a quality praised throughout the dynastic histories. 礼 is verbal here ("to treat with 礼"); 贤 xián = the worthy; 下士 = lower-ranked scholars.

e: "inside responds, outside coordinates" — inside-outside cooperation; a coordinated attack from within and without
d: 里 (inside) + 应 (yīng, to respond, to correspond) + 外 (outside) + 合 (to coordinate, to join). A military and strategic idiom: the force inside a city or position responds to the force attacking from outside, each coordinating with the other.

e: as it should be by reason; a matter of course
d: Literally "what reason makes ought-to-be-so," something so right and natural that it needs no defense. 当然 ("of course") and 应当 ("ought to") share the 当 of fitting necessity. Sometimes used critically, of someone who takes a kindness as 理所当然 ("for granted").

e: Principle is one, but its manifestations are many — the unity of diversity in Neo-Confucian metaphysics
d: Formulated by Cheng Yi, developed by Zhu Xi. 理一 = principle is singular and universal; 分殊 = its particularizations are diverse. The classic image: the moon reflected in ten thousand pools of water.

e: bold with right on your side: speaking firmly because the principle is clearly yours
d: Lit: principle-straight-spirit-strong. When the 理 is on your side, your 气 (spirit, breath) is strong, so you can speak up with full confidence and no guilt.

e: strength falls short of the heart: the will is there but the ability is not
d: Lit: strength-not-follow-heart. Said when one wants to do something but lacks the strength or means to carry it through, the gap between intention and capacity.

e: within one's power; as far as one is able
d: Literally "what one's strength can reach," the things that lie within one's ability to do. The bright mirror of 无能为力: 我会尽力所能及 ("I'll do all I can"). Again built on 能, the capacity at the root of "possible."

e: to endure every hardship — to pass through countless trials to reach a goal
d: 历 (to pass through) + 尽 (exhaust, to the full) + 艰辛 (hardship). The phrase fits Xuanzang's journey exactly: deserts, mountains, thirst, and danger endured over sixteen years for the sake of the texts.

e: grows better with time: the longer it lasts, the fresher and more valued it becomes
d: 历久 lìjiǔ = to pass through a long time, to endure; 弥 mí = all the more, increasingly; 新 xīn = new, fresh. Lit: "having lasted long, all the more new." Said of friendships, classic works, traditions, and well-made things that do not fade but gain in worth as the years accumulate. 这部经典作品历久弥新。

e: vivid before the eyes: every detail clear in memory as if still happening
d: 历历 lìlì is a reduplication meaning "one by one, distinctly, item by item," the same clarity-of-sequence sense that runs through 历; 在目 zài mù = "before the eyes." The phrase describes a memory so sharp that each scene appears in clear order in the mind's eye. 童年的往事至今历历在目。

e: to become a Buddha on the spot
d: Usually in the full proverb 放下屠刀，立地成佛: lay down the butcher's knife and become a Buddha where you stand. Chan's radical claim that awakening is instantaneous and open even to the worst, now the standard phrase for the possibility of immediate reform.

e: "interest-harm relationship" — a relationship involving mutual stakes and risks
d: Lit: benefit-harm-relationship. Describes a situation where parties are bound by shared interests and shared risks , where what benefits or harms one affects the others. 他们之间有复杂的利害关系，不能轻易分开。"There are complex stakes between them , they can't be easily separated."

e: unbroken and continuous — stretching on without interruption
d: 连绵 liánmián = continuous, uninterrupted (as mountains rolling one into the next, or rain falling without pause). 不断 = without cessation. Used for mountain ranges, rain, difficulty, sorrow, and any phenomenon that continues without obvious end.

e: page after page, tablet after tablet — excessively wordy, verbose
d: 篇 = a piece of writing; 累牍 = pile of writing tablets (classical). Together: pieces of writing linked in succession and accumulated into piles. A pejorative idiom for excessive verbosity: writing that goes on and on without saying much.

e: pity the fragrance, cherish the jade: to be tender toward women
d: 香 (fragrance) and 玉 (jade) both stand for a beautiful woman. To treat women with gentleness and care. Literary, sometimes ironic.

e: drill the troops and feed the horses: ready oneself for the contest
d: 练 here is its oldest active sense, to drill. The image is an army putting in the reps before battle, so the phrase travels easily to any team or person training hard ahead of a test.

e: practiced and worldly, mature and steady
d: 练达 means seasoned in the ways of the world; pairs with 老成 (mature beyond one's years). A literary compliment for someone whose poise comes from experience, not age alone.

e: good medicine is bitter to the mouth: honest advice is hard to hear
d: From the Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ. Often completed by 忠言逆耳 (loyal words grate on the ear). Used to soften unwelcome but useful criticism.

e: "both defeated, both hurt" — a mutually destructive outcome; both sides lose
d: 两败 (both defeated) + 俱伤 (both injured). A conflict in which neither side wins and both come away damaged, the lose-lose result of a fight pushed too far: 这样争下去只会两败俱伤 (going on fighting like this will only hurt both sides).

e: two hearts delighting in each other — mutual affection
d: A classical phrase for mutual romantic fondness, where 悦 yuè (to delight in, akin to 喜欢) is shared by both sides. It names the ideal of love that is returned, two people who like and are gladdened by each other, and is often quoted in the context of relationships and marriage.

e: "complete the good of both" — a solution good for both sides; the best of both worlds
d: 两全 (keep both whole, satisfy both) + 其美 (their goodness). A way of handling things that serves both parties or both goals without sacrificing either, the win-win outcome: 找一个两全其美的办法 (to find a solution good for both sides).

e: measure your strength, then act: do only what you can manage
d: 量 liàng (to assess, here in the assessing sense) + 力 lì (strength) + 而 ér (and then) + 行 xíng (to act). Gauge how much you are capable of, and act within that limit. A counsel of prudence: take on what your resources, ability, and circumstances can actually support, rather than overreaching.

e: measure income to set spending: live within your means
d: 量 liàng (to gauge) + 入 rù (income, what comes in) + 为 wéi (to make, to determine) + 出 chū (expenditure, what goes out). Let the size of your income decide the size of your spending.

Literally "sparse, sparse, not even a few," describing something so scarce it can almost be counted on one hand. Here 几 ("a few") takes its statement sense rather than its question sense. The mirror image of 多多益善.

e: all the ancestors of the line, generation upon generation
d: 列 (arrayed, successive) + 祖 + 列 + 宗. A formulaic invocation of the entire ancestral chain, used in formal toasts, funeral eulogies, and solemn declarations where one speaks on behalf of the whole family line. The repetition of 列 creates a sense of unbroken succession stretching backward.

e: "between neighbors and the neighborhood" — community bonds; relations among people living nearby
d: 邻 (lín, neighbor) + 里 (the neighborhood unit) + 之间 (between). Uses 里 in its oldest sense , the bounded residential community of the Zhou system.

e: clasping the Buddha's feet at the last minute — cramming
d: From a proverb about neglecting incense in ordinary times and embracing the statue's feet only when disaster looms (平时不烧香，临时抱佛脚). The universal student condition, named without mercy. Usable for any deferred preparation: visas, taxes, wedding speeches.

e: "scattered like stray stars" — sparse and scattered; bits and pieces here and there
d: A reduplication of 零星 (scattered, sporadic), itself 零 (scattered drops) plus 星 (stars, scattered points of light).

e: so enthralled as to forget to leave: lingering, reluctant to go home
d: 流连 liúlián = to linger, to be unable to tear oneself away; 忘返 wàng fǎn = to forget to return.

e: to disown all six kinships — utterly cold-blooded, recognizing no family bond
d: Lit: six-relatives-not-recognize. The classical six kinships are father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, child. Said of someone who in the pursuit of power or self-interest will not even acknowledge their own kin.

e: "the six spirits have no master" — panic-stricken; at a total loss
d: 六神 (the six spirits) are the guardian spirits believed in Daoist physiology to govern the vital organs (heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, spleen, gallbladder). When they are 无主 (without a master, leaderless), the person loses all composure.

e: at sixty, the ear follows — one can hear without resistance
"frost flies in the sixth month" — a sign of grievous injustice
d: 六月 (the sixth lunar month, high summer) plus 飞霜 (flying frost). Frost in midsummer is an impossibility that heaven produces only in response to a wrong so great it disturbs the natural order.

e: dragon flying, phoenix dancing — describes bold, unrestrained calligraphy
d: Lit: dragon-fly phoenix-dance. Originally a description of grand, sweeping calligraphy where the strokes move with the energy of mythic creatures. Now used both admiringly (fluid, powerful brushwork) and ironically (illegible scrawl that only the writer understands).

e: dragon and tiger fighting — two powerful forces in fierce competition
d: 龙 lóng + 争 zhēng (to contend; to compete) + 虎 hǔ (tiger) + 斗 dòu (to fight; to contend). Used when two equally formidable opponents , companies, athletes, armies, political factions , clash with serious intensity. Neither side is diminished; both are worthy adversaries. 这场决赛简直是龙争虎斗，双方势均力敌。

e: "on the road no one picks up what others have dropped": the mark of a well-governed society
d: From the Hánfēizǐ (Legalist text, 3rd century BCE), describing the ideal state under good rule. Paired with 夜不闭户 yè bù bì hù ("at night doors are not bolted").

e: to act following ones nature: to do as one's disposition prompts
d: Literally "to follow nature and act." To behave according to one's true temperament rather than calculation or constraint. It can praise an honest, unaffected spirit or, in a cooler reading, describe someone who simply acts on impulse without weighing the consequences.

e: green trees forming shade — lush, leafy, and cool
d: 绿树 lǜshù (green trees) + 成 chéng (to form) + 阴 yīn (shade). Trees grown so full that their crowns join into continuous shade, a picture of a flourishing, well-grown garden or avenue in high summer. Here 阴 is the welcome, cooling shadow, the same positive sense as 阴凉. 几十年过去，当年的小树苗如今已绿树成阴。

e: "chaotic seven, messy eight" — in complete disorder; a total mess
d: 乱 (chaotic) + 七八 (seven-eight) + 糟 (rotten, spoiled). One of the most common expressions in spoken Mandarin for utter disorder, whether of a messy room, a tangled situation, or muddled thinking. The embedded 七八 again uses the clashing seven-and-eight to mean jumbled, every-which-way.

e: if you fall behind, you will be beaten — the fundamental lesson of the century of humiliation
d: The defining phrase of modern Chinese nationalist historiography. Attributed to various leaders; popularized by Deng Xiaoping. The phrase frames national development not as aspiration but as existential necessity: weakness invites predation, therefore modernization is survival.

e: fallen blossoms and flowing water — spring's end; utter defeat
d: Lit: falling-flowers flowing-water. A classical image from Tang and Song poetry for the beauty of spring's end. Also used for utter defeat: 打得落花流水 "beaten to pieces."

e: to throw stones at someone who has fallen in a well — to kick someone when they're down
d: Lit: fall-well-down-stone. The act of throwing rocks on top of someone already trapped in a well. Vivid idiom for betrayal or cruelty toward someone already in misfortune.

e: fallen leaves return to the root — everyone returns to their origins
d: Lit: fallen-leaves-return-root. The universal Chinese sentiment about homeland: no matter how far one has traveled or how long one has been away, the natural ending is to return to one's place of origin.

e: Mazu's divine power manifests — a miracle attributed to her
d: 显灵 xiǎn líng (lit. "spirit manifests") is the standard phrase for a deity's miraculous intervention. 妈祖显灵 is used when a ship survives a storm, a prayer is answered, or an illness is healed , any event attributed to Mazu's protective intervention.

e: numb and inhumane; deadened to feeling — both physical and moral
d: 麻木 mámù (numb; without sensation , 麻 hemp, suggesting the prickling of nerves; 木 wood, suggesting deadness) + 不仁 bùrén (without humaneness; without feeling). Originally a medical term for physical numbness , limbs that have lost sensation.

e: immediate success upon arrival — "when the cavalry arrives, victory follows"
d: Lit: horse-arrive-success. Originally a wish for military campaigns, deeply resonant with the Mongol cavalry tradition that shook the known world. Used today as a congratulatory phrase for new endeavors. 祝你马到成功！ "Wishing you swift success!"
The doubled form of 马虎. Used both for sloppy work and, self-deprecatingly, to answer "how are you?" with a shrugging "just so-so."

e: to bury the head and toil hard: to work diligently without distraction
d: Lit: bury-head-bitter-work. To lower one's head and labor away, absorbed in the task and indifferent to praise or notice. The picture is of someone bent over their work, head down.

e: saints fill the streets — everyone already has the innate moral knowledge to be a sage
d: Said to have been uttered by Wang Yangming after a student asked skeptically whether ordinary people could really possess 良知. His response: walk out onto any busy street and observe; anyone who acts from their innate moral sense in that moment is a sage.

e: a face full of spring breeze: beaming, radiant with joy
d: Lit: full-face-spring-wind. The whole face glowing like a warm spring day, said of someone visibly pleased, content, or flush with good fortune.

e: a chest full of hot blood: brimming with fervor
d: 满腔 a full chest, 热血 hot blood. Describes youthful idealism and the will to throw oneself into a cause. Warm and slightly literary in tone.

e: the whole room glows — a radiant, welcoming presence fills the space
d: Lit: room-full-give-off-radiance. Used for a beautiful person or a remarkable guest whose presence lights up a room. A formal compliment in social and literary contexts.

e: to return fully laden — to come home with rich gains
d: 满载 (loaded full) + 而归 (and return). The image of Xuanzang re-entering Chang'an with 657 manuscripts after sixteen years abroad. Now a common phrase for any return rich in results , from a successful trip, a fruitful search, or a profitable venture. The opposite is 一无所获 "to come back empty-handed."

p: mǎn zhāo sǔn, qiān shòu yì
e: "fullness invites loss; humility attracts benefit" — the cosmological argument for modesty
d: From the 尚书 (Shangshu, Book of Documents), one of the Five Classics , among the oldest extant Chinese prose.

h: 满纸荒唐言，一把辛酸泪。
p: mǎn zhǐ huāngtáng yán, yī bǎ xīnsuān lèi.
e: A whole page of absurd words, a fistful of bitter tears.
d: From Cao Xueqin's own opening verse, his description of the book and of the grief that went into it. The pairing of seeming absurdity (a tale of stones and dreams) with real suffering captures the novel's double nature as fantasy and as a wound from the author's own ruined life.

Lit: slow-work-produce-fine-goods. The Chinese counterpart to "haste makes waste." A proverb rather than a classical four-character 成语 in the strict sense, but widely used and culturally important. Invoked to defend careful, unhurried craftsmanship against pressure for speed.

e: slow and methodical; unhurried and in proper order
d: Lit: slow-stitch-this-manage. Describes someone who does everything at an unhurried, measured pace and in proper sequence. Can be neutral (a composed, methodical person) or slightly pejorative (someone frustratingly slow to act).

e: careless and inattentive: with no thought passing through the mind
d: Lit: idly not passing-through the heart. 经心 means to take to heart, to attend to. To do something 漫不经心 is to do it absent-mindedly, paying it no real attention.
The spear that can pierce anything meets the shield that can stop anything: the story behind China's word for contradiction.

e: beauty beyond what the eye can take in — overwhelmingly beautiful
