d: Lit: beauty-not-able-to-receive/contain. Used for spectacular natural scenery, festivals, or exhibitions where there is simply too much beauty to absorb at once.

e: matched gates and doors: of equal social standing (for a marriage)
d: Lit: gate-matching-door-matching. The old principle that the two families in a marriage should be of comparable rank and wealth. Still used, sometimes critically, of pairing by status.

e: the gateway like a marketplace: thronged with visitors
d: Lit: gate-courtyard-like-market. Said of a household or office so busy with callers that the entrance resembles a crowded market. Its opposite is 门可罗雀, a gate so deserted you could net sparrows in it.

e: "to press one's hand to the heart and question oneself" — honest self-examination; to look inward without flinching
d: 扪 mén (to press or feel with the hand) + 心 + 自 (self) + 问 (to question). The gesture of placing one's hand over one's heart and asking honestly: what do I know? what did I actually do? It is the physical enactment of consulting 良心 directly, without evasion.

e: muddled and only half-aware: in a fog
d: A vivid reduplication pairing 懵 (měng, dazed) with 懂 (dǒng, understand) to describe a hazy, half-comprehending state, like a child too young to grasp what is happening or a person fresh out of sleep.

e: "Meng Jiangnu weeping at the Great Wall" — grief strong enough to move stone
d: One of China's four great folk legends (四大民间故事 sì dà mínjiān gùshì). Meng Jiangnu's husband Fan Xiliang was conscripted to build the Qin wall and died of exhaustion.

e: Mencius's mother moves three times — the importance of environment in education
d: Not from the Mencius text itself but from the Lienüzhuan 列女传 (Biographies of Exemplary Women), attributed to Liu Xiang 刘向 (77–6 BCE).

e: To Realise You Are Lost and Turn Back
d: Four characters that describe one of the most human experiences: taking a wrong road, recognising it, and finding the way home. The Chinese idiom for course-correction done with dignity.

e: enervating music: sounds thought to soften the will and sap the spirit
d: Lit: dispirited music. A classical term of disapproval for music seen as decadent and weakening, the kind moralists blamed for a ruler's downfall. Still used, half-seriously, of overly sentimental songs.

e: "face doesn't change color" — unruffled; keeping composure under pressure; poker-faced
d: Lit: face-not-change-color. The mark of composure under pressure , your face doesn't betray fear, surprise, or discomfort. 他面不改色地接受了批评，继续进行演讲。"He received the criticism without changing expression and continued his speech." Often admired as a sign of courage or self-discipline.

e: face red, ears crimson — flushed with anger, embarrassment, or the heat of argument
d: 面 miàn (face) + 红 hóng (red) + 耳 ěr (ears) + 赤 chì (the deeper crimson). The face and ears flush red from a surge of emotion, most often a heated argument or acute embarrassment. 两个人争得面红耳赤，谁也不让谁。

e: every aspect covered; thorough in all directions
d: 面 miàn (face; surface; aspect) + 面 + 俱 jù (all; together) + 到 (arrived at). Arrival has reached every face, every surface, every angle of the matter. Used to praise comprehensive coverage , a plan that misses nothing, a speech that addresses every concern, an analysis that leaves no gap.

e: a face with the color of greens: gaunt and sallow from hunger
d: Lit: face-has-vegetable-color. 菜色 is the wan, greenish pallor of someone who has eaten nothing but wild greens, with no grain or meat. The phrase paints a face worn down by famine or hardship.

e: a wondrous brush gives birth to flowers — gifted writing that makes words bloom
d: Lit: wondrous-brush-give birth-flowers. From a Tang dynasty story about the poet Li Bai dreaming that his brush sprouted flowers, foretelling his literary gifts. Used to praise writing of exceptional beauty or imagination , prose or verse that transforms language into something alive.

e: miraculous hands bring back the spring; masterly healing
d: 妙手 (wondrous hands) + 回春 (return spring, restore life's season). The stock phrase of gratitude to a doctor, embroidered on the silk banners (锦旗 jǐnqí) that patients present to hospital departments, a living custom: the walls of a respected clinic hang red with them.

e: the people can scarcely survive: a populace plunged into misery
d: Literally "the people have no means to make a living." A grim phrase for times of misrule, war, or disaster when ordinary people cannot even keep themselves alive. 聊 liáo here is the classical sense "to rely on, to depend on for," so 不聊生 means having nothing to depend on for life.

e: to the people, food is heaven: nothing matters more than feeding the people
d: Literally "the people take food as heaven." An ancient maxim of statecraft: the first and highest concern of any ruler is that the people have enough to eat. Still quoted constantly in everyday life, often half-jokingly, to defend the seriousness of a good meal.

e: name does not match reality — the condition 正名 diagnoses
d: 名 (name) + 不 (does not) + 副 (match, correspond to) + 实 (reality). The set phrase for the gap that 正名 targets.

e: the reputation is not falsely spread: to live up to one's name; to be as good as people say
d: Lit: the name is not emptily passed around. Said of a person or thing whose fame turns out to be well deserved, the praise that circulated was no exaggeration. Here 传 keeps the chuán reading, the spreading of a reputation.

e: existing in name but not in reality
d: Literally "the name survives, the reality is dead," describing something that keeps its title or form while its substance has vanished, an alliance, a rule, or an institution that is hollow inside. The 名 versus 实 contrast, the gap between what is called and what truly is, that 其实 itself points to.

Literally "the name fits its reality," said of someone or something that truly lives up to its reputation or title. 名 (name) and 实 (reality) match. The opposite is 名不副实 ("the name does not match the reality"), all show, no substance. Note the shared 其实 morphemes 其 and 实.

e: one's name fell behind Sun Shan's — to fail an examination
d: Sun Shan, a Song-dynasty wit, passed the provincial exam in last place. Asked by a neighbor whether the neighbor's son had passed, he answered in verse: "The last name on the list was Sun Shan; your worthy son came after Sun Shan." The gentlest failure notice in the language, still the standard lite…

e: name and reality correspond — the goal of 正名
d: 名 (name) + 实 (reality) + 相符 (mutually correspond, match). The affirmative formulation of what 正名 aims to restore. Where 名不副实 names the problem and 名正言顺 names the condition of legitimacy in action, 名实相符 states the standard of alignment itself.

e: the name is right and the speech follows smoothly — acting with proper authority and justification
d: Lit: name-correct speech-flows. Directly from the Analects 13.3 argument: when the name is rectified, speech follows naturally, and what follows from speech can be accomplished. Used today when someone has the proper credentials or title to do something , "now that you have the title, you can act."

e: to perceive the finest detail — exceptional discernment
d: Lit: bright-observe-autumn-hair-tip. 秋毫 = the impossibly fine tip of an animal's autumn coat. Used of leaders and judges who miss nothing. Its opposite: 不见舆薪 bùjiàn yú xīn "unable to see a cartload of firewood", missing what's obvious.

e: yesterday's news — past its prime, no longer relevant
d: Lit: tomorrow's chrysanthemum. Chrysanthemums peak at the Double Ninth Festival (重阳节); by tomorrow they are wilted and past. Used of news, opportunities, or people who are no longer timely.

h: 明月几时有？把酒问青天。
p: míng yuè jǐ shí yǒu? bǎ jiǔ wèn qīng tiān.
e: When did the bright moon first appear? Cup in hand, I ask the blue sky.
d: Opening of Su Shi's 水调歌头 (Prelude to Water Melody), written on the Mid-Autumn Festival while missing his younger brother Su Zhe.

e: the wise protect themselves; prudent self-preservation
d: From the Book of Odes, where it praised wise self-conduct. Two millennia of court politics turned it ambivalent: today it usually criticizes the colleague who sees the problem and says nothing, keeping their own 身 safe. A compliment in the Zhou dynasty, a workplace accusation now.

e: to knowingly do wrong: to break a rule while fully aware it is wrong
d: 明 (míng, clearly) + 知 (zhī, to know) + 故 (deliberately, the willed-action sense) + 犯 (fàn, to violate, to offend). To commit an offense while clearly knowing it is forbidden, the opposite of an honest mistake.

e: to ask knowing the answer — a rhetorical or teasing question
d: Lit: clearly-know-yet-ask. For when someone already knows the answer but asks anyway, either to tease, to confirm, or to draw out a confession. 你明知故问！"You already know the answer; why are you asking?"

e: written in one's fate — destined; predestined
d: Lit: in-one's-fate written-and-fixed. The classic phrase for fatalism: this was always going to happen. Extremely common in romantic narratives, films, and everyday speech when reflecting on life's significant turns.

e: crossing the river by feeling for stones — Deng's gradualist pragmatism
d: The most important political metaphor of the reform era. 摸 (to grope, to feel one's way) + 着 (progressive aspect) + 石头 (stones) + 过河 (cross the river).

e: worn down from crown to heel — total self-sacrifice for the world's benefit
d: 摩 mó (to wear down; to rub) + 顶 dǐng (crown of the head) + 放 fàng (to reach as far as) + 踵 zhǒng (heel).

e: perhaps he did — a charge without evidence; judicial murder by innuendo
d: Chancellor Qin Hui's response when asked what evidence existed for Yue Fei's treason charge: 莫须有, variously translated as "perhaps," "maybe there was a reason," or "need it necessarily be?" The phrase captures the essence of political show-trial logic: the accusation is sufficient; evidence is irrel…

e: to stick rigidly to established rules
d: The natural antonym of 与时俱进. 墨守 refers to Mozi's legendary skill at defensive warfare: holding a position without yielding. The phrase criticizes inflexibility and mechanical adherence to convention.

e: "eyes not turning from the pupil" — to stare fixedly, riveted
d: 目 (eye) + 不转 (not turning) + 睛 (pupil). Eyes so fixed on something that even the pupils don't move. Used for complete absorption in watching a performance, a fight, or any gripping sight.

e: "no people in the eye" — arrogant; treating no one as worthy of notice
d: 目 (eye) + 中 (within) + 无 (without) + 人 (people). Looking out from one's eye and seeing no one worth registering , arrogance so total that others become invisible. A criticism of conceit and contempt. 目空一切 (eye-empty-everything) intensifies this further: not even things are worth looking at.

e: a jumble of accents: speech mixing many regional tongues
d: Lit: southern resonance and northern tones. Said of speech that mixes accents from all over, or of a gathering where many dialects are heard at once. Here 调 takes the diào reading, "accent, manner of speech."

e: "going south in the shafts, tracks heading north" — completely self-contradictory
d: From the Zhànguó Cè: a man in the state of Wèi claimed he was going to the state of Chǔ (which lies south) but pointed his carriage north. When told he was heading the wrong way, he replied that his horse was fast, his driver skilled, and he had plenty of provisions, all the wrong justifications.

e: rare and precious is muddleheadedness — wise to sometimes not see clearly
d: The famous inversion, from the Qing painter-official Zheng Banqiao, who inscribed it as a scroll: for a clear-sighted person, letting some things stay blurry is the harder and wiser art. Hung in studies and offices ever since as a license not to litigate every wrong.

e: hard to divide and hard to untangle: locked together, evenly matched
d: Lit: hard-to-separate-hard-to-loosen. Of a contest too close to call, or of people so entwined, whether fighting or in love, that they cannot be pulled apart.

e: hard to untie, hard to part: locked together
d: Lit: hard 难 to untie 解, hard 难 to separate 分. Two sides so entangled they cannot be pulled apart: a deadlocked contest, a fierce struggle, or two people inseparably close. 双方打得难解难分 = the two sides fought to a standstill.

e: inside and outside are distinct: insiders and outsiders are treated differently
d: Lit: inside-outside-have-distinction. The principle that there is a proper line between those within a family, group, or nation and those without, and that the two are not handled the same way.

e: troubles within, pressures without: beset on every side
d: A state or organization squeezed simultaneously by internal worry and external pressure. Common in political and business commentary; a near twin of 内忧外患.

e: able to bend and able to stretch — flexible and adaptable
d: Lit: can-yield-can-extend. Describes someone who knows when to be humble and when to assert themselves , a virtue prized in Chinese social thought. 大丈夫能屈能伸 "A real man of character can yield and can rise again." 屈 = to yield, bow; 伸 = to stretch out, extend.

e: the capable bear the heavier burden; the able do more work
d: 能者 = the capable one; one who can + 多劳 = works more, bears more labor. A maxim that can be used approvingly (the talented should take on more responsibility) or ironically (the competent get punished with extra tasks).

e: a clay Bodhisattva crossing a river — unable to save even oneself
d: Lit: clay-bodhisattva-cross-river. 菩萨 púsà (Bodhisattva) is made of clay , crossing water would destroy it. Used to say someone is in no position to help others when they can barely save themselves. 泥菩萨过河，自身难保。

An extremely common conversational turn, throwing the question back to the other person. The particle 呢 ne softens it and invites their view. One of the most natural ways to ask for an opinion in spoken Chinese, and a good phrase to keep a conversation going.

e: holding up a flower, smiling faintly — wordless understanding
d: Chan's founding legend, recorded in Song-era lamp histories: the Buddha silently held up a flower before the assembly, and only Mahākāśyapa smiled, receiving the transmission outside words. Cited for any perfect unspoken communication between two people who need no explanation.

e: rich in years and strong in force — in the prime of life
d: Lit: year-rich-strength-strong. Used to describe someone in their prime: still young enough to have full physical and mental energy, experienced enough to have skill and judgment. The ideal working age. 他正值年富力强之时 "He is at the prime of his powers." A compliment to someone in their 30s–50s.

e: to keep thinking of without ever forgetting — to hold something constantly in mind
d: Lit: thought-after-thought, never forgetting. 念念 doubles the character to mean "moment after moment of mind." Used for an attachment, a wish, or a person one cannot let go of: 他对故乡念念不忘 (he never stops thinking of his hometown).

e: to mutter words under one breath: to chant or murmur incantations
d: Lit: muttering-and-having-words. Originally of a priest or sorcerer murmuring a spell, now of anyone muttering steadily to themselves, whether praying, reciting, or grumbling.

e: to think of it and dwell on it — to keep a matter constantly before the mind
d: A classical phrase from the Book of Documents (书经): 兹 zī means "this." To think of this and be present to this , to give a duty or concern unbroken attention. More literary than the others, used in formal or written contexts to describe devotion to a cause or responsibility one never sets aside.

e: birds singing, flowers fragrant: a beautiful spring scene
d: A stock phrase for an idyllic countryside in spring, the birds talking and the blossoms in scent. Warm and common in description.

p: níng wéi yù suì, bù wéi wǎ quán
e: Better to be shattered jade than intact tile — choose integrity over ignoble survival
d: Lit: rather be jade-shattered, not be tile-whole. The contrast is between two kinds of material: jade, which is rare, beautiful, and breaks rather than bends; and roof tile (瓦 wǎ), which is common, dull, and merely functional.

e: a small test of the ox-cleaver: great talent on a minor task
d: From the cook Páo Dīng of the Zhuāngzǐ, whose ox-carving blade glides through every joint. A heavy cleaver lightly tried, said when a capable person handles an easy job and shows the skill in reserve.

e: a pretense becomes real — what was performed turns out to be true
d: Lit: do-fake-become-real. For situations where pretending leads to the actual outcome: fake engagement turns into a real one, a play-acted role becomes the person's real life.

e: to arrange soldiers and deploy units: to marshal forces
d: A military set phrase, sibling to 排兵布阵. Describes a commander laying out troops in formation; now applied to organizing a team or lineup before a contest or launch.

e: Cook Ding carves the ox; acting in perfect accord with natural structure
d: 庖丁 Pāodīng (Cook Ding , 庖 páo = kitchen, cook; 丁 Dīng = a name/title) + 解 jiě (to separate; to cut apart; to resolve; to understand , the character shows a horn + knife + cow) + 牛 niú (ox; cattle). Zhuangzi's most celebrated parable, from the third chapter (养生主 , The Secret of Caring for Life).

p: pǎo le héshàng pǎo bu liǎo miào
e: "the monk may run, but the temple cannot run" — even if the person flees, the institution stays put
d: A folk saying, not a classical chengyu, but functionally fixed. The proverb captures a specific reasoning about accountability: a debtor or wrongdoer may try to flee, but the property, family, or institution they are tied to will remain, and can be held responsible.

e: "to run the dragon costume" — to play a minor role; to be a bit-part player
d: From traditional Chinese opera. 龙套 lóngtào is the costume worn by the chorus of attendants (soldiers, servants, courtiers) who fill out a scene without lines. To 跑龙套 is to be one of these background figures: present, busy, but never central.

e: to band together for evil: to collude in wrongdoing
d: Lit: friends-allying to-do evil. 朋比 is to band together as a clique, 为奸 to commit villainy. A sharply negative idiom for cronies who join forces for corrupt or treacherous ends, the dark side of company kept on a level footing.

e: to have friends all over the world
d: A warm saying praising someone with a wide circle of friends everywhere. 遍 biàn means "all over," 天下 "under heaven, the whole world." Often paired with the encouraging proverb 在家靠父母，出门靠朋友 ("at home you rely on parents; away from home you rely on friends"), which captures the practical importance of…

e: cloaked in stars, capped with the moon — toiling from before dawn until after dark
d: To wear the stars as a cape and the moon as a hat is to be outdoors working while they are up. Said admiringly of farmers, delivery riders, and anyone on the early-and-late grind: 他披星戴月地工作，就为了孩子上大学。He works from starlight to moonlight, all so his child can attend university.

e: splitting the head and covering the face: full in the face, without holding back
d: Describes a torrent that lands straight on you, a downpour of rain or a barrage of scolding, leaving no chance to dodge.

e: the courage of a common man: reckless bravery without strategy
d: 匹夫 pǐfū is an ordinary fellow of no rank. The phrase names the brute, headlong courage of one who rushes in to fight without thought or plan, contrasted with the cool, calculated valor of a true leader. It is a gentle put-down: brave, but foolishly so.

e: safe and sound, nothing amiss: all is calm and well
d: Lit: peaceful-safe-no-matter. A reassuring summary that nothing has gone wrong: a journey passed without incident, a household at peace. The 无事 here is the formal cousin of colloquial 没事.

e: to split the autumn colors evenly: to share equally, to be evenly matched
d: Lit: evenly-divide-autumn-scenery. Two sides each take half, as if dividing the beauty of autumn. Used when rivals are so closely matched that neither comes out ahead.

e: a level heart and quiet breath: calm and composed
d: Lit: level-heart-quiet-breath. To approach something with a settled mind and even temper, neither agitated nor hasty. 平心静气地谈 "to talk it over calmly."

e: "level and easy, close to people" — approachable; unpretentious; accessible
d: 平易 (flat and easy , without obstacles or pretension) + 近 (close to; approachable) + 人 (people). A person who is 平易近人 does not stand on ceremony, does not use their position as a barrier, and can be approached by ordinary people without formality or anxiety.

e: to judge the head and discuss the feet: to nitpick and find fault
d: Lit: appraise-head-discuss-feet. Originally about appraising a person's looks head to toe; now it means to carp over trifles and make petty, unwanted criticisms of others.

e: to meet by chance: like duckweed drifting together on water
d: Lit: duckweed-water mutually-meet. Floating duckweed has no fixed place, so the phrase describes strangers who meet briefly by accident and then drift apart again.

e: smash the cooking pots and sink the boats — to commit fully with no route of retreat
d: From Xiang Yu's strategy at the Battle of Julu (207 BCE): after crossing the river to attack Qin's army, he ordered the boats sunk and the cooking pots smashed, leaving his men with three days' rations and no possibility of retreat. They fought with total desperation and won.

e: smash the Four Olds — destroy old ideas, culture, customs, and habits
d: The central slogan of the Cultural Revolution's attack on traditional Chinese civilization. 破 (smash, break) + 四旧 (the Four Olds).

e: to universally deliver all sentient beings from suffering
d: A Buddhist phrase (from Guanyin's vow) applied also to Mazu, who is often assimilated with the Goddess of Mercy in folk practice. 普度 pǔdù = universally deliver; 众生 zhòngshēng = all living beings.

e: "seven scattered, eight fallen" — scattered and broken up; in pieces
d: 七零 (sevens scattered) and 八落 (eights fallen): things strewn about, broken apart, no longer whole. Used of an army routed and dispersed, of belongings scattered, or of a once-unified group now fragmented.

e: "seven up, eight down" — nervous and unsettled; anxious about the outcome
d: Seven and eight are the neighbors of ten who cannot agree on direction. Seven goes up, eight goes down: the image is of something that cannot find rest, oscillating without resolution. The idiom describes the feeling of anxiety before a result, the inner turbulence of waiting without knowing.

Sun Wukong's power to transform himself into seventy-two different forms, from a fly to a temple. Used as a chengyu for boundless adaptability and resourcefulness, the capacity to change shape to fit any situation, and applied admiringly to anyone strikingly versatile or quick to adapt.

e: "seven mouths, eight tongues" — everyone talking at once; a clamor of voices
d: 七嘴 (seven mouths) and 八舌 (eight tongues): so many people speaking at the same time that no single voice can be made out. Describes a crowd all offering opinions at once, a noisy discussion where everyone interrupts everyone.

Literally "aligned hearts, joined strength", everyone striving together as one. A close cousin of 同心协力, stressing that all hearts are lined up in the same direction. The collective togetherness that 一起 points toward when a group acts as a team.

e: its appearance not outstanding — plain-featured; ordinary-looking
d: 其 qí (its) + 貌 mào (appearance; face) + 不扬 bù yáng (not elevated; not distinguished). Used of people with unremarkable physical appearance, often with an implied "but capable": the phrase sets up the contrast between appearance and substance.

e: to bring back from the dead — to revive a desperate situation
d: Lit: raise-dead-return-life. Originally medical (miraculous cures); now used for companies, projects, and relationships revived against all odds.

e: breath urgent, composure ruined: flustered and furious, beside oneself with rage
d: Pictures someone so panicked or enraged that their composure has fallen apart. 败坏 doubles "defeated" and "ruined." Common in narration for a person who has lost their cool and is lashing out.

e: spirit that could swallow mountains and rivers — magnificent, all-encompassing force
d: Lit: qi-swallow-mountain-river. A classical idiom for heroic grandeur: the qi of a great army, a historical figure, or a piece of calligraphy or poetry so powerful it seems to contain all of nature within it. Often used in literary and historical commentary.

e: magnificent spirit that fills the mountains and rivers
d: Lit: qi-strong-mountain-river. Similar to 气吞山河 but with a sense of steadiness rather than swallowing, the qi standing as firm and vast as mountains and rivers. Used for patriotic spirit, heroic resolve, or great art. A phrase from Wen Tianxiang's 正气歌 tradition.

e: just right; arriving at exactly the right point
d: 恰 qià (just; exactly) + 到 dào (arrive at) + 好 hǎo (good; right) + 处 chù (place; point). Arriving at precisely the right place: the perfectly calibrated amount, the perfectly timed remark, the execution that is neither too much nor too little.

e: exactly to its measure: just right, neither too much nor too little
d: Lit: precisely-matching-its-portion. Praise for words or actions pitched at exactly the right degree. Here 分 takes the fèn reading, the proper allotted measure.

e: a thousand changes, ten thousand transformations: endlessly changing; protean
d: 千 qiān = thousand, 万 wàn = ten thousand, the two largest round numbers paired for the sense of "countless." Lit: "a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations." Describes anything in ceaseless, dazzling flux: clouds, markets, a magician's tricks, the moves of a skilled fighter. 舞台上的灯光千变万化。

e: a thousand methods and a hundred schemes: by every conceivable means
d: Lit: thousand-methods-hundred-plans. Stronger than 想方设法, often with a hint that the effort is dogged or even scheming. 千方百计地想办法 "to try every trick in the book."

e: pointed at by a thousand men: condemned by everyone
d: Literally "what a thousand men point their fingers at." It describes a person reviled by the whole public, the target of universal blame and reproach. To be 千夫所指 is to stand utterly condemned in the eyes of the crowd, a heavy figure for public disgrace.

e: a peerless masterpiece: a work unmatched through the ages
d: Literally "a song unmatched in a thousand ages." Here 千古 means all the ages, and 绝唱 the supreme, unrepeatable performance. Reserved for a poem, song, or work of art so fine that nothing across the centuries can equal it.

e: "a thousand armies, ten thousand horses" — an overwhelming force; a vast host
d: 千军 (a thousand armies) and 万马 (ten thousand horses): a military host so large it cannot be counted. The phrase pictures an unstoppable onrush of force and is applied to any overwhelming mass, an army, a flood of competitors, a tide of demand.

e: "a thousand jun hanging by one hair" — a moment of extreme peril; hanging by a thread
d: 千钧 (a thousand jun, an enormous weight, the 钧 being an ancient heavy measure) suspended by 一发 (a single hair). The image is of a crushing weight held by the thinnest possible thread, an instant of utmost danger in which the slightest thing decides catastrophe or escape.

p: qiānlǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià
e: "a thousand-li journey begins beneath the feet" — every great endeavor starts with a single step
d: From the Daodejing, chapter 64. 千里 (a thousand li) + 之 (connecting particle) + 行 (journey, travel) + 始 (to begin) + 于 (at, from) + 足下 (beneath the feet).

p: qiān lǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià.
e: A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
d: From chapter 64, now a chengyu used worldwide. The surrounding passage teaches that great things grow from small beginnings and that the wise act early, while problems are still tiny and easy to handle: the tree that fills an armspan grew from a sprout, the nine-storey tower rose from a heap of eart…

e: a thousand people, a thousand faces — each one different
d: Often used to describe the terracotta warriors, whose faces are all individual. As a general chengyu it means that every person (or every case, or every product) is distinct, with no two alike, and it can praise rich variety or warn against treating different things as the same.

e: a thousand threads and ten thousand strands: countless intricate connections
d: Lit: thousand-silk-ten-thousand-threads. Used of relationships or matters knit together by innumerable fine ties: 千丝万缕的联系 "connections beyond counting." The literal silk threads behind every abstract 系.

e: "a thousand pains, ten thousand toils" — untold hardships; every kind of suffering
d: 千辛 (a thousand bitternesses) and 万苦 (ten thousand toils): hardship piled on hardship beyond counting. Used to describe the immense effort and suffering endured to reach a goal: 历尽千辛万苦 (to have gone through every kind of hardship).

e: "the humbly modest exemplary person" — the junzi whose modesty is doubled and genuine
d: From the 易经 (Yijing), first line of hexagram 15 谦 Qiān: 谦谦君子，用涉大川，吉 (The humbly modest exemplary person , it is advantageous to cross the great river. Good fortune). The doubling of 谦谦 marks the quality as thorough and genuine rather than surface-level.

e: "the lesson of the overturned cart ahead" — learn from the mistakes of those who came before
d: 前 (in front) + 车 (cart) + 之 (possessive) + 鉴 (mirror; lesson; to take as a warning). A cart that has already overturned lies visible on the road ahead of you , it is the past made legible, a warning you can see precisely because the past stands in front.

e: "the front one falls, the next one follows" — wave after wave of sacrifice; undeterred succession
d: 前 (front; those ahead) + 仆 pū (to fall forward, to fall face-down) + 后 (back; those behind) + 继 jì (to continue; to succeed). Those in the front ranks fall; those behind step up to continue.

Literally "the prior cause and the later result", the whole chain from why to what-happened. To know the 前因后果 is to understand a matter completely, from the reason a 为什么 seeks to the outcome it explains. 因 (cause) and 果 (effect, "fruit") are the two poles of explanation.

e: money can reach the gods — money can accomplish anything
d: A cynical proverb about the power of money to overcome any obstacle. 通神 = to reach the divine, suggesting even the sacred can be bought. The Tang-dynasty origin makes this one of the oldest commentaries on corruption in Chinese literature.

e: to shift unseen and transform in silence: to influence imperceptibly over time
d: 潜 qián = hidden, submerged, 移 yí = to shift, 默 mò = silent, 化 huà = to transform. Lit: "shifting while submerged, transforming in silence." Describes the slow, unnoticed way an environment, a teacher, or a habit gradually changes a person's character or thinking without any single dramatic moment.

p: qiè ér bù shě, jīn shí kě lòu
e: Persevere without giving up, and you can engrave even metal and stone
d: From 劝学. The full passage contrasts: if you chisel but give up, you cannot even cut rotten wood; if you persevere without stopping, you can engrave metal and stone.

e: close with no gap between: utterly intimate, inseparable
d: Lit: intimate-close-without-gap. Of a friendship or bond so tight that no space, no estrangement, divides the two. Here 间 takes the jiàn reading, the gap as separation.

e: keep worthy ministers close and petty men far
d: From Zhuge Liang's Chushibiao (出师表), the memorial he submitted before the northern campaigns, diagnosing why the Former Han rose and the Later Han fell.

e: qin and se playing in harmony — a happy and loving marriage
d: 琴 qín (seven-string zither) and 瑟 sè (larger twenty-five string zither) are the classical paired instruments. When they sound together in harmony, they are the image of a couple in accord. A literary idiom for marital happiness, used in wedding toasts and poetry.
Indigo is made from the indigo plant, yet it is bluer than the plant itself. Xunzi's image for the student who surpasses the teacher through sustained effort.

p: qīng chū yú lán ér shèng yú lán
e: Blue comes from indigo but surpasses indigo — the student surpasses the teacher
d: From 劝学 (Encouraging Learning), the opening chapter of the Xunzi. The original context is an argument about the power of education to transform: the product (blue dye) surpasses its source (the indigo plant) through processing.

e: to act rashly and recklessly: to move without due thought
d: Lit: light-lifting-reckless-moving. A warning against hasty, ill-considered action, often 不要轻举妄动 "do not act rashly," said when caution and patience are called for.

e: to topple states and cities: a woman of overwhelming beauty
d: 倾 qīng = to overturn, to topple; 国 guó = state; 城 chéng = city. The image is hyperbolic: a beauty so dazzling that rulers neglect their duties and whole cities and states fall because of her.

e: pure and true — the Chinese term for halal and for Islam's monotheism
d: 清 qīng (pure, clear) + 真 zhēn (true, genuine). The standard Chinese translation of the Islamic concept of divine purity and absolute transcendence. Applied in Chinese to: halal food (清真饮食), mosques (清真寺 , "pure truth temple"), and informally to Islamic identity.

e: unable to restrain one's feelings: cannot help oneself
d: Lit: feeling-not-self-restrain. When emotion wells up too strongly to hold back: 她情不自禁地哭了 "she could not help crying." 禁 here is jīn, "to bear; to restrain."

e: to exhaust the troops in endless war: reckless militarism
d: Literally "drain the soldiers, abuse the martial." A sharp condemnation of a ruler who wages war without end, squandering lives and resources in aggression for its own sake. 黩 dú means to defile or abuse, so 黩武 is the abuse of military force.

e: "the road's end, the last stretch": at the end of one's resources; cornered, no way forward
d: 穷 qióng (exhausted) + 途 tú (way) + 末 mò (final) + 路 lù (road). Used for someone whose options have run out: a bankrupt business, a defeated army, a person at the end of their rope. Slightly literary in register.

e: seek common ground while keeping differences: agree where you can, set the rest aside
d: Lit: seek-sameness-preserve-difference. A principle of diplomacy and negotiation: build on what is shared without forcing every disagreement to be resolved first.

e: yield and you will be preserved — the paradox of strength through softness
d: Daodejing 22: 曲则全，枉则直，洼则盈. "Yield and you will be preserved; bend and you will be straightened; hollow and you will be filled." The full paradoxical sequence of Daoist counterintuition.

e: driving out ghosts and warding off evil — the exorcistic function
d: Lit: drive-ghost-ward-evil. Captures the apotropaic (protective, evil-averting) function that shamanism shares with folk religion broadly.

e: countable on bent fingers, a mere handful
d: 屈指 (bend the fingers) + 可数 (can be counted). The vivid opposite of 不计其数: so few you can tally them on one hand. 像他这样的人才屈指可数 "Talents like him can be counted on one hand." Note 数 here is shǔ (to count), the verb reading, against shù (number) in 不计其数.

e: to take over and replace it: to supplant another and assume their place
d: Lit: take it, and replace it. From the Records of the Grand Historian, where the young Xiang Yu, seeing the First Emperor's procession, vows that he could take the emperor's place. Now used for any decisive supplanting of one thing by another.

e: to fetch the scriptures — to go and learn from a master source
d: Literally "to obtain the sutras," from Xuanzang's mission and its retelling in 西游记.

e: take strengths to補 compensate weaknesses — learn from others
d: Lit: take-long-补-short. The standard phrase for learning from others to compensate for one's own deficiencies. 互相取长补短 "learn from each other's strengths to make up for each other's weaknesses" is the common collaborative formulation.

e: "to go and then come back again" — to depart and return unexpectedly
d: 去 qù (to leave) + 而 ér (but; and then) + 复 fù (again; to return) + 返 fǎn (to turn back). Someone who had departed comes back, often unexpectedly or after a significant interval.

e: indifferent to going or staying — free of attachment to outcome
d: From the famous couplet: 宠辱不惊，去留无意 , "Undisturbed by honor or disgrace; indifferent to going or staying." A Daoist attitude of equanimity and non-attachment. 去 (go/leave) contrasts with 留 (stay/remain). The phrase captures the ideal of acting without being determined by results.

e: "remove the false, preserve the true" — to sift out falsehood and keep what is genuine
d: 去 wěi = send away the false. 存 cún = preserve; 真 zhēn = the true. The epistemological program of discernment: not just believing what you are told but actively removing the counterfeit to preserve what is real.

e: to go all out: to throw one's full strength at a task
d: Lit: with-full-strength-to-go-toward. To commit every ounce of effort to something, holding nothing back. The everyday phrase for total commitment, whether to a contest, a project, or a rescue.

e: fully absorbed: to concentrate every bit of attention on one thing
d: Lit: whole-spirit-pour-into. With one's entire mind poured into a single focus, oblivious to all else. The phrase for deep, undivided concentration.

e: with whole heart and whole mind: wholeheartedly, with total devotion
d: Lit: whole-heart-whole-intent. The 心 (heart) and 意 (intent) doubled to mean nothing held back: 全心全意为人民服务 "to serve the people wholeheartedly." The strongest everyday way to say one is fully committed.

e: a flock of dragons with no head: a leaderless, directionless group
d: Lit: flock-dragons-without-head. A phrase from the Book of Changes: many capable members but no one to lead them, so the group drifts. Used of an organization left rudderless after its leader is gone.

e: heat and fire toward the sky: a buzzing, full-tilt scene
d: The image is a fire roaring up at the heavens. Used for a worksite, campaign, or rehearsal humming with energy. Common in news and everyday speech.

e: hot tears filling the eye sockets: moved to tears
d: 热泪 hot tears, 盈眶 brimming the eye rims. For the moment emotion wells up and the eyes flood. Used for reunions, awards, and stirring speeches.

e: human will can overcome heaven — perseverance defeats fate
d: The Maoist rejoinder to classical fatalism. 人定 = human resolution and determination; 胜 = to overcome; 天 = heaven/fate. Against the traditional acceptance of 天命, this phrase asserts that collective human effort can reshape nature and destiny.

e: every person fully uses their talents; no talent is wasted
d: Lit: person-exhaust-their-talent. A governance and organizational ideal: the right people in the right roles, fully realizing their abilities. Often paired with 物尽其用 wù jìn qí yòng (every object fully utilized).

e: men worn out and horses spent: an army exhausted
d: The classic picture of a column at the end of a long march, fighters and mounts alike drained. Frequent in historical novels such as the Sānguó Yǎnyì.

e: a human face with the heart of a beast: a cruel person behind a civil mask
d: Not built on 社 itself, but a classic measure of how a person fits or fails the bonds of human society: someone who looks like one of us yet behaves with brute cruelty. A reminder that belonging to a 社会 is judged by conduct, not appearance.

e: a human life is a matter of Heaven; "lives are at stake," used to underscore extreme gravity
d: 人命 "human life" plus 关天 "concerns Heaven." The phrase invoked when human lives are on the line in medical, legal, or rescue contexts, to communicate that ordinary calculations no longer apply. The implicit logic: a life belongs to Heaven; touching it is a cosmic, not merely human, matter.

e: a mountain of people, a sea of people — an enormous crowd
d: Lit: person-mountain-person-sea. The go-to phrase for describing massive crowds: national holidays, concerts, train stations during Spring Festival rush. Pairing 山 (mountain) with 海 (sea), the two largest natural forms, captures the sense of scale without irony.

e: humans and spirits communing — the fundamental premise of shamanism
d: Lit: human-spirit-mutually-communicate. The cosmological axiom that makes shamanism possible: the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is permeable, and certain human specialists can cross it.

e: human plans yield to Heaven's plans — fate overrides strategy
d: Lit: human calculations are no match for Heaven's calculations. A fatalist proverb at the heart of folk cosmology: 谋事在人，成事在天 (planning is human, success is Heaven's). Used when the best-laid plans go awry.

h: 人往高处走，水往低处流
p: rén wǎng gāo chù zǒu, shuǐ wǎng dī chù liú
e: "people move toward high places; water flows to low places" — the natural human drive for self-improvement; ambition as gravity
d: A folk proverb rather than a classical four-character chengyu, but one of the most widely cited sayings about ambition and social mobility in Mandarin. Water follows physical gravity downward; people follow social gravity upward.

p: rén wèi cái sǐ, niǎo wèi shí wáng
e: people die for money; birds die for food
d: 财 cái = wealth, property. One of the most widely quoted Chinese proverbs about greed and human nature, a parallel structure comparing human ambition to animal survival instinct. Sobering, not condemnatory; an observation about the force of desire.

e: whether hearts face toward or turn away: popular support or opposition
d: Lit: people's-hearts, facing-or-backing. 向 is to face toward (support), 背 to turn one's back (oppose). The phrase names the balance of public sentiment that decides whether a cause or a ruler will stand.

e: what people say is to be feared
d: A shorter, more colloquial formulation of the same truth: public opinion is a force that should not be underestimated. Less analytical than 三人成虎, more emotionally immediate. Often used in the context of reputation and social pressure.

p: rén zài Cáo yíng xīn zài Hàn
e: body in Cao's camp, heart in Han — physically present but mentally elsewhere; loyalty divided
d: From Romance of the Three Kingdoms: Guan Yu was held in Cao Cao's camp but his heart remained loyal to Liu Bei's Han cause. The 在…在 parallel structure contrasts physical location (body) with emotional location (heart).

p: rén zài jiānghú shēn bù yóu jǐ
e: in the rivers-and-lakes world, one's body is not one's own — once entered, you are bound by its rules
d: The defining 江湖 saying. Used seriously to explain why one cannot simply walk away from obligations , and humorously to explain why you have to attend yet another obligatory dinner, meeting, or social engagement.

e: humaneness, righteousness, the Way, and virtue — the full Confucian moral vocabulary
d: The four great concepts of Confucian ethics strung together: 仁 rén (humaneness), 义 yì (righteousness), 道 dào (the Way , the correct path of conduct), 德 dé (virtue , moral power accumulated through right conduct). Together they describe the ideal moral life.

e: the benevolent person loves others — the most concise definition of 仁
d: From Mencius (4B:28). The simplest, most direct statement of the first virtue. 仁 is not an abstract principle but an orientation toward actual people. Love here (爱 ài) means caring about the genuine wellbeing of others, not sentimental attachment.

p: rén zhě yào shān, zhì zhě yào shuǐ
e: "the benevolent love mountains, the wise love water"
d: The companion form of the Analects couplet, often quoted with the order reversed. 仁 (benevolence) and 智 (wisdom) are matched to mountain (immobile, supporting) and water (mobile, responsive) respectively.

From Mencius (孟子). The political claim that follows from 仁 as a virtue of rule: a ruler who genuinely cares for the people will have no one willing to make war against them, because no one wants to fight a benefactor.

e: humaneness to the utmost, righteousness to its limit — to do everything one possibly can
d: Said of someone who has discharged every moral obligation, exhausted every avenue of help or forgiveness, usually before walking away. Often used right before delivering a hard refusal: "I have done everything humanly possible; the rest is not on me."

e: to take a thief for a father: to serve one's enemy as a benefactor
d: A harsh condemnation, aimed at a traitor or collaborator who submits to the very people who wronged him. The image inverts the sacred father-son bond into betrayal.

e: to acknowledge one's ancestors and return to the lineage
d: Lit: recognize-ancestor-return-lineage. Used for those who were separated from their family (by adoption, diaspora, or historical disruption) and formally reconnect with their ancestral line. A profoundly significant act in Chinese social life.

Literally "to take on the toil and take on the grumbling," to shoulder hard work and even unfair blame without complaint. A warm compliment for a dependable, uncomplaining worker, and a quietly admired virtue in the Chinese workplace.

e: to be at the mercy of others; to be slaughtered at will by whoever wants to
d: Lit: let-people-slaughter-carve. The extreme end of the 被 spectrum , not just being acted upon but being vulnerable to anyone who chooses to exploit you. 宰割 = to slaughter and carve up (animals, and by extension, the weak).

e: "the burden is heavy, the road is far" — great responsibility with a long journey ahead
d: From the Analects of Confucius (论语): 仁以为己任，不亦重乎？死而后已，不亦远乎？(Is taking benevolence as one's charge not heavy? Does the journey end only at death , is that not far?) Used to describe serious long-term undertakings: social reform, academic work, national development. Conveys gravitas without complaint.

e: accumulate day by day, build up month by month — the power of small consistent effort
d: Lit: day-accumulate-month-build. The Chinese formulation of compounding: small daily efforts accumulate into transformative results over time. Used to encourage consistent study, practice, and work. 日积月累，功到自然成 "accumulate consistently and success will naturally follow."

e: changing by the day and the month — rapid, ceaseless progress
d: Literally "new each day, different each month," for change so fast it is visible from one stretch of time to the next. The standard phrase for the breakneck pace of modern development, especially technology and the transformation of cities, the felt texture of living in the 现代 age.

e: glory and splendor, wealth and rank: a life of luxury and high station
d: Four near-synonyms stacked for weight. Often used wistfully or critically, the worldly prize that classical heroes are urged to see through.

e: "melt together, thread through": to master a subject by integrating all its parts
d: 融 róng (to melt; to merge) + 会 huì (to come together) + 贯 guàn (to thread through; to run a string through) + 通 (to penetrate fully).

e: the soft overcomes the hard; yielding defeats force
d: 柔弱 róuruò (soft; yielding; pliant) + 胜 shèng (to overcome; to defeat; to surpass) + 刚强 gāngqiáng (hard; strong; rigid; forceful). Daodejing chapter 78: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻坚强者莫之能胜 (nothing in the world is as soft as water, yet nothing surpasses it in wearing away the hard and strong).

e: like fire and like white reeds: in full, blazing swing
d: Lit: like-fire-like-white-flowers. 荼 is the white flower of a reed. From an account of an army arrayed in red and white, the phrase now describes a movement or campaign surging ahead at full intensity.

e: "like thunder piercing the ear" — a name of thunderous fame
d: 如 (like) + 雷 (thunder) + 贯 (to pierce, to pass through) + 耳 (ear). A famous name entering the ear with the force of thunder.

e: like the sun at its zenith — at the height of power or fame
d: Lit: like-sun-middle-sky. Used to describe someone or something at the apex of their power, influence, or popularity. 他的事业如日中天 "his career is at its zenith." Can refer to a person, a dynasty, a company, or a cultural trend.

e: as if a heavy load were set down: deeply relieved
d: Lit: as-if-releasing-a-heavy-burden. The feeling of relief once a worry or duty is finally over, the body lightening as the weight comes off. 长舒一口气 "to let out a long breath" is its companion image.

e: like a fish that has found water — to be in one's element; perfectly suited to one's environment
d: A fish out of water dies; a fish in water is entirely itself. This chengyu describes the state of someone who has found the exact environment where they thrive , a new job that suits them perfectly, a community where they feel at home. 他在新公司如鱼得水，如虎添翼。

e: to achieve one's wish; things went as hoped
d: The positive counterpart: wishes fulfilled, intention and outcome aligned. 如愿以偿 and 事与愿违 are natural antonyms: the same structure (relation of wish to outcome) with opposite results. Pairing them in commentary about uncertain situations (whether things went well or not) is a common rhetorical move.

e: entering the earth brings peace — may they rest in peace
d: Lit: enter-earth-become-peaceful. The traditional Chinese expression for the peace of burial: entering the earth is how the deceased find rest. Used in discussions of funerary customs and in consoling the bereaved.

e: too sharp to be withstood: an irresistible force
d: Lit: so sharp it cannot be matched. Here 当 means to stand against or block. Said of an advance, an army, or a momentum that nothing can stop.

e: a timely snow foretells a good harvest
d: 瑞 ruì (auspicious) + 雪 xuě (snow) + 兆 zhào (to portend) + 丰年 fēngnián (a year of abundance). A farmer's proverb with real agronomy behind it: a heavy winter snow insulates the wheat from killing cold, kills overwintering pests, and melts into spring soil moisture.

e: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse
d: His horse ran off. His neighbours grieved. He shrugged. The Daoist parable that became China's word for the unknowability of fortune.

e: the governance of the Three Dynasties — the Confucian golden age
d: The Three Dynasties (Xia, Shang, Zhou) collectively were idealized by Confucians as the golden age of moral government, a standard against which all later dynasties were measured and found wanting. 三代 remains a byword for ideal antiquity in Chinese intellectual discourse.

e: the dead of night — the third watch, past midnight
d: 三更 (third night watch, 11 pm to 1 am) + 半夜 (middle of the night). The 更 is gēng, first tone. A fixed phrase for any unreasonably late hour. 你三更半夜打电话干什么? "What are you calling at this hour for?" Still in active everyday use; most speakers do not connect it to the premodern watch system.

e: "three visits to the thatched cottage" — to seek out a person of talent with great persistence and sincerity
d: The most celebrated episode from Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Liu Bei, ruler of Shu, visits the hermit Zhuge Liang three times at his remote thatched cottage before Zhuge Liang agrees to leave seclusion and serve as his strategist.

e: the Three Principles of the People — nationalism, democracy, livelihood
d: Sun Yat-sen's political program, still the official ideology of the Republic of China (Taiwan). The phrase is so embedded in Chinese political vocabulary that it functions almost as a set term.
A minister warns his king: if three people all claim there is a tiger in the marketplace, even the skeptical will believe it. The Zhanguo Ce parable of rumor that outlasts the warning against it.

p: sān rén xíng, bì yǒu wǒ shī
e: where three walk together, one of them is sure to be my teacher
d: From the Analects (论语). Confucius's most-quoted statement on learning: in any company of three people, there will be something to learn , from the better among them by emulation, from the worse by avoidance.

e: "three heads and six arms" — superhuman ability; able to do many things at once
d: 三头 (three heads) and 六臂 (six arms), the form of certain fierce Buddhist and Daoist deities such as Nezha, who can fight and act on many fronts at once.

e: "three hearts, two intentions" — indecisive; half-hearted; wavering
d: Three hearts pulling in different directions, two sets of intentions competing: the image is of someone who cannot commit. Used to criticize a lack of decisiveness or sincerity in a relationship, a task, or a position. 做事不能三心二意 (You can't do things half-heartedly).

e: "three words, two phrases" — in a few words; briefly
d: 三言 (three words) and 两语 (two phrases): just a handful of words, said briefly. Used to mean something can be (or cannot be) explained in a sentence or two: 三言两语说不清 (it can't be explained in a few words).

e: three yang lines open into prosperity: an auspicious fresh start, a New Year blessing
d: From the hexagram 泰 (peace) in the Book of Changes, whose lower three lines are 阳, marking yang rising as winter turns to spring. A traditional New Year greeting wishing renewal and good fortune for the year ahead.

e: fierce in appearance but cowardly within — all bark and no bite
d: Lit: color-fierce-inside-timid. A Confucian observation from the Analects: those who appear stern and imposing externally (色厉) but are weak-willed inside (内荏). The opposite of the virtuous person, whose outer bearing matches inner substance.

e: many monks, little porridge — too many claimants for scarce resources
d: The monastery breakfast as economic model. Used for job markets (百个人抢一个岗位，僧多粥少), housing, research funding, and concert tickets. The pictorial economy of the phrase, one queue and one pot, is why it beats the abstract word for scarcity in daily speech.

e: kill the chicken to warn the monkey: punish one to frighten the rest
d: Make an example of a minor offender so the watching crowd falls into line. Common in talk of office discipline and political crackdowns.

e: to smear blood on the lips as an oath — to seal a solemn covenant
d: The ritual procedure of the Spring and Autumn covenant assembly (盟会 ménghuì): participants touched their lips with the blood of a sacrificial animal , usually a bull or horse , while swearing the covenant terms. The act bound the parties through ritual sanction, not just political agreement.

e: "mountains high, water long" — virtue or reputation that endures across time
d: From a Northern Song memorial by Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹) describing the legacy of a virtuous official: 云山苍苍，江水泱泱；先生之风，山高水长 ("the cloudy mountains stretch dark; the rivers run wide; the master's spirit , high as the mountains, long as the rivers").
Clear mountains, lovely waters. The standard Chinese phrase for a picturesque landscape: four characters that compress the whole aesthetic vocabulary of natural beauty.

e: "the mountains are exhausted, the waters are at their end" — at the end of one's resources
d: From Lu You (陆游, Song dynasty), 游山西村: 山穷水尽疑无路，柳暗花明又一村 ("when the mountains are spent and the waters are done and there seems to be no road , there, beyond the dim willows and bright flowers, is another village").

e: mountains piled on mountains, waters winding through waters — a seemingly hopeless impasse
d: From a poem by Lu You 陆游. Full line: 山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村, "Mountain on mountain, water on water, seemingly no path; then through dark willows and bright flowers, a village appears." The proverb for finding hope when all seems lost.

e: cut the complex and move toward the simple: prune the excess
d: 删 to delete, 繁 the complicated, 就 to go toward, 简 the simple. An editor's motto, applied to prose, procedures, and design alike.

e: good and evil are rewarded accordingly — karmic accounting
d: The foundational moral logic of the City God's record-keeping function. 善 shàn = virtue; 恶 è = evil; 有报 yǒu bào = has retribution/reward. The phrase asserts that no deed escapes accounting, even if human courts miss it, because the City God has the complete ledger.

e: good beginning, good ending; to see something through properly from start to finish
d: Lit: good-start-good-end. The virtue of completing what one begins, and completing it well. 终 zhōng (end, conclusion) is the Classical Chinese counterpart to the grammatical 了 , both mark the reaching of an end. This idiom captures the moral weight of completion.

e: to wound heaven and harm reason: utterly immoral
d: An act so cruel it offends both heaven and natural law. Strong condemnation of conscienceless deeds.

e: the highest good is like water — effortless giving that sustains without striving
d: Daodejing, Chapter 8. Functions as a classical four-character literary phrase rather than an everyday idiom. Cited in calligraphy, philosophy, and any context invoking the Daoist ideal of natural, uncontending benefit.

e: The highest good is like water.
d: From chapter 8. Water is the master image of the Daodejing: it benefits all things without contending, it seeks the low places that everyone else disdains, and in this very humility it comes closest to the 道.

e: "hands moving up and down" — to manipulate facts; to connive
d: From the Zuǒzhuàn (左传), Spring and Autumn period. A general signaled with his hand upward or downward to indicate whether a captured soldier was high-ranking (ransom-worthy) or low-ranking (irrelevant) , the signal determined the truth, not the facts.

e: "what the top does, the bottom imitates" — those in power set the moral tone
d: A foundational principle of Confucian political thought: the ruler's virtue or vice flows downward through society. If the one above is corrupt, those below will follow. If the one above is upright, the people will follow that too. 上 and 下 carry the full social hierarchy in two strokes.

A polite, slightly formal way to ask someone to wait briefly, 片刻 ("a short moment") being the written cousin of 一会儿. Heard in service settings and on the phone, the courteous register where 等一会儿 would be too casual.

e: "seen little, amazed by much" — making a fuss about ordinary things
d: 少见 (having seen few things) + 多怪 (finding much to be strange/surprising). When you haven't seen much of the world, ordinary things seem remarkable. A mild criticism of provinciality or naïvety: someone who marvels at things a more experienced person takes for granted.

e: to sacrifice oneself for others: selfless devotion to others' good
d: Lit: give-up-self-for-others. The highest praise for selflessness, setting one's own interests aside for the sake of other people. The 己 here is exactly the self that 舍 (to give up) renounces.

e: to give up one's life and forget death; to face danger without thought of self
d: A standard high-register chengyu for selfless courage, used for soldiers, rescue workers, doctors during epidemics. The phrase doesn't contain 命 directly but belongs to its semantic field: it names the willingness to set down the command-to-live for something larger.

e: if not I, then who? — the burden falls to me
the body is not controlled by oneself — driven by circumstances beyond one's will
d: 身 shēn (body; self) + 不 bù (not) + 由 yóu (controlled by; following from) + 己 jǐ (oneself). One's own body belongs to external forces , obligation, circumstance, social pressure, or fate. The counterpart to agency: when 他 (the other, external) overrides 己 (the self).

e: to practice with one's own body and strength; to live what one preaches
d: 身 and 体 here are both verbs in the classical grammar: to embody personally (身) and to enact (体力行, carry out with strength). The Confucian ideal of the teacher whose conduct is the curriculum. Modern usage praises leaders who do rather than direct: 环保不能只喊口号，要身体力行。

e: deep thought, mature deliberation — to think long and carefully before acting
d: 深 shēn (deep) + 思 sī (think) + 熟 shú (mature; thoroughly cooked) + 虑 lǜ (to deliberate; to consider). A four-character description of the deliberative ideal: thought that has gone deep and has been given time to mature, like food that has cooked through completely.

e: appearing like a deity, vanishing like a ghost — moving unpredictably, appearing and disappearing without warning
d: Lit: spirit-emerge-ghost-disappear. 出 is to emerge, appear; 没 is to sink, vanish. The pairing of 神 (divine, above) and 鬼 (ghostly, below) creates a complete spectrum of supernatural unpredictability , appearing from nowhere, vanishing the same way.

e: careful attention to death rites and honoring distant ancestors
d: From the Analects (论语): 慎终追远，民德归厚矣. "When the people are careful about death rites and diligently honor distant ancestors, the virtue of the people will return to richness." Confucius's most concise statement of why ancestor veneration matters: it cultivates moral seriousness in the living.

e: living dragon, active tiger — bursting with energy and vitality
d: 生 shēng (alive; living) + 龙 lóng + 活 huó (active; lively) + 虎 hǔ (tiger). Used to describe a person , especially a child, an athlete, or anyone at the peak of their physical vitality , who radiates robust, irrepressible energy. 这些孩子个个生龙活虎，根本停不下来。

e: life generating life without ceasing — the endless renewal of existence
d: A Daoist cosmological phrase: life perpetually generating more life. Used in nature writing, philosophical prose, and speeches about cultural continuity.

e: to share life and death together — a bond through the deepest adversity
d: Lit: life-death-with-together. Used for close comrades, soldiers, and couples who have endured extreme hardship. The deepest statement of loyalty.

p: shēng yú yōuhuàn, sǐ yú ānlè.
e: One lives through hardship and worry; one dies from comfort and pleasure.
d: Mencius 6B:15. The full passage argues this through historical examples: great figures of the past were all tempered through adversity before they could accomplish anything.

e: "feign east, strike west" — strategic deception; misdirection before attacking
d: Lit: declare-east-strike-west. A classic military stratagem from the Sun Tzu tradition , make noise in the east to draw attention, then attack from the west. Used broadly for any deceptive misdirection tactic in business, politics, or argument. 他用声东击西的策略迷惑了对手。

e: ten years at a cold window — long, austere years of study
d: The image of the exam candidate reading through winters without heat. The full couplet adds the payoff: ten years at the cold window unknown, one exam success and the world knows your name (十年寒窗无人问，一举成名天下知). Modern parents invoke it during gaokao season with full sincerity.

p: shí nián shù mù, bǎi nián shù rén
e: "ten years to grow a tree, a hundred years to cultivate a person" — education takes far longer than any other cultivation
d: From the classical text 管子 Guǎnzi. Growing a tree requires ten years of patience: planting, watering, waiting. Cultivating a human being , educating, civilizing, forming character , requires ten times longer. The century-scale horizon is a deliberate rebuke to impatience.

e: perfect in every way — ten-complete and ten-beautiful, with nothing lacking
d: The most-used idiom of perfection in Chinese. The doubling of 十 means completeness is measured twice , in wholeness and in beauty , so that neither a technical nor an aesthetic standard is left unmet.

e: time will not wait for me — seize the moment; there is no time to lose
d: Lit: time-not-me-wait. A classical inversion , the subject (时, time) is placed before the negation, with "me" as object, producing the archaic feel of a proverb. The phrase frames time as an agent with no personal loyalty: it moves whether you are ready or not.

e: time passes, circumstances change — things are different now; that was then
d: 时过 (time has passed) + 境迁 (the situation has shifted , 境 jìng: circumstances, context; 迁 qiān: to move, to change). Used to acknowledge that what was true, appropriate, or possible in the past no longer applies , without judgment, simply as a statement of temporal fact.

e: the hour is not early: it is getting late
d: A common set expression rather than a classical chengyu. Used to signal politely that time has slipped on, often as a cue to wrap up or take one's leave: 时候不早了，我该走了 "it is getting late, I should go."

e: when the time comes, fortune turns — one's luck changes for the better
d: Lit: time-comes fortune-turns. Fortune is not fixed; it turns like a wheel. Used when someone's luck dramatically improves after a period of misfortune. The Daoist wheel of fortune encoded in a four-character phrase.
Great figures are made by the conditions of their age, not by innate destiny alone, the circumstances create the opportunity for greatness.

e: to seek truth from facts — address problems realistically
d: A classical phrase, later a famous modern slogan, meaning to approach a 问题 on the basis of facts rather than wishful thinking or ideology. 实事 (real matters) + 求是 (seek what is so). The standard expression for a pragmatic, evidence-based way of analysing and solving problems.

e: to harbor a wicked scheme: to act with malicious intent
d: A colloquial set phrase, 使坏 (to scheme) plus 心眼 (mind, intention). Describes someone secretly plotting harm rather than acting openly. Everyday spoken register, not classical.

e: scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant: the four classes of old society
d: The traditional ranking of occupations, with the farmer placed second only to the scholar and above the merchant, a clue to how high agriculture stood in the Confucian moral order.

e: the eighth wonder of the world
d: The popular epithet attached to the terracotta army since foreign dignitaries applied it after the discovery.

e: generation after generation: for all the generations to come
d: A doubling of 世 (age) and 代 (generation), each repeated for emphasis. Describes something passed down or continuing without break across every generation, as in a craft, a duty, or a family living on the same land.

e: a haven of peace: an idyllic refuge cut off from the troubled world
d: Lit: a peach-blossom spring beyond the world. From Tao Yuanming's fable of a fisherman who stumbles on a hidden valley untouched by war and time. Now any tranquil place sheltered from the strife and bustle of ordinary life.

e: half the work, double the result: maximum output from minimum effort
d: Lit: work-half-achievement-double. The ideal of efficiency: accomplishing more by working smarter. From Mencius (孟子). Its mirror image is 事倍功半 shì bèi gōng bàn (double the work, half the result), wasted, inefficient effort.

e: double the effort, half the result
d: A related but distinct phrase: where 事与愿违 says the outcome diverged from the wish without specifying the ratio, 事倍功半 specifically describes disproportionate effort yielding inadequate results.

e: "nothing happens more than three times" — the third time is the last; do not push beyond three
d: A folk saying rather than a classical text quotation: three is the outer limit of tolerance or recurrence.

Literally "when a matter arises, there is a cause", nothing comes out of nowhere. It is the quiet conviction behind every 为什么: ask the question and there will be a 因 (cause) to find. The 因 here is the same one in 因为 ("because").

e: now that things have come to this
d: Literally "matters have arrived at the present," a set opener used when a situation has reached its current, often difficult, point and one must face it: 事到如今，只能这样了 ("now that it's come to this, this is all we can do"). Built on 如今 (nowadays, the present).

e: the affair has passed and the circumstances have changed
d: 事 (the matter) 过 (has passed) 境 (circumstances) 迁 (have shifted). Note 过 in its full verbal sense, the same morpheme that grammaticalized into the experiential particle. Used to wave off old grievances: 事过境迁，别再提了 "It's all in the past, don't bring it up again."

e: things go contrary to ones wishes
d: Traced to Ruan Ji of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove: a literary formulation of the gap between intention and outcome, resigned rather than accusatory, with no blame assigned.

e: things depend on human effort — nothing is impossible with effort
d: Lit: matters-located-in-human-doing. The outcome of things lies in human action, not fate or circumstance. An optimistic proverb of agency: no matter how difficult, the result is in human hands. 不要灰心，事在人为。

Literally "the momentum lies in must-be-done", a course of action that circumstances make unavoidable. It is certainty of the necessary kind, the 必 ("must") that 一定 and 必须 both touch, applied to events that simply have to proceed.

e: right and wrong turned upside down — moral inversion
d: Lit: right-wrong-overturned-upended. Used when injustice prevails, when blame is assigned to the innocent, or when someone deliberately distorts moral reality. 他把是非颠倒，让人无法接受。Strong condemnation in formal and classical register.

e: right and wrong, correct and incorrect — the full moral spectrum of a situation
d: Lit: right-wrong-correct-incorrect. A compound of two pairs: 是非 (right/wrong as a classical pair) and 对错 (correct/incorrect as a modern pair). Used to describe careful moral judgment of a complex situation. 分清是非对错 = "to clearly distinguish right from wrong in the situation."

e: right and wrong clearly divided: drawing a sharp line between them
d: Lit: right-wrong-divide-clear. Said in praise of someone with firm moral judgment who does not blur what is right with what is wrong.

e: right and wrong, crooked and straight: the true merits of a case
d: Lit: right-wrong-crooked-straight. The four poles by which a dispute is judged. To 分清是非曲直 is to sort out who is truly in the right, free of bias.

e: to praise the ancient and disparage the present
d: Lit: right-ancient-wrong-present. The bias of treating old things as inherently superior to contemporary ones. Appears in debates about tradition versus modernity, canonical texts versus living practice. Qin Shihuang's advisors warned him about scholars guilty of this very tendency.

e: hand never releasing the scroll — to be an insatiable reader
d: Lit: hand-not-release-scroll. To be so devoted to books that you never put them down. A compliment for scholars. 卷 juǎn = scroll; the classical form of the book.

e: the hand arrives and the capture is made — easily accomplished
d: Lit: hand-arrives-capture-comes. Used to describe a task accomplished with ease and confidence , the expert reaches out and the thing is done. An expression of mastery making difficulty look effortless. 对他来说，这件事手到擒来 "For him, this was a cinch."

e: hands busy, feet disordered — flustered and disorganized
d: Lit: hands-busy-feet-chaotic. The image of someone scrambling in a panic, hands and feet moving in disordered haste. Used to describe being overwhelmed and disorganized: the opposite of calm competence. 他一到过年就手忙脚乱 "Around New Year, he's always running around in a flustered state."

e: "hands and feet without placement" — at a complete loss, not knowing what to do
d: 手 (hands) + 足 (feet) + 无措 (nowhere to place them). So flustered that your hands and feet don't know where to go. From the Analects (Book XIII): Confucius warns that without ritual propriety, the people will be 手足无措.

e: the affection of hands and feet: the bond between brothers and sisters
d: Lit: hand-foot's-feeling. 手足 (hands and feet) is a classical image for siblings, who are as inseparable as one's own limbs. The phrase names the deep tie between brothers and sisters.

e: to have kept watch for a long while: to wait faithfully and at length
d: Lit: keep-watch-much-time. Said of someone who has been standing by patiently for a long stretch, often awaiting a person or an awaited moment. 守候 pairs the vigil of 守 with the waiting of 候.

e: to watch out for and help one another
d: From the Mencius: neighbors keeping watch and lending aid to each other, the ideal of a community that protects its own. 守望 (to keep watch) + 相助 (to help one another). Invoked for solidarity in hard times.

e: Guarding the Stump, Waiting for Rabbits
d: A rabbit ran headlong into a tree stump. The farmer dropped his plough and watched the stump for the rest of his life.

e: the first finger you bend to count: second to none, the very best
d: Lit: first-bend-one-finger. When you count off the best on your fingers, this is the one you bend down first. Used to rank a person or thing as the foremost in its field. 他在这个行业首屈一指 "He is second to none in this industry."

e: to be controlled by others; to be subject to another's power
d: Lit: receive-control-by-people. The standard formal expression for being under another's power, being constrained by external forces rather than acting freely. Common in diplomatic, strategic, and business contexts. The grammatical structure 受…于 is classical , modern equivalent would be 被人控制.

p: shū tóng wén, chē tóng guǐ
e: unified script, standardized axle widths — the rhetorical formula of systemic national unity
d: Still quoted in policy arguments about national standards: language standardization, infrastructure compatibility, technical regulation. The pairing condenses the Qin unification logic: physical connectivity (roads) plus cultural connectivity (writing) equals empire.

e: a family with a fragrance of books — a family of scholars and learning
d: Lit: book-fragrance-door-lineage. A family where books are the tradition and education runs through the generations. High cultural prestige in Chinese society. 书香 shūxiāng "the fragrance of books" is itself a vivid compound.

p: shú dú Táng shī sān bǎi shǒu
e: read three hundred Tang poems until you know them by heart — and you'll be able to compose poetry yourself
d: From the preface to the famous Qing-dynasty anthology Three Hundred Tang Poems: 熟读唐诗三百首，不会作诗也会吟. The locus classicus for the Chinese theory of learning by saturated recitation. The full saying ends "even if you can't compose, you'll be able to chant" , competence emerges from soaking in the corpus.

e: recite the classics but forget your ancestors
d: From the Zuozhuan: a minister who could cite all historical precedents of his state but could not name his own ancestral lineage was mocked with this phrase. Used for ingratitude, forgetting one's origins, or adopting foreign ways at the expense of one's own heritage.

e: when water flows, a channel forms
d: Literally "when the water arrives, the channel is made", success comes naturally once conditions ripen, with no forcing. It is the gentle counterpart to 终于's hard-won arrival: the long-awaited outcome that, in the end, simply falls into place.

e: water drips and the stone is bored through: small force, long time
d: The same image reordered, traced to the Han text Hàn Shū. Stresses the result, the worn-through stone, as proof that small efforts accumulate.

e: water and fire cannot coexist — irreconcilably opposed
d: Water extinguishes fire; fire evaporates water. The two simply cannot occupy the same space. Used for people, factions, or ideas in absolute opposition. 他们两人水火不容 "Those two are completely incompatible."

e: "not even water can leak through": packed solid; completely blocked or surrounded
d: 水 shuǐ (water) + 泄 xiè (to leak; to drain out) + 不 bù (not) + 通 (to pass through). So densely packed that not even a drop of water could trickle out.

e: when the water rises the boat rises too: gains that lift everything along with the tide
d: Originally a Chán Buddhist phrase. Used when one rising element pulls others up with it, whether prices, status, or a whole industry.

e: fishing the moon out of water — chasing an illusion
d: Lit: water-inside-fish-moon. The moon's reflection in a pond looks real but cannot be grasped. Used for futile efforts chasing something impossible. A Buddhist parable: mistaking the reflection for reality.

e: with the wind, with the water — smooth sailing; everything going well without obstruction
d: A wish and a description: wind at your back, current in your favor , nothing impeding progress. 祝你顺风顺水！(Wishing you smooth sailing!) is a common departure blessing. The 风水 imagery is natural: when wind and water cooperate, travel is easy; when they oppose, nothing moves.

e: let things take their natural course; go with the flow; accord with what is self-so
d: 顺 shùn (to follow; to go along with; to accord with; to flow downstream) + 其 qí (its; their; that) + 自然 zìrán (nature; the natural; self-so , 自 zì = self, 然 rán = thus/so: what is so of itself, without external imposition). The modern everyday expression for the principle underlying 无为.

e: push the boat along with the current: go with the flow and make the easy move
d: When circumstances already lean your way, you give a light push and take the credit. Often used for a decision that costs nothing because the moment favors it.

e: "accord with Heaven, respond to humanity" — acting in alignment with both cosmic order and popular sentiment
d: Lit: accord-Heaven-respond-humanity. A classical formula used to describe righteous political action or revolution: the actor is both aligned with Heaven's pattern and responding to the genuine needs of the people.

p: shuō Cáo Cāo, Cáo Cāo dào
e: speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives — speak of the devil
d: The exact Chinese equivalent of "speak of the devil." Said the instant someone shows up just as you were talking about them. It is the most common everyday phrase in which Cao Cao's name survives, owed to his reputation, in the stories, for moving with sudden speed.

p: shuō cáo cāo, cáo cāo dào.
e: Speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives.
d: The Chinese equivalent of "speak of the devil," drawn from the novel's portrait of Cao Cao as swift and unexpectedly present. Said when a person appears just as they are being talked about. One of the clearest examples of how thoroughly the Romance's characters entered everyday speech.

e: to do what one says — to be as good as one's word
d: 说 shuō (to say) + 到 dào (reach the point of) + 做 + 到. Literally "say it to the point, do it to the point." A high compliment: this is a person whose words and deeds match, who does not promise idly. The structure leans on 做到 (to achieve, to follow through).

e: to start telling it makes a long story: it is a long story
d: Lit: to-speak-of-it-the-words-grow-long. The standard preface to a complicated explanation, the Chinese equivalent of "well, it's a long story."

e: say one, not two — a person whose word is final; absolute authority
d: Lit: say-one-not-two. To speak once and have it stand; not to be contradicted. Describes a figure of absolute authority within their domain. Can be used admiringly (a decisive leader) or critically (an autocrat). 他在公司里说一不二。Tā zài gōngsī lǐ shuō yī bù èr. "In the company, what he says goes."

e: to refuse to own up to one's debts even in death — utterly unwilling to acknowledge fault
d: Lit: die-not-recognize-account. Said of someone who, when caught out, doubles down rather than admitting anything. The 死 here is "to-the-death," intensifying the refusal.

p: sǐ ér fù shēng, zài shì wéi rén
e: to die and come back to life; to be reborn into the world
d: 再世 (again-in-the-world) is the classical expression for reincarnation or miraculous revival. Used both literally (near-death recovery) and figuratively (total transformation of a situation or person). 再世英雄 (a hero reborn in a new era).

e: to die away and come back: to the point of fainting and reviving
d: Lit: die-go-live-come, pairing 死 and 活. Describes extremity of feeling or pain so severe one seems to faint and revive: to cry 哭得死去活来 (to weep oneself into a faint), to be beaten half to death.

e: "dying for face, living in torment" — to suffer rather than ask for help because of pride
d: A seven-character folk saying rather than a classical 成语, but extremely widely used. Describes the pattern of letting one's face-consciousness cause unnecessary suffering , not asking for help, not admitting failure, not seeking medical attention, because doing so would cost face.

e: to die other than by one's allotted fate: to meet an unnatural death
d: Lit: die-by-not-fate. 于 marks the cause of death, and 非命 (not one's natural span) signals an accident, violence, or disaster rather than a peaceful end.
