e: to make one's home in all four seas — at home anywhere; cosmopolitan; rootless wandering
d: 四海 = the four seas = everywhere under heaven. 为 = to treat as; to make into. The whole globe is one's household. Used for travelers, exiles, and those rootlessly at ease anywhere. Both admiring (cosmopolitan freedom) and elegiac (loss of fixed roots) , depending on context.

e: "four faces, eight directions" — from every direction; from everywhere
d: The most common chengyu using 方. 四面 (the four faces of a square; the four sides) + 八方 (the eight directions). Used for crowds, news, demands, attacks , anything converging from every direction. 来自四面八方的客人 (guests from all over).

e: "Chu songs on all four sides" — besieged on every side; utterly isolated
d: From the fall of Xiang Yu, the Hegemon-King of Chu, at the battle of Gaixia (202 BCE). Surrounded by Han forces, Xiang Yu heard his enemies singing the songs of his own homeland of Chu from every direction, and concluded that Chu had already fallen and his men had deserted to the enemy.

e: "reaching in four and through eight" — accessible in every direction; well-connected
d: 四通 (passing through in the four directions) plus 八达 (extending out the eight ways). Used of roads, railways, and transport networks that radiate to everywhere, and by extension of any hub that connects in all directions. A 交通四通八达 city is one you can reach and leave by any route.

e: seemingly right but actually wrong; plausible but false
d: Lit: seem-right-but-wrong. Used for arguments, claims, or reasoning that appear correct on the surface but are fundamentally flawed. The danger zone of logical errors , specious reasoning that passes for truth. Appears in classical philosophy and remains common in intellectual criticism.

e: if you escort the Buddha, escort him all the way west: finish what you start, see help through to the end
d: A colloquial saying drawing on the westward journey of Buddhist pilgrimage. Urges you not to abandon a kindness or a task halfway, but to carry it to completion.

e: to send off the old and welcome the new: ring out the old year, ring in the new
d: A New Year and year-end phrase, balancing 送 (sending off) the old against 迎 (welcoming) the new. Common on greeting cards and in festival speeches.

e: to send off those leaving and welcome those arriving: the endless round of social hospitality
d: Traces to the Lǐjì (Book of Rites). Describes the constant ceremony of receiving guests and seeing them off, often with a faint note of how exhausting such social duty becomes.

e: "follow the karmic current" — to go with the flow; to accept what fate brings; non-attachment
d: Lit: follow-karmic-connection. A Buddhist and Daoist attitude of non-attachment: accepting outcomes without forcing them, trusting the flow of conditions rather than imposing a rigid agenda. Has become a widely used life philosophy and response to uncertainty or disappointment. 随缘吧，强求没用。

e: the years spare no one — time is merciless; age catches up with everyone
d: 岁月 suìyuè (years and months , a classical compound for the flow of time) + 不饶 bù ráo (shows no mercy, does not spare). A cousin-phrase to 时不我待, but the mood is different: less urgent, more resigned. Where 时不我待 urges action, 岁月不饶人 acknowledges what cannot be undone.

e: the years pass like a weaver's shuttle — time flies
d: Lit: years-months-like-shuttle. 岁月 = years and months (time). 梭 suō = the weaver's shuttle that flies back and forth at great speed. The Chinese "time flies," usually said with a mixture of nostalgia and wonder at how quickly life passes.

e: "the one of whom I speak" — the beloved, the one I yearn for
d: From the Shijing (诗经) poem 蒹葭 ("Reeds"). One of the most famous lines of classical poetry, and the locus classicus for 伊 as feminine third person. The poem itself is gender-ambiguous in the classical text but read across two millennia as referring to a beloved woman across the river.

e: all before one is swept aside: to carry all before one, irresistible
d: Lit: wherever-faced, grass-flattens. 所向 is "wherever one turns," 披靡 the way grass bends flat before the wind. Said of an army or a force so strong that everything in its path gives way.

e: stones from other hills — outside perspectives can polish your own jade
d: From the Book of Songs (诗经): "stones from other hills can be used to grind jade." External viewpoints, foreign models, and outside criticism all carry value that self-regard misses. 他山 (other hills) + 之 (possessive particle) + 石 (stones).

e: Grand Duke Jiang fishes: those who are willing will take the bait
d: From 太公钓鱼，愿者上钩. The sage Jiang Ziya fished with a straight, baitless hook, waiting for King Wen to seek him out. Said of letting the willing come of their own accord rather than forcing them.

e: an age of great peace and prosperity — the ideal the Taiping name invoked, and failed to deliver
d: 太平 (great peace) + 盛世 (flourishing age, era of prosperity). The four-character compound describes the classical Chinese political ideal: an era in which the realm is at peace, governance is just, harvests are abundant, and the common people live without fear.

Literally "the night-blooming cereus shows itself once," for something splendid that lasts only a moment and is gone. The flower opens for a single short while in the night, then withers. A poignant image of fleeting brilliance, the shadow side of "a little while."

e: to chat and laugh with verve: lively, easy conversation
d: Lit: talk-laugh wind-rises, as if a fresh breeze sprang up from the talk. Describes a person who holds a room with relaxed, witty conversation. A warm compliment to a host or a speaker.

e: to sigh that one need look no further: the very acme of perfection
d: Lit: sigh-that-viewing-stops-here. From the Zuozhuan, where a guest praised a performance as so fine that watching could end there, nothing better remaining to see. High praise for the best of its kind.

e: dignified and upright: open, honorable, with nothing to hide
d: Reduplicated from 堂正. Said of someone who acts squarely and aboveboard, facing things head-on rather than scheming in the shadows. 堂堂正正做人 "to live as an upright person."

e: hide your brightness and nurture your obscurity — keep a low international profile while building strength
d: 韬光 (conceal one's brilliance) + 养晦 (cultivate obscurity, from 晦 = darkness, the dark of the moon).

e: peaches and plums fill the world: a teacher's students are everywhere
d: Lit: peach-plum-fill-the-world. 桃李 (peach and plum trees) stand for a teacher's 弟子, the disciples cultivated over a lifetime. To say someone's 桃李满天下 is high praise for a great educator.

e: the Oath of the Peach Garden — sworn brotherhood
d: The scene in which Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swear an oath of brotherhood in a peach orchard, vowing to live and die for one another and their shared cause.

e: ask a price, return a price: to haggle, bargain
d: Acts out the back-and-forth of the marketplace, one side naming a figure and the other countering. Extended to any drawn-out negotiation over terms.

e: unable to laugh or cry: caught between amusement and dismay
d: Lit: crying-laughing-both-wrong. Neither weeping nor laughing fits the situation, the awkward state of finding something at once absurd and exasperating. 令人啼笑皆非 "leaves one not knowing whether to laugh or cry."

e: clarified butter poured over the crown — sudden, total illumination
d: 醍醐, the finest essence refined from milk, was a Buddhist metaphor for the ultimate teaching; pouring it over the head is enlightenment received in one stream. Used for explanations so good they reorganize your understanding: a lecture, a mentor's single remark.

e: grand in structure and fine in thought: a work both vast and meticulous
d: Lit: body-large-thought-fine. Praise for a major work, a book or system, whose overall framework is grand while its detailed reasoning is precise. Here 体 is the structure or framework of the whole.

e: the body without a patch of whole skin: wounded all over, or torn apart in criticism
d: Lit: body-without-intact-skin. Literally beaten until no skin is unbroken; figuratively, an argument or piece of work refuted or criticized so thoroughly that nothing is left standing.

e: to carry out the Way on Heaven's behalf
d: The slogan on the great banner of the Liangshan outlaws, claiming that in punishing the corrupt and protecting the weak they act as the agents of Heaven's justice where the earthly state has failed.

e: "heaven-bestowed good fate" — a heaven-sent destined match; a blessed union
d: Lit: heaven-bestow-good-fate. The most auspicious framing for a destined romantic match , one that heaven itself has arranged and blessed. Used in wedding toasts, blessings, and romantic contexts when the match seems particularly right. 他们的婚姻真是天赐良缘，两个人都幸福极了。

e: heaven and earth as my witness — swearing to one's sincerity before the cosmos
d: A folk oath formula invoking Heaven and Earth as moral witnesses. 我天地良心地告诉你. "I'm telling you in all sincerity, with heaven and earth as my witness." Reveals how folk religion makes the cosmos itself a moral guarantor.

e: "heaven overturned, earth capsized" — a total upheaval; world-reversing change
d: 翻 fān (to overturn; to flip) + 覆 fù (to capsize). When the cosmos itself is described as flipped, the image captures change so total that the existing order has been inverted. Used for dramatic historical upheavals or situations where everything has changed beyond recognition. 经历了这场变革，国家发生了天翻地覆的变化。

e: Heaven is high and the emperor is far away
d: In a remote place, central authority cannot reach, so local powers do as they please. A wry comment on how rules dissolve with distance from the capital, still used for any situation where oversight is too far off to matter and people act with impunity.

e: Heavenly Empress, Holy Mother — Mazu's full honorific
d: The full formal title combines 天后 (Heavenly Empress, the highest imperial designation) with 圣母 Shèngmǔ (Holy Mother, a term shared with the Blessed Virgin in Catholic contexts, creating interesting resonance in Fujian where Portuguese missionaries arrived in the 16th century).

e: self-evident truth; axiomatic — too obvious to argue about
d: Lit: heaven's warp and earth's weft. 经 jīng = warp threads (the vertical structural threads in a loom); 义 yì = weft and righteous pattern. Together they constitute the fabric of moral reality , what is simply given. "孩子要孝顺父母，这是天经地义的事。

e: heaven's decree is hard to defy; fate is difficult to resist
d: 天命 tiānmìng (Mandate of Heaven; fate) + 难 nán (difficult) + 违 wéi (to defy; to go against). The phrase works in both the political and personal register.

e: the mandate has found its home — used of the rightful heir to power, the person heaven has chosen
d: 所归 suǒ guī (where it belongs; where it returns to). As a chengyu, 天命所归 is a verdict, not a prediction. It is said after the fact: this person succeeded, therefore heaven wanted them to succeed.

e: heaven south, earth north — from all corners of the world; talking about everything under the sun
d: 南 nán = south; 北 běi = north. The phrase works in two ways. Used of people: 天南地北的朋友 (friends from all corners of the world , scattered to the four directions, heaven-south and earth-north).

e: Heaven and humanity in sympathetic resonance — cosmic and human realms in constant responsive dialogue
d: 感 gǎn = to feel, to resonate; 应 yìng = to respond. The Han Confucian doctrine , systematized by 董仲舒 Dǒng Zhòngshū , that Heaven responds to human affairs and humans respond to Heaven's movements, all mediated through the five phases and Yin-Yang cycles.

e: "Heaven and humanity as one body" — the complete unity of cosmic and human orders
d: A variant formulation of 天人合一, with 体 (body; substance) replacing 合一 (united as one). 一体 emphasizes organic embodied unity , Heaven and humanity are not merely in accord but constitute a single body, a single substance.

p: tiān shí dì lì rén hé
e: "Heaven's timing, Earth's advantages, human harmony" — the three conditions for success
d: From Mencius (2A.1): the convergence of the right moment from Heaven, favorable terrain from Earth, and human solidarity. A practical expression of 天人合一 in strategic thought: success requires alignment with all three orders simultaneously.

p: tiānxià dà shì, fēn jiǔ bì hé
e: the great tendency of all-under-heaven: long divided, must unite; long united, must divide
d: The opening principle of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). A cyclical theory of political history: unity and division alternate as inevitably as the seasons. Endlessly cited in Chinese political discourse to frame any current period as part of a longer historical rhythm.

e: "all under heaven is at peace" — universal peace and order
d: 天下 tiānxià (all under heaven , the entire world as governed territory) + 太平 (great peace). The ideal end-state of Confucian governance and the dream of every dynasty: a world so well-ordered that there is nothing left to struggle against.

e: the world belongs to all — the realm is the public good, not private property
d: Sun Yat-sen's personal motto, drawn from the ancient Book of Rites. Inscribed on buildings and monuments across Taiwan and mainland China. The phrase directly opposes the Confucian concept of dynasties as family property (家天下 jiā tiānxià, "the realm as one family's possession").

e: all crows under heaven are equally black — it's the same everywhere; they're all the same
d: Usually cynical: no matter where you go, officials/bosses/people of that type are all equally corrupt/problematic/the same. 当官的天下乌鸦一般黑 (Officials everywhere are equally corrupt , all crows under heaven are black.) A statement of resigned cynicism about systemic problems.

p: tiānxià wú bù sàn zhī yánxí.
e: No feast under heaven goes on forever; every banquet must end.
d: A proverb woven through the novel and epitomising its theme of impermanence: every gathering, however joyful, must break up, just as the splendour of the Jia family must pass. Used widely in Chinese to console at partings and to acknowledge that good times, like all things, come to an end.

h: 天下无难事只怕有心人
p: tiānxià wú nán shì, zhǐ pà yǒuxīn rén
e: under heaven there are no difficult things — only fear the determined person
d: Determination overcomes all obstacles , there is nothing under heaven so hard that a truly committed person cannot accomplish it. A companion to 功夫不负有心人. 有心人 yǒuxīn rén = a person of resolve and intention. Used as encouragement in the face of daunting tasks: 天下无难事，只怕有心人，你一定能做到。

e: the rise and fall of the realm is the responsibility of every common person
d: Attributed to the late Ming / early Qing Confucian scholar 顾炎武 Gù Yánwǔ (1613–1682), though the current form was popularized by Liang Qichao in the late Qing. A founding text of Chinese civic patriotism.

e: the ends of the earth — sky-edge, sea-corner
d: Lit: sky-edge sea-corner. The farthest, most remote reaches of the world. High frequency in romantic poetry and pop songs about separation and longing.

e: seamless; flawless — not a flaw to be found
d: Lit: heaven's robe has no seams. The garments of heavenly beings are woven whole , no stitching, no joins. Used to praise flawless plans, flawless stories, and flawless alibis. When applied to an alibi, the idiom carries a slight edge: seamlessness itself can be suspicious.

e: a favored child of Heaven: one singularly blessed by fortune
d: Lit: Heaven's-spoiled-child. Originally said of the Xiongnu nomads who boasted Heaven's favor; now used of anyone who seems destined for success, sometimes with a touch of envy.

e: a union made by Heaven: a match made in heaven
d: Lit: Heaven-made union. A classical blessing for a marriage, suggesting the couple was destined to come together. Still used today on wedding scrolls and congratulations.

e: to stir up trouble and drive a wedge: to set people against each other
d: Lit: stir-up and sow-division. To deliberately create a gap between people who were close, by rumor or provocation. 离间 (jiàn) is to open a rift where there was none.
铁 (iron) intensifies 哥们儿. The metaphor is metal: a friendship that won't bend or rust. Reserved for the few friends you would drop everything for.

e: "listen and yet not hear" — to hear without registering; selective inattention
d: 听 (the act of listening) + 而 (and yet, connecting contrast) + 不闻 (not actually hearing). The distinction between 听 (the directed act) and 闻 (what the ear actually receives) sharpens into an idiom: you can perform the physical act of listening without anything penetrating.

e: to leave it to Heaven — to accept fate without struggle
d: Lit: listen-Heaven follow-fate. To stop fighting and let things take their natural course. Can be stoic acceptance or passive resignation depending on context. One of the most common fate-related expressions in everyday Chinese.

通 tōng (to connect, to pass through) + 灵 líng (spirit; efficacious; miraculous). The ability to communicate with spirits , the defining capacity of a shaman. In contemporary Chinese, 通灵 also appears in discussions of psychic ability, mediumship, and supernatural sensitivity more broadly.

e: "through to feeling, reaching to reason": sensible, reasonable, understanding
d: 通 (to be through to) + 情 qíng (human feeling; the way people are) + 达 dá (to reach) + 理 lǐ (reason; principle). A person who is 通情达理 understands both how people feel and what reason requires, and weighs the two fairly.

High praise for writing or speech: 通俗 (accessible, popular) and 易懂 (easy to understand) together describe an explanation pitched so clearly that anyone can follow it. The standard compliment for good teaching.

e: sharing the same sickness, they pity each other: fellow sufferers sympathize
d: From the Wú Yuè Chūnqiū. People who endure the same hardship feel a natural bond, the way two patients in one ward understand each other without explanation.

Literally "together the sweet, shared the bitter", to go through good times and bad side by side. It captures the deepest sense of 跟 as "with", a togetherness that holds through difficulty. Here 同 ("together") plays the accompanying role 跟 carries in speech.

e: of one heart and one virtue — fully unified in purpose and conduct
d: Lit: same-heart-same-virtue. The phrase for a group whose members share both inner orientation (心) and outward conduct (德). Used of teams, families, and political coalitions to describe rare and full unity , not just agreement on a goal but alignment on the moral terms by which it will be pursued.

e: to work together with one heart
d: Literally "same heart, joined strength", to pull together toward a shared goal in full unity. It is the spirit behind 一起努力 ("work hard together") raised to its ideal: not just acting jointly, but acting as one mind and one effort.

e: in the same boat, crossing together: united by a common difficulty
d: Lit: same-boat-jointly-cross. People who, sharing one boat, must row together to reach the far shore. The classical image for setting aside differences in the face of a shared crisis.

e: pain in the heart and ache in the head: bitterly grieved and resentful
d: Lit: pain-heart-ache-head. To feel grief and indignation so deep that heart and head both ache. Used for bitter regret or anger over a wrong or a loss. 对这种浪费，他感到痛心疾首 "He was bitterly grieved at such waste."

e: clear and logical at every point: well-reasoned and articulate
d: Lit: every-head-is-the-way. Said of speech or analysis that is orderly and convincing from start to finish, with each point landing soundly. 说得头头是道 "to argue every point convincingly."

e: heavy on top and light on the feet: top-heavy and unstable
d: Lit: head-heavy-feet-light. Used of anything badly balanced, with too much weight or emphasis at the top: a wobbling structure, a lopsided plan, or a dizzy, unsteady feeling.

e: throw a peach, return a plum: to repay a kindness in kind; mutual gift-giving
d: This idiom shares the verb 投 tóu (to throw; to give) that drives 投票, though it does not contain 票 itself, so it sits here as a near neighbor on the 投 thread rather than a 票 idiom. 投桃报李 comes from the Shījīng (Book of Songs): you toss me a peach, I send back a plum.

e: to advance by leaps and bounds: to progress at great speed
d: Lit: sudden-fly-fierce-advance. Said of rapid, dramatic progress in study, technology, or an economy. 科技突飞猛进 "technology advances by leaps and bounds."

e: nothing but an empty name — a title with no substance behind it
d: 徒 (merely, only) + 有 (have) + 虚名 (empty name). The sharpest everyday formulation of what 正名 opposes. A famous general who wins no battles is 徒有虚名. A top university whose graduates learn nothing is 徒有虚名.

e: the Tumu Crisis — the catastrophic defeat in which a Chinese emperor was captured by nomads
d: The 1449 capture of Emperor Yingzong at Tumu Fortress (土木堡 Tǔmùbǎo) by Oirat Mongols under Esen Khan. A turning point that ended Ming offensive posture against the steppe and initiated the Great Wall rebuilding program. Used as a metonym for military disaster born of imperial overreach.

e: push out the old and bring forth the new
d: To discard the outdated and create something new, the constant renewal that drives a thing forward into its modern form. Used of art, technology, and institutions that modernize by building fresh work on inherited foundations rather than simply repeating the past.

e: shed the womb, swap the bones: a total transformation
d: From Daoist alchemy, on the adept reborn into an immortal frame. Modern usage praises a genuine, root-and-branch change for the better.

e: the awl-tip comes through the bag — talent that emerges despite obstacles
d: From the Shǐjì (史记, Records of the Grand Historian). 颖 yǐng = the pointed tip of an awl. 脱 tuō = to escape; to break free. An awl placed in a bag will always eventually poke through: genuine talent, given any opportunity, will emerge and make itself visible.

e: Confucian on the outside, Legalist on the inside — the structural formula of Chinese imperial governance
d: A modern scholarly formulation summarizing two thousand years of Chinese governance. 外 wài = outer, exterior; 内 nèi = inner, interior. The outer face of government (edicts, titles, rituals, examination texts) was thoroughly Confucian.

e: returning the jade intact to Zhao — restoring something to its owner undamaged
d: From the Shiji biography of 蔺相如 Lin Xiangru, who carried the priceless 和氏璧 jade to the powerful state of Qin, saw through Qin's bad faith, and brought the jade safely home to Zhao through sheer nerve and cunning.

e: finished egg: to be done for, ruined, all over
d: Not a four-character chengyu but a fixed colloquial expression. 完 (wán, to finish) + 蛋 marks total collapse: 完蛋了 (wándàn le) means we're finished, it's all over.

e: perfect and without flaw — utterly complete
d: 完美 (perfect) + 无 wú (without) + 缺 quē (defect, lack, gap). Flawless to the point that nothing is missing and nothing could be improved. The two halves reinforce each other: 完美 asserts wholeness, 无缺 denies any gap.

e: the matter is finished and all is well — done and dusted
d: 完 (to finish) + 事 shì (matter) + 大吉 dàjí (greatly auspicious, all is well). Said with relief when a task is over and one can stop worrying about it , "that's that, we're done." Sometimes carries a faint note of cutting corners, of treating the mere finishing as the whole point.

e: evergreen through ten thousand ages — enduring forever
d: 万古 (ten-thousand ages, all of history) + 长青 (ever-green, perennially fresh). Used for ideas, institutions, or relationships that are wished to last beyond ordinary time.

e: the ten-thousand-li Great Wall — symbol of colossal collective effort
d: 万里 wànlǐ (ten thousand li) is figurative hyperbole. The wall's actual total length across all dynasties is approximately 21,196 km. Used metaphorically for any enormous undertaking requiring sustained collective effort.

e: "the ten-thousand-li long march" — the 1934–1935 retreat of the Red Army; any prolonged and arduous undertaking
d: 万里 (ten thousand li , vast) + 长征 (long expedition, long march). The Chinese Communist Party's Long March (1934–1935) covered approximately 12,000 kilometers as the Red Army retreated from Nationalist forces. 万里 again functions as rhetorical superlative rather than measurement.

p: wàn shì jù bèi, zhǐ qiàn dōngfēng
e: all ten thousand things are ready; only the east wind is lacking
d: From the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). Before the Battle of Red Cliffs (208 CE), Zhuge Liang tells Zhou Yu that the plan is complete in every respect , except that the wind is blowing in the wrong direction to set the enemy fleet alight.

p: wàn shì jù bèi, zhǐ qiàn dōngfēng.
e: Everything is ready; we lack only the east wind.
d: From the eve of Red Cliffs, when the allies' fire-attack plan was fully prepared but needed a wind from the east to carry the flames into Cao Cao's fleet. The line is now a common chengyu for a situation in which all preparations are complete and only one final, decisive condition is missing.

e: all things renewed — the entire world refreshed and reborn
d: 万 (ten thousand; all) + 象 (phenomena; appearances) + 更新 (to renew). The 更 is gēng, first tone. A classic New Year phrase; appears on Spring Festival banners alongside 春回大地 (spring returns to the earth).

p: wàn zhàng gāo lóu píng dì qǐ
e: A tower ten thousand zhang tall rises from flat ground
d: The folk proverb that answers impatience: every immeasurable height begins on ordinary earth.

e: ten thousand hearts as one — united as one body
d: 万众 wànzhòng = the ten thousand people / the multitudes. 一心 = one heart / one mind. Used for collective unity in times of national effort or crisis. A rallying phrase in political rhetoric and public discourse , the aspiration that multiplicity collapses back into the cosmological One.

e: ten thousand purples, a thousand reds — a riot of color; abundant beauty
d: From the Song dynasty poet Zhu Xi 朱熹: 等闲识得东风面，万紫千红总是春 , "It is easy to recognize the face of the east wind: ten thousand purples and a thousand reds , it is all spring." The phrase moved from the poem into common use as the standard expression for spring's visual abundance.

e: the music of a doomed state — decadent art that signals decline
d: From the Liji 礼记: licentious music signals a state in moral collapse. Used today to criticize art deemed nihilistic or culturally destructive.

e: mend the sheep pen after the sheep is lost
d: From the Zhanguo Ce: a man loses sheep through a hole in his pen and is told he is too late to repair it. A neighbor corrects the fatalist: remediation after a loss is not too late, it is exactly right.

p: wáng yáng bǔ láo, wéi shí wèi wǎn
e: mend the pen after the sheep is lost — it is not yet too late
d: The extended form of the idiom, almost always cited together. The second half (为时未晚, not yet too late) is the direct answer to the fatalist in the original story. The full eight-character phrase is common enough to function as a single fixed saying.

e: lose a sheep, gain an ox
d: A related phrase (not a classical chengyu in the same sense) used to describe a small loss that leads to an unexpected larger gain: the silver lining formulation. Where 亡羊补牢 is about repair, 亡羊得牛 is about serendipitous compensation. The shared 亡羊 makes the pair memorable.

e: a constant stream of coming and going — uninterrupted traffic
d: 往 wǎng (to go toward) + 来 (to come) + 不绝 (without cessation). Describes a place or relationship with continuous back-and-forth movement: traffic, commerce, correspondence, social connection. 街上人来人往，好不热闹 "People coming and going on the street , what a lively scene!"

e: rebirth in the Pure Land — the aspiration fulfilled at death
d: The central Pure Land aspiration: to depart this world and arrive in Amitābha's Pure Land at death. In eulogies and memorial contexts: "She has been reborn in the Pure Land" 她已往生净土 is the standard Buddhist formulation for death.

e: the past is like drifting smoke
d: Literally "bygone matters are like smoke", the past fading and dispersing beyond grasp. Here 往 takes its time sense, 往事 ("past events"), and the phrase carries a gentle melancholy about how what is gone slips away. The mirror of 往 reaching backward rather than ahead.

e: to work with selfless devotion; absorbed work
to see only the dust and never catch up: to be hopelessly outdistanced
d: Literally "to gaze at the dust and be unable to reach." One can see only the dust kicked up by someone far ahead, with no hope of catching them. Used to admit that another is so far superior or so far in front that one cannot hope to match them.

e: to quench thirst by gazing at plums
d: From a tale of Cao Cao, who told thirsty troops that plum groves lay ahead, so the thought of sour plums made their mouths water and eased their thirst. It means consoling oneself with an empty hope or imagined prospect. The 望 of gazing-toward is the same root that gives 希望 its reach.

e: hoping your daughter will become a phoenix — parental ambition for daughters
d: The female counterpart to 望子成龙 wàng zǐ chéng lóng (hoping your son will become a dragon). 凤 fèng (phoenix) is the female auspicious creature paired with 龙 (dragon). The phoenix (凤凰 fènghuáng) represents feminine grace, beauty, and virtue.

e: gazing till the eyes would bore through: aching with anticipation
d: Eyes straining at the road so hard they might pierce the distance. Describes longing for someone's return or news that will not come.

e: to hope ones son becomes a dragon: to long for ones child to succeed greatly
d: Literally "to hope the son becomes a dragon," the dragon being the emblem of supreme success and distinction. The classic expression of parental ambition: the deep hope that ones child will rise high in life. A close partner phrase, 望女成凤, hopes the daughter becomes a phoenix.

e: alarming words to startle the listener: scaremongering
d: Here 危 carries its older sense of high-pitched, alarming speech. Used to dismiss someone exaggerating a threat to frighten an audience. Mildly critical register.

e: danger lies in dawn-and-dusk: peril is imminent, near death
d: Sānguó Zhì era usage. 旦夕 is the span of a single day; the danger is so close it could fall within hours. Used for a dying patient or a regime about to collapse.

e: the leather cord worn through three times — the archetype of devoted scholarship
d: 韦 wéi = leather; 编 biān = cord, binding; 三绝 sān jué = worn through three times. Classical books were written on bamboo strips bound together with cords of leather or silk.

e: to compromise to keep the peace: to bend and yield so the whole holds together
d: Lit: bend-crooked-seek-wholeness. To swallow grievances and make concessions in order to preserve a relationship or an arrangement intact. Here 全 is the intact whole one bends in order to save.

e: to do evil; to commit crimes and wrongdoing
d: Lit: do-wrong-make-evil. 非 (wrong) and 歹 dǎi (bad, evil) pair up to name flagrant wrongdoing. Said of those who run riot doing harm: 为非作歹的歹徒 "evildoers who run amok."

e: to be a henchman for the tiger; to help the powerful oppress others
d: Lit: for-tiger-act-as-ghost-of-the-slain. In Chinese folklore, the ghost of someone eaten by a tiger becomes a 伥 , a spirit that lures future victims to the tiger. To 为虎作伥 is to be co-opted into serving the very power that devoured you.

e: to rid the people of a scourge
d: To eliminate a menace for the public good, as a hero kills a man-eating beast. Praising tone, used for someone who removes a real threat.

e: to be a teacher and model for others: to set an example worthy of imitation
d: 为人 wéi rén = to act as, to be for others. 师 shī = teacher. 表 biǎo = model; the standard others measure themselves against. To serve as a moral and intellectual example, especially said of teachers who must embody what they teach.

p: wéi xué rì yì, wéi dào rì sǔn.
e: In pursuit of learning, every day something is gained. In pursuit of the Dao, every day something is dropped.
d: Chapter 48. The contrast with Confucius's emphasis on continuous learning and accumulation of knowledge is probably deliberate. The Daodejing does not reject learning but insists that the Dao requires a different movement: subtraction rather than addition, unlearning rather than accumulation.

From the Book of Songs (诗经, Shījīng): the bird weaves its nest before the rains arrive. The counterpart to 亡羊补牢 , prevention before the fact. Together the two idioms cover the complete cycle of crisis management: prepare if you can, and repair decisively if prevention fails.

e: "review the old to understand the new" — the scholar's relationship to tradition
d: 温 (wēn, to warm; to review , warm water used to reheat food, hence to re-examine) + 故 (gù, old; former) + 知 (zhī, to know) + 新 (new). From the Analects of Confucius, Chapter 2.11: 子曰，温故而知新，可以为师矣。

e: the writing does not match the topic: off the point, irrelevant
d: Lit: writing-not-match-topic. Said of an essay or answer that wanders away from what was asked, or of a reply that misses the actual question. The classic teacher's note on a stray composition.

e: the four treasures of the study: brush, ink, paper, inkstone
d: 文房 is the scholar's study, the writing 房; 四宝 are its four treasures: 笔 (brush), 墨 (ink), 纸 (paper), 砚 (inkstone). The phrase names the classical toolkit of Chinese calligraphy and painting.

e: accomplished in both letters and arms: master of both pen and sword
d: Literally "civil and martial, both complete." The classic praise for a complete person who excels at both scholarship and fighting, the brush and the blade. The ideal whole human being in the traditional view, equally at home in the study and on the field.

e: writing carries the Way — literature serves moral truth
d: The classical Chinese theory of literature: writing is not merely aesthetic entertainment but a vehicle for moral truth (道 Dào). Proposed by Han Yu (韩愈) in the Tang Dynasty and central to the Chinese literary tradition.

e: refined in manner and solid in substance — the cultivated gentleman
d: From the Analects: 文质彬彬，然后君子. "When refinement (文) and substance (质) are balanced, then you have the gentleman." The ideal of 文 is not mere surface polish but the harmonious integration of outward culture with inner integrity. 彬彬 = harmonious, balanced.

e: hear the cock and rise to practice swordplay: diligent self-discipline
d: From the Jin Shu account of Zǔ Tì (祖逖), who woke at the rooster's first crow to drill with his sword. A praise word for someone who studies or trains relentlessly.

e: as stable as Mount Tai — utterly immovable, rock solid
d: Mount Tai (泰山, Shandong), the most sacred of the Five Peaks and site of imperial Heaven-sacrifice. Used to praise a person's composure, a government's stability, or a company's financial health.

e: to aspire to rule China — lit. "to inquire about the cauldrons of the Central Plains"
d: From a Spring and Autumn anecdote: the king of Chu asked Zhou envoys about the weight of the Nine Cauldrons (九鼎), signaling his ambition to displace the Zhou. 问鼎 became permanently associated with political ambition at the highest level.

e: the crux of the problem; the key issue
d: A very common phrase pairing 问题 with 关键 (key, crux) to point at the heart of a matter: 问题的关键在于… ("the crux of the problem lies in…"). Used constantly in analysis and discussion to single out what really matters, the decisive point on which everything turns.

e: "questioning the heart and finding no guilt" — to have a clear conscience; to be at peace with what one has done
d: 问 (to question; to examine) + 心 + 无愧 (without guilt; nothing to be ashamed of). To question one's own 心 and find no 愧 (guilt, shame) is the state of moral peace that comes from acting according to 良心. Used as an aspiration and as a claim. 我做这件事问心无愧。(In doing this, I have nothing on my conscience.)

e: I don't think it matters either way; I have no preference.
d: A useful everyday phrase pairing 觉得 with 无所谓 (it makes no difference, I don't mind). Used to signal an easygoing, no-strong-opinion stance when asked to choose. Shows how 觉得 frames even a non-opinion as a personal impression.

e: to go one's own way; to act as one always has
sleep on brushwood and taste gall — sustained self-discipline in pursuit of a long-deferred goal
d: From the story of 越王勾践 Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn, king of Yue, defeated and humiliated by the king of Wu around 494 BCE.

p: wū lòu piān féng lián yè yǔ
e: the roof leaks, and then it rains all night — misfortunes come in clusters
d: The Chinese equivalent of "when it rains, it pours." A leaking roof is already misfortune; continuous rain compounds it. Often quoted as half-proverb with the paired line: 船迟又遇打头风 (the boat is delayed and then hits a headwind). Very natural in everyday speech.

e: to groan without being sick: to complain for no reason
d: A literary critic's jab at writers who manufacture sorrow they do not feel. Now applied to anyone who dramatizes trivial troubles or affects suffering for effect.

e: "nothing comes to the right of it" — unrivaled; the best of its kind
d: 无 (nothing; none) + 出 (to go beyond; to surpass) + 其 (its; this) + 右 (right side). In classical Chinese ranking, the person or thing of highest rank occupied the rightmost position in certain formal arrangements. "Nothing surpasses it to the right" means nothing ranks higher.

e: all-pervading; present everywhere; reaching every corner
d: 无 wú (without; no) + 处 chù (place) + 不 bù (not) + 到 (arrive). There is no place that is not arrived at. The double negative , no place that has not been reached , produces the emphatic positive: total pervasiveness.

e: everywhere; omnipresent — present in every place
d: Lit: no-place-not-present. The double negative (无处 "no place" + 不在 "not present") creates a strong universal affirmative: present in every place without exception. Used for things that are all-pervasive , technology, a scent, an influence. 他的影响力无处不在。

e: impossible to grasp; no way to get a handle on it
d: Lit: no-way-from-grasp. Used when a situation is too fluid, complex, or uncertain to control or predict. The physical image of reaching for something and finding no surface to grip carries directly into this idiom.

e: no ground on which to hold oneself: too ashamed to show one's face
d: 无地 = no place; 自容 = to hold or hide oneself. So ashamed that there is nowhere on earth to put oneself. 容 here is the holding sense turned inward: no space will contain a person's shame. 听到批评，他羞愧得无地自容。(At the criticism, he was so ashamed he wished the ground would swallow him.)

e: "unrelated to the important" — trivial; beside the point; not worth worrying about
d: Lit: no-connection-tense-important. Used to dismiss irrelevant details or minor concerns. 这些细节无关紧要，我们不要在这里浪费时间。"These details are beside the point , let's not waste time on them." Often used as a diplomatic way to redirect a conversation.

e: of no help to the matter: useless, achieving nothing
d: Lit: no-help-to-the-matter. Here 于 means "to, with respect to," so the phrase is literally "brings no benefit to the situation." Said of an effort or remedy that fails to change anything.

e: a treasure beyond price: a priceless thing
d: 无价 (without price) marks what no sum could buy. Used for a rare heirloom, a one-of-a-kind artwork, or, warmly, for a person or a friendship.

e: nothing can be done about it — helpless; resigned; having no recourse
d: 无 (nothing) + 可 (can) + 奈何 (what can be done; how to deal with). The expression of pure helplessness: there is no available action. 无可奈何，只能接受。(There was nothing to be done; one could only accept it.) One of the most-used classical phrases in modern speech.

e: unsung hero — a hero without a name
d: Lit: without-name hero. Someone who performs heroic deeds without receiving fame or recognition. The tension between 名 (name, recognition) and 实 (substance, actual contribution) compressed into a phrase.

e: powerless; unable to do anything about it
d: Lit: have-no-ability-to-act-with-force. 无能 = lacking ability; 为力 = to exert effort/force. The standard idiom for expressing helplessness in the face of a problem. 对于这件事，我也无能为力 "I am also powerless over this matter." Formal and literary; widely used.

p: wú shì bù dēng sānbǎo diàn
e: one doesn't visit the Three Jewels hall without a reason — never come empty-handed or without purpose
d: The 三宝殿 is the hall of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, Sangha) , you don't enter it for nothing. The proverb is used to say: if someone is coming to see you or asking something, they must want something.

e: governing through non-action — the ideal Daoist political order
d: The political application of 无为: the sage ruler does so little that people think they accomplished everything themselves. 太上，下知有之 (Daodejing 17): "The best ruler , the people merely know he exists." The phrase is widely used today for management styles that empower rather than micromanage.

e: no gap worth striking — flawless, impeccable, impossible to fault
d: 无 (no) + 懈 (slack; gap; weak point) + 可 (worth) + 击 (to strike). If there is no gap worth attacking, the argument or plan is airtight. 他的计划无懈可击。(His plan is flawless.) Common in formal debate and written argument.

e: "five lights, ten colors" — multicolored and dazzling; richly varied
d: 五光 (five kinds of light) and 十色 (ten colors) together evoke a brilliant, shifting display. Used both literally, for lights and decorations that glitter in every hue, and figuratively for a world or a scene that is varied, glamorous, and a little dazzling.

e: the five lakes and four seas: from every corner of the land
d: A sweep of the whole country. Used warmly for people gathered from everywhere: 我们来自五湖四海。

e: "five limbs to the ground" — to prostrate fully; to admire with complete humility
d: 五体 (the five parts of the body: the two knees, the two elbows or hands, and the head) plus 投地 (cast to the ground). It names the Buddhist full prostration in which all five touch the floor, the deepest bodily gesture of reverence.

e: the five phases generating and overcoming each other — the self-regulating logic of the cosmos
d: The technical summary of the two cycles. 相生 xiāngshēng = mutual generation; 相克 xiāngkè = mutual overcoming/control. Together they describe a homeostatic system: generation without overcoming leads to excess; overcoming without generation leads to stagnation.

e: five shades, six colors — a riot of colors; multicolored
d: Lit: five-shades-six-colors. The standard idiom for anything vibrantly multicolored. 五 and 六 are figurative numbers (like English "many"); the compound just means extremely colorful. 市场上五颜六色的花朵 "the market's riot of colorful flowers."

e: Wu Song fights the tiger — fearless strength against great odds
d: The most famous single episode in the novel: the hero Wu Song, drunk and alone on Jingyang Ridge, kills a man-eating tiger with his bare hands.

e: highly skilled in martial arts: a formidable fighter
d: Literally "martial skill high and strong." Describes a person of outstanding fighting ability, a master whose technique is far above the ordinary. 武艺 is the craft of arms, the practised techniques of combat; 高强 marks it as superior.

e: things change, stars shift — time passes and the world turns over
d: From Wang Bo's Tang-dynasty Pavilion of Prince Teng poem: 物换星移几度秋, "things change, stars shift, how many autumns now?" The stars' slow precession as the clock of dynasties. Used for nostalgia at scale: returning to a transformed hometown, rereading an old diary.

e: when things reach their extreme, they necessarily reverse — the law of cyclical transformation
d: 物 wù = things; 极 jí = extreme, apex; 必 bì = necessarily; 反 fǎn = to reverse. This is the fundamental law of Yin-Yang cosmology, applicable to all phenomena: the hottest summer carries the seed of winter; the most powerful dynasty carries the seed of its decline; a pendulum at its extreme cannot stay…

e: "let everything exhaust its use" — no waste; make the most of every resource
d: 物 wù = things; resources; material. 尽 jìn = to exhaust; to use fully. Let every thing fully deploy its capacity, leaving nothing wasted. A principle of material ethics as much as economics: the proper relationship between a person and the world's resources is stewardship, not waste.

e: the goods fine and the price cheap: excellent value for money
d: The four-character verdict every shopper hopes to pronounce: good quality and a low price at once. Standard praise in advertising and casual recommendation alike.

e: things remain but people have changed — the bittersweet feeling of returning to a place where everything looks the same but everyone is gone
d: Lit: things-are-people-not. A key phrase in classical Chinese poetry for the emotional experience of historical rupture: looking at unchanged landscapes after dynasties have fallen. Deeply appropriate to the Yuan-Ming transition, when the same cities stood but an entire ruling order had vanished.

e: things gather by kind: like attracts like, birds of a feather flock together
d: Lit: things-by-kind-gather. From the idea that creatures of a sort come together; often paired with 人以群分 "people divide into groups," and used, sometimes pointedly, of who keeps company with whom.

e: To Stray onto the Wrong Road
d: The four-character idiom for taking a wrong turn, whether morally, professionally, or literally. Where 迷途知返 describes the recovery, 误入歧途 describes the moment things went wrong.

e: "looking at flowers through mist" — seeing something obscurely, without clarity
d: 雾 (mist, fog) + 里 (inside, within) + 看花 (looking at flowers). The object of perception is real, but the medium prevents clear sight. Used for situations where the truth is obscured , murky political signals, ambiguous intentions, confusing circumstances.

e: "the evening sun descends in the west" — dusk; things in decline
d: 夕阳 (setting sun) + 西 (west) + 下 (to descend). A classic image from Tang dynasty poetry: the sun dropping below the western horizon. Used literally for beautiful sunsets and metaphorically for the decline of an era, a career, or a life.

e: the Western Pure Land — and by extension, any paradise or blissful realm
d: The formal name 西方极乐世界 Xīfāng Jílè Shìjiè is abbreviated to 西方极乐 in common usage. In pure religious context: Amitābha's Buddha-field. In broader cultural use: any ideal realm of beauty, abundance, and peace.

e: "every breath mutually connected" — closely and inextricably interconnected
d: Lit: breath-breath-mutually-connected. 息 = breath. The image: two systems breathing in such synchrony that they cannot be separated. Used for things that are organically and necessarily connected. 这两个问题息息相关，解决一个就能推动另一个。"These two issues are inextricably linked , solving one will advance the other."

e: grinning cheekily: to behave with a flippant, unserious grin
d: A face stuck in a smirk, used to describe someone who refuses to take a moment seriously. Often a parent's rebuke to a child who jokes through a scolding.

e: to grow so used to a thing that it seems ordinary
d: Lit: practice-take-to-be-normal. What was once strange or hard becomes routine through repetition, until one no longer notices it. Often said of bad habits or hardships one has stopped questioning.

e: move the post, establish credibility — demonstrate that stated commitments will be honored
d: Shang Yang's wooden post demonstration before his Qin reforms: post a reward, honor it fully, establish that the state means what it says.

e: joy beyond what one hoped — overjoyed by surprise
d: 喜 (delight) arriving from outside (外) the range of expectation (望). The precise word for good news you did not dare hope for: the scholarship, the recovered wallet, the friend at the airport gate. Stronger and more specific than 很高兴.

e: as long as you like it, that's enough
d: A warm everyday phrase, not a classical chengyu, used when giving a gift or making a choice for someone: if you like it, that's all that matters. It captures a generous, easygoing attitude and is one of the most common natural uses of 喜欢 in spoken Chinese.

e: brimming with joy: radiant with a festive, happy spirit
d: Lit: festive air spilling over. 洋洋 paints joy overflowing in every direction. Said of a face, a household, or a whole town lit up with celebration, a stock phrase at weddings and the New Year.

e: glad to hear and pleased to see — popular and well-liked
d: Describes something the public genuinely enjoys and welcomes, literally "glad to hear it and happy to see it." 喜 (glad) and 乐 lè (happy) pair with 闻 (hear) and 见 (see). Often used of art, entertainment, or activities that are widely and warmly received.

e: joy takes shape in the face: visibly delighted
d: Lit: joy 喜 takes form 形 upon 于 the complexion 色. Happiness that cannot be hidden and shows plainly on the face. Here 形 is verbal, "to take shape, to appear," a clear window onto the verb sense of the character.

Literally "the early-comers and the later-arrivers", the order of precedence set by who came first. It rests on the same 先 ("first") and 后 ("after") that frame 然后, here applied to fairness in turn-taking and priority. The natural order of a queue.

e: "first courtesy, then arms" — try diplomacy before resorting to force
d: From the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). The classical strategic principle: open with 礼 (courteous communication), and only if that fails escalate to 兵 (military force or coercive action).

e: what enters first becomes master: first impressions dominate later judgment
d: Lit: first-enter-become-master. The idea that lodges in the mind earliest takes the seat of authority and colors everything after it, the classical name for the grip of a first impression or a prior bias.

e: petty men first, gentlemen after — settle terms up front
d: The contract-signing proverb: state the money, the split, and the deadlines with un-gentlemanly explicitness now, so that everyone can afford to be a gentleman later. Spoken at the start of partnerships between friends precisely because friendship is what it protects.

e: the note beyond the strings: an unspoken meaning, the overtone behind the words
d: Lit: outside-the-string's sound. The sense a speaker implies without saying it outright, like the overtones a plucked string sets ringing. To catch the 弦外之音 is to hear what someone really means.

e: obvious; plain to see: needing no explanation
d: Lit: evident-and-easy-to-see. The 而 joins "evident" to "easily seen," so plain that it is grasped at a glance. Often opens a sentence stating something taken as self-evident.

e: to appear in person and teach by example: to instruct from one's own experience
d: Lit: show-the-body-and-expound-the-teaching. Originally Buddhist, of a deity appearing in bodily form to preach. Now it means to teach others by drawing on what one has personally lived through.

e: to complement each other: two things that reinforce and complete one another
d: Lit: mutually-assist mutually-complete. Said of two factors that work together so that each makes the other stronger, like theory and practice or form and content.

e: to be close and loving — mutual affection between people
d: Lit: mutually-close mutually-love. The standard phrase for loving harmony in a family or couple. Often used in toasts and wedding speeches.

h: 相濡以沫，不如相忘于江湖
p: xiāng rú yǐ mò, bùrú xiāng wàng yú jiānghú
e: Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes than to sustain each other with spit
d: From 大宗师. The first half, 相濡以沫, has become an independent chengyu meaning "mutual support and care in difficult circumstances" (the fish sustaining each other in a drying puddle). Used positively for devoted couples or friends who help each other through hardship.

e: to depend on one another for life; to be each other's only support
d: 相依 "mutually depending" plus 为命 "for life." Said of two people whose survival depends on each other: a widow and her child, two siblings orphaned together, an old couple in their final years. Carries deep emotional weight; not used lightly. Often appears in family stories and biographical writing.

e: incense smoke; the vitality of a temple's active veneration
d: Literally "incense fire" or "incense smoke," but 香火 carries meanings beyond the physical act of burning. A temple with 香火鼎盛 xiānghuo dǐngshèng (incense burning vigorously) is a temple with a healthy, active congregation, good reputation, and real spiritual efficacy.

e: to think of squares and devise methods: to try every possible means
d: Lit: think-method-set-up-method. To rack one's brains for a way through, doing whatever it takes. 方 and 法 here both carry the "method" sense, doubled for emphasis.

e: to let the mind wander into improper territory; lost in fantasy
d: 想 xiǎng (to think; to imagine) + 入 rù (to enter; to go into) + 非非 fēifēi (beyond right and wrong; in Buddhist usage, the realm beyond ordinary thought).

e: a small dish on a plate: a piece of cake, an easy matter
d: Lit: small-dish-one-saucer. A 小菜 is a minor side dish, trivial next to the main course, so 小菜一碟 means a task so easy it is hardly worth mentioning. 这对我来说是小菜一碟 "this is a piece of cake for me."

p: xiǎohái méi niáng, shuō lái huà cháng
e: the child has no mother: it's a long story
d: A 歇后语 (xiēhòuyǔ) two-part saying. The literal image, a motherless child, sets up the punchline 说来话长, "it's a long story." Spoken as a preface when the backstory is tangled and the speaker hardly knows where to begin.

e: just a kid, only a child
d: Colloquial set phrase. The trailing 家 marks a category of person; said dismissively or fondly of someone too young to know better. "你一个小孩子家懂什么。"
Describes adult behavior that is petty or babyish. The 气 (qì) suffix turns a noun into a temperament. Everyday spoken register: "他这样太小孩子气了。"

e: the petty man gets his moment — power in unworthy hands
d: 得志 is achieving one's ambitions; attached to 小人 it names the special insufferability of the schemer promoted. The stock description of the new supervisor swaggering through a department, and of every court favorite in the historical novels.

e: to make a big production of a small topic — to overreact
d: 小 xiǎo (small) + 题 tí (topic, subject) + 大 dà (big) + 做 (to make, to treat). Originally from the examination tradition, where a trivial topic was expanded into a grand essay; now it means blowing a minor matter out of proportion.

e: with extreme care and caution; treading very lightly
d: Lit: small-heart wing-wing. The 翼翼 reduplication comes from the Shijing (Classic of Poetry) where it described birds folding their wings carefully.

e: a dagger hidden in a smile: friendly on the surface, treacherous beneath
d: Lit: laugh-inside hide-knife. Traced to the Tang minister Lǐ Yìfǔ, whose mild smile masked a ruthless heart. Names a person whose warmth is a weapon, the dark twin of 微笑.

e: hold the emperor to command the lords — rule through a puppet figurehead
d: Cao Cao's signature strategy: control a powerless legitimate ruler and issue your own orders in their name. Now a standard idiom for anyone who wields real power from behind a respectable figurehead, in politics or business. It names the gap between formal authority and actual control.

Lit: heart-not-present-there. 焉 yān is a classical demonstrative "there." The heart/mind (心 xīn , the seat of consciousness in Chinese tradition) is absent from the place where the body sits. Used to describe distraction, daydreaming, or emotional distance during a conversation or task. 他上课时总是心不在焉。

e: heart-urgent, fire-scorching — desperately impatient and anxious
d: Lit: heart-urgent-fire-scorch. The sensation of being so anxious that you feel fire scorching your insides. Used for people in unbearable suspense, waiting for important news.

e: heart anxious as if burning: consumed with worry
d: 焚 (fén) is to set ablaze. The heart so 急 it feels on fire, used for someone waiting in agony for urgent news. Literary and intense.

e: quick heart, straight mouth — frank and direct by nature
d: Lit: heart-fast-mouth-straight. A description of someone whose inner state and outer speech are perfectly aligned: no strategic filtering, no diplomatic softening. Used as a compliment among people who value directness, and occasionally as an excuse after saying something pointed.

e: heart vast, spirit at ease — expansive peace and contentment in beautiful surroundings
d: 旷 kuàng = open; vast (like an open plain). 怡 yí = pleased; comfortable. The specific feeling of contentment and openness experienced in a beautiful landscape, after a burden lifts, or at a moment of rare clarity. Common at scenic spots: 站在山顶，令人心旷神怡。

e: "heart receives, spirit understands" — to understand without words; to grasp intuitively
d: Lit: heart-receive-spirit-comprehend. The ideal of Chinese social understanding: no explicit statement is needed. You see, you understand, you nod. This is 意思 operating at its highest level , the meaning is fully communicated without ever being spoken. 他点了点头，心领神会。

e: heart full and wishes fulfilled: perfectly content and satisfied
d: Lit: heart-full-intent-satisfied. Pairs 心 and 意 again, both filled to the brim. Said of someone wanting for nothing, the calm fullness of having one's desires met.

e: heart and mind unsettled: distracted and uneasy
d: Lit: heart-spirit-not-settled. Said of a restless, distracted state in which the mind cannot come to rest, often from worry or anticipation. The opposite of 镇定.

p: xīn wài wú lǐ, xīn wài wú wù
e: outside the mind there is no principle; outside the mind there are no things
d: Two formulations of Wang Yangming's central thesis in their most direct form. 心外无理 xīn wài wú lǐ directly contradicts Zhu Xi: principle is not outside the mind awaiting investigation.

e: may what the heart wishes come true
d: 心 xīn (heart) + 想 xiǎng (think; wish) + 事 shì (matter; affair) + 成 chéng (to succeed; to be accomplished). A blessing structure: heart-wishes turn into accomplished realities. Among the most common felicitations in Chinese , standard at New Year (新年快乐，心想事成！), birthdays, and before examinations.

e: with one's whole heart and every thought — to dwell on something constantly
d: A doubled, rhythmic phrase stacking 心 (heart) and 念 (thought): every beat of the heart, every flicker of mind, bent on one object. 她心心念念想回家 (her every thought is set on going home).

e: heart imprinting on heart — deep mutual understanding; soul connection
d: 印 yìn = seal; to stamp. Like two wax seals pressed together making a perfect impression , silent, complete correspondence between two people's inner worlds. 他们心心相印，不需要多说话就能理解彼此。

e: hearts share the rhinoceros horn — telepathic understanding; being on the same wavelength
d: From a Tang poem by Li Shangyin (李商隐): 身无彩凤双飞翼，心有灵犀一点通. The rhinoceros horn was believed in classical natural philosophy to have a channel running through its center , an image of two hearts with a shared passage between them, allowing understanding to flow without words.

e: mind like a monkey, will like a horse — a restless, unsettled mind
d: A Buddhist-Daoist image, central to the novel's allegory, of the mind as an unruly monkey and the will as a bolting horse, leaping and galloping where it pleases. The Monkey King is literally the 心猿, the mind-monkey, who must be tamed.

e: the heart knows and the belly is clear — everyone understands, nobody says it
d: Knowledge distributed through the torso: heart knowing, belly bright. The phrase for open secrets: the office 心知肚明 about why the manager left; both negotiators 心知肚明 about the real bottom line. Understanding at its most silent.

e: flourishing and thriving: full of vigor and growth
d: Lit: joyful-joyful, facing-flourishing. 欣欣 is the look of glad, vigorous growth; 向荣 is turning toward flourishing. Said of plants in full bloom, and by extension of a thriving enterprise or society.

e: the new replaces the old: metabolism; constant renewal
d: Lit: new and old, replacing and discharging. The scientific term for metabolism, the body taking in the new and expelling the spent. Figuratively, the natural cycle by which fresh things supersede worn-out ones in any system.

e: to open the mouth like a river — to speak carelessly; to say whatever comes to mind without regard for truth
d: 信 xìn here shifts sense: 信 kǒu = to trust one's mouth, to follow wherever the mouth goes (the archaic sense of 信 as "to follow freely"). 开河 kāi hé = to open a river, to let it flow unobstructed.

e: pick up casually with a free hand — to write or create with effortless skill
d: Lit: trust-hand-pick up-come. Used of writers, calligraphers, and scholars who produce refined work without apparent effort. The idiom implies deep mastery: the hand moves freely because the mind no longer needs to deliberate. Often said of someone who writes beautifully on demand.

e: arrayed like stars, spread like chess pieces — dotted everywhere
d: 星罗 (netted like stars) + 棋布 (laid out like go stones). The standard descriptor for anything scattered densely across a landscape: lakes on a delta, islands in an archipelago, convenience stores in Shanghai. The two images, night sky and go board, are both grids the classical eye knew intimately.

e: a single spark can set the prairie ablaze
d: 星星 here is the spark sense of 星. The image of fire racing across a plain is ancient (the Book of Documents already warns of fire on the grassland), but the phrase's modern fame comes from Mao Zedong's 1930 essay taking it as a title, arguing a small revolutionary force could ignite the country.

e: a walking corpse, a moving piece of flesh — alive in body but dead in spirit
d: Lit: walking-corpse, walking-flesh. Said of someone who has lost the inner life that makes a person alive in any meaningful sense , going through motions without thought, feeling, or purpose. Sharp, almost cruel; reserved for those judged to have given up entirely.

e: every trade produces its champion — every line of work has its top practitioner
d: Lit: every-row produces a 状元 (the top scholar in the imperial exam). The folk-wisdom rebuttal to anyone who says one trade is beneath another: every trade has its master, every craft has its top practitioner, and excellence is available wherever you are.

e: like drifting clouds and flowing water — natural, effortless, unforced
d: Lit: walking-clouds, flowing-water. The classical praise for prose, calligraphy, conversation, or any skilled action that has reached the point of unforced motion. The sister-image to 自然 (naturalness): the result is fluid because nothing is being held against the grain.

e: walk throughout the world — to travel the world boldly
d: The romantic image of the 江湖 adventurer or itinerant scholar: someone who has traveled all under Heaven, accumulating experience and connections. The phrase captures the Chinese ideal of the person who has moved through the world and is at home everywhere.

e: a lone form, a single shadow: solitary and without companions
d: Lit: the form is alone, the shadow is single. The mirror image of 形影不离: here there is only one form and its one shadow, no one alongside. A literary, somewhat melancholy phrase for a person who is utterly on their own.

e: all shapes and colors: of every kind, all sorts
d: Lit: shape-shape, color-color. The reduplication piles up variety: people, goods, schemes, opinions of every imaginable kind. 形形色色的人 = all sorts of people. Often carries a faint edge of "a mixed bag," not all of it admirable.

e: form and shadow never part: inseparable
d: Lit: form and shadow do not separate. A shadow follows its form everywhere; two people who are 形影不离 are constant companions, always together. Warm and affectionate, used for close friends, devoted couples, or a child who will not leave a parent's side.

e: spirits high, expression ablaze — in jubilant high spirits
d: Originally literary criticism: Liu Xie's Wenxin Diaolong used 兴高而采烈 to praise the poet Ji Kang's lofty inspiration and brilliant style. The phrase migrated from describing writing to describing faces, and now marks any scene of visible collective joy: children on the last day of school arrive 兴高采烈.

e: the lessons of rise and fall — the standard analytical frame for the Taiping in modern Chinese historiography
d: 兴 (rise, flourish) + 亡 (fall, perish) + 教训 (lesson, warning). Not a fixed classical chengyu but a recurring analytical phrase in modern Chinese historical writing, particularly in discussions of the Taiping.

e: a matter of life and death: bearing directly on survival
d: Literally "bearing on life itself." Here 性命 means life, the vital nature that animates the body. The phrase marks something as gravely serious, a matter on which survival hangs, as in 性命攸关的决定, a life-or-death decision.

e: much ill fortune, little good — the outlook is grim
d: 多 and 少 as a probability report: on the scale of outcomes, the bad end is heavy. The stock phrase of thriller narration and worried families when someone has gone missing; expect it in every wuxia novel's darkest chapter.

The full set of siblings named in birth-order pairs: 兄 (elder brother), 弟 (younger brother), 姐 (elder sister), 妹 (younger sister). A staple four-character phrase, and one of the few common ones to carry 姐 directly.

e: sharing joys and sorrows: bound together by a common fate
d: Lit: joy-sorrow-mutually-connected. Two parties so closely tied that whatever befalls one befalls the other, the deep 关系 in which fortunes rise and fall as one.

e: to watch from the sidelines with folded arms: to look on without lifting a finger
d: Lit: sleeve-hands-aside-watch. With hands tucked in the sleeves, the onlooker stands by and does nothing while others struggle. A reproach for passivity and refusal to help.

e: "a mind as open as a valley" — profound receptivity; the deepest form of intellectual humility
d: The Daoist counterpart to the Confucian 谦谦君子. Where the Confucian formulation focuses on the social expression of humility in hierarchical relationships, 虚怀若谷 focuses on the inner orientation , the mind that has genuinely emptied itself of the need to be right, to have known first, to defend its exi…

e: to have only its surface: impressive on the outside but hollow within; all show and no substance
d: 虚 xū = empty; hollow; in vain. 有其表 yǒu qí biǎo = to have (only) its outer appearance. The phrase describes something or someone that looks fine on the surface but lacks real worth underneath. 这家公司虚有其表，其实早就负债累累。

e: the noisy guest usurps the host: a secondary thing overshadows the main one
d: Lit: clamoring-guest-seizes-host. Said when something minor draws all the attention away from what should be central, like a sideshow that swallows the main event or a flashy detail that buries the point.

p: xuē jiān nǎodai wǎng lǐ zuān
e: to sharpen one's head and bore in: to push to the front of the queue
d: A colloquial saying, not a classical 成语, paired here with 加塞儿 (jiāsāir, to cut the line). Mentioned to contrast the orderly 排队 ideal with the elbows-out reality of a crowded queue.

e: Learning cannot stop — the process of cultivation has no natural endpoint
d: Opening line of the Xunzi and of the 劝学 chapter, the programmatic statement of Xunzi's entire educational philosophy. 已 yǐ: to stop, to cease. The philosophical force follows from the 性恶论: if goodness is not innate but must be cultivated, then the cultivation is never complete by its own logic.

e: to study and constantly practice what one has learned — the joy of learning
d: The opening phrase of the Analects (1.1). 时 shí means "at the right times" or "constantly/regularly"; Confucius is describing not cramming but sustained, rhythmic practice. 习 xí originally depicted a young bird practicing flight: iteration until mastery.

p: xué ér shí xí zhī, bù yì yuè hū?
e: Is it not a pleasure to learn and repeatedly practice what you have learned?
d: Opening line of the Analects (1.1). The word 说 here is read yuè, an archaic form of 悦 "pleased, delighted." The passage continues: "Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar? Is it not a mark of the noble person not to be resentful when others do not recognize him?" Three questions that establi…

e: excel in learning, then enter officialdom
d: From the Analects (子张 chapter): the formulation attributed to Confucius's disciple Zixia establishing the connection between scholarly achievement and public service. 优 (yōu) means to excel, to have surplus capacity; 仕 (shì) means to serve in office.

e: "learning fills five carts" — immensely learned; erudite
d: 学 (learning) is 富 (rich enough) to fill 五车 (five cartloads of books). The image comes from an age when books were bamboo strips, so that a serious library was measured by the cartload. Originally said of the philosopher Hui Shi, whose writings were said to fill five carts.

e: learning has no boundary — there is always more to know
d: Lit: learning-has-no-stopping-point. The classical formulation of intellectual humility , no matter how much one has learned, the frontier of knowledge remains inexhaustible. Used to encourage continued study and to discourage complacency.

e: learn in order to apply — practical application of knowledge
d: Lit: learn-by-means-of-reach-use. The Confucian insistence that learning is not ornamental but practical: knowledge must be applied in action to have value. The opposite of empty book-learning (书呆子 shū dāizi, "bookworm" in the pejorative sense).

e: frost on top of snow — to make a bad situation even worse
d: 雪 xuě (snow) + 上 shàng (on top of) + 加 jiā (to add) + 霜 shuāng (frost). Frost piled on snow already covering the ground: one hardship stacked on another. The everyday equivalent of "to rub salt in the wound" or "when it rains, it pours." 他刚失业，妻子又生病了，真是雪上加霜。

e: to send charcoal in the snow: timely help when it is needed most
d: The image is bringing fuel to someone freezing in a blizzard. Praises aid that arrives at the moment of real need, the warm counterpart of 锦上添花 (adding flowers to brocade), which only embellishes what is already fine. Still in everyday use.

e: blood and flesh linked: tied as closely as flesh to blood
d: A near-twin of 骨肉相连, stressing the living, circulating closeness between people, or between an individual and a cause they cannot separate from.

e: to advance step by step in order
d: Literally "following the sequence, advancing gradually", to progress in proper order without rushing. It is the principle behind any 先…然后…最后 plan: each step in its turn, the next only after the last. A watchword in learning and training.

e: trained to a standard: well-drilled, disciplined
d: 素 here means a long-cultivated grounding. Praises a team, unit, or staff whose competence is visibly the product of systematic 训练 rather than luck.

e: not a crow or sparrow to be heard — dead silence
d: The silence so complete even the loudest birds have stopped. The stock description of a classroom after a hard question, a courtroom before a verdict, a banquet after an unwise toast. Its cousin 悄无声息 describes stealth rather than hush.

e: strict in disciplining oneself: hold yourself to a high standard
d: Lit: strict-toward-disciplining-self. Often paired with 宽以待人, "lenient toward others," to describe the admired character who is hard on the self and gentle with everyone else.

e: words that always hit the mark; speech that is measured and unfailingly accurate
d: From Analects XI.14: Confucius describes a man who rarely speaks , 不言则已，一言必中: but when he does, always hits the target. 中 zhòng here means "center; bull's-eye," not "middle." The standard for speech that earns its right to be heard: few words, each one aimed and landing.

e: "words cannot exhaust meaning" — the inadequacy of language; what remains unsaid
d: Lit: words-not-exhaust-meaning. A classical lament about the limits of language , that what one truly means always exceeds what words can carry. Found in literary correspondence, essays, and poetry. Often appears at the end of letters: 语言有限，言不尽意。

e: to teach by word and by example: to instruct both through speech and through one's own conduct
d: Lit: words pass it on, the body teaches it. Describes the ideal of a teacher or parent who not only explains in words (言传) but also models the lesson through their own actions (身教). The deeper teaching is the one carried by example.

e: to speak and be trustworthy — to be as good as one's word
d: 言 yán (to speak; words) + 而 ér (and; then; connecting two qualities) + 有 yǒu (to have; to possess) + 信 xìn (trustworthiness).

e: let the words return to the main story: to get back to the main topic
d: Lit: words return to the proper narrative. A storyteller's phrase, after a digression, for steering back to the central thread. Notably 传 takes the zhuàn reading here, since 正传 means the main body of the tale, the narrative proper, not a casual transmission.

e: brief words, complete meaning — concise and comprehensive
d: 简 jiǎn = brief, few; 意 yì = meaning, intention; 赅 gāi = complete, thorough (a relatively rare character used almost exclusively in this idiom). The highest praise for a piece of writing or a speaker: nothing wasted, nothing missing.

e: "words heard, plans followed" — to comply with every word and plan
d: 言 (words) + 听 (heeded) + 计 (plans, strategies) + 从 (followed). Whatever someone says is accepted; whatever they plan is implemented. Used to describe a relationship of complete compliance , a ruler who accepts all counsel from a trusted advisor, or a person who follows another uncritically.

e: words and actions align — to practice what you preach
d: 言 yán (words) + 行 xíng (actions) + 一致 yīzhì (consistent; in agreement). The Confucian virtue of correspondence between speech and conduct. Used as a positive description of trustworthy, reliable people, and as a standard against which behaviour is measured.

e: covering one's ears to steal the bell — self-deception
d: From the Lüshi Chunqiu: a thief found the great bell of the fallen Fan clan too heavy to carry, decided to break it up, and covered his own ears against the clang so no one would hear.

e: eyes blurring, vision tangling — dazzled, overwhelmed by abundance
d: Lit: eye-flower-tangle-disorder. Used for the sensory overload of a busy market, a fireworks display, a dazzling performance: too much beauty or activity to take in at once. Almost always positive in tone (the overload of richness, not chaos).

e: to feel proud and elated; to finally breathe out after long suffering
d: Lit: raise-eyebrows-exhale-qi. The physical sensation of relief and pride after enduring hardship or injustice. The eyebrows lift, the breath that was held in tension is finally released. Used for vindication, promotion after years of struggle, or national pride after historical humiliation.

e: play up strengths, avoid weaknesses: lean into what you do well
d: Common in advice and strategy contexts; the practical companion to 取长补短.

e: obey openly, defy in secret — to comply in appearance while resisting in private
d: 阳 yáng (openly) + 奉 fèng (to obey; to comply) + 阴 yīn (covertly) + 违 wéi (to disobey). To nod and agree to someone's face while quietly doing the opposite behind their back. The phrase turns on the 阴 / 阳 contrast of overt and covert: the visible compliance is 阳, the hidden defiance is 阴.

e: to support the family and feed its mouths: to provide for one's household
d: Lit: support-family-keep-alive-mouths. Here 活 is causative, to keep alive by feeding. The duty of the breadwinner to put food on the table and sustain everyone under the roof.

e: to chew and gnaw on words — nitpicking at wording; pedantic attention to phrasing
d: 咬 = to bite; 嚼 = to chew. Vividly imagines someone masticating language rather than simply reading it. Can be used approvingly (careful, attentive reading) or critically (pedantry, missing the point). Context determines the register.

e: the medicine arrives, the illness is gone: an instant, effective cure
d: A praise phrase for a skilled doctor or a decisive remedy. Extended to any solution that fixes a problem cleanly and at once.

p: yào fēng dé fēng, yào yǔ dé yǔ
e: want wind, get wind; want rain, get rain — getting whatever one wishes
d: Used to describe someone who gets everything they ask for: a pampered child, a powerful person, someone in a position where nothing is refused. The parallelism of 要…得… (want…obtain…) is the construction backbone. Can be admiring or envious. 他在家里要风得风，要雨得雨，什么都不缺。

e: mastery of one's work comes from diligence: skill is born of effort
d: Lit: work, refined-through, diligence. From Han Yu's essay on study: 业精于勤，荒于嬉, "mastery comes from diligence and is ruined by play." A maxim that one's craft or learning is perfected only through steady, hard application.
He decorated his palace with dragons, until a real one appeared. The idiom for loving what you only love in the abstract.

e: to cancel with one stroke of the pen: to write off entirely
d: Lit: one-stroke-cross-out. With a single line drawn through the ledger, a debt or a past grievance is wiped clean. Used of forgiving a debt or letting an old matter be settled and forgotten.

e: "to cross over in a single step" — to clear an obstacle in one move
d: Not a classical 成语 but a fixed conversational formula. Often used in development and policy rhetoric: 一步跨过工业化 "to leap past industrialization in a single step." Carries a faint flavor of skipping stages: sometimes admiring (decisive progress), sometimes ironic (rushing through what should have been…

e: "one step, one footprint" — steady, methodical progress
d: Lit: each step leaves exactly one footprint; nothing rushed, nothing skipped. A modern proverb for diligent, unhurried work that builds on itself. Often used in career advice, study guidance, and praise for craftsmen.

e: one sings, a hundred answer: a single voice draws a crowd of agreement
d: One person 唱 starts the note and a hundred others 和 (hè) chime in. Used for an idea or call that instantly wins broad, eager support.

e: one sings, the other echoes: to chime in and back each other up
d: Originally one voice leads and another harmonizes (和 hè, to respond in tune). Now usually mildly negative: two people egging each other on or colluding to push the same line.

e: fixed and unchanging; rigidly the same — set in stone; never varying
d: 成 chéng here carries its classical sense of "established; fixed; accomplished." Lit: "once established, not changing." The phrase carries a critical edge, describing something or someone that has refused all adaptation.

e: touch and it ignites — a situation on the verge of explosion
d: Lit: one-touch-immediately-fire. A crisis situation where the slightest action will trigger an explosion: political tensions, a fragile negotiation, volatile emotions. Originally describing hair-trigger mechanisms, now widely applied to any situation of extreme tension.

Literally "one stamp of the foot and it is done," to accomplish something in a single easy stroke. Most often used in the negative, to warn that hard things cannot be done all at once: 学语言不能一蹴而就 ("you can't master a language in one go"). The single-action 一 again, the cousin of 一下子.

e: a dot and a drop: bit by bit, little by little
d: Lit: one-dot-one-drop. The small increments by which patient effort accumulates. 一点一滴地积累 "to build up bit by bit."

e: not moving a muscle: perfectly still, motionless
d: Lit: one-move-not-move. The everyday phrase for total stillness, a person frozen in place, an animal holding its breath. The doubled 动 frames the stillness as the complete absence of motion.

p: yī ér zài, zài ér sān
e: once, then again, then a third time — time after time; repeatedly
