感 gǎn (to feel) + 情 qíng (feeling). The broad word for emotional feeling, and especially the affection that builds up between people: 他们感情很好 "they have a close bond." Also "to develop feelings": 日久生情 "feelings grow with time."

e: to infect; to inspire; to spread into
d: 感 gǎn + 染 rǎn (to dye; to stain; to spread, as dye spreads through cloth). The same word covers pathogen transmission and emotional contagion, both understood as resonance spreading from one body to another, rooted in the classical cosmology of qì 气.

感 gǎn + 伤 shāng (wound; grief). The heart wounded by what it feels. Tender, autumnal. The feeling of parting, of beauty that cannot last. A key register in classical Chinese poetry and the ci 词 lyric tradition.

感 gǎn + 受 shòu (to receive; to undergo; to be a recipient). Something comes to you and is taken in. Emphasizes the experiential process rather than the end-state, richer and more embodied than 感觉. Common in art criticism, travel writing, and introspective prose.

e: to exclaim with feeling; to marvel
d: 感 gǎn + 叹 tàn (to sigh; to exclaim). When emotion erupts as an exclamation. Memorable fact: 感叹号 gǎntànhào = the exclamation mark (!). The character literally encodes the grammar of feeling.

e: felt insight; wisdom from lived experience
d: 感 gǎn + 悟 wù (to awaken; enlightenment; the word for Buddhist satori). Insight that comes from experience touching the heart. Deeper than knowledge.

感 gǎn + 谢 xiè (to thank; originally: water overflowing, pouring out one's feelings). Warmer and more sincere than 谢谢. Standard in writing, speeches, and formal situations. Also functions as a noun in 表示感谢.

感 gǎn + 应 yìng (to respond; to echo). Used in both physics (电磁感应 diàncí gǎnyìng, electromagnetic induction) and classical cosmology. The doctrine of 天人感应 tiān rén gǎnyìng, Heaven and humanity in constant resonant dialogue, is a pillar of Han Confucian thought.
感 gǎn + 知 zhī (to know; cognition). Perception as an act of knowing: the full cycle from sensation to understanding. The most formal and academic of the four.

Bottoms up , "dry cup." The standard toast call, implying the glass is to be emptied. Contrasted with 随意 (suíyì, "as you like"), which allows partial drinking. 干杯 is the stronger and more committed version. Refusing to 干杯 with someone who has singled you out for a toast is a social rebuff.

e: to work; to do manual labor
d: 干 gàn (to do, to labor) + 活 huó (work, a task). The everyday spoken phrase for doing physical or hands-on work. Colloquial and slightly blue-collar in flavor, the verb you reach for about chores, jobs on a site, or work around the house.
Stems and Branches: the shorthand for the combined system of Ten Heavenly Stems and Twelve Earthly Branches used to name years, months, days, and two-hour periods.

e: just now · already · formerly, the past-pointing adverbs
d: 刚 gāng (just now) places an action in the immediate past: 他刚走 (he just left). 已经 yǐjīng (already) pairs with 了 to mark a completed state: 我已经吃了 (I've already eaten). 以前 yǐqián (before, formerly) frames a whole clause in the past: 我以前住在上海 (I used to live in Shanghai).

刚 gāng (just; barely) + 才 cái. A time word for the very recent past, the moment that has only just passed: 刚才他还在这儿 "he was still here just now." Here 才 keeps its sense of a threshold only just crossed.
钢 gāng (steel) + 笔 bǐ. The fountain pen, named for its steel nib. Its cousins fill out the modern desk: 圆珠笔 yuánzhūbǐ (ballpoint), 毛笔 máobǐ (brush), 铅笔 qiānbǐ (pencil).

e: height difference; high and low; relative level; social hierarchy
d: 高 (high) + 低 (low). The paired antonym compound that covers any vertical differential: the height gap between two objects, the difference in quality between two options, or the gap in social standing between two people.
"High boron-silicon glass," resistant to thermal shock. 耐热 (nàirè) is heat-resistant, 温差 (wēnchā) the temperature difference it can survive, 爆裂 (bàoliè) bursting or shattering.
高 (high) + 山 (mountain). A tall mountain , the compound appears in geography, poetry, and cultural discourse.

高 (high, superior) + 手 (hand; skill; person with a skill). A superior hand , someone with excellent technique. 象棋高手 (chess master); 编程高手 (programming expert); 武林高手 (martial arts master, from wuxia fiction). Colloquial and approving. The opposite is 新手 xīnshǒu (newcomer, novice).

Trains are booked on the official 12306 app or site (it has an English version) or through travel apps, and your passport is the ticket: it is checked at the station entrance and at the gate. 动车 (dòngchē) are slightly slower bullet trains. Arrive early; large stations have security checks.

e: so happy (she) jumped up — adj + 得 + result
d: 得 can also follow an adjective (not just a verb) when the adjective itself takes a result clause. The structure is Adj + 得 + [result] , "so [adj] that [result]." This is the correlative "so…that" pattern.

e: the two brothers; the pair of bros

d: The base word: 哥 doubled, the second syllable toned down to neutral. Standard everyday term for one's own older brother, and a child can also use it for an unrelated older boy.
哥 + 们 (plural) + the Beijing 儿 ending. Close male friends, sworn-brother style. Singular or plural, it marks loyalty between guys; northern and casual, common in Beijing speech.

e: to sing (in praise); singing as an art
d: 歌 gē (song) + 唱 chàng (to sing). More formal and elevated than 唱歌. Used for singing as a discipline and for singing in celebration: 歌唱家 gēchàngjiā is a professional vocalist, and 歌唱祖国 means to sing the praises of one's homeland.

e: song lyrics; the words of a song
d: 歌 gē (song) + 词 cí (wording). The words set to music, as opposed to 曲 qǔ, the melody. A songwriter is often credited separately for 作词 zuòcí (writing the lyrics) and 作曲 zuòqǔ (composing the tune).
歌 (song) plus 剧 (drama). A sung drama; the term used for Western-style opera, as distinct from 京剧 (jīngjù) Peking opera.
歌 (song) plus 曲 (tune, melody). 歌 leans on the lyrics, 曲 on the music; together they name a song as a finished piece. Slightly more formal than a bare 歌.

歌 gē (song) + 手 shǒu (skilled person). The standard word for a professional singer. This -手 suffix pattern for skilled persons: 歌手 singer, 选手 athlete/contestant, 鼓手 drummer, 射手 archer/shooter, 旗手 flag-bearer.

e: to reform; leather; to strip away

d: 革 gé (leather; to strip; to change) plus 命. Originally classical: to remove the Mandate of Heaven (天命) from a dynasty that had lost it, the pre-modern theory of legitimate dynastic overthrow.

e: investigation of things; rectification of affairs
d: A term from the Great Learning 大学, interpreted radically differently by Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming. For Zhu Xi: the patient investigation of external things to grasp their 理.

e: individual; a small number of; exceptional
d: 个 gè (single) + 别 bié (separate; other). Either "one by one, individually" (个别谈话 "to talk to people one at a time") or "only a few, exceptional" (个别情况 "a few isolated cases").

e: individual; personal; in one's own view
d: 个 gè (single) + 人 rén (person). The single person set against the group, and by extension "personal, private": 个人观点 "a personal opinion," 个人信息 "personal information." Its foil is 集体 jítǐ (the collective).
个 gè (single) + 体 tǐ (body; entity). A single unit within a larger whole, used in biology and economics alike: 个体差异 "individual differences," 个体户 "a self-employed business owner."

个 gè (individual) + 性 xìng (nature). The traits that distinguish one person from another, the stamp of the individual: 有个性 "to have a strong personality, to be distinctive," 个性化 "personalized, customized." Often praised as a mark of a person who is not interchangeable with the crowd.
个 gè + 子 zi (noun-suffix). A person's height or physical build: 高个子 "tall build," 矮个子 "short build," 个子很高 "very tall." Used of the whole frame of a person, not a measured number.

e: everyone gets what they need; each to their proper place

d: 各 gè (each; every) + 其 qí (its). Used in classical and formal modern Chinese to indicate that each member of a set has its own distinct version of something. Common in philosophical and legal prose where precision about individuals within a group matters.

各 gè (each) + 自 zì (self). Each person doing a thing for their own self, separately: 各自回家 "each went home on their own." A near relative of 己, built on the same idea of the individual self set apart from the group.

e: to give face; to show respect; to honor someone's standing
d: 给 (to give) + 面子. To actively enhance or protect someone else's face. Can mean: attending their event (your presence honors them), publicly praising them, deferring to them in front of others, or not challenging them when they are wrong , to spare their embarrassment.

e: fundamental; basic; (with a negative) at all
d: 根 gēn (root) + 本 běn (root). The two words for "root" doubled. As an adjective, fundamental or essential: 根本问题 "the fundamental issue." As an adverb with a negative, it means "not at all": 我根本不知道 "I had no idea whatsoever."
更 gèng (even more) + 多 duō (many; much). The most frequent collocation for comparative quantity. Appears in both spoken and written registers without restriction.
更 gēng (to change) + 改 gǎi (to alter; to revise). A formal compound for changing plans, decisions, or documents. More official in tone than 改变 gǎibiàn and preferred in administrative contexts.
更 gèng + 好 hǎo (good). The quintessential comparison pair. Appears in everyday speech, advertising, and formal writing with equal frequency.

e: let alone; much less; to say nothing of
d: 更 gèng + 何况 hékuàng (how much more; not to mention). A rhetorical connective that escalates from a difficult or surprising premise to an even more extreme conclusion. Introduces the harder case: if X is already the case, 更何况 Y is the clincher.

更 gēng (to change) + 换 huàn (to swap; to exchange). To replace one thing with another of the same kind: a part, a component, a person in a role. Emphasizes substitution more than 更改, which emphasizes revision.

更 gèng + 加 jiā (to add; to increase). A compound adverb that amplifies the degree of 更 further. Preferred in formal writing, speeches, and academic prose. In speech, bare 更 is more natural; 更加 in conversation can sound slightly elevated.

e: to update; to renew; to replace with something new
d: 更 gēng (to change; to replace) + 新 (new). To make new again: to update software (更新系统), to renew a contract (更新合同), to replace aging infrastructure (更新设备). A standard verb in technology, administration, and policy. 持续更新 (continuous updating) is a phrase familiar to every software user.

更 gēng (to change) + 衣 yī (clothes; garment). To change one's clothing. Formal and classical in register; in modern spoken Chinese 换衣服 huàn yīfu is more natural. Survives today primarily in 更衣室 gēngyīshì (changing room; locker room).

工程 gōngchéng (engineering; project , lit. "work + process") + 师 shī (master; teacher; professional). Engineer , one of the most respected professional titles in China, associated with the nation's modernization drive. 工程 alone means a large project or undertaking: 三峡工程 = Three Gorges Project.

e: time and effort; trouble spent on a task
d: 工 gōng (work, labor) + 夫 fū (effort). The time and care put into doing something: 花工夫 to spend effort, 没工夫 to have no time. It measures the investment a task demands rather than the skill it yields, the cost side of mastery.

工 gōng (labor; work) + 业 yè (sector). Manufacturing industry as a branch of the economy: 重工业 "heavy industry," 工业化 "industrialization." Paired with 农业 (agriculture) in the standard rhetoric of national development.

工 gōng (work; skill) + 艺 yì (art; skill; technique). Craft as the intersection of technical skill and artistry. 工艺品 gōngyìpǐn = handicraft item; artisan product. 传统工艺 = traditional crafts. 工艺美术 = arts and crafts (as a discipline).

e: kōan — a paradoxical case used as a meditation object
d: 公 gōng (public) + 案 àn (case/record). Originally a legal term: a judicial precedent. In Chan, a 公案 is a recorded exchange between a master and student, or a question posed by the master, used as a meditation object.
The allowed deviation from a dimension. Tight tolerances cost money; for parts that thread or seal against each other they decide whether the product works. 超差 (chāochā) is out of tolerance.

公 gōng (public; common) + 德. The virtue owed to strangers and the shared world: not littering, not jumping queues, not playing music loudly on the train. 没有公德心 "to lack civic-mindedness" is a routine complaint; 社会公德 "social public ethics" is one of the standard categories in civic discourse.
公 gōng (public) + 共 gòng (common; together). Belonging to or used by the community at large: 公共汽车 "public bus," 公共场所 "public place." The plain modifier for anything held in common.
公 (male) + 鸡 (chicken). The crowing bird of the farmyard, the one Shuōwén praised for knowing the hour.
公 gōng (metric) + 斤 jīn (a traditional unit of weight, about half a kilo). The standard kilogram. The 公 again marks the international unit against the older 斤.
公 gōng (public) + 开 kāi (to open). Out in the open rather than hidden: as an adjective, 公开信 "an open letter"; as a verb, 公开秘密 "to make a secret public." The opposite of 秘密 mìmì (secret).

Serving chopsticks , a second pair of chopsticks placed at the table for taking from shared dishes, kept separate from the pair used for eating. The practice is hygienic and has become more widespread post-2020. At formal banquets, a serving spoon (公勺 gōng sháo) may accompany each dish.
公 (gōng, public, metric/standardized) + 里 (Chinese li, 500 m). The standard modern unit of distance in China: 公里 = 1 kilometer = 2 市里 (shìlǐ, "market li," the standard li of 500 m).

e: citizen (a legal member of a state)
d: 公 gōng (public, common) + 民. The legal-political term for a citizen: a person who holds the nationality of a state and bears its rights and obligations. The standard word in constitutional and legal contexts, paired with 权利 quánlì (rights) and 义务 yìwù (duties).
公 gōng (public; impartial) + 平 píng (level). Even-handed dealing that favors no side: 公平竞争 "fair competition," 这不公平 "that's not fair." The everyday word for fairness.
公 gōng (public; common) + 认 rèn. Publicly recognized. The word for consensus recognition: a writer is 公认 the best of her generation; a fact is 公认 to be true.
Formula: "public pattern," a form that holds generally. 套公式 (tào gōngshì, "slot into the formula") is the study-hall phrase for plug-and-chug problem solving.
公 gōng (public; common) + 司 sī (to manage; an office). A jointly run enterprise, a body managed in common: 一家公司 "a company." Note the contrast with the homophone 私 sī (private).
公 gōng (public) + 园 yuán (garden). A garden held in common, open to all, as opposed to a private 花园 huāyuán. One of the first 公 words a beginner meets.
A Chinese company binds itself with its red seal more than with a signature. 合同专用章 (hétong zhuānyòngzhāng) is a seal used only for contracts and is equally valid.

公 gōng (impartial) + 正 zhèng (upright). The public standard joined to the straight line: justice as judgment held to the same mark for all. Common of judges, verdicts, and arbiters: 公正的判决 "a fair verdict."

e: merit; accumulated virtue from good deeds; karmic credit
d: 功 gōng (meritorious achievement; effort; skill) + 德 dé (virtue; moral force). The accumulated virtue that comes from righteous acts , most alive in Buddhist and popular religious usage, where performing good deeds (捐款, helping the poor, building a temple) generates 功德 that benefits the giver in this…

e: homework; schoolwork; preparation; research done before a task
d: 功 gōng (work; effort) + 课 kè (lesson; course). Originally: the work (功夫) one does for one's lessons (课).

功 gōng (merit) + 劳 láo (toil; labor). The credit owed to someone for hard work that produced real results. Used to acknowledge contribution: 这是大家的功劳 = this is everyone's accomplishment. The modest counterpart is 苦劳 kǔláo, credit merely for effort even without success.

e: utility; benefit — the Mohist evaluative standard
d: 功 gōng (merit; effect) + 利 lì (benefit; profit). The criterion Mozi applied to every institution, practice, and policy: does it enrich the state, increase the population, and benefit the people? If not, it should be eliminated regardless of tradition or aesthetic value.

功 gōng (work; merit) + 能 néng (ability; can). The work that something is able to do , its function. Appears everywhere: product features (软件功能 , software features), biology (心脏的功能 , the function of the heart), linguistics (句子的功能 , the function of a sentence).

功 gōng (effect) + 效 xiào (effect; result). The efficacy of a medicine, treatment, or method, the actual beneficial result it achieves. Especially common in medicine and traditional Chinese health: 这种药的功效很好 = this medicine is very effective.

e: to pursue (a degree, a field of study); to read-for
d: 攻 gōng (to attack; to apply oneself to) + 读. The verb for actively pursuing advanced study , a master's, a doctorate, a specialty. The 攻 conveys the sense of going at it, attacking the subject rather than passively absorbing.

供 gōng (to provide) + 应 yìng (to meet a need). To supply goods or services to meet a demand: 供应商 (supplier), 供应链 (supply chain), 供不应求 (supply falls short of demand). The yìng here is the answering of a need with provision.

恭 gōng (respectful) + 喜 xǐ (joy). To respectfully share in someone's happiness. Doubled as 恭喜恭喜 it is the warm spoken "congratulations," and 恭喜发财 gōngxǐ fācái is the standard New Year greeting wishing wealth.

The classic New Year greeting: "congratulations and may you get rich." Especially used in Southern China and the diaspora. The Cantonese pronunciation (gung1 hei2 faat3 choi4) is equally well-known internationally.
共 gòng (together; shared) + 同 tóng (same). Held in common by all parties: 共同的目标 "a shared goal," 共同努力 "to strive together." Stronger and more formal than 一起.

e: to communicate; to bridge; to reach an understanding
d: 沟 gōu (a ditch; a channel; a conduit) + 通 (to connect; to make pass through). Originally to link two waterways by a channel; now overwhelmingly used for communication between people: to open a channel of understanding so meaning can flow back and forth.
狗 + 叫 (jiào, to call out, cry). The plain way to say a dog is barking. 汪汪 (wāngwāng) is the onomatopoeia for the sound itself.
狗 + 熊 (xióng, bear). Literally a dog-bear, the colloquial name for the Asian black bear. Figuratively 狗熊 brands a coward, the opposite of a 英雄 (yīngxióng, hero), a pun that turns on the rhyme.

e: wolfberry / goji berry — the ubiquitous health supplement
lone soul, wild ghost — a wandering spirit with no family or anchor
d: 孤 gū (lone; orphaned; isolated) + 魂 hún (soul) + 野 yě (wild; untamed; in the open) + 鬼 guǐ (ghost). The classical and still-current phrase for a spirit with no one to care for it , no family performing rites, no ancestral hall, no spirit tablet.

古 gǔ (old-fashioned) + 板 bǎn (stiff, a board). Describes someone set in old ways and unwilling to bend: 思想古板 "old-fashioned in outlook," 古板的老师 "a stuffy, rigid teacher." Less about strangeness than about humourless inflexibility.

古 gǔ (ancient; old) + 城 chéng (city). A city or walled district that preserves its historic fabric. The phrase covers both whole heritage towns, such as the 丽江古城 (Lijiang Old Town) and 平遥古城 (Pingyao Old Town), and the old quarter inside a modern city.

古 gǔ (ancient) + 代 dài (era). The distant past as a historical age, the time of the old dynasties, sages, and classics: 古代文学 "classical literature," 古代史 "ancient history." Stands opposite 现代 (modern) and 近代 (the recent, early-modern past).

古 gǔ (ancient) + 典 diǎn (canon, standard work). Pertaining to the classical heritage and its refined standards: 古典文学 "classical literature," 古典音乐 "classical music," 古典美 "classical beauty." Marks something as belonging to a venerable, canonical tradition rather than the modern or popular.

e: an antique; a curio; an old fogey (figurative)
d: 古 gǔ (ancient) + 董 dǒng (to collect, to keep). A prized old object valued for its age and craft: 古董家具 "antique furniture," 收藏古董 "to collect antiques." Used figuratively of a person hopelessly behind the times, an "old relic."

古 gǔ (old, out of step) + 怪 guài (strange). Describes a person, temper, or thing that is peculiar and hard to predict: 性格古怪 "an eccentric character," 古怪的脾气 "an odd temper." Carries a sense of not fitting ordinary norms, often a little hard to get along with.

古 gǔ (ancient) + 老 lǎo (old). Describes something of great age that has endured: an 古老的传统 age-old tradition, an 古老的文明 ancient civilisation, an 古老的传说 old legend. It praises longevity and depth of roots rather than fixing a date.

e: old-tree tea — material from trees over 100 years old
bone-force; structural strength in a stroke
fixed; to fix in place; regular
d: 固 gù (solid; firm) + 定 dìng (fixed). Held firmly in one place or pattern, not movable or variable: 固定收入 "a fixed income," 把架子固定在墙上 "to fix the shelf to the wall."

e: the Forbidden City; the Old Palace
d: 故 (old, former) + 宫 (gōng, palace). Literally "the Old Palace," the formal Chinese name for the former imperial palace complex in Beijing, known in English as the Forbidden City. It was the residence of emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties and is now the Palace Museum (故宫博物院, Gùgōng Bówùyuàn).

e: old friends; old acquaintances; former associates
d: 故 (gù, old; former; intentional; reason , a hand holding a stick, the old way of doing things) + 旧 (old). Old friends, specifically those known from a previous period of life. A literary and somewhat formal term; 老朋友 (lǎo péngyou) is the colloquial equivalent.

e: old friend; an acquaintance from former days
d: 故 (old, former) + 人 (rén, person). An old friend, specifically one known from an earlier period of life, now perhaps far away or long unseen. 故人 belongs to the literary and poetic register, common in classical verse about parting and reunion; the everyday equivalent is 老朋友 (lǎo péngyou).

e: storybook; picture book with a narrative
d: 故事 gùshì (story) + 书 shū (book). A storybook , the most common type of book for children learning to read. 讲故事 jiǎng gùshì = "to tell a story" (the standard phrase). 听故事 tīng gùshì = "to listen to a story." 故事情节 gùshì qíngjié = "plot, storyline."

故 (old, former) + 乡 (xiāng, countryside, native village). The place one is from, charged with the weight of belonging and longing. 故乡 is the literary and emotional register; the plainer 家乡 (jiāxiāng) is more neutral and everyday.
故 (deliberate) + 意 (yì, intention, will, mind). To do something on purpose, with conscious intent. Used adverbially: 他故意迟到 (he was late on purpose), 不是故意的 (didn't mean to, it wasn't intentional).
故 (cause; here, an underlying fault) + 障 (zhàng, obstruction, barrier). A malfunction in a machine or system: something with a cause behind it that obstructs normal operation.

e: to consider face; to save face for someone; to protect dignity
d: 顾 gù (to consider; to look after; to take into account). 顾面子 means to take face into consideration when making decisions or acting , whether one's own face or someone else's. More deliberate and conscious than simply 给面子. Suggests a thoughtful navigation of face dynamics.
顾 gù (to look after; to consider) + 问 wèn (to ask). The person one turns to and asks for counsel: 法律顾问 "legal adviser," 技术顾问 "technical consultant." Literally the one whom you regard and question.

e: hexagram; trigram; the unit of the system
d: 卦 guà is the technical term for both the six-line hexagrams and the three-line trigrams (distinguished as 六爻卦 liù yáo guà and 三爻卦 sān yáo guà when precision is needed). The character depicts a hand 卜 over a ground 土 , divination.
To register at a hospital: hang a number. 挂个专家号 is booking the senior specialist; 挂不上号 is the national complaint about famous hospitals.

e: hanging her mat to calm the storm
d: A convoy of ships was caught in a typhoon. Crew members and merchants, terrified, invoked Mazu. Her red skirt (or in some versions a red lantern) was seen at the masthead: she was present. The storm subsided.

e: "That explains it!" Synonym for 难怪 with the same function
d: "That explains it!" Synonym for 难怪 with the same function. Slightly more drawn out and emphatic. 怪不得他不来 ("that's why he didn't come").

e: Emperor Guan — deified general, god of war and righteousness
d: Guan Yu 关羽 (d. 220 CE), the historical Three Kingdoms general celebrated for his loyalty and righteousness 义 yì, was progressively deified over the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties, eventually receiving the title 关圣帝君 (Holy Emperor Guan).

e: to show concern and care for (warm, often institutional)
to power off (a device); to switch off a phone

d: "The key is" or "what matters is." Marks the core of an argument. Useful when you want to highlight the deciding factor among several you have just laid out: 关键在于时间 ("the key is timing").
关 guān (to join; pass) + 节 jié (joint). An anatomical joint, the hinge where bones meet: 膝关节 "knee joint." By extension, a critical juncture in a matter, the place where things turn.

e: correlation; connection; to be associated with
d: 关 (connection) + 联 (to join; to link). More formal and analytical than 关系 , used for logical correlations, data relationships, and systematic connections. Common in academic, research, and analytical writing. 相互关联 xiānghù guānlián = mutually correlated; interconnected.

e: to close the door; (of a shop) to close for the day or for good
to lock up; to shut in; to imprison
to affect; to have a bearing on; to be relevant to
d: 关系到 (lit. "the relationship reaches to") means that something has a bearing on, affects, or is relevant to something else. Used for high-stakes matters where the connection is important to note explicitly. Common in official, journalistic, and persuasive writing.
网 wǎng = net; network. 关系网 is the spider's web of personal connections , who you know, who they know, and the overlapping obligations and trust that run through the web.

A common fixed expression used to characterize something as having major consequences or importance. 重大 zhòngdà = major, significant. Used in formal registers to signal that a decision, situation, or event carries real weight and should be treated with corresponding seriousness.

关 (to concern; to be connected to) + 心 (heart). The heart connected to something , caring. One of the most important relational verbs in Chinese. Both the action of caring and the expression of concern. High frequency in family, friendship, and professional contexts.
关 guān (to connect) + 于 yú (to). Marks the subject matter of a book, talk, or document: 关于历史的书 "a book about history." Where 对于 frames an attitude, 关于 frames a topic.

e: Guan Yu — the archetype of loyalty and honour
d: The red-faced sworn brother of Liu Bei, towering in loyalty and martial valour, who refuses every bribe and honour Cao Cao offers to keep him.

e: to pay attention to; to follow closely; attention; concern
d: 关 (to concern; to connect) + 注 (to pour; to focus , water pouring into a single point). Focused, sustained attention toward something important. In digital contexts, 关注 means to follow someone's account (social media).

e: "Gazing at the Vast Sea" — an early landscape poem
d: Written after Cao Cao's northern campaign of 207 CE, often cited as the first fully realized landscape poem in the tradition. The poet gazes from a cliff and the sea, swallowing sun and moon, becomes the mirror of his own ambition.

e: to observe; to watch closely; observation
d: 观 guān (to look) + 察 chá (to examine). To watch with attention in order to learn something: a scientist, a doctor, or a detective 观察 their subject. Stronger and more deliberate than simply watching.
观 guān (view) + 点 diǎn (point). The particular angle from which you regard an issue: 我同意你的观点 "I agree with your view." The opinion you argue from, lighter and more debatable than a fixed 观念.

e: to watch; to view (an event or show)
d: 观 guān (to view) + 看 kàn (to look). To watch a performance, game, or spectacle. A slightly formal partner to the everyday 看 kàn, fitting for events that draw an audience.

观 guān (view) + 念 niàn (thought). A deeper, more settled idea than a 观点: the concepts and assumptions one lives by, often slow to change. 传统观念 "traditional notions," 时间观念 "a sense of time / punctuality."

e: Guanyin — bodhisattva of compassion, the most beloved in China
d: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara ("the one who perceives the sounds of the world"). One of the most significant transformations in Chinese Buddhist history: in Indian and Central Asian Buddhism, Avalokiteśvara is male.

Also called the 观经 Guān Jīng. A narrative framed by Queen Vaidehi's suffering (her son has imprisoned her husband, King Bimbisāra): she asks Śākyamuni to teach her how to reach a realm free from suffering.

e: visualization — contemplating the Pure Land and Amitābha in detail
d: 观 guān (contemplate; observe) + 想 xiǎng (imagine; think). The more advanced and demanding practice outlined in the 观无量寿经 (Contemplation Sutra): systematic visualization of the Western Pure Land (its jeweled trees, lotus pools, the thrones, the light) and ultimately of Amitābha himself in full detail…

e: the bodhisattva 观自在 by another name

d: 观 guān (to watch) + 众 zhòng (the many, a crowd). The watching crowd: the audience at a show, the spectators at a game, the viewers of a broadcast. Its cousins are 听众 tīngzhòng (listeners) and 读者 dúzhě (readers).

e: coffin — the most important object in traditional death culture
d: The coffin (棺材 guāncai) was traditionally a major family investment: solid wood, red lacquered, with auspicious carvings. The quality of the coffin reflected both the family's means and its filial devotion.
管 guǎn (to govern; to be in charge of) + 理 lǐ (to put in order). To run and oversee an organization, system, or resource: 管理公司 "to manage a company," 时间管理 "time management."

e: the bare verb: habits, facts, general truths
d: The unmarked verb is the default for habitual actions and standing facts, usually anchored by a frequency word: 我每天喝咖啡 (I drink coffee every day), 他住在北京 (he lives in Beijing), 地球绕太阳转 (the earth orbits the sun). No particle needed; adding 了 here would wrongly signal a completed event.

光 guāng (light; beam) + 明 míng (bright). More elevated and abstract than 明亮. Used in spiritual and political registers: 光明大道 "the road of light" (a righteous path), 走向光明 "moving toward the light." The opposite is 黑暗 hēi'àn darkness.
The speed of light. Colloquially any blinding speed: 光速下班 is leaving work the second the clock strikes, a usage every office knows.

e: time; the passing days (literally "light and shadow")
d: 光 guāng (light) + 阴 yīn (shadow). The most poetic word for time in Chinese, naming the days by the very thing that measures them: the alternation of sunlight and shade, day and night, sweeping across the ground like the shadow on a sundial.
广 (guǎng, broad, expansive) + 东 (east). "The broad eastern region": the province that was the easternmost of the early southern territories brought under Tang-Song dynasty control.

e: the Palace of Vast Cold — the Moon Palace

d: 逛 (to stroll, wander) + 街 (street). A verb-object pair: to roam the streets with no fixed errand, window-shopping as much as buying. The default leisure activity in any Chinese city.

e: to stipulate; a rule; a regulation
d: 规 guī (rule; compass) + 定 dìng (to fix). To lay down a rule in advance, and the rule so laid down. 按照规定 ànzhào guīdìng "according to the regulations." The formal, institutional cousin of 决定.

硅胶 (guījiāo) is silicone; 密封圈 (mìfēngquān) is any sealing ring or gasket. Food-grade silicone should not smell; 异味 (yìwèi, an odd smell) and 发黄 (fāhuáng, yellowing) are the common complaints. 漏水 (lòushuǐ) is a leak.
AABB reduplication of 鬼祟 (guǐsuì, surreptitious; stealthy). The reduplication intensifies and gives the phrase a rhythmic, memorable quality. 祟 suì originally means the malign influence of spirits.

鬼 guǐ + 话 huà (speech; talk). Literally "ghost speech" , nonsense, lies, deceptive talk. The logic: ghosts mislead and confuse; speech that misleads and confuses is ghost-speech. 说鬼话 (to speak ghost talk) = to talk rubbish, to lie.

鬼 guǐ (ghost) + 魂 hún (soul; spirit). The ghost or spirit of a deceased person , the closest equivalent to the English "ghost" in its neutral, descriptive sense. Less colloquially charged than 鬼 alone. 闹鬼 (nàoguǐ, spirits making trouble) describes a haunting; 闹鬼的地方 is a haunted place.

Ghost Month: the seventh month of the lunar calendar, during which the gates of the underworld are held to open and the spirits of the dead roam freely. Considered an inauspicious period for weddings, starting new businesses, moving house, or making major decisions.
The polite way to refer to the other side's company; 贵厂 (guì chǎng) for a factory. Your own side is plain 我们公司 or 我们. 贵 is the same character as "expensive," here meaning "honoured."
滚 (gǔn, to roll) + 蛋: a blunt order to get out. The image is of telling someone to roll away like a dropped egg. It is rude and forceful, used only in anger.

Airs of the States , the 160 regional folk songs that form the first and largest section of the 诗经. The word 风 carries the sense of "wind" or "air" , something that moves through a region, picking up its local character.
国 (nation) plus 歌 (song). The official song of a country, sung standing at ceremonies and medal podiums.

国 guó (nation) + 画 huà (painting). The native tradition of brush-and-ink painting on silk or paper, kin to calligraphy. Short for 中国画 Zhōngguóhuà, and set against 油画 yóuhuà, the imported oil-painting tradition.
国 guó + 际 jì (boundary; border; between). "Between countries." The standard word for anything international: 国际机场 international airport · 国际关系 international relations · 国际化 internationalization.

e: national conditions; the state of the nation
d: 国 (country) + 情 (conditions, circumstances, feelings). The specific circumstances of a given country , its history, population, resources, culture, and current state.

果 guǒ (fruit) + 仁. The general category term: any kernel or "nutmeat." Wang Yangming and other Neo-Confucians explicitly used this image as the metaphor for moral 仁: a 果仁 is what gives the fruit its capacity to generate the next tree, just as 仁 is what gives a person the capacity to relate fully to…
果 (guǒ, fruit) + 肉 (flesh). The soft edible part between the skin and the pit, the meat of the fruit.
果 guǒ (fruit) + 实 shí (the ripened, full thing). The fruit a plant bears, and by extension the rewards of effort: 劳动的果实 "the fruits of labor." This is the seed-and-fruit sense of 实 made explicit.

e: to pass the pass; to clear a hurdle, exam, or test

d: 过 (guò, to cross) + 河 (river). A verb-object pair, to get to the far bank. It anchors several proverbs, since crossing water is the classic image of a one-way commitment.

e: "you've overpraised me" — a deflection of excessive praise
d: 过 guò (to exceed; to go too far) + 奖 jiǎng (to praise; to commend; an award) + 了 le (completion/change-of-state particle). A slightly more sophisticated deflection than 哪里哪里 , conceding that some praise may be warranted but asserting that the speaker has gone beyond what is accurate.

e: the past; to pass; to go over to
d: 过 guò (to pass; to cross; to go beyond) + 去 qù (away). As a noun: the past , what has passed away from the present. As a verb: to go over to (move across and away to a location). Both meanings share the same root image: time or a person crossing and moving beyond the current point.

e: after a while; in a little while
d: "After a spell passes," used to push something a short way into the future: 过一会儿再打给你 ("I'll call you back in a little while"). 过 (to pass) marks the elapsing of the short time. A close, even softer relative is 等会儿 / 待会儿 ("in a bit, later"), the ready phrase for "hold on / later."

e: "still far from good enough" — modest self-assessment; "I have a long way to go"
d: 还 hái (still; yet) + 差 chà (to fall short; to be lacking) + 得 de (degree complement marker) + 远 yuǎn (far). A self-deprecating phrase that positions the speaker as still well short of a standard , pointing forward to future growth rather than backward at achievement.

The most versatile of the three hedges. As a standalone response to "how was it?" or "how are you?", 还好 reads as "fine, okay, not bad." As an opener to a clause, it shifts to "fortunately, luckily" , the speaker is noting that things didn't go as badly as they might have.

Used in questions that offer the listener a choice between two (or more) options: A 还是 B？It signals "which one?" and asks for a pick. A choice question with 还是 does not also take 吗, since 还是 already makes it a question. The options can be nouns, verbs, or whole clauses.

e: forget it; never mind; on second thought, no

d: "One more thing" or "and another point." Marks the addition of a further item to a list of points you are making. Common in explanations and arguments where you are building up to a conclusion.
孩 paired with 童 (child, youngster). A bookish, slightly elevated word for children, common in writing and formal speech rather than casual talk.

孩 (child) plus the neutral-tone suffix 子, which turns many one-syllable nouns into stable everyday words. 孩子 is the default word for a child and also the word a parent uses for a son or daughter of any age.

p: háizi jiào yǔ lín shī le
e: the child got soaked by the rain (colloquial 叫 passive)
d: 叫 jiào as passive marker: Subject + 叫 + Agent + Verb + Result. The most distinctly northern/colloquial of the three. Rain soaking a child is the kind of minor adversarial act that all four passive markers handle naturally.
海 (hǎi, sea) plus 报: a public announcement spread far and wide. The word for a poster or playbill, the kind pasted on a wall to advertise a film or a show.
海 hǎi (sea) + 边 biān (edge; side). The edge where land meets sea, the place you go to be beside the water: 去海边度假 "to vacation at the seaside."
海 hǎi (sea) + 岛 dǎo (island). A piece of land surrounded by sea. Where 岛 alone is any island, 海岛 stresses the open-sea setting, far from the mainland.
海 hǎi (sea) + 关 guān (pass; barrier). The customs authority that inspects goods crossing a border, named for the sea-passage through which trade once arrived: 过海关 "to clear customs."
海 hǎi (sea) + 军 jūn (army; armed force). The naval branch of the military, the "sea army." Its siblings are 陆军 lùjūn (the army, "land force") and 空军 kōngjūn (the air force).

Shanghai style: the cosmopolitan, eclectic aesthetic and cultural orientation associated with Shanghai. Applied to art, architecture, cuisine, fashion, and urban manners. A term of both pride and occasional condescension from those outside Shanghai.
海 hǎi (sea) + 洋 yáng (the open ocean). The full body of the world's salt water, the scientific and grand register: 海洋生物 "marine life," 太平洋是最大的海洋 "the Pacific is the largest ocean."

e: to fall ill, to be sick
d: 害 (to be afflicted by) + 病 (illness). The causative branch: to be struck down by sickness. Colloquial and slightly regional; 生病 (shēngbìng) is the neutral standard.
害 (harmful) + 虫 (insect). An insect that damages crops or carries disease. Its counterpart is 益虫 (yìchóng), a beneficial insect.
害 (dread) reinforced by 怕 (to fear). The default spoken verb for fear of a concrete thing or outcome. Takes an object directly or stands alone.
害 (to suffer a feeling) + 羞 (shame). To be visited by shyness, the blush of being seen. Describes a person's manner, not a one-off act.

含 is "to contain." The pair 含税 / 不含税 appears on almost every RMB quotation; 含运费 (hán yùnfèi) is freight included, 含包装 packaging included. The same 含 works for anything the price might or might not cover.

e: cold food — the ancient festival Qīngmíng absorbed
Han Fei — greatest Legalist theorist, student of Xunzi
d: 韩非 (280–233 BCE): a prince of the state of Han who studied under Xunzi and became the most systematic theorist of Legalism 法家. His text, the 韩非子 Hánfēizǐ, synthesizes earlier Legalist thought and provides the fullest account of governance through law 法, technique 术, and power 势.

汉 Hàn (the dynastic name) + 朝 cháo (dynasty, court). The dynasty (206 BCE to 220 CE) whose name became the name of a people. A defining golden age of unified empire, remembered as the standard for later eras.

Former subjects of the Jin dynasty, including Han, Jurchen, Khitan, and Koreans. Conquered earlier, treated with somewhat less suspicion than southerners. Had somewhat greater access to lower official positions.

e: Sinology; the study of Chinese language and civilization
d: 汉 Hàn (Chinese) + 学 xué (study, learning). The academic study of Chinese language, texts, and culture, especially as pursued by scholars outside China. A 汉学家 hànxuéjiā is a sinologist.

汉 Hàn (the Han) + 语 yǔ (language, speech). The standard scholarly name for the Chinese language, framed by ethnicity rather than country. Its sister 中文 zhōngwén leans toward the written language, while 普通话 pǔtōnghuà names the standard Mandarin spoken form.

e: "Han elements" — commercially inspired garments that aren't structurally hànfú
the Han ethnicity; the Han people
d: 汉 Hàn (of Han) + 族 zú (clan, ethnic group). The majority ethnic group of China, named after the Han dynasty. Set against the 少数民族 shǎoshù mínzú, the country's many minority peoples.
Spaceflight: "sailing the heavens," on the model of 航海 (seafaring). 航天员 is the official word for China's astronauts; the industry is 航天工程, space engineering.

e: not at all, not in the least

d: Heroic and expansive , the alternative 词 style, characterized by large-scale historical and philosophical subjects, martial energy, and a willingness to use the lyric form for ideas rather than feelings alone. Su Shi and Xin Qiji are its defining practitioners.
Appended to a proposal, it softens a request into a negotiation: 我们明天再说，好不好? Its siblings 行不行 and 可不可以 climb the same ladder of politeness; children deploy 好不好 serially until granted.

e: with great difficulty; finally after much effort

d: 好 hǎo (good) + 处 chù (place; aspect; point). The good points of something: its advantages. Contrast: 坏处 huàichù (bad points; disadvantages).

e: a brave fellow; a stout-hearted hero
d: 好 hǎo (good) + 汉 hàn (fellow). A bold, admirable man, the heroic outlaw or stalwart of old novels. The saying 好汉不吃眼前亏 "a wise fellow does not take a loss he can avoid" shows its everyday use.
好 (good) + 喝 (drink): pleasant to drink. Mandarin splits "tasty" by mouth-action, so liquids are 好喝 while solid food is 好吃 (hǎo chī), good to eat.

e: done; ready; okay; alright (change of state)
d: 好 + 了 (change-of-state marker) = has become ready/done/okay. One of the most frequent two-syllable expressions in spoken Mandarin. Announces completion, signals readiness, and in reduplicated form (好了好了) means "alright, enough, okay."

A close friend, the most common way to mark closeness. 好 hǎo (good) stacks directly in front. For an even closer bond there is 知己 zhījǐ, "one who knows me," a soulmate-friend who truly understands you, a notion with deep roots in classical Chinese friendship.
好 hào (fond of) + 奇 qí (the strange, the unusual). Fond of the unusual , curious. 好奇心 hàoqíxīn = curiosity (the heart of fondness for strangeness).

Good things come in pairs: the principle that favors even numbers and pairing in gifts, decorations, and arrangements. Matched pairs of objects (candles, vases, figurines) are standard for weddings and auspicious occasions.
好 hǎo (good; well) + 听 (to listen). The auditory parallel of 好看 hǎokàn (nice-looking). Applied to music, voices, songs, and speech.

e: good brothers — polite euphemism for wandering hungry ghosts
d: 好 hǎo (good) + 兄弟 xiōngdì (brothers). The Taiwanese term of respect used in place of 鬼 during Ghost Month. Addressing spirits as "good brothers" acknowledges their presence without the provocation of calling them ghosts; it is also an appeal to fraternal feeling.
喝 (drink) + 茶 (tea). 喝茶 also names the social ritual of sitting down together; "请喝茶" is both an offer of tea and an invitation to talk.
喝 (drink) + 酒 (liquor). The default verb for drinking alcohol of any kind, from beer to baijiu. Central to banquet culture, where 喝酒 carries social obligation.
喝 (drink) + 咖啡 (coffee). Like 喝茶, the phrase doubles as a soft social invitation: "改天一起喝咖啡" means let's meet up sometime.
喝 (drink) + 水 (water). The first sentence most learners build with this character, and the everyday reminder a Chinese host or parent will repeat constantly.
喝 (drink) + 完 (finished), another resultative: drink to completion, drain the glass. 完 marks the liquid as gone.
喝 (drink) + 醉 (drunk), a resultative compound: the 醉 is the result of the 喝. Often expanded to 喝醉了 (hē zuì le) for the completed state, "got drunk".

e: to merge; to combine; to amalgamate
d: 合 hé (to join) + 并 bìng (to combine side by side). To merge separate units into one: 两个部门合并了 "the two departments merged." Common in business, administration, and biology.

合 hé (to join, to combine) + 唱 chàng (to sing). Voices joined into one: a chorus, or the act of singing together. 合唱团 héchàngtuán is a choir. Contrast with 独唱 dúchàng, a solo, where one voice stands alone.

e: to merge into one; to unite into a single whole
d: 合 hé (to combine; to close) + 而 ér (and then; thereby) + 为 wéi (become) + 一. A classical four-character phrase describing the merging of separate things into wholeness. Used in philosophy, business mergers, artistic synthesis, and descriptions of cultural fusion.
合 hé (to fit; to accord with) + 法 fǎ (law). In accordance with the law, on the right side of the line: 合法权利 "lawful rights." Its opposite is 非法 fēifǎ (illegal) or 违法 wéifǎ (to break the law).
合 hé (to accord with) + 理 lǐ (reason; principle). Something that accords with reason or fairness: 合理的价格 "a reasonable price," 合理安排 "a sensible arrangement." Its opposite is 不合理.

e: to close (a book, lid, door); to shut
d: 合 hé (to close) + 上 shàng (a result complement: shut to). To bring two edges together so a thing is closed: 合上书 "close the book," 合上盖子 "put the lid on."
合 hé (to fit) + 适 shì (to be apt). An adjective describing something that fits the situation well: 合适的工作 "a suitable job," 大小合适 "the right size." Its opposite is 不合适.
Contract. 签合同 (qiān hétong) is to sign one. The parties inside it, 甲方 and 乙方 (Party A and Party B), have become everyday slang for client and vendor.
合 hé (to join) + 作 zuò (to do; to work). To join efforts and work as one. The everyday word for partnership of every scale, from two classmates to two nations: 合作伙伴 "a cooperation partner."

e: why must; there is no need to; why go so far?
d: 何 hé (why; what; how , the classical interrogative) + 必 bì (must; certainly). A rhetorical question that questions the necessity of an action, usually suggesting that the action is excessive, unnecessary, or misguided.
和 hé (harmony) + 平 píng (calm). Peace as the opposite of war and conflict: 世界和平 "world peace," 和平谈判 "peace talks," 和平相处 "to live together in peace."
和谐 (héxié, harmonious; in harmony) + 社会. The governing ideal articulated by Hu Jintao in 2004.
河 (river) + 边 (biān, edge / side). The strip of ground along a river, where people walk, fish, and wash. One of the first place-words a beginner builds with 河.
河 (river) + 流 (liú, to flow / a current). The generic technical term for a river as a flowing body of water, the word a geography textbook or a news report reaches for.
河 (river) + 水 (shuǐ, water). The water of a river as a substance, distinct from sea water 海水 (hǎishuǐ) or rain. Common in the proverb about minding your own affairs.

The Great Bend: the large northern loop of the Yellow River into Inner Mongolia. The fertile irrigated land within the bend has been farmed since antiquity and was historically a zone of contest between Han Chinese settlers and nomadic peoples of the steppe.

核 hé (nucleus; kernel; seed, as in 核武器 nuclear weapons) + 心 xīn (heart). The innermost, hardest, most essential center. Where 中心 is the geometric center, 核心 is the conceptual kernel, what everything else wraps around. Heavily used in political discourse, business strategy, and academic writing.

黑 hēi (black) + 暗 àn (dim; dark; unlit). Physical darkness, and by easy extension moral or social darkness: an age, a society, or a regime described as 黑暗 is corrupt and oppressive, a world where justice cannot be seen. 旧社会很黑暗 (the old society was full of darkness) is a stock phrase.
黑 hēi (black) + 板 bǎn (board; plank). The classroom blackboard, a high-frequency HSK word and a useful anchor for the plain color sense.

e: dark tea & pu-erh — the other tea category prized for aging

d: 黑 hēi (black; illicit) + 客 kè (guest; visitor). The standard Chinese word for a hacker. It works on two levels at once: phonetically 黑客 echoes the English "hacker," and semantically it reads as "black guest," the uninvited intruder who enters a system in the dark.

黑 hēi (black; dark) + 马 mǎ (horse). A direct calque of the English "dark horse," now fully naturalized: a competitor nobody expected who surges from obscurity to win. Used constantly in sports, elections, business, and entertainment competitions.

黑 hēi + 色 sè (color). The neutral word for black as a color. Unlike its English counterpart, black in classical Chinese cosmology was not purely negative: in the 五行 (Five Phases) system, black is the color of Water, of the North, of winter, and of the kidneys, a respectable and necessary part of the…

e: the criminal underworld; organized crime; the mob
d: 黑 hēi (illicit) + 社会 shèhuì (society). Organized crime and the world it inhabits, the "black society" running parallel to and beneath the legitimate one.
黑 hēi (illicit; off the books) + 市 shì (market). A market operating outside legal channels, where goods or currency change hands at unofficial prices.

e: many, a lot: plain and understated
d: 很多 is the everyday "many, a lot": 很多人 (many people), 很多问题 (many questions). 不少, literally "not few", says the same thing through understatement, and often carries a note of mild surprise: 他认识不少人 (he knows quite a few people).

e: to span across; to stretch across
d: 横 (héng, horizontal) + 跨. The verb of choice for bridges, viaducts, and any long structure that reaches from one side to the other. Also figurative for periods or regions: 横跨三个朝代 "spanning three dynasties," 横跨三大洲 "stretching across three continents."

e: red envelope; a cash gift; a digital money packet
d: 红 hóng + 包 bāo (packet; bundle). The red paper envelope filled with money, given to children at New Year, to a couple at their wedding, and to employees as a bonus. The red is the point: the envelope blesses the money inside.

红 hóng (red) + 茶 chá (tea). Fully oxidized tea, the category English calls black tea. The Chinese name describes the amber-red color of the infusion in the cup; the English name describes the near-black color of the oxidized leaf.
红 (hóng, red) + 灯 (light): the red traffic signal that means stop. Here 灯 has shed every trace of flame and means pure colored signal. Its partner is 绿灯 (lǜdēng), the green light to go.

红 hóng (red; auspicious) + 火 huǒ (fire). A business, a celebration, or a neighborhood that is 红火 is booming, bustling, full of warmth and prosperity. The image fuses the lucky red with the energy of fire: a scene so lively it glows.

e: the Red Army; the early Chinese Communist military force
d: 红 hóng (red; revolutionary) + 军 jūn (army). The Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army, the Communist fighting force from 1927 until it was renamed in the late 1930s.

e: to blush; to flush red (with anger or embarrassment)
d: 红 (red) + 脸 (face). The cheeks going red, whether from shyness or from a flare of temper. 脸红 (liǎnhóng) reverses the order for the same blush; 红脸 also names the stern, blunt role someone plays in a good-cop bad-cop pairing.

红 hóng (red) + 绿 lǜ (green) + 灯 dēng (light; lamp). The everyday word for a traffic signal, built from its two decisive colors with red named first. 闯红灯 (chuǎng hóngdēng) is to run a red light, a common phrase that has also become a metaphor for breaking a rule that everyone agrees on.

e: a favored person; someone in favor with the powerful; a star
d: 红 hóng (popular; in favor) + 人 rén (person). Someone basking in favor, whether a boss's trusted lieutenant, a court favorite, or a rising celebrity. The metaphor runs straight from the color: to be 红 is to be celebrated, so a 红人 is a person bathed in that good fortune.

红 hóng + 色 sè (color). The neutral term for red as a color, but watch the second sense: 红色 also means "revolutionary" or "Communist" in political contexts. 红色旅游 (red tourism) is travel to revolutionary historical sites; 红色经典 (red classics) are the canonical works of revolutionary culture.

红 hóng (red) + 十字 shízì (cross). The International Committee of the Red Cross, established 1863. The Chinese translation renders the emblem directly: the red 十-shaped cross. The full institutional name is 红十字国际委员会 Hóng Shízì Guójì Wěiyuánhuì.

e: red thread of fate; also: a line that must not be crossed
d: 红 hóng (red , the color of luck, celebration, and vital force in Chinese culture) + 线 xiàn (thread; line). The red thread of fate in romantic mythology.

后 hòu (after; later) + 代 dài (generation). The generations that come after: 子孙后代 "children and grandchildren, all later generations." Used both for one's own line of descendants and, more broadly, for posterity as a whole.

e: the rear; behind the front line
d: 后 (rear) + 方 (direction; side; region). The military and formal register word for the rear area behind a front line or forward position. Contrasted with 前方 qiánfāng (the front, the forward area). Also used metaphorically for the support structure behind any endeavor: family, logistics, home base.

e: the imperial harem; the rear palace
d: 后 (rear; and the empress sense) + 宫 (palace). The residential complex at the back of the imperial enclosure housing the emperor's wives and concubines. The term plays on both senses of 后: the rear palace (spatially, at the back) and the palace of the 后 (the empress and her female hierarchy).

后 (after) + 来 (to come; to arrive). "What came after" , subsequent events in a narrative or sequence. 后来 always refers to the past relative to a reference point already established: you set the scene, then 后来 picks up the story.
后 (rear) + 门 (door; gate). Literally the door at the back of a building. Figuratively: an unofficial, informal, or improper channel for getting something done.

e: behind; at the back; in the rear
d: 后 (behind) + 面 (face; side; direction). The most common spatial word for "behind" in everyday Mandarin. Used for physical position relative to a reference point. Interchangeable with 后边 hòubian in many contexts; 后面 is slightly more formal.

后 hòu (after; later) + 世 shì (generation). The generations who come after us: 流芳后世 "to leave a good name to posterity," 后世子孙 "descendants of later generations." Looks forward to those who will inherit and remember.

后 hòu (after; behind; later) + 天 tiān (day). Chinese has dedicated words for two days in either direction of today: 前天 qiántiān / 昨天 zuótiān / 今天 jīntiān / 明天 míngtiān / 后天 hòutiān. Beyond that, you count: 三天后 sān tiān hòu (three days later).

e: to wait for a bus or train
d: 候 hòu (to wait) + 车 chē (vehicle). To wait for transport. Seen everywhere on station signage: 候车室 hòuchēshì "waiting room," 候车厅 "waiting hall."
候 hòu (season) + 鸟 niǎo (bird). The bird that moves with the season, contrasted with 留鸟 liúniǎo, the resident bird that stays year-round.

e: to wait to see a doctor
d: 候 hòu (to wait) + 诊 zhěn (to examine medically). To wait for a medical consultation. The room where patients sit is the 候诊室 hòuzhěnshì.
忽 hū (sudden, to neglect) + 然 rán (-ly). Marks an event arriving without warning: 忽然下雨 "it suddenly began to rain." Usually placed before the verb. Near-synonym of 突然.

Huzhou brush , brushes made in Huzhou, Zhejiang province, regarded as the finest in China. The term is used as a quality designation, much as "Huizhou ink" signals quality in the ink category. Huzhou brush-making has been a continuous craft tradition for over a thousand years.
湖 (lake) plus 面 (surface): the open face of the water, the plane that mirrors sky and mountain.
湖 (lake) plus 南 (south): the province south of Dongting Lake, known for spicy cuisine and as Mao Zedong's birthplace.
湖 (lake) plus 畔 (pàn, bank, edge): the land at the water's rim, a literary word for a lakeshore walk or dwelling.
湖 (lake) plus 泊 (pō, a still pool). The pairing is the standard geographic term for lakes taken as a class, the word a textbook or atlas uses.
湖 (lake) plus 水 (water): the water of a lake itself, often invoked for its stillness and color.
互 hù (mutual) + 相 xiāng (each other). Placed before a verb, it says the action runs in both directions between two or more parties: 互相帮助 "to help each other," 互相理解 "to understand one another."
户 hù (door; household) + 外 wài (outside). Literally "outside the door," the open air beyond a building. Common in 户外运动 "outdoor sports" and 户外活动 "outdoor activities."

护 (protect, the 护 of 保护) + 士 (officer, the scholar-gentleman suffix of 战士 soldier and 博士 PhD). Coined when modern nursing arrived in the late Qing; the profession's day, 护士节, falls on Florence Nightingale's birthday, May 12.
花 huā (mixed-color) + 白 bái (white). Of hair or a beard, mixed black and white, grizzled: 花白的头发 "grizzled hair." The "many-colored" sense of 花 applied to the heads of the middle-aged.

e: tisanes & herbal infusions — not true tea

d: 花 huā (flower) + 朵 duǒ (the measure word for blooms). A flower viewed as an individual blossom, slightly more literary than bare 花. Children are often called 祖国的花朵, "the flowers of the motherland."
花 huā (to spend) + 费 fèi (fee, to expend). A more formal word for spending, and also a noun meaning the expense itself: 生活花费 "living expenses." Heavier and more written than bare 花.

Sichuan pepper , the dried husk of the prickly ash berry, not related to black pepper or chili pepper. Contains hydroxy-alpha sanshool, which activates the same receptor as light touch and low-frequency vibration, producing the characteristic tingling numbness on the tongue and lips.

The decorated red sedan chair in which the bride was traditionally carried to the wedding. The chair was ornately painted and curtained, surrounded by musicians and attendants. The tradition has been revived in some contemporary weddings as a heritage element.
花 huā (to spend) + 钱 qián (money). The basic verb-object phrase for spending money. Often split by an amount: 花了不少钱 "spent quite a lot of money," 花很多钱 "spend a lot."

e: to spend time; to take time
d: 花 huā (to spend) + 时间 shíjiān (time). To spend or take time on something. The same verb 花 covers time as well as money, where English needs a different word for each.
花 huā (patterned) + 样 yàng (shape, kind). A decorative pattern or a fancy variation, and by extension a trick or gimmick: 玩花样 "to play tricks," 花样滑冰 "figure skating."
花 huā (flower) + 园 yuán (garden, plot). A garden, a cultivated plot of flowers and plants. 植物园 zhíwùyuán is a botanical garden; 动物园 dòngwùyuán, a zoo, keeps the same 园.

e: Huayan — the jewel-net philosophy of total interpenetration
d: Based on the 华严经 Huáyán Jīng (Avatamsaka Sutra), Huayan developed the most philosophically ambitious vision in Chinese Buddhism: the mutual interpenetration and non-obstruction of all phenomena.
滑 huá (to slide; slippery) + 雪 xuě (snow). To ski, literally "to slide on snow." The word covers downhill skiing and snowboarding alike in casual use.
To resolve a contradiction, a common phrase in management, diplomacy, and mediation contexts. 化解 (huàjiě) means to dissolve or resolve; 化 alone means to transform or change.

e: to turn into; to become; to be reduced to
d: 化 huà (to transform) + 为 wéi (to be; to become), a literary verb of becoming. 化为 marks a complete turning of one thing into another, often dramatic and frequently with a sense of dissolution or loss.

e: transforming inborn nature and establishing the deliberately cultivated
d: 化 huà (transform) + 性 xìng (inborn nature) + 起 qǐ (establish, raise up) + 伪 wèi (deliberate cultivation). The Xunzian formula for what moral education accomplishes: it transforms what is innate and establishes in its place the cultivated.
Chemistry: transformation-study. 化学反应 is a chemical reaction; 化学式 (huàxuéshì) is a chemical formula, read left to right like grammar.

Literally "to mark off an era," used as an adjective for something so significant it divides history into before and after: 划时代的发明 ("an epoch-making invention"). 划 (to mark, to divide) plus 时代. The strongest everyday word for a development that changes the age itself.
画 huà (to draw) + 画 huà (a picture). A verb-object pair, literally "to draw a drawing," the everyday way to say one is drawing or painting. The first 画 is the action, the second is what it produces.

画 huà (to paint; to draw; a painting) + 家 jiā. One who has made painting their home. The 家 suffix elevates the painter from a craftsperson to a master, implying sustained creative commitment and a body of work rather than mere technical skill.

e: a scene; an image (on a screen or in a picture); a frame
d: 画 huà (picture) + 面 miàn (surface; face). The visible surface of a picture or screen: the framed image you see in a film, a photo, or a painting. 画面很美 "the image is beautiful."

e: "Coming back to what we were saying" or "on the other hand
d: "Coming back to what we were saying" or "on the other hand." Marks a return to a previous thread, often with a contrasting take. Useful for acknowledging a counterpoint to your own argument: "but coming back to it, you do have a point that…"
话 huà (speech; talk) + 题 tí (topic). What a conversation is about: 换个话题 "change the subject," 热门话题 "a hot topic." It frames the heading of talk rather than writing.

e: nostalgia; to reminisce; longing for the past
d: 怀 (huái, to hold in the heart; to cherish , heart 忄+ 衣 clothing, the sense of something held close) + 旧 (old). Nostalgia as an emotional posture: the conscious holding of the past with affection.

e: to cherish the memory of; to reminisce

d: Huaiyang cuisine: the specific tradition of the Yangzhou-Huai'an axis, considered the most technically refined of Chinese culinary traditions and the foundation of state banquet cooking.
坏 (bad) + 处 (point, aspect). The disadvantage or harm of something, the standard counterpart to 好处 (hǎochu, benefit). Weighed up when deciding whether something is worth doing.
坏 (bad) + 蛋 (egg). A literal rotten egg, used figuratively for a scoundrel. Colloquial and elastic: a genuine insult when angry, a flirtatious tease between a couple when said with a smile.
坏 (to break down) + 了 (change-of-state particle). The everyday way to say a device or appliance has stopped working, or that food has gone off. Also a spoken exclamation: 坏了！ "Uh-oh, this is bad!"
坏 (bad) + 人 (person). The default word a child learns for the villain in a story or the stranger to avoid. Broad and moral, covering everyone from the cartoon antagonist to a genuine criminal.

e: to cheer; to hail with joy
d: 欢 huān (joy) + 呼 hū (to shout; to call). To shout for joy, the sound a crowd makes in celebration: 欢呼声 "cheers," 人们欢呼雀跃 "people cheered and jumped for joy."
欢 huān (joy) + 快 kuài (fast; quick). Joy with a quick, light tempo: a brisk and cheerful mood. Often said of music, rhythm, and movement: 欢快的旋律 "a lively melody," 欢快的舞步 "brisk, cheerful dance steps."
欢 huān (joy) + 乐 lè (happy; glad). Joy of the shared, festive kind: a celebration, a holiday, a crowd in good spirits. 欢乐的气氛 "a joyful atmosphere." More outward and communal than the quiet 高兴.
欢 (joyful) plus 送 (see off). To send someone off with celebration: a farewell party for a retiring colleague or a graduating class. The opposite number of 欢迎 (huānyíng), to welcome.

e: to be jubilant; to seethe with joy
d: 欢 huān (joy) + 腾 téng (to leap; to surge). A crowd boiling over with joy, leaping and shouting. Said of stadiums, squares, and whole towns at a great moment: 全场欢腾 "the whole place erupted in jubilation."
欢 huān (merry) + 喜 xǐ (glad). A warm, somewhat colloquial word for being happy and pleased, common in the south and in the phrase 欢欢喜喜 "all merry and glad," and in 皆大欢喜 "everyone happy."

欢 huān (joy) + 迎 yíng (to greet; to meet). To receive someone gladly. Also the set greeting 欢迎 "welcome!" and the shop sign 欢迎光临 "welcome, please come in." 受欢迎 shòu huānyíng means "popular; well-liked."

幻 huàn (illusion; phantom; to change; to vanish) + 想 xiǎng (thought; imagination). Thinking directed at what is illusory or impossible: fantasy, wishful thinking, daydreaming. Carries a mildly critical register , implies the thought has decoupled from reality.
换 (swap) + 班 (shift). To trade work shifts with a coworker, or for one shift to hand over to the next. The swap is of time slots rather than objects.
换 (swap) + 车 (vehicle). To get off one bus, train, or subway line and board another. The word every commuter says at an interchange station; 换乘 (huànchéng) is the signboard version.

"Let's change the subject." Direct topic-change marker, used when the current thread has run its course or when you want to move on from something uncomfortable. Slightly more deliberate than 对了; signals an intentional shift rather than a stumble onto something new.
Literally swap a sentence and say it: 换 (swap) + 句话 (a sentence) + 说 (say). A fixed connective that restates a point another way, exactly like English "to put it differently."
换 (swap) + 钱 (money). A verb-object pair for converting currency or breaking a large note into small ones. The default phrase at any bank counter or exchange window.
换 (swap) + 衣服 (clothes). The everyday house phrase: take off what you are wearing and put on something else. The same frame builds 换鞋 (change shoes) and 换床单 (change the sheets).

皇 huáng (august; emperor) + 后 (the commanding consort). The principal wife of a reigning emperor in the Chinese imperial system. A formal title with specific ritual privileges and a defined role in the imperial hierarchy.

e: yellow tea — the rarest of the six categories
Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine

d: 黄 (huáng, yellow) + 河 (river). The silt-yellow river of north China, cradle of early Chinese civilization. Here 河 returns to its oldest job, naming this exact river, with 黄 added once 河 stopped meaning it by default.

黄 huáng (yellow) + 金 jīn (gold/metal). The word for gold as a metal (yellow gold). Also used figuratively: 黄金时代 "golden age" · 黄金地段 "prime location" · 黄金周 "Golden Week" (national holidays). 金 alone can also mean gold, but 黄金 is the explicit metallic sense.

e: Huang-Lao school; the syncretic Daoist-Legalist school that governed early Han China
d: 黄 Huáng (Yellow Emperor 黄帝, the legendary sage-ruler of antiquity) + 老 Lǎo (Laozi 老子) + 之学 (the learning of).

The almanac: literally "yellow calendar," named for the imperial yellow of the official calendar. An annual publication (now also a mobile app feature) that gives day-by-day auspiciousness ratings based on the traditional calendrical system.
黄 (huáng, yellow) + 牛, literally the yellow ox of the fields. In cities it became slang for a ticket scalper, from the way scalpers swarm and jostle like a milling herd.

The Loess Plateau: the wind-deposited silt plateau of northwestern China that gives the Yellow River its color and its sediment load. Covering approximately 640,000 km², it is one of the largest loess deposits on earth and the cradle of earliest Chinese agriculture.

Huizhou ink , ink sticks produced in the Huizhou region of Anhui province, regarded as the finest in China. Huizhou is also home to the She inkstone 歙砚 and Xuan paper, making Anhui province the geographic center of the Four Treasures tradition.

Huizhou merchants: the merchant class from the southern Anhui mountain region who dominated certain sectors of Chinese commerce (especially salt, timber, and pawnbroking) from the Song through the Qing dynasty.
回 (huí, to return) plus 报 (to requite): to give back in kind. Used for repaying kindness and, in finance, for the return on an investment.

e: to answer; to reply; an answer
d: 回 huí (back) + 答 dá (to respond). To send a response back to a question: 回答问题 "to answer a question." As a noun, the answer itself: 一个满意的回答 "a satisfactory answer."

e: "Coming back to what we were talking about
d: "Coming back to what we were talking about." Returns to an earlier thread after a digression. Particularly useful in longer conversations where you want to close out a tangent and pick up the original point.

e: to go home; to return home
d: 回 huí (to return) + 家 jiā (home). One of the most common V+location phrases in the language. The directional verb 回 indicates movement back toward an origin point: home as the natural destination of return, not merely a place you happen to go.

回 huí (to return; to turn back) + 来 lái (toward here). To turn and come back toward the speaker's reference point, usually home, a shared location, or where you were before leaving. The counterpart is 回去 huíqù (to go back, returning away from the speaker).

e: To return a gift , to reciprocate with a gift of one's own
d: To return a gift , to reciprocate with a gift of one's own. 回礼 is expected and its absence is noticed. The return gift should be roughly equivalent in value to the original but need not be identical in kind. Returning a gift of equal or slightly higher value is considered courteous.

e: to turn one's head; later; to repent
d: 回 huí (turn back) + 头 tóu (head). To turn the head around, and by extension "in a little while" (回头见 "see you later") or to turn back from a wrong path (回头是岸 "to repent is to reach the shore").

e: to recall; to look back on; a memory
d: 回 huí (turn back) + 忆 yì (to remember). To turn the mind back to the past. As a noun, a remembered scene: 美好的回忆 "fond memories." The eddy here loops through time rather than space.

A factory that quotes in dollars but pays its costs in RMB carries the exchange risk and may ask to reprice when the rate moves. 汇率波动 (huìlǜ bōdòng) is fluctuation. Agree a reference rate, or a band within which the price stays fixed.

e: can speak Chinese — learned through study and practice
d: 会 indicates that a skill was acquired through learning, training, or practice. The speaker once did not have this ability and now does , through effort. This is the fundamental meaning: know how to.

A short written summary of decisions, owners, and dates, sent the same day. Offering to write it yourself means your version becomes the record. 白纸黑字 (báizhǐ hēizì, "black ink on white paper") is the idiom for having it in writing.

绘 huì (to depict) + 画 huà (to paint). A more formal word than 画画, naming painting as a discipline or art form: 绘画艺术 "the art of painting." Used in writing and in talk about fine art rather than casual sketching.

e: Huike — second patriarch; the arm in the snow
d: Huike (487–593 CE) is remembered for two things: the snow-and-arm story of his fierce aspiration, and the exchange above about the unfindable mind , which is itself a kōan on the non-existence of a substantial, locatable self.

e: Huineng — sixth patriarch; the Platform Sutra; Southern Chan
d: Huineng (638–713 CE) is the most historically consequential figure in Chinese Chan. An illiterate woodcutter from Guangdong, he achieved sudden recognition of his original nature upon hearing a line from the Diamond Sutra.

e: Huiyuan (334–416 CE) — Eastern Jin dynasty founder
d: Huiyuan is revered as the first patriarch of Chinese Pure Land Buddhism, though he did not use that term himself.

婚 hūn (marriage) + 礼 lǐ (rite; ceremony). Wedding as ritual. The 礼 suffix creates ceremony words for life's great transitions: 婚礼 wedding · 葬礼 zànglǐ funeral · 成人礼 chéngrénlǐ coming-of-age ceremony · 开幕礼 kāimùlǐ opening ceremony.

婚 hūn (marriage, 女 woman + 昏 dusk, from the tradition of evening weddings) + 姻 yīn (marriage-alliance; matrimony, 女 woman + 因 cause/connection). The formal compound for marriage. 婚礼 hūnlǐ = wedding ceremony. 结婚 jiéhūn = to get married. 离婚 líhūn = to divorce.

e: activity; event; to move about; to exercise
d: 活 huó (lively) + 动 dòng (to move). As a noun, an organized activity or event; as a verb, to move one's body, to stretch and stir after sitting still. The lively-and-moving pair names anything that gets people up and going.

e: work; a job; a task; a piece of work
d: 活 huó (work) + the retroflex 儿 (ér) ending, typical of northern colloquial speech. The concrete job itself: the work to be done, often skilled handwork. A fine piece of craftsmanship is 好活儿 (good work).

Living Buddha , the Chinese term for a recognized reincarnation (tulku in Tibetan). Not precisely "Buddha" in the doctrinal sense but a lama whose successive rebirths are identified and confirmed by the tradition. The Dalai Lama and Panchen Lama are the most senior examples.

活 huó (lively) + 泼 pō (to splash, itself a water word). A doubled water image, the splash of a living current, describing a bright, spirited, outgoing temperament. Most natural for children and young people: 活泼可爱 (lively and adorable).
活 huó = living, alive. Used in folk speech to describe a person of extraordinary virtue or generosity , a doctor who heals the poor without payment, a neighbor who gives without being asked.

活 huó (to live) + 着 zhe (the durative marker, an ongoing state). To be in the state of being alive, as opposed to 死了 (dead). Yú Huá's famous novel 《活着》 takes the word as its whole subject: simply going on living through everything.

火 huǒ + 车 chē (vehicle; cart). Named when steam locomotives first arrived in China , "fire-powered cart." The word has outlasted the steam era. 高铁 gāotiě (high-speed rail) is now preferred for bullet trains, but 火车 remains in universal use.

火 huǒ + 锅 guō (pot; wok). A simmering communal pot at the table , the quintessential Chinese social meal. 吃火锅 = to eat hotpot, one of the most common social dining activities. Regional varieties: 四川火锅 Sichuan hotpot (numbing-spicy 麻辣), 北京涮羊肉 Beijing lamb hotpot (clear broth).

e: the right heat and timing; (by extension) the right moment or level of skill
d: 火 huǒ (fire) + 候 hou (the timing of). In cooking, the exact control of heat and duration that makes or ruins a dish. Figuratively, the ripeness of a moment or the maturity of a skill: 火候到了 "the moment is ripe."
火 huǒ (fire) + 山 shān (mountain). A fire-mountain. Strikingly direct. Related: 火山爆发 volcanic eruption · 活火山 active volcano · 死火山 extinct volcano · 休眠火山 dormant volcano.

The fire star twice over: the red planet of the five-phase planet names, and the everyday spark from a fire or a grinder's wheel. Internet slang added a third life: a 火星人 (Martian) is someone hopelessly behind on the news.
火 huǒ + 焰 yàn (flame , itself contains the fire radical 火). Used for actual flames and for intensity: 熊熊火焰 "roaring flames." Also in compound idioms: 火焰般的热情 "flame-like passion."

或 (perhaps; one possibility) + 者 (the said one; that case). Originally meaning "one possibility or the other," 或者 grammaticalized into a straightforward conjunction meaning "or." It works across both spoken and written registers, unlike 还是 hái shì (which is restricted to questions) or 抑或 yìhuò (whic…
货 huò (goods; commodity) + 物 wù (thing). Goods as freight or stock in trade, the things that move through commerce: 运送货物 "to transport goods," 货物清单 "a manifest of cargo."

e: wok breath; the scorched aroma of high-heat cooking

d: A 乩童 (also written 乩手 jīshǒu or 乩身 jīshēn) is a human medium through whom a deity speaks and acts. During trance, the medium is said to be ridden by the god (神明附身 shénmíng fùshēn).

e: sharp spontaneous exchange — the master tests the student
d: 机 jī (opportunity; trigger) + 锋 fēng (blade; sharpness). The live Chan exchange: master and student meet in the present moment, and the master uses any available means , a question, a non-sequitur, a shout, a gesture , to test whether the student is genuinely awake or merely performing understanding…

e: quick-witted; resourceful; clever in the moment
d: 机 jī (opportunity; mechanism; key moment , originally a trigger mechanism on a crossbow, the precisely timed release point) + 智 zhì (intelligence; discernment). Wisdom that activates at the right moment: the quick intelligence that reads a situation instantly and responds with precision.
肌 (jī, muscle tissue) + 肉 (flesh). The fibrous flesh that moves the body; both characters carry the 月 flesh-radical.
鸡 (jī, chicken) + 蛋 (egg): the default egg in Chinese kitchens. When a recipe or menu just says egg, it means a hen's egg, so 鸡蛋 is one of the first nouns most learners cook with.
鸡 (chicken) + 肉 (ròu, meat). The flesh on the menu, as opposed to the live bird. Pair it with 牛肉 (niúròu, beef) and 猪肉 (zhūròu, pork) to name the everyday meats.

e: to accumulate virtue · good karma; meritorious deeds
d: 积善 jī shàn: 积 jī (to accumulate; to pile up over time) + 善 shàn. The idea that individual good acts deposit something durable in a person's character or fate , virtue as a slow savings account rather than a single decision.

e: basic; fundamental; (基本上) basically, on the whole
d: 基 jī (foundation) + 本 běn (root). The base layer of something: 基本功 jīběngōng (basic skills), 基本工资 (base salary). The adverb 基本上 jīběnshàng means "basically, by and large."

基本 jīběn (basic; fundamental) + 功 gōng (skill). The foundational skills of any discipline, the drills a beginner must master before anything else: scales for a musician, stances for a martial artist, strokes for a calligrapher.
Gene: sounds like the English, means "basic cause." 转基因 (zhuǎnjīyīn, transgenic/GMO) is the charged supermarket word built on it.

e: excited; agitated; stirred up; worked up
d: 激 jī (to rouse; to surge) + 动 dòng (to stir). A fast, strong emotional stirring, joy, anger, or agitation that one can barely sit still through: 太激动了 "so excited," 别激动 "calm down."

e: to pass the imperial examination; to place in the rankings
d: 及 jí (to reach; to attain) + 第 dì (rank). To succeed in the civil-service exam and be placed in the official order. A historical and literary term; the modern equivalent is 考上 kǎoshàng (to test into).
及 (reach) + 格 (the standard grid): to reach the mark, customarily 60 out of 100. 不及格 is failing, and the near-miss score of 59 is proverbial for agony: 59分 is one point short of relief.

Auspicious, lucky, propitious , the standard term for something considered to bring good fortune. A number, date, phrase, or object that is 吉利 is sought after and displayed. Its opposite: 不吉利 (bù jílì), inauspicious.

e: extremely; utterly; in the highest degree
d: 极 jí (extreme; pole; utmost) + 其 qí (its; that). "Its extreme" , intensifier placing something at the outer limit of its property. More formal and emphatic than 非常 fēicháng or 很 hěn. Common in written evaluations, literary description, and critical prose.
急 (urgent) + 救 (jiù, to save). Saving in haste. The set term for first aid and emergency rescue: 急救箱 (jíjiùxiāng) is a first-aid kit, 急救车 (jíjiùchē) an ambulance.
急 (urgent) + 忙 (máng, busy). An adverb of manner: doing something fast because time is short. It sits right before the verb to color the action with haste.
急 (impatient) + 性子 (xìngzi, temperament). Someone whose nature is to rush, who cannot stand waiting. The opposite is 慢性子 (mànxìngzi), an unhurried, easygoing type.

急 (urgent) + 诊 (zhěn, to diagnose). Emergency consultation. 急诊 is the hospital department you go to when something cannot wait, the Chinese counterpart of the emergency room. 看急诊 (kàn jízhěn) means to go to the ER.
