疾 (jí) and 病 are near-synonyms paired into one formal noun. In classical usage 疾 was the slight ailment and 病 the serious one; fused together, 疾病 is the neutral cover term for disease in medical and official language.

e: the truth of the origin of suffering — craving and clinging
d: 集 jí = accumulation, gathering. Sanskrit samudaya: arising. The cause of suffering is 贪爱 tān'ài (craving/clinging, also translated 渴爱 kě'ài, thirst): the driven, compulsive wanting and clinging to pleasant experiences, the desperate aversion to unpleasant ones, and the delusion of a fixed self that…
集 jí (to gather) + 体 tǐ (body). A gathered body of people acting as one: 集体活动 "a group activity," 集体主义 "collectivism." Set against the individual, 个人 gèrén.

e: collective wisdom; the shared intelligence of a group
d: 集体 jítǐ (collective; group; the body of people together) + 智慧. The wisdom that emerges from a group deliberating, pooling experience, and correcting one another , greater than any individual's 智慧 alone.

Asks about a small, countable number, typically under ten, and must be followed by a measure word: 几个 ("how many"), 几本 ("how many volumes"), 几位 ("how many people," polite). It assumes the answer is small, so it is the word for guests, family members, hours, or days.

Outside questions, 几 + measure word means "a few": 几个朋友 (a few friends), 几本书 (a few books), 前几天 (a few days ago). The same word asks "how many?" when the expected answer is small; the statement and question readings are told apart by context and intonation.
几 jǐ (how many; a few) + 个 ge. Either a question ("how many?") or a vague small number ("a few"), depending on context: 几个人 "how many people?" or "a few people."
Geometry. Classical Chinese for "how much?", repurposed by Xu Guangqi and Matteo Ricci in their 1607 translation of Euclid. Both senses live on: one in the classroom, one in Cao Cao's poetry.

己 jǐ (one's own) + 见 jiàn (view). The opinion that is distinctly one's own, valued for independence but cautioned against when it hardens into obstinacy. Lives in 固执己见, "to cling stubbornly to one's own view."

e: what one does not desire (for oneself)

d: Cancellations, postponements, rejections, and suspensions are natural territory for 被. The subject (plan) is acted upon by an impersonal or unspecified authority. The adversative flavor is clear: the plan was ended by something outside its (or its creator's) control.
To calculate, to compute. The formal verb behind 计算机 (jìsuànjī, computer, "calculating machine") and 计算器 (jìsuànqì, calculator). Colloquial speech often just says 算 (suàn).
记 jì (to record) + 笔记 bǐjì (notes). The standard phrase for taking notes: in class, in a meeting, during a lecture. The verb-object construction: 上课要记笔记 (take notes in class).
记 jì (to keep in mind) + 得 de (a resultative marker). To have something still held in memory, the everyday word for remembering: 我记得他 "I remember him." Its opposite is 忘记 wàngjì (to forget).

e: a mark; a sign (made to remember by)
d: 记 jì (to mark) + 号 hào (sign, number). A mark made deliberately so you can find or recall a spot: 做记号 "to make a mark." Often a tick beside a line or a fold in a page.
记 jì (to write down) + 录 lù (to copy, to register). To set something down in writing, and the written result itself. Also the "record" that is broken in sport: 世界记录 "world record."
记 jì (to remember) + 忆 yì (to recall, recollect). The faculty of memory and its contents, more formal and abstract than 记得: 童年的记忆 "childhood memories," 记忆力 jìyìlì "the power of memory."
记 jì (to record) + 者 zhě (one who). Literally "one who records," the reporter whose work is to set down and report events: 新闻记者 "a news reporter."

e: to remember firmly; to commit to memory
d: 记 jì (to keep in mind) + 住 zhù (a resultative meaning "to stay fast"). To make something stick so it will not slip away: 记住这个号码 "memorize this number." The 住 stresses that the memory has caught and held.

祭祖 (lit. "offering to ancestors") is the ritual presentation of food, incense, and goods to deceased family members. The offering table holds cooked dishes (often the ancestor's favorite foods in life), rice, fruit, and wine. Incense is lit and prostrations (拜 bài) are made.

e: Jixia Academy — the Warring States research university
d: Established by the state of Qi near its capital Linzi (临淄 Líncí) in the early 4th century BCE, operating for about a century. Scholars from all schools received state stipends and official titles without bureaucratic duties.

加 jiā (to add; to increase) + 快 kuài (fast). Adding more speed to something already in motion. Common in official and news language for policy goals, construction schedules, and economic development; equally at home in everyday speech.
加 (jiā, to add) plus 热 (heat): to add heat, to warm something up. The verb on the microwave button and the recipe step.

e: in addition; plus; adding to this

d: 扫一扫 (sǎo yi sǎo) is "scan"; one person shows their QR code (二维码 èrwéimǎ), the other scans. 我扫你 means "I'll scan yours." 拉群 (lā qún) is to create a group chat, the norm for an order with several people on each side.
加油 (jiāyóu, to add fuel) + 站 (station): the place a car stops to refuel. Note that 加油 doubles as the cheer "let's go! keep it up!", literally "add oil," but here it is strictly the fuel sense.
To pick up with chopsticks: the specific verb for the gripping action of chopsticks. 夹菜 (jiā cài) is to pick up food from a shared dish.

To pick food for someone else , placing food from a shared dish into another person's bowl as a gesture of care and hospitality. The action is performed with chopsticks and directed toward honored guests, elders, or someone whose preferences you are attending to.

e: auspicious festival; festive holiday — literary register
d: 佳 jiā (excellent; fine; auspicious) + 节 jié (festival; season; node). A slightly elevated term for a holiday or festival occasion, preferred in literary and formal contexts over the more neutral 节日 (jiérì).
佳 jiā (fine; good) + 音 yīn (word; news). The good news one hopes for, slightly formal in tone: 静候佳音 "to await good news quietly," a polite way to say you are hoping for a favorable reply.

家 jiā (home) + 常 cháng (ordinary; often; constant). The routine of domestic life: meals, small talk, everyday rhythms. A warmly neutral word that positions the homely and ordinary as valuable rather than inferior.

e: family tradition; values passed through generations
d: 家 jiā (family) + 风 fēng (wind; custom; style; ethos). The invisible ethos that blows through a family across generations: the unspoken values, behavioral norms, and character traits transmitted from parents to children.

家 jiā (family) + 规 guī (rules; regulations; norms). The explicit code of conduct of a household, the spoken version of what 家风 transmits implicitly. Distinguished families in imperial China often had written 家规 codifying expectations for children's conduct, study, and marriage.

e: family-country sentiment; patriotic feeling rooted in personal bonds
d: 家 (family) + 国 (country) + 情怀 qínghuái (feeling, sentiment, cherished aspiration). The emotional bond that flows from family love outward to love of country: the Confucian ladder enacted as feeling.

家 jiā + 人 rén (person/people). The people of the home. More intimate and emotionally warm than the formal compound 家庭成员 (family members, bureaucratic). 家人 feels like "my people": those who share your roof and your life.

Family; household. The nuclear unit of parents and children who share a home. 家庭作业 (jiātíng zuòyè, homework , lit. "family work") and 家庭医生 (jiātíng yīshēng, family doctor) show the compound in everyday use. The term carries a warmth and domesticity that the more formal 家族 lacks.

家 jiā + 乡 xiāng (countryside; native place, the rural origin point). The place where 家 was first made. A place of origin rather than merely an address: family roots, ancestral connections, formative landscape. Central to Chinese identity, deeply tied to belonging and longing.

Clan; extended family network; lineage group sharing a surname. 家族企业 (jiāzú qǐyè) is a family business , often meaning a business controlled across generations by a single clan. The word implies shared ancestry, shared surname, and historically shared clan property and ancestral hall (祠堂 cítáng).

e: Jiayu Pass — western terminus of the Ming wall
oracle bone script — the earliest Chinese writing
d: 甲 jiǎ (shell / armor) + 骨 gǔ (bone) + 文 wén (writing). Writing incised on turtle plastrons (腹甲 fùjiǎ) and ox scapulae (肩胛骨 jiānjiǎgǔ) used for royal divination during the Late Shang period. Over 4,000 distinct graphs have been identified; roughly 2,000 are deciphered.
假 jiǎ (false; supposed) + 如 rú (suppose). A slightly more formal "if," at home with imagined or hypothetical cases: 假如我是你 "supposing I were you." Interchangeable with 如果 in most sentences.
价 (price) + 格 (a fixed standard, a slot). The settled, stated price of a good, the figure printed on the tag or quoted by the seller. The everyday word for what something costs.
价 (price) + 值 (to be worth). The abstract worth of a thing, an act, or an idea, far beyond any market figure. Carries the moral and intellectual sense, as in 价值观 (jiàzhíguān), a set of values.

Dowry , the goods the bride's family sends with her to the new home. Traditionally included furniture, bedding, household items, and valuable objects. The dowry and betrothal gifts are understood as a two-way transfer that balances the exchange between families.

兼 jiān (jointly; all together; simultaneously) + 爱 ài (love; care). The central Mohist doctrine: love that makes no distinction by relationship, proximity, or social standing. Contrasted directly with the Confucian 爱有差等 ài yǒu chā děng (love is graded by degree of relationship).

e: to reduce; to decrease; to diminish
d: 减 jiǎn (to subtract, to reduce) + 少 (few, less). To make less: to reduce a quantity, frequency, or intensity. 减少污染 (reduce pollution); 减少开支 (cut expenditure); 人数减少了 (the number of people decreased). The standard verb for any reduction in quantity.

e: abbreviated-character tablature — the guqin's notational system
d: 减 jiǎn (reduce; abbreviate) + 字 zì (character) + 谱 pǔ (notation; score). Developed in the Tang dynasty, used continuously since. Each composite character encodes string number, finger, position, and technique in a single glyph. Over 3,000 pieces survive in this notation.

From a lab, often for a named standard: LFGB, FDA, and the like are said as letters. 认证 (rènzhèng) is certification, 证书 (zhèngshū) the certificate. Check the report's date and which material it covers.
简 (pared down) + 便 (convenient). A method or procedure that is both simple and easy to use, with no fuss in the steps.
简 (brief) + 称 (to call, a name). The shortened form of a long name: 北大 for 北京大学, 联合国 from its full title. As a verb, to abbreviate something as.
简 (slip, hence pared down) + 单 (single, plain). The everyday word for simple, whether a task, an idea, or a person who is uncomplicated. Negated as 不简单 it flips to mean impressive, no small feat.
"To put it simply" or "in short." Introduces a condensed version of a longer explanation. Useful when you have been speaking at length and want to summarize the core point.
简 (pared down) + 短 (short). Brief in the sense of few words: a brief speech, a brief reply, a brief note. The narrow slip rendered literal as length.

简 (simple) + 化 (the -ize / -ify suffix, to turn into). To make a process, a procedure, or a script simpler. The very term 简体字 (jiǎntǐzì), simplified characters, is the product of this verb applied to writing itself.
简 (brief) + 介 (to introduce). The short blurb that sums up a book, a company, a film, or a person. The about-line under a profile is a 简介.
简 (brief) + 历 (one's history, experience). A condensed record of your schooling and work, the document you send with a job application. Literally a brief life-history.

简 jiǎn (simple; brief; bamboo slip, an early writing surface) + 体 tǐ (form; style) + 字 zì. Introduced in mainland China in the 1950s–1960s under the People's Republic, with the goal of increasing literacy rates.
简 (plainly) + 直 (straight, directly). An adverb of emphasis: put plainly and directly, it amounts to. Used to push a statement to its extreme, often with a touch of exasperation or wonder.

e: see a ghost! — absurd! ridiculous! what the hell!
d: 见 jiàn (to see; to encounter) + 鬼 guǐ (ghost). Literally "see a ghost!" — used as an exclamation of disbelief, exasperation, or dismissal of something absurd. Equivalent to "what the hell!" or "that makes no sense!" Does not carry strong profanity weight.

e: to meet; to see one another (in person)
d: 见 jiàn (to see) + 面 miàn (face). Literally "to see faces," the everyday verb for meeting someone in person. It is a separable verb: 见了一面 "met once," 见过面 "have met before."

建 jiàn (to build, to establish) + 国 (country, state). The founding of a state. 建国以来 (since the founding of the country) is a common phrase that, depending on speaker, refers to 1912 (Republic) or 1949 (People's Republic). 国庆节 (National Day, October 1) marks the 1949 建国.
Architecture, building. 建筑师 (jiànzhùshī) is an architect, distinct from the 工程师 who makes the building stand up. As a verb, 建 alone means to build: 建一座桥, build a bridge.

健 (robust) + 康 (well, at ease). The formal health word: 健康码 was the pandemic-era health code, 健康证 the food-worker's health certificate, and 亚健康 ("sub-health") the popular term for run-down-but-not-sick, a category Chinese wellness culture takes seriously.

健 (strengthen) + 身 (body). The gym era's verb: 健身房 is the gym, 健身教练 the personal trainer. The park's older exercise culture keeps its own verb, 锻炼, so the generations can be told apart by which word they use.

Originally specifically the Yangtze River (长江 Chángjiāng , the Long River), which is so dominant in Chinese geography that 江 alone referred to it. Over time 江 generalized to any large river, while smaller rivers typically use 河 hé.

North of the Yangtze. In local usage, particularly in Nanjing and Shanghai, this refers to the area immediately north of the river, considered rougher and less cosmopolitan than Jiangnan. A mild regional insult in some contexts.

e: the debts and vendettas of the martial world; the cycle of obligation and revenge
d: 江湖 + 恩 ēn (grace; debt of kindness) + 怨 yuàn (grievance; resentment). The engine of wuxia narratives: every favor creates an obligation, every wrong creates a grievance. The 江湖 keeps score across generations , a debt unpaid by the father falls to the son.

e: a person of the rivers-and-lakes world; someone who lives by the code
d: The person defined by their membership in the 江湖 , not just someone who passes through it, but someone whose identity is constituted by it. 江湖人 abide by a parallel moral code: loyalty to sworn brothers (义气 yìqi), repayment of debts and favors, the obligation to right wrongs.

e: south of the Yangtze; the culturally and economically rich lower Yangtze region
d: 江 jiāng (the Yangtze) + 南 nán (south). The region south of the Yangtze , centred on present-day Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Shanghai , is the most romanticized landscape in classical Chinese poetry. 江南 means silk, canals, spring rain, white walls, and scholar gardens.

e: Jiang Qing, Mao's wife, Gang of Four leader
every generation of rivers and mountains produces its talented people; each era brings forth its own greatness
d: From Zhao Yi's (赵翼) 18th-century poem 论诗 (On Poetry): 江山代有才人出，各领风骚数百年 (every generation of rivers and mountains produces its talented people; each holds sway for hundreds of years).

e: the future; in the future; what is coming
d: 将 jiāng (about to; will; the near future) + 来 lái (coming; arriving). What is about to arrive, the future approaching. 将来 refers to the general future (not an immediate event). Slightly more formal than 以后 yǐhòu. Contrast: 未来 wèilái (the future, lit.

e: to speak; to explain; to lecture
to mind one's manners; to be attentive to politeness
d: 讲 jiǎng (to attend to; to value; to make a point of) + 礼貌. The active form: not just having manners but consciously practicing them. Common in parental instruction and educational contexts. 讲礼貌 is what 有礼貌 looks like as a discipline rather than a state.

e: to be civilized; to behave with proper manners
d: The everyday descendant of the classical sense, deployed across public-conduct campaigns. Bus stops, parks, and tourist sites carry signs urging citizens to 讲文明 (be civilized) and 讲礼貌 (be polite).

e: to descend; to lower; to fall
to reduce; to lower; to bring down
d: 降 jiàng (to descend, to lower , as in altitude, rank, or intensity) + 低 (low). The standard transitive verb for reducing a measurable value: 降低价格 (lower the price); 降低风险 (reduce the risk); 降低标准 (lower the standard).

e: to cut the price, mark down
d: 降 (to lower) + 价 (price). To bring a price down, to discount. Its opposite is 涨价 (zhǎngjià), to raise the price. Both are verb-object compounds, so an amount can split them: 降了价.

e: to land; to descend (aircraft); to come down
d: 降 jiàng (to descend, to lower) + 落 luò (to land). The standard word for an aircraft landing. Also used for anything descending to earth: 降落伞 jiànglùosǎn = parachute.
交 jiāo (to cross) + 错 cuò (crosswise). The original "crossing" sense, with no fault implied: lines, paths, or branches weaving across one another. 纵横交错 describes a network running every which way.
交 (mutual) + 换 (swap). A two-way exchange where both sides hand something over: gifts, contact details, opinions, prisoners. More formal and reciprocal than a plain 换.

e: cross-collar wrapping right-over-left — the defining feature of hànfú

d: A verb-object phrase: 交 jiāo (to associate with, to form bonds) + 朋友. To make a single friend is 交个朋友 (with 个 splitting the phrase). The same 交 appears in 交流 (to exchange, communicate) and 社交 (social interaction), all built on the sense of mutual exchange.
Also 货期 (huòqī). Ask when the clock starts: from deposit received, from sample approval, or from materials arriving. 延期 (yánqī) is a delay; 赶货 (gǎnhuò) is rushing an order.

交 jiāo (to cross; to exchange; mutual) + 通 (to go through; to connect). The crossing-and-passing of people and vehicles: the whole system of movement through a place. 交通 covers traffic in the everyday sense (交通堵塞, a traffic jam) and transport as a category (交通工具, means of transport).
交通 (jiāotōng, traffic) + 灯 (light): the three-color signal at an intersection. Also called 红绿灯 (hónglǜdēng), literally the red-green light.

e: noodle topping; the garnish that makes the bowl
arrogant; proud (positive or negative depending on context)
d: 骄 jiāo (arrogant; a rearing horse , the original pictograph showed an unruly horse rearing up on its hind legs) + 傲 ào (proud; disdainful; lofty). The primary antonym of 谦虚. In moral discourse, always negative , 骄傲是谦虚的对立面 (arrogance is the opposite of humility).

角 jiǎo (corner) + 落 luò (to settle, to land). The place where things come to rest in the corner, a nook. Both literally (a room's corner) and figuratively (a quiet, tucked-away place in the world). The name of this site: 角落書屋.

e: dumplings — the northern New Year food
d: The quintessential northern Chinese New Year food, eaten at midnight on New Year's Eve in many northern households. The shape resembles the 元宝 yuánbǎo (ancient sycee gold ingots), making them symbols of wealth.
Dumpling wrapper, literally "dumpling skin." Sold pre-made in supermarkets, but making them by hand is considered superior.

脚 jiǎo + 本 běn (root; book; basis). The script for a play, film, or shoot , and, in the modern technical vocabulary, a programming script (a JavaScript file is a JS 脚本). The 脚 here gestures at the foundational text that the performance or program is built on.

脚 jiǎo + 步 bù (step). Both the literal sound of footsteps and the figurative pace of progress. 听见脚步声 "to hear footsteps"; 加快脚步 "to quicken one's pace"; 跟上时代的脚步 "to keep up with the pace of the times."

e: underfoot; right beneath one; (also) at the present moment
d: 脚 jiǎo + 下 xià (below). Literally under the foot , the immediate ground one is standing on. By extension, "right here, right now," especially in the older expression 脚下 used for the immediate present.

e: footprint; the mark of a foot
d: 脚 jiǎo + 印 yìn (mark; seal; print). Both the literal print of a foot in mud or snow, and the figurative traces someone has left behind: 留下脚印 "to leave footprints" can describe an explorer's path or a person's life-marks.

脚 jiǎo + 趾 zhǐ (toe; finger of the foot). The standard word for toe. Note the partner term: 手指 shǒuzhǐ "finger" (literally "hand-finger") , Chinese carefully distinguishes hand-fingers from foot-fingers.

e: to be a stickler; to take something too seriously
d: 较 jiào (to compare; to dispute) + 真. To insist on getting the real, exact, literal version of something , usually said with mild disapproval. The cousin of 认真 with the dial turned past serviceable into pedantic.
教 (to teach) + 练 (to drill). The one who teaches by drilling: a sports coach, a driving instructor, a fitness trainer.
教 jiào (to teach) + 师 shī (master; expert). The formal word for a teacher as a profession, common in writing and titles. In direct address the warmer 老师 lǎoshī is used instead.
教 jiào (to teach) + 室 shì (room). The room where teaching happens. Watch the tone of 室 (shì), and do not confuse it with 教师 jiàoshī (teacher); the two words differ only in the second syllable.

e: to teach (as a profession); to be a teacher
d: 教 jiāo (to teach) + 书 shū (books). Literally "to teach books," the standard way to say one teaches for a living. Note the first-tone jiāo here, the colloquial verb reading.
教 jiào (religion) + 堂 táng (hall). The hall of worship, a church building. The community of believers, by contrast, is 教会 jiàohuì.

e: a lesson (learned the hard way); to reprimand
d: 教 jiào (to teach) + 训 xùn (to admonish). As a noun, the lesson drawn from a mistake or setback: 吸取教训 "to learn the lesson." As a verb, to scold or take someone to task.

教 jiào (to teach) + 育 yù (to raise; to nurture). The whole enterprise of teaching and bringing up, as both a noun and a verb: 高等教育 "higher education," 教育孩子 "to bring up a child." This is the formal jiào reading.

The fermentation pit: the earthen or stone pit in which the fermented grain mash (酒醅 jiǔpēi) undergoes anaerobic fermentation. Old pits with established microbial ecosystems are considered the most valuable assets of a distillery.

"Staircase price": the unit price falls as quantity rises. Asking for a tier table is the cleanest way to learn the factory's real cost curve, and it moves the conversation from "lower the price" to "at what quantity."

e: to come into contact, to engage with
d: 接 (to touch) + 触 (chù, to make contact). Two surfaces meet, or two people start dealing with each other. Used for physical contact and for first encounters with ideas, fields, or strangers.
接 (receive) + 电话 (diànhuà, phone call). To take up a ringing call and connect the line. The hand that closes the gap now closes a circuit.

e: to approach; to be close to; to approximate
d: 接 jiē (to connect; to receive; to meet) + 近 (near). To connect by closing the gap , a more formal and abstract verb than 靠近.

e: one after another; in succession; repeatedly
d: 接 jiē (to join; to connect) + 连 lián (in a series). An adverb meaning that events occur in close, repeated succession, each new one arriving before the last has finished registering. Often reinforced as 接连不断 (continuously, without a break).

e: to pick someone up, to meet someone
d: 接 (to meet) + 人 (rén, person). To go to a station, airport, or door and collect a person who is arriving. The everyday counterpart to ceremonial 迎接.
接 (receive) + 受 (shòu, to be given). The hand takes what is offered and keeps it. Used for offers, opinions, criticism, conditions, anything you take in and agree to.
A clear, polite refusal. Stronger than 有点难, softer than 不行. Pair it with the reason and what you could accept.
接 (join) + 着 (zhe, continuing aspect). One action takes the baton from the one before it. Use it to mean "and then, right after that," or "go on (doing something)."

The opening of the closing mantra. Even taken out of liturgical context, these lines carry a strong recognizable rhythm in Chinese Buddhist culture; readers and listeners hear the rest of the mantra by implication when these first phrases sound.
街 (street) + 道 (road, way). The everyday word for a city street. In administrative use it also names the smallest urban division, the 街道办事处 (jiēdào bànshìchù), a neighborhood subdistrict office.
街 (street) + 坊 (a city ward). The people who share your street, your neighbors in the old close-knit sense. 街坊邻居 (jiēfang línjū) is the warm collective phrase for the whole neighborhood.
街 jiē (street) + 角 jiǎo (corner). The physical corner where two streets meet. In narrative, the street corner is a classic site of waiting, meeting, and chance encounter.
街 (street) + 区 (district, zone). A block or built-up quarter bounded by streets. Common in urban planning and real-estate talk: 商业街区 (shāngyè jiēqū) a commercial district.
街 (street) + 头 (head, end). The mouth of a street or the streetside in general. It frames public, open-air activity: 街头艺人 (jiētóu yìrén) a street performer, 街头篮球 (jiētóu lánqiú) streetball.

e: critical juncture; the pivot point of a situation
d: 节 jié (joint) + 骨 gǔ (bone) + 眼. The eye at the joint of the bone , the precise small spot at which a thing turns. Colloquial; almost always paired with 上 in 节骨眼上 "at the critical juncture."

节 (jié, section; festival; segment) + 目 (item). A listed performance item or broadcast segment. 电视节目 (TV program); 春节联欢晚会节目 (Spring Festival Gala items). The word traveled from variety show programs into streaming, where 综艺节目 means a variety program and 节目单 is a program schedule.

节 jié (node; joint; festival) + 日 rì (day). The standard word for a festival or public holiday. 传统节日 chuántǒng jiérì = traditional holiday (Spring Festival, Mid-Autumn, Dragon Boat). 法定节假日 fǎdìng jiàjià rì = statutory public holiday. 情人节 Qíngrén Jié = Valentine's Day (lit. "lover's day").
A short greeting at Chinese New Year and the Mid-Autumn Festival maintains the relationship between orders. 新年快乐 or 中秋快乐 with a line of thanks is enough.

e: to save; to cut down on; to use sparingly
d: 节 jié (restrain) + 省 shěng (to economize; to spare). To save money, time, or effort by using less of it: 节省时间 "save time," 节省开支 "cut expenses." The hands-on, daily-budget cousin of 节约.

Mozi condemned extravagant funerals, elaborate music, and luxury consumption on utilitarian grounds: if a practice does not benefit the people, enrich the state, and increase the population, it is harmful. His critique of Confucian ritual was direct and sustained.

节 jié (restrain) + 约 yuē (to bind; to limit). To hold consumption within bounds, especially of shared or large-scale resources: 节约用水 "conserve water," 节约能源 "conserve energy." The word of public campaigns and stated principle.

e: simple burial; against elaborate funerary practice
d: Three inches of wood for the coffin; three garments for the body; no grave mound. 节葬 is the direct application of 节用 to death. It was a pointed attack on the bronze-vessel burial culture of Mozi's era , the practice of entombing rulers with vast quantities of ritual bronzes, servants, and goods.

e: to restrain; to be moderate; temperance
d: 节 jié (restrain) + 制 zhì (to control). To hold one's appetites or conduct within limits: 饮食节制 "moderation in eating and drinking." The inward, moral side of 节, keeping a thing from running past its proper bound.
结 jié (to conclude) + 果 guǒ (fruit; result). The outcome a process ties off into. Also a connective: "as it turned out." Read this way it is jiéguǒ; the verb "to bear fruit" reads jiē guǒ instead.

e: to combine; to integrate; to unite
d: 结 jié (to tie) + 合 hé (to join). To bring two things together so they work as one: 理论与实践结合 "to combine theory with practice." Abstract and constructive, used of ideas, methods, and elements, not of physical knots.

结 jié (to tie) + 婚 hūn (marriage). To tie the marriage bond, the standard word for getting married. A separable verb: 结过婚 "have been married," 结了婚 "got married." Its opposite is 离婚 líhūn (to divorce).

结 jié (to tie, to knot, to conclude) + 论. The conclusion that an argument or investigation arrives at: the point where reasoning is tied off. 下结论 xià jiélùn "to draw a conclusion," 得出结论 déchū jiélùn "to reach a conclusion."

e: to settle in full: to pay off
sturdy; durable; (of a body) strong and solid
d: 结 jiē (to bear fruit; to form) + 实 shi (solid). Built to last, not flimsy: 这张桌子很结实 "this table is very sturdy." Of a person it means strongly built: 身体结实 "physically robust." Note the toneless reading jiēshi here, distinct from 结 jié elsewhere.

e: to end; to finish; to conclude
d: 结 jié (to tie off) + 束 shù (to bind; a bundle). To bring an event or period to its close: 会议结束了 "the meeting is over." Its opposite is 开始 kāishǐ (to begin).

e: to form a karmic bond; to connect; to begin a meaningful relationship
d: 结 jié (to tie; to form; to knot) + 缘. To tie a karmic thread , to form a connection that carries the weight of 缘分.
姐 (elder sister) plus 夫 (husband) names the man married to one's older sister. Chinese kinship marks the relation precisely, distinct from 妹夫 (mèifu), a younger sister's husband.
The doubled character is the everyday word for one's older sister. The second 姐 takes a neutral tone, giving the warm, soft cadence Chinese kinship terms favor.
姐 (elder sister) plus 妹 (younger sister) yokes the two into a single word for "sisters" as a pair or group, and by extension a tight circle of close female friends.

e: to remove; to lift; to terminate (a state or obligation)
d: 解 jiě + 除 chú (to remove; to do away with). To untie and clear away. Used for lifting a binding state or formal tie: 解除警报 = lift an alert; 解除合同 = terminate a contract; 解除武装 = disarm; 解除疲劳 = relieve fatigue. More formal than 解开, it dissolves an arrangement or condition rather than a physical knot.

e: to answer; to solve and explain; a solution
d: 解 jiě + 答 dá (to answer; to reply). To unravel and answer. Used for working out and explaining the answer to a question or problem, especially in study: 解答疑问 = answer a question; 标准解答 = the standard solution.

e: to interpret; to construe; to make sense of
d: 解 jiě (to untie; to dissolve; to explain) + 读. The standard verb for interpretive reading , of a text, a result, a signal, a person's behaviour. Where 阅读 is comprehending what is plainly there, 解读 is going after what is implicit.

解 jiě + 放 fàng (to release; to set free). To untie and let go. The standard word for liberating people from bondage, oppression, or restraint: 解放思想 = free up one's thinking; 解放双手 = free one's hands (from drudgery).

e: to unseal; to lift a lockdown

d: 解 jiě + 雇 gù (to hire; to employ). To undo the hiring. The formal word for dismissing someone from a job, the legal counterpart to the colloquial 炒鱿鱼 chǎo yóuyú (lit. stir-fry the squid). 解雇 separates the worker from the employment tie, the same "undoing a bind" logic applied to a contract of work.

e: to solve; to resolve; to settle
d: 解 jiě + 决 jué (to decide; to settle). To undo and settle. The all-purpose verb for solving a problem or settling a matter: 解决问题 = solve a problem; 解决困难 = overcome a difficulty; 想办法解决 = find a way to settle it.

e: to untie; to undo; to unfasten
d: 解 jiě + 开 kāi (to open). The most literal 解-word: to untie a knot, undo a button, unfasten a rope. By extension it covers loosening any bind, even a metaphorical one: 解开心结 = untie the knot in one's heart, resolve an inner tension. The picture of separating the bound thing is right on the surface.
解 jiě + 渴 kě (thirst; thirsty). To undo thirst. The everyday verb-object phrase for slaking thirst: 喝水解渴 = drink water to quench thirst; 西瓜很解渴 = watermelon is very thirst-quenching.

e: to explain; to interpret; an explanation
d: 解 jiě + 释 shì (to release; to elucidate). To open a thing up and let its sense out. The everyday word for explaining: 解释原因 = explain the reason; 做出解释 = give an explanation. It also covers defending oneself: 解释误会 = clear up a misunderstanding. Where 解决 settles a problem, 解释 makes a meaning plain.

e: liberation; release; to be freed from bondage or constraint
d: 解 jiě (to untie; to release; to dissolve) + 脱 tuō (to escape; to shed; to free oneself from). In Buddhist context: liberation from 轮回, the shedding of karmic bondage and conditioned existence.

e: interface; the surface between two systems
d: 界 (boundary; boundary marker) + 面 (surface; face). The surface at the boundary between two things. In technology and computing: the user interface (用户界面 yònghù jièmiàn), screen interface. In science: the interface between two phases or systems.
借 (lend) + 给 (give to). Pinning 给 after 借 fixes the direction outward: the subject is the one handing the object over.

e: to learn from, draw on as a model
d: 借 (to borrow) + 鉴 (mirror, to reflect on). To borrow another's experience as a mirror for your own, taking what is useful from a model or precedent.
借 (to borrow) + 口 (mouth). A "borrowed mouth," words you reach for that are not the true reason. As a noun it is the excuse itself; as a verb, "to use as a pretext."
借 (borrow/lend) + 钱 (money). A verb-object pair whose direction depends on the prepositions around it: 向他借钱 is borrowing from him, 借钱给他 is lending to him.

e: to draw on, with the help of
d: 借 (to make use of) + 助 (aid). To accomplish something by leaning on an external tool, force, or person. Formal register, common in writing.

e: this life; the present life; this age
d: 今 jīn (present; now) + 世 shì (life; age). The life one is living now, set against 前世 (a former life) and 来世 (the next): 今生今世 "this very life." Can also mean the present age in a more general sense.

今 jīn (now; the present moment) + 天 tiān (day). The word for "today" encodes "the now-day." Chinese time words are nouns that typically occupy the topic position at the start of a sentence, before the verb; they work differently from English adverbs like "today."

e: today I mainly want to discuss
d: Sets the agenda. Saying it early, with numbered points, is the strongest move a visitor has: it decides what gets talked about and in what order. Follow with 第一 (dì-yī), 第二, 第三, and close each topic with 这个先到这里 ("let's leave this one here for now").
The market half-kilo. 一斤多少钱 ("how much per jin?") is the essential market question. Originally a pictograph of an axe, which is still its job as a radical.

e: weight; one's true worth or standing
d: 斤 jīn (catty) + 两 liǎng (tael), the two traditional units of weight, hence "weight" in general, and figuratively a person's substance or worth. 掂量掂量自己的斤两 (to weigh up one's own worth) means to take an honest measure of what one can really do.

e: the Diamond Sutra; the foundational text of Chan Buddhism
d: The full title is 金刚般若波罗蜜经 (Jīngāng bōrě bōluómì jīng), the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra. The diamond image is the cutting power of 般若 that severs every clinging.

e: golden flowers — the prized mold colonies in Fu Brick

d: 金 jīn (gold) + 钱 qián (coin; money). A slightly elevated or literary term for money. Used in formal writing and in philosophical contexts: 金钱不是万能的 "Money is not omnipotent." Compare: 钱 (everyday "money"), 金钱 (money as an abstraction or moral question), 财富 cáifù (wealth/riches).

Epigraphy: the study of inscriptions on bronze and stone. The scholarly discipline that underlies serious seal carving: to carve seal script well, one must have studied the ancient bronzes and stone inscriptions from which the script derives.

e: golden bud — the premium single-bud grade
to do one's utmost; to try one's best
d: 尽 jìn (to exhaust; to the limit) + 力 lì (effort). To use up all the effort one has, to spare nothing: 我会尽力 "I will do my best," 尽力而为 "do all one can."

e: do what you can as a human, then accept Heaven's decree
the end; the very end; the limit
d: 尽 jìn (to exhaust, to use up) + 头 tóu (end). The point where a thing runs out: the far end of a road, the limit of a stretch. 路的尽头 "the end of the road."
紧 (close, tight) + 跟 (gēn, to follow). To follow with no gap. Physical (stay right behind) or figurative (紧跟时代, keep pace with the times).

紧 (pressing) + 急 (jí, hurried, anxious). Two words for urgency stacked together, intensifying each other. The register of sirens, evacuations, and red-banner notices: 紧急出口 (emergency exit), 紧急情况 (emergency situation).
The doubled form intensifies the grip. 紧紧 describes an action done with full, unrelenting tightness, often a hold or an embrace that won't let go.
紧 (taut) + 张 (zhāng, to stretch open). A surface pulled tight from both ends. Used for nerves before an exam, the tension in a thriller, and resources stretched thin (时间紧张, time is short).

近 jìn (near; close; recent) + 来 lái (coming; approaching the present). "What has come near," the recent past approaching the present. A slightly more formal or literary synonym of 最近 zuìjìn. Common in formal speech, writing, and news contexts.

e: in recent years; over recent years
d: 近 (recent) + 年 (year) + 来 (coming from , a directional particle marking elapsed duration). Time that has been coming toward the present moment across recent years. A standard phrase in news, academic writing, and formal speech: 近年来，中国的城市化速度加快 (in recent years, China's urbanization has accelerated).

e: in the near future; recently; in the near term
d: 近 (near) + 期 qī (a period of time; a term; a scheduled point). A time period that is near , used for both the recent past and the near future depending on context. 近期内 (within the near term); 近期计划 (near-term plans). The period implied is typically weeks to a few months, not years.
近 (near) + 视 shì (to see; vision). Seeing only what is near , the clinical and colloquial term for myopia. 近视眼镜 (myopia glasses , corrective lenses); 高度近视 (high myopia, severe nearsightedness).
进 jìn (to advance) + 步 bù (a step). To move forward step by step, hence to improve. Works as a verb (你进步了 "you've improved") and as a noun (很大的进步 "great progress").

e: to go into town; to go to the city
d: 进 jìn (to enter) + 城 chéng (city; town). A verb-object phrase: to go into the city. The expression preserves the old sense of the city as a bounded place one literally enters, crossing from outside to inside.
跟进 (gēnjìn) is to follow up, 催 (cuī) to chase. Ask for photos as well as words; a picture of goods on the line settles more than 快了 (kuài le, "nearly there").
Evolution: advance-transformation. 进化论 is Darwin's theory; gamers use 进化 for level-ups, which Darwin might have minded. The neutral scholarly variant is 演化.

e: to import; imports; entrance (of a place)
d: 进 jìn (to take in) + 口 kǒu (mouth; opening). To bring goods in across a border, the opposite of 出口 chūkǒu (to export). The same word also names a physical "entrance," the opening you go in through.
进 jìn (to enter) + 来 lái (to come). To enter moving toward where the speaker is. 请进来 "please come in" is what you say from inside a room to someone at the door.

e: to go in (away from the speaker)
d: 进 jìn (to enter) + 去 qù (to go). To enter moving away from where the speaker stands. From outside a building you tell someone 你先进去 "you go in first."

e: to enter; to go into (a place or stage)
d: 进 jìn (to enter) + 入 rù (to go in). A more formal "to enter," used of physical spaces and of abstract stages alike: 进入房间 "enter the room," 进入新阶段 "enter a new phase."

e: palace graduate — the highest examination degree
d: The degree conferred on all who passed the palace examination (殿试). Literally "advanced to scholar" or "presented scholar." Receiving the 进士 degree placed a candidate in the imperial bureaucracy; specific posting and rank depended on one's place in the final ranking.

e: to make a pilgrimage offering incense
to carry out; to be in progress; to conduct
d: 进 jìn (to advance; to enter) + 行 xíng. The all-purpose formal verb for "to carry out" , used before two-syllable activity nouns: 进行讨论 "carry out a discussion," 进行调查 "conduct an investigation," 进行比赛 "hold a competition." Functions like a grammaticalized "do" for activities that are too dignified for…
进 jìn (to advance) + 展 zhǎn (to unfold). The headway a task, plan, or situation makes over time: 工作有了进展 "the work has made progress." More about an undertaking than a person.
经 jīng (to pass through; constant) + 常 cháng (constant). The standard adverb for an action that recurs as a regular habit: 我经常去那家店 "I go to that shop often." Stresses regularity, not just repetition.
经 jīng (canon) + 典 diǎn (standard text; canon). A proven, enduring work, or the quality of being a touchstone: 经典电影 "a classic film," 文学经典 "literary classics."

e: to pass through; to go by; (after) the course of
d: 经 jīng (pass through) + 过 guò (cross over). To travel through a place, or to go through a process. As a noun it names the whole course of events: 事情的经过 "how the matter unfolded."

经 jīng (manage; order) + 济 jì (aid; relieve). A shortening of 经世济民, "to order the age and aid the people." Now the standard word for the economy, and as an adjective "economical, thrifty": 经济实惠 "good value for money."

e: Special Economic Zone — the instrument of the opening
d: 经济 (economy, economic) + 特区 (special zone, from 特 special/exceptional + 区 zone/district). The bounded territories where market rules applied before they were extended nationally: 改革开放's experimental method made spatial.
经 jīng (manage) + 理 lǐ (to put in order). The one who runs the day-to-day affairs of a business: 总经理 zǒngjīnglǐ "general manager," 部门经理 "department manager."

e: to experience; experience; what one has been through
d: 经 jīng (to pass through; warp threads; to undergo) + 历 lì (to go through). The most common everyday word for living through something and for the sum of what one has lived through. As a verb it takes events as objects: you 经历 a war, a hardship, a change.

经 jīng (warp thread; main channel) + 络 luò (network thread; connecting channel). Together they describe the body's energy network: 12 primary 经 channels + 8 extraordinary 奇经八脉 vessels + an extensive network of 络 branch channels. The basis of acupuncture, acupressure, and qigong.

e: mosque school education — traditional Islamic learning
d: 经堂教育 (mosque school education, lit. "sutra hall education," using the Buddhist term 经堂 for a building devoted to sacred texts) is the traditional system by which Hui Muslim boys study Arabic, Persian, and Islamic jurisprudence under an imam (阿訇 āhōng, from Persian ākhund).

经 jīng (pass through) + 验 yàn (to test; verify). The practical know-how gathered by having passed through and tested much: 工作经验 "work experience." Distinct from 经历, which is the events themselves rather than the lessons drawn from them.

e: a pleasant surprise; to be pleasantly surprised
d: 惊 jīng (startled) + 喜 xǐ (joy). The happy jolt of an unexpected good thing: 一个惊喜 "a surprise (gift or event)," 又惊又喜 "both startled and delighted."
精 (refined, essential) + 简 (pared down). To trim away the excess and keep only what is needed, used of staff, budgets, text, and organizations. Sharper and more deliberate than plain 简化.

The method of spiritual victory , Ah Q psychological mechanism of reframing defeats as victories. Lu Xun intended this as a portrait of a national psychological defense mechanism: the substitution of internal narrative for genuine change.

e: spiritual civilization; cultural-moral development as a policy domain
d: A signature term of post-1978 reform-era political vocabulary, paired with 物质文明 (wùzhì wénmíng, material civilization).

e: to be proficient in; to master; to have a thorough command of
d: 精 jīng (refined; essence; finely worked) + 通 (to be all the way through). To have passed thoroughly through a field down to its fine grain: full mastery, not mere acquaintance. 精通 is reserved for genuine expertise: 精通三门外语 (fluent in three foreign languages), 精通法律 (thoroughly versed in law).

e: Pure Land Buddhism — the most widely practiced school in China
d: Pure Land centers on faith in Amitābha Buddha 阿弥陀佛 Āmítuófó and the aspiration to be reborn in his Western Pure Land 西方极乐世界, from which enlightenment is easy to attain. The primary practice is 念佛 niànfó (recitation of Amitābha's name).
Return the host's toast once the host has toasted you, standing and holding the glass with both hands. A short toast in Chinese is worth more than a long one in English.

e: To toast , to offer a drink as a gesture of respect
d: To toast , to offer a drink as a gesture of respect. 敬 means "to respect" or "to offer respectfully"; 酒 means "alcoholic drink." The act of toasting at a Chinese meal is a structured social protocol, not a casual gesture.

e: still-form qigong; seated or standing meditation
d: 静 jìng (still; quiet) + 功 gōng (practice). Qigong performed without external movement: seated meditation, standing post (站桩 zhàn zhuāng), or lying-down practices. The body is still while breath and attention cultivate interior movement of qi.

Nine Songs: the series of eleven shamanic hymns attributed to Qu Yuan, addressing the gods of the Chu pantheon. Among the most directly religious texts in the 楚辞, they preserve the ritual language of Chu shamanism within a literary frame.

e: double nine — colloquial shorthand; homophonic longevity wish
d: 九 jiǔ (nine) + 九 jiǔ (nine). The colloquial compressed name for the festival, and a sound-based wish: 九九 is homophonous with 久久 (jiǔ jiǔ, for a long time; lasting), turning the calendar date into an expression of the wish for long life.

The multiplication table: memorized in China as a chant of 45 compressed phrases from 一一得一 (1×1=1) to 九九八十一 (9×9=81). The chant begins with the smaller number, which is why it runs from 1×1 up rather than 9×9 down as in some other traditions.

Kowloon, "Nine Dragons," the peninsula ceded to Britain in 1860. The name comes from a legend that eight mountains in the area represented eight dragons; a Qing emperor passing through added himself as the ninth.

e: the supreme position; the imperial throne
d: 九五 (the Nine-Five, the fifth yang line of the Qian hexagram, the "flying dragon in the heavens") + 之尊 (the honored, the exalted). The throne itself, the supreme position of the emperor. To 登上九五之尊 is to ascend the throne.

e: the highest heavens; the ninth sky
d: 九 jiǔ + 霄 xiāo (the upper sky; the clouds). The ninefold heaven, the very top of the sky, as high as the cosmos reaches.

九 jiǔ + 月 yuè (month). September in the solar calendar. The ninth day of the ninth lunar month is the Double Ninth Festival (重阳节 Chóngyáng Jié), when the doubled nine (the highest yang) is celebrated by climbing heights and honoring the elderly, the day's name 重阳 meaning "double yang." So 九月初九 (the…

e: the Nine Provinces; all of China
d: 九 jiǔ + 州 zhōu (province; region). The nine ancient provinces into which the legendary sage-king Yu was said to have divided the land after taming the floods. 九州 became a poetic name for the whole of China, the entire civilized realm: 九州大地 (the great land of the nine provinces).

e: long ago; from the distant past; far back in time
d: 久 jiǔ (long; for a long time) + 远 yuǎn (far). Temporal distance mapped onto the same word as spatial distance. 久远 specifically emphasizes the antiquity of something , a tradition, a custom, a wound, a memory. Literary and slightly formal.

酒 jiǔ (alcohol; wine; liquor) + 鬼 guǐ (ghost). A drunkard , someone possessed by alcohol to the point of losing themselves. The pattern is productive: 赌鬼 (dǔguǐ) is a compulsive gambler, 烟鬼 (yānguǐ) is a heavy smoker, 色鬼 (sèguǐ) is a lecher.

e: drinking capacity: how much alcohol one can hold
d: 酒 jiǔ (alcohol) + 量 liàng (capacity). A person's tolerance for drink, the amount they can take before they are affected. A culturally loaded word at the banquet table, where 酒量好 (a good capacity) is treated as a social asset: 他酒量很大 (he can really hold his drink).

The drinking table , refers not just to the physical table but to the entire social ritual of the banquet. 酒桌文化 (jiǔzhuō wénhuà) is "drinking table culture," often discussed critically for its excesses.

e: the old calendar; the lunar calendar
d: 旧 (old) + 历 (lì, calendar; to pass through). The traditional lunisolar calendar, officially called 农历 (nónglì, agricultural calendar) or 阴历 (yīnlì, lunar calendar).

e: the old era; the old order
d: 旧 (old) + 时代 (shídài, era, age , time + generation). A period that has ended and been superseded. The phrase carries strong evaluative loading: in Communist-era writing, 旧时代 nearly always means the pre-1949 Republican or imperial period, and the connotation is negative.

旧 (former) + 址 (zhǐ, site, address , earth 土 + stop 止, the place where one stops/settles). The location of something that has moved or no longer exists. Appears on historical markers, museum labels, and administrative documents.
救 (rescue) + 护 (hù, protect) + 车 (chē, vehicle). The "rescue-and-protect vehicle." Hear a siren in a Chinese city and this is the word.

e: to save someone's life; to revive (the dying)
d: 救 jiù (to rescue) + 活 huó (alive) as a resultative ending. To rescue with the result of being alive: 活 here marks the outcome, that the rescue succeeded and the person lives. The same pattern builds 养活 yǎnghuó (to support, to keep alive by feeding).

救 (rescue) + 火 (huǒ, fire). Counterintuitively this means "to put out a fire," not to save the fire; here 救 keeps its Shuōwén sense of 止, halting the disaster. The same logic gives 救灾 (jiùzāi, disaster relief).
救 (rescue) + 济 (jì, to aid, to cross over). Material relief for the poor or disaster-struck: food, money, shelter. This is 救 in its social-welfare register.

救 (rescue) + 命 (mìng, life). Literally "save a life." As a shout it is the standard Chinese cry of distress, the equivalent of "Help!" As a verb-object phrase it describes the act of saving someone from death.
救 (rescue) + 人 (rén, person). The general act of pulling a person out of danger, whether from water, fire, illness, or ruin.
救 (rescue) + 援 (yuán, to aid, to reach a hand). A coordinated, often large-scale rescue effort: teams, equipment, logistics. The default word for earthquake and mountain rescue.

e: nearby; at a convenient location close by
d: 就 jiù (then; right there; to conform to; to make use of what is present) + 近 (near). Making use of what is nearby , going to the closest available option rather than traveling farther.

e: precisely; exactly; even if; it's just that
d: 就 jiù (then; precisely; at once) + 是. Multiple functions make 就是 one of the most versatile particles in spoken Mandarin.

e: that is to say / in other words
it's just that simple; merely this easy
d: 就 in this usage minimizes or dismisses: it is merely, just, only this , simpler or smaller than one might have expected. 就这样 "just like this, that's all" and 就这么 "it's simply this" are extremely common in casual speech for dismissing complexity or closing a matter.

居 jū (to dwell, to reside) + 民. A person defined by where they live rather than by their nationality: the residents of a building, a neighbourhood, a city, a region. The everyday administrative word, as in 居民区 jūmínqū (a residential district) and 城市居民 (urban residents).

e: chrysanthemum — the flower of the ninth month
d: 菊 jú (chrysanthemum) + 花 huā (flower; blossom). The chrysanthemum blooms in the ninth and tenth lunar months, when most flowering plants have finished. This timing made it a literary symbol of resilience, late-life achievement, and the refusal to conform to expected seasonal rhythms.

e: Grand Master — the head of the Mohist organization
d: 巨 jù (great; chief) + 子 zǐ (master). The elected or designated leader of the Mohist order, holding authority over all members. The 巨子 could direct members to travel, take on defense contracts for states, and enforce the school's internal law.

句 jù (sentence) + 号 hào (mark; sign). The punctuation mark that closes a sentence, written in Chinese as a small hollow circle 。 rather than a dot. Idiomatically 画上句号 "to draw the full stop" means to bring something to a close.

句 jù (sentence) + 子 zi (noun-suffix). The everyday word for a complete sentence as a grammatical unit: 一个句子 "one sentence," 简单的句子 "a simple sentence." The building block every grammar lesson works with.

具 jù (to possess, to furnish) + 体 tǐ (body, form). Having a definite body, hence concrete and specific as against vague or abstract. Its opposite is 抽象 chōuxiàng (abstract): 具体的例子 "a concrete example."

e: to possess (a quality, characteristic, or abstract attribute)
d: 具 jù (to possess; equipped with; concrete tool) + 有. Formal written register. Used specifically to assert that a subject possesses an abstract quality, characteristic, feature, or capacity , not physical objects. 具有能力 (to possess ability), 具有价值 (to have value), 具有代表性 (to be representative).

"As far as I know." A hedge that acknowledges your information may be incomplete. Useful when stating something you believe to be true but do not want to assert with full confidence. Carries a slightly bookish, considered tone.
距 (jù, to be apart) plus 离 (to be apart). A noun for the measured space between two points, and also a verb for being that far apart. Used for physical and emotional distance alike.
决 jué (to resolve; to break through) + 定 dìng (to settle). To bring a choice to rest, and also the decision itself. 做决定 zuò juédìng "to make a decision." The most common everyday word for deciding.

e: Quatrain , four lines of five or seven characters
d: Quatrain , four lines of five or seven characters. The most concentrated Tang form.
军 (military) + 队 (formed unit). The standing army as an institution, the original martial home of 队 made explicit.

e: ruler and subject — hierarchical, mutually obligated
d: The political relationship. The ruler (君 jūn) is obligated to govern benevolently and justly; the subject (臣 chén) is obligated to serve loyally and to remonstrate when the ruler errs. 忠 zhōng (loyalty) is the core virtue for the subject; 仁政 rénzhèng (benevolent governance) for the ruler.
Ruler, minister, assistant, envoy: the four functional roles within a compound herbal formula.

p: jūn jūn, chén chén, fù fù, zǐ zǐ
e: let the ruler rule, minister minister, father father, son son
d: The Analects 12.11 formula for 正名 in practice, given when Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius about governance. Each binome repeats the same character twice: the first instance is the title, the second is the standard the title entails.

A binding agreement resting on personal honor and the parties' characters, without legal documentation. The term assumes both sides are junzi , people whose word is their commitment. Widely used in modern business and political contexts where formal contracts are either inappropriate or impossible.

e: commandery-county system — China's foundational administrative structure
d: 36 commanderies (郡) at unification (later expanded to over 40), subdivided into counties (县). Officials were appointed from the center, paid salaries, and could be dismissed, creating administrative accountability upward rather than hereditary independence downward.
咖啡 kāfēi (coffee) + 馆. The modern counterpart to the 茶馆, a place to sit with a laptop or a friend. The 馆 suffix quietly marks it as a public establishment.

Kashgar , the westernmost major city in China, situated at the edge of the Tarim Basin near the Kyrgyz and Tajik borders. Historically the greatest bazaar city on the Silk Road, where the northern and southern routes reconverged. The old city (老城 lǎochéng) retains much of its traditional character.
开 (kāi, to open, to switch on) + 灯 (lamp): the verb-object phrase for switching a light on. Its opposite is 关灯 (guān dēng), to turn the light off.

e: to open up; open (in attitude or policy)
to start work; to begin construction
to bloom; to blossom; to flower
d: 开 kāi (to open) + 花 huā (flower). To come into bloom, said of a plant opening its flowers. Figuratively, of an effort that bears fruit: 遍地开花 "blooming everywhere," spreading and flourishing.

e: to hold a meeting; to attend a meeting
to power on (a device); to start filming
to open one's mouth — to speak (especially after a silence, or to ask for something)
to open the door; (of a shop) to open for business
d: 开 kāi (to open) + 门 mén (door). To open a door, and idiomatically for a shop to open: 商店几点开门？ "What time does the shop open?" Its pair is 关门 guānmén, to close.

e: to make a mold; to commission tooling
d: The step that commits real money. 开新模 is new tooling; 共模 (gòngmú) or 公模 (gōngmú) is a shared or public mold the factory already owns, cheaper but not exclusive to you. 私模 (sīmú) is a private mold for one customer.

e: the beginning; the start; at first
d: 开 kāi (to open) + 头 tóu (head, end). The opening end of something: the start of a story, a year, a task. 一开头 "right at the start." Both a noun (the beginning) and a verb (to begin).

开 kāi (open) + 心 xīn (heart). Lit. "open heart." The heart is opened, unblocked, free. One of the most common everyday happiness words in Mandarin, lighter and more colloquial than 高兴 gāoxìng (pleased, glad) and more immediate than 幸福 xìngfú (lasting happiness; bliss).

e: school starts; the start of term

d: 楷 kǎi (model; standard) + 书 shū (writing). The standard script , the foundation that every calligrapher must master before attempting other styles. Print fonts are based on regular script. 不会楷书，不学草书 "Don't attempt cursive without mastering regular script" , the traditional maxim.

Karez: the ancient underground irrigation system that made Turpan's agricultural oasis possible. A network of vertical shafts connected by horizontal tunnels channels glacial meltwater from the Tianshan foothills to fields in the desert basin.

e: to see a doctor; to seek medical treatment
d: 看 (to look at, to examine) + 病 (illness). The verb covers both sides of the clinical encounter: the patient "looks at" the illness by going to be treated, and the doctor "looks at" the illness to diagnose it. Context distinguishes who is doing the looking. 我去看病 (I'm going to see a doctor).

e: to look down on; to disdain; to have contempt for
d: 看 (to look) + 不起 (cannot rise up to). The potential complement 不起 indicates inability to raise the gaze high enough , to look up to. Contempt as a failure of elevation. Its opposite is 看得起 kàndéqǐ (to respect, to think well of, to regard highly). 他看不起任何人 , He has contempt for everyone.

e: to see through; to figure out
d: 看 (kàn, to look) + 穿 (to pierce, as a result complement). The gaze bores all the way through the surface, you see through a lie, a disguise, a scheme. 穿 here is the original drilling sense turned to the mind: the look penetrates and reaches the truth behind.

e: to see; to catch sight of
d: 看 kàn (to look) + 到 dào (arrive). Looking that arrived at its object: perception confirmed. 看到 asserts that the visual information reached awareness. Without 到, 看 is merely the act of looking, which may or may not result in seeing.

看 (to watch) + 电视 (television). 看 is the default verb for watching screens: 看电影 (to watch a film), 看视频 (to watch a video), 看直播 (to watch a live stream), 看比赛 (to watch a match). The verb doesn't change regardless of the medium , 看 covers any directed visual consumption of moving images.
看 (kàn, to look) plus 懂. The visual counterpart to 听懂: to read a text, watch a film, or view a chart and grasp it.

看 (to look) + 法 (method, way). A held view as a particular way of looking at something. 你对这件事有什么看法？ (What's your view on this matter?). More formal and substantive than 意见 yìjiàn (opinion, suggestion). 世界观 shìjièguān (worldview) extends the same logic: how the world appears from your vantage.

e: to favor; to back; to be bullish on
d: 看 (to see, to judge) + 好 (as good/positive). To evaluate something as likely to succeed or worth supporting. Widely used in investment contexts (看好这只股票 , bullish on this stock), sports prediction (我看好他们赢 , I favor them to win), and interpersonal support (我很看好你 , I have high hopes for you).

h: 看见 · 看完 · 看懂
d: 看 combines with resultative complements to specify the outcome of the looking. 看见 kànjiàn (to catch sight of , result: visual contact made). 看完 kànwán (to finish reading or watching , result: completion). 看懂 kàndǒng (to read and understand , result: comprehension).

e: watched twice; read it through twice
d: 了 with a frequency complement (遍 biàn = complete passes through, 次 cì = times, 回 huí = times in colloquial speech). Marks the action as having been performed a counted number of complete cycles. The quantification of repetition implies completion of each cycle.
看门 (kānmén, to watch the gate) + 狗. A dog that guards the door. Figuratively it names anything that stands watch, including the software process that restarts a crashed system.

e: to visit a friend; to go see someone
d: 看 extends naturally from visual attention to social attention: going to see someone implies caring, checking in, tending to the relationship. 看朋友 (visit a friend), 看望 kànwàng (to visit and care for, especially an elder or patient), 探望 tànwàng (to pay a visit, more formal).

看 (to look at) + 书 (book). The standard way to say "to read" in Mandarin , specifically reading for comprehension or leisure. 读书 dúshū overlaps but emphasizes reading aloud or formal study; 看书 is the unmarked everyday verb for sitting with a book.

Commissioned by the Kangxi Emperor 康熙帝, completed 1716. 47,035 characters organized under 214 radicals. The definitive classical reference work, still consulted by scholars of classical Chinese today.

e: archaeology; to study antiquity through remains
d: 考 kǎo (to examine, to investigate) + 古 gǔ (the ancient). To investigate the past through its physical remains: 考古学 "archaeology (the discipline)," 考古发现 "an archaeological discovery." The verb of unearthing and reading 古迹, the traces the past left in the ground.

e: to approach; to draw near; to get close to
d: 靠 kào (to lean against; to approach; to rely on) + 近 (near). To lean close , the verb of physical approach. 靠近 carries the movement more explicitly than 接近: it often describes the final stage of approach, closing the last stretch of distance.

科 kē (branch; category; department) + 学 xué (learning; -ology). Lit. "categorized learning" , the systematic division of knowledge into disciplines. Coined as a translation for Western "science" in the late 19th century.
科学 kēxué (science, lit. "the study of branches/categories") + 家 jiā. One who has made science their home.

e: prostration — kowtow — the physical language of reverence
d: 磕头 (kowtow, lit. "knock head") is the full prostration: kneeling and touching the forehead to the floor.
可 kě (can; worthy of) + 爱 ài (love). Worthy of being loved: cute, adorable. One of the most-used adjectives in everyday Mandarin. Used for children, animals, cartoon characters, and endearing people.

e: evidently; it can be seen that; clearly
d: 可 (can; worth) + 见 (to see; to understand). "Can be seen" , used to introduce a logical inference or conclusion drawn from evidence. A formal connector common in essays and arguments.
可 (worth) + 靠 (to lean on; to rely on). Worth leaning on. Used for people, sources of information, systems, and promises.

A very common stack: 可能 ("possibly") plus the modal 会 ("will / be likely to"), giving "might, may well." 明天可能会变冷 ("it might turn cold tomorrow"). The 会 adds the sense of a future tendency, so 可能会 feels a touch more about what is likely to happen, while bare 可能 just flags that something is possible.

可能 kěnéng (possible) + 性 xìng (-ness). The abstract noun "possibility," built by attaching the -ity suffix to the adjective 可能: 有可能性 "there is a possibility," 很大的可能性 "a strong likelihood." A model case of how 性 turns a quality into a countable, discussable thing.
可 (worth) + 怕 (to fear). Worth fearing. Used for things that inspire genuine dread , horror films, dangerous situations, extreme weather, powerful people.

e: unfortunately; what a pity; it is a shame that
d: 可 (worth) + 惜 (to pity; to regret the loss of something). Worth regretting. Functions as an adjective (这很可惜 , this is a pity) and as a sentential adverb opening a clause (可惜他没来 , unfortunately he did not come).

可 kě (worthy of; -able) + 笑 xiào (laugh). Worthy of being laughed at: ridiculous, absurd. Built on the same 可 + verb pattern as 可爱 (worthy of love → cute) and 可怕 (worthy of fear → frightening). Often carries a sting.

e: can; may; it is permissible to; acceptable; not bad
d: The most versatile 可-compound. 可 (permitted/possible) + 以 (by means of; using). As a modal verb it covers both capability and permission. As a colloquial adjective it means "acceptable" or "not bad." It is the go-to answer when someone asks if something is okay.

e: May I come in? — requesting permission
d: 可以 is the canonical permission modal. It asks or grants social authorization , whether rules, norms, context, or a person in authority allows an action. The asker knows they have the physical ability; the question is whether they have the social right.

克 kè (to overcome) + 己 jǐ (self). To conquer one's own impulses, the Confucian ideal of self-mastery. The root of 克己复礼, "subdue the self and return to ritual," and of 克己奉公, "curb oneself and serve the public good."

刻 (kè), to carve or engrave, joins 苦 (kǔ) to describe effort that bites in: study or training pursued through self-denial. A 刻苦 student drills past comfort, the way a blade is sharpened against stone.

Factories like to name famous customers. The useful questions are which markets they ship to, and how much of the output the largest customer takes (占比 zhànbǐ, share), since a dominant customer gets the line first in peak season.
The Hakka people, literally "guest family people," so named because they arrived in the regions where they settled as migrants, after earlier inhabitants.

Guest star: a star that appears briefly and then fades, i.e., a nova or supernova. Chinese court astronomers maintained careful records of guest stars for astrological-political interpretation: a guest star in a particular mansion was a portent for specific ministers, regions, or dynasties.
课 kè (lesson) + 本 běn (volume). The book for a course of study. A close synonym is 教科书 jiàokēshū, slightly more formal.
课堂 kètáng (classroom) + 笔记 bǐjì. Notes taken during class. 借笔记 jiè bǐjì = to borrow someone's notes. 整理笔记 zhěnglǐ bǐjì = to organize/clean up one's notes.
肯 kěn (to be willing; to assent) + 定 dìng (to settle). To settle a thing as yes: as an adverb, "certainly," and as a verb, "to affirm, to confirm." Its opposite is 否定 fǒudìng (to negate; negative).
空 kōng (empty) + 间 jiān (space). Empty space, both physical and figurative: 没有空间 "no room," 发展空间 "room to grow." Paired with 时间, the two name space and time together.
空 (sky, air) plus 姐 is the colloquial word for a female flight attendant, literally a "sky sister." It is a clipped, affectionate everyday term beside the formal 空中小姐 (kōngzhōng xiǎojiě).

空 kōng (empty; void; sky) + 气 qì. The physical substance of the atmosphere, what you breathe. Also used metaphorically for social atmosphere: 房间里的空气很紧张 "the air in the room was tense." The same word covers oxygen and social mood.

口 kǒu (mouth) + 才 cái (talent). Literally "mouth-talent," the ability to speak well and persuasively: 他很有口才 "he is very eloquent." One of a family of 才 compounds naming a specific gift, alongside 文才 wéncái (literary talent).

e: manner of speaking; breath smell; implied attitude
d: 口 kǒu (mouth) + 气 qì. Operates on two levels: (1) the qi from the mouth, literally breath smell (口气重 "bad breath"); (2) the implied attitude and tone in what someone says, what their words reveal about how they feel. 你这个口气 "That tone of yours…" carries reproach.

Mouth-Chan: enlightenment talked rather than lived, generalized into anyone's verbal habit. 他的口头禅是"没问题" means "no problem" is his catchphrase. One of the most useful conversation words about conversation.

口 kǒu (mouth) + 味 wèi (flavor; taste). Both the objective flavor of food and the subjective preference of a taster. 这不合我的口味 "This doesn't suit my taste." 口味重 kǒuwèi zhòng = "strong-flavored preferences" , liking bold, heavy flavors.

口 kǒu (mouth) + 吻 wěn (lips; to kiss, the form of the mouth). The shape of what comes from the mouth, the distinctive way a person speaks, implying their perspective and attitude. More literary than 口气, used in written analysis, narration, and formal commentary.
口 kǒu (mouth) + 音 yīn (sound). The sound a particular mouth gives a language, marking where the speaker is from: 南方口音 "a southern accent," 带口音 "to have an accent."
Often the most practical settlement, since you hold the next payment. Agree the amount in writing before deducting.

苦 kǔ = suffering, bitterness, difficulty. Sanskrit dukkha: a wheel whose axle is off-center, generating grinding rather than smooth motion. The Buddha's first noble truth: life as ordinarily lived is characterized by dukkha.

苦 (bitter, hard) plus 力 (lì, strength) names grueling physical labor and, historically, the laborer himself. The English word "coolie" carries this same syllable. In modern speech 干苦力 means to do back-breaking work.

e: to train hard, to drill relentlessly
d: Here 苦 works as an adverb on 练 (liàn, to train): to practice bitterly, to grind. The word frames mastery as something earned through painful repetition rather than talent.

苦 (bitter) joins 难 (nàn, calamity, disaster) to name suffering on a large, often historical scale: famine, war, oppression. Weightier than everyday hardship, 苦难 belongs to the language of nations and generations.
苦 (bitter) plus 心 (xīn, heart, mind) names the trouble one's heart goes through for someone else's sake. 一片苦心 (yí piàn kǔxīn) is a heartful of well-meant pains, often unrecognized.

苦 (bitter) plus 衷 (zhōng, inner feelings) names the private difficulty behind a person's puzzling choice, the bitterness they cannot say aloud. To have a 苦衷 is to act badly for a reason you keep hidden.
Containment covers goods not yet shipped. Ask the factory to check 库存 and the work in progress (在制品 zàizhìpǐn) before anything else leaves.

e: to boast; to praise (phonetic of 跨)
to take a stride; a step
d: 跨 + 步 (bù, step). The base physical sense , a single deliberate stride, often a long one. Used in athletics, dance, military drill, and figuratively for any decisive move forward.

e: span (of a bridge, an era, a project)
d: 跨 + 度 (dù, degree; measure). The measurable distance from one support to another , originally an architectural and engineering term (the 跨度 of an arch or bridge), now extended to time spans, salary ranges, age gaps, and the scope of a project or career.
跨 + 国 (guó, country). 跨国公司 (kuàguó gōngsī, multinational corporation) is the canonical compound. Also 跨国婚姻 (cross-national marriage), 跨国合作 (cross-national cooperation), 跨国犯罪 (transnational crime).

e: to step over; to get past
d: 跨 + 过 (guò, to pass). The everyday verb of stepping over a low obstacle: a threshold, a puddle, a fallen branch. By extension, getting past a difficulty in a single move. Common with 门槛 ménkǎn (threshold) , both literal and metaphorical.

跨 + 界 (jiè, field; domain). A buzzword in entertainment, design, and business since the 2000s: an actor turning singer, a fashion brand collaborating with a tech company, a novelist directing a film. 跨界合作 (kuàjiè hézuò) "crossover collaboration" appears constantly in marketing copy.

跨 + 境 (jìng, border; territory). The standard term in trade and law. 跨境电商 (kuàjìng diànshāng, cross-border e-commerce) is one of the most-used compounds in contemporary business writing. 跨境 carries a more administrative tone than 跨国; 国 invokes the country, 境 the legal frontier.

e: to cross over into the new year
d: 跨 + 年 (nián, year). The standard verb for what one does on New Year's Eve , celebrating through midnight from the old year into the new. 跨年晚会 (kuànián wǎnhuì) "New Year's Eve gala" is the genre name for the live-broadcast countdown shows.

e: to mount; to step up onto (astride)
d: 跨 + 上 (shàng, up; onto). To swing one leg over and mount: a horse, a bicycle, a motorcycle, a stage. The verb preserves the original image of legs spread on either side. The poetic phrase 跨上战马 kuà shàng zhànmǎ "to mount the war-horse" recurs throughout classical narrative and modern wuxia.

跨 kuà (to straddle, to cross over) + 文化 (culture). Cross-cultural: spanning or bridging different cultural contexts. 跨文化交际 kuà wénhuà jiāojì (intercultural communication) is an academic field. 跨文化婚姻 (cross-cultural marriage) appears in demographic and social discussions.

跨 + 学科 (xuékē, academic discipline). The standard rendering of "interdisciplinary" in Chinese academic writing. 跨学科研究 (kuà xuékē yánjiū) "interdisciplinary research" is now a frequent funding category.

The modifier form, suffixing 式 (shì, type/style) to make an adjective. Most common in 跨越式发展 (kuàyuè shì fāzhǎn, "leap-forward development"), the standard term in Chinese policy and journalism for skipping intermediate stages of economic or technological growth.

Spoken prices use 块 for the main unit, 毛 for tenths, 分 for hundredths; written prices use 元, 角, 分. The trailing unit is often dropped: 四块一 is 4.10, 三块八五 is 3.85. Factories apply the same words to dollars, so add 美金 (měijīn) or 人民币 (rénmínbì) when it could be either.

e: be quick; a bit faster; hurry
d: 快 kuài (fast) + 点 diǎn (a little; somewhat , the softening particle). The most colloquial way to tell someone to speed up. Tonal in its delivery: said gently it is a nudge, said sharply it is impatient.

e: carefree; cheerful; lively and at ease
d: 快 kuài (unobstructed) + 活 huó (alive; living; moving freely). The image is life flowing without constraint. Carries a slightly old-fashioned or literary flavor in modern Mandarin, but remains warm and vivid in fiction and colloquial northern speech. Describes people who seem naturally unburdened.

快 kuài (released; unobstructed) + 乐 lè (music; joy; ease). The standard word for happiness in modern Mandarin: it is an adjective predicate, a pre-noun modifier, and a noun. Appears in greetings and fixed phrases far more than the simple 快 alone.

快 kuài (fast) + 速 sù (speed; velocity). The compound reinforces both components, producing the most neutral, all-purpose word for fast in formal or written Chinese. Works as an adjective before nouns or as an adverb before verbs.
Chopstick rest: a small ceramic or metal rest placed beside the bowl to lay chopsticks on between bites. Used in formal settings; absent in casual ones.

宽 kuān (wide; broad) + 容 róng (to hold). To hold broadly: a generous, forgiving disposition that leaves wide room for others' faults. Where 容忍 is a grudging act, 宽容 is an admired character trait. The 宽 (wide) intensifies the holding image directly: a broad vessel spills less.
狂 kuáng (wild; unrestrained) + 欢 huān (joy). Joy turned up to its loudest: unrestrained revelry. 狂欢节 kuánghuānjié is the standard word for Carnival, and 狂欢 names any wild, all-out celebration.

e: earth; pure yin; the receptive; hexagram 2 of the Yijing
d: Six broken yin lines: ䷁. The second hexagram represents pure receptive capacity, responsiveness, sustaining, nurturing, the mother principle, earth, the minister. 坤 does not passively endure; it actively receives, nurtures, and brings to fruition what 乾 initiates.
困 (trapped) + 境 (situation, circumstance). A predicament you are stuck inside, with no obvious exit. Stronger and more structural than 困难: a 困境 is the whole walled situation, not a single problem.
困 (sleepy) + 倦 (weary, jaded). The settled, heavy tiredness that pulls a person toward sleep. More literary than 犯困, fitting written description of a long day's fatigue.

困 (hemmed in) + 难 (hard). The everyday word for a problem that resists you, or for the strained circumstances a person lives through. Works as both a noun (a difficulty) and an adjective (difficult, hard-up).
困 (sleepy) + 意 (feeling, inclination). The sensation of sleepiness itself, the rising pull you can either fight off or give in to.

e: there's not enough time; too late to do something
d: 来 lái (to come; to reach) + 不 bù (not) + 及 jí (to reach; to catch up to). The time has not come far enough to reach this action, so there is not enough time. Opposite: 来得及 lái de jí (there is still time; still possible).

e: (he/she/it) has come; has arrived; here it is
d: 来 lái (to come) + 了 le (completion/change-of-state particle). The arrival has been completed: the thing or person is now here. One of the most basic and high-frequency phrases in Mandarin.

e: the next life; the afterlife; the life to come
d: 来 lái (coming) + 世 shì (life). The life that follows this one in the Buddhist cycle of rebirth: 来世再相见 "to meet again in the next life." Paired with 前世 (a former life) and 今世 (this life) to span the chain of rebirths.

e: source; origin; where something comes from
d: 来 lái (to come) + 源 yuán (source; origin; spring, where water comes from). "The place from which it comes." Used for the source of funding (资金来源), information (信息来源), authority (权力来源), and anything whose origin needs to be named.

e: to come from; to originate from; hailing from
d: 来 lái (to come; to arrive) + 自 zì (from; self; origin). The standard formal expression for geographic or conceptual origin. Used for people (来自北京), ideas (这个想法来自实验), data (数据来自2023年), and institutions (来自联合国的报告).

朗 lǎng (clear; bright; resonant) + 读. The school-room and literary register for reading aloud , the kind of reading where pronunciation, rhythm, and feeling matter. Standard exercise in Chinese language classes.

e: aged white tea — white tea stored for 3+ years

d: 老 (old/established) + 百 (hundred) + 姓 (surname; clan). Lit. "the hundred old clans": the established common families as opposed to the aristocracy. The standard term for ordinary people, used across the political spectrum.

老 lǎo + 板 bǎn (plank; board, extended to the person in charge). The everyday term for boss, owner, or the person in charge of a business. In restaurants, calling out 老板！is the standard way to get the owner's attention.
老 lǎo (old; familiar prefix) + 公 gōng (elder male). The warm, everyday word a woman uses for her husband, paired with 老婆 lǎopó (wife). More casual than 丈夫 zhàngfu.

e: a seasoned worldly person; a streetwise veteran; an old hand
d: 老 lǎo (old; experienced) + 江湖 (the wanderers' world). A person who has been around , who has seen the tricks, navigated the codes, survived the dangers, and accumulated knowledge with scars.
老 (old) + 练 (tempered). Weathered by long practice into steadiness: a veteran's unflappable competence. Praises judgment and poise, not just technical speed.

A friend of long standing. 老 lǎo (old) marks the length of the friendship, not the person's age. A warm word, often used on reunion: 老朋友了 ("we go way back"). The opposite, a new friend, is 新朋友 xīn péngyou.

老人 lǎorén (elderly person; old person) + 节 jié (festival; designated day). The official civic designation established in 1989, co-locating a state-recognized day honoring elderly citizens with the existing Double Ninth Festival.

e: teacher — the most common honorific in Chinese education
d: 老 lǎo (venerable) + 师 shī (master; teacher; expert). The standard term for teacher at all levels, from elementary school through university. Used as a title of address (王老师 "Teacher Wang") and as a term of respect for anyone with expertise to transmit.

老 lǎo (established; true) + 实 shí (solid; real). Meaning cluster: (1) honest and straightforward (他很老实，不会骗人 "he's very honest, won't deceive anyone"); (2) well-behaved, obedient (孩子今天很老实 "the child is well-behaved today"); (3) naive, easy to take advantage of (别太老实了 "don't be too naive").
