平 píng (level) + 等 děng (rank). Equal standing, no rank set above another: 人人平等 "everyone is equal," 男女平等 "equality of men and women." More about status than about fairness in dealings.

e: average; on average; to even out
d: 平 píng (even) + 均 jūn (equal). The arithmetic mean, the level reached when a total is shared out evenly: 平均分 "average score," 平均年龄 "average age," 平均分配 "to distribute evenly."
平 píng (flat) + 面 miàn (surface; face). A flat surface, and in geometry a plane. Also the modifier in 平面设计 píngmiàn shèjì "graphic design," the flat, two-dimensional kind.

e: commoner; an ordinary person (vs the elite)
d: 平 píng (level, ordinary, common) + 民. An ordinary person without rank, wealth, or official position: the commoner as opposed to nobles, officials, or celebrities. 平民百姓 píngmín bǎixìng is a fixed pairing meaning the common folk, the man and woman in the street.
平 píng (level) + 稳 wěn (steady; firm). Moving or sitting on an even keel, without jolts or swings: 平稳着陆 "a smooth landing," 物价平稳 "prices are stable."
评 (to judge, comment) + 价 (worth). To weigh something and assign it a worth: a teacher's assessment, a customer's review, a verdict on a person's conduct. Works as both verb and noun.

e: to review, to comment; a review, a commentary
d: 评 píng (to appraise, to judge) + 论. To pass critical judgement on something, or the resulting commentary. A film review, a book review, a comment posted under an article (评论区 pínglùnqū "the comments section") are all 评论.
破 (to break, smash) + 坏 (to ruin). Two near-synonyms doubled for force. Destroys physical things (buildings, environment) and abstract ones alike (trust, an atmosphere, a plan, the rules).

保佑 bǎoyòu = to protect and bless. The standard phrase spoken when lighting incense or making an offering at a temple or home shrine. Used across all levels of religious engagement, from deeply devout practitioners to secular cultural observers marking a family occasion.

心肠 xīncháng = the heart-and-gut, the moral center of a person. 菩萨心肠 describes someone of exceptional compassion and forgiveness , a person who cannot bear to see others suffer and who gives without calculation.

e: the uncarved block — original simplicity before social shaping
d: 朴 pǔ: unworked wood, the block before the sculptor's chisel. The Daoist image for the original undivided state of human nature and reality, before categories, distinctions, desires, and social roles have carved it into something particular.

Pudong: the eastern bank of the Huangpu River and its hinterland, designated a special economic development zone in 1990. Its skyline of supertall towers built since the 1990s is the visual symbol of reform-era China.

e: universal deliverance — community feast for the unnamed dead
d: 普 pǔ (universal; general) + 度 dù (to cross over; to ferry across; to deliver). A feast laid out publicly , on street corners, in courtyards, at temple forecourts , specifically for the hungry ghosts who have no living descendants to offer for them.

e: Pu'er — the aged, fermented dark tea
d: Named after Pu'er city, Yunnan , the trading hub of the ancient Tea Horse Road. A post-fermented tea that improves with age like wine; some vintage cakes sell for astronomical sums. The microbial fermentation process (渥堆 wòduī for ripe pu'er) is unique among teas. 生普 shēng pǔ (raw) vs.

普 pǔ (widespread; universal) + 通 (general; running throughout). Widespread and holding everywhere: the quality of being ordinary, the common case rather than the special one. 普通人 (an ordinary person), 普通话 (the common spoken standard, Mandarin).

e: the seven emotions and six desires; the full range of human feeling
d: 七情 (the seven emotions: joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, aversion, desire) + 六欲 (the six desires of the senses). Together they name the complete inner life of a human being.

e: the Qixi Festival; the Chinese Valentine's Day
d: 七 qī + 夕 xī (evening). The seventh evening of the seventh lunar month, the annual meeting of the Weaver Girl (织女) and the Cowherd (牛郎). Once a women's festival for praying for skill in needlework (乞巧, "begging for cleverness"), it is now celebrated as a day for lovers.

七 qī + 月 yuè (month). July in the solar calendar. The seventh lunar month is the Ghost Month (鬼月), when the gates of the underworld are believed to open and spirits roam among the living; its fifteenth day is the Ghost Festival (中元节).
妻 qī (wife) + 子 zi (suffix). The standard modern word for wife. Note the tone: in classical Chinese 妻子 qīzǐ meant "wife and children," but the modern toneless reading qīzi means the wife alone.

e: to look forward to; to anticipate

d: 期 qī (a fixed period) + 间 jiān (interval). A defined stretch of time, often used after an event to mean "during": 假期期间 "during the holidays," 会议期间 "in the course of the meeting."

e: to expect; expectation; to set hopes on
d: 期 qī (a set time, to anticipate) + 望 wàng (to look toward). To expect something of someone or some outcome, with a definite hope and often a standard behind it: 不要辜负大家的期望 "do not let down everyone's expectations." Weightier and more formal than 希望.

e: the state of Qi — first hegemon's domain

p: Qí Huán Gōng yǔ Guǎn Zhòng
e: Duke Huan of Qi and Guan Zhong — the classical model of ruler and reforming minister
d: 齐桓公 Qí Huán Gōng (r. 685–643 BCE) became the dominant power of the early Spring and Autumn through the administrative genius of his minister 管仲 Guǎn Zhòng. The partnership became the canonical Chinese example of a ruler who provides authority and a minister who provides competence.

e: complete (in range); all there; fully stocked
d: 齐 qí (even; all present) + 全 quán (complete). Said of a set or selection where every needed item is on hand: 设备齐全 "fully equipped," 品种齐全 "a complete range of varieties." Stresses that nothing in the expected range is missing.

其 qí (that; those) + 次 cì (order; rank; next). "Next in that sequence" , used to introduce the second point in a ranked list, following 首先 shǒuxiān (first of all) or 第一 dì yī. Slightly more formal than 然后 ránhòu, which is purely sequential.

其 qí (that; those) + 他 tā (other). "Those others" , anything outside the named set. The variant 其它 qítā uses the non-human 它 and is preferred when referring to things rather than people, though in practice 其他 covers both.

e: the rest; the remainder; the others
d: 其 qí (those) + 余 yú (remainder; surplus; what is left). "Those that remain" , refers to everything in a set that has not already been specified. More formal than 其他; 其余 often implies a complete remainder (everything else), while 其他 may just mean "various others."

其 qí (its; that) + 中 zhōng (middle; within). "Within that" or "among them" , used to pick out elements from a previously named set. One of the most frequent formal connectives in written Chinese, where English might say "of these" or "among which."

e: cheongsam — Manchu-derived dress, distinct from hànfú

d: 企 qǐ (to stand on tiptoe; to aspire) + 业 yè (undertaking). A business organization: 国有企业 "state-owned enterprise," 私营企业 "private enterprise," 企业家 "entrepreneur." The standard term for a firm as a legal and economic body.

e: to take the first steps, starting point
to draft (a document); to draw up
d: 起 qǐ (to begin; to raise) + 草 cǎo (draft). To compose the first version of a formal text, a contract, law, speech, or plan. 起草合同 "to draft a contract."
"Order-starting quantity," often per colour or per SKU rather than per order. Ask which. Factories will usually trade a lower MOQ for a higher unit price.
起 (to rise) plus 飞 (to fly): to rise into flight. Used literally of aircraft leaving the runway and figuratively of an economy or career that is about to surge.

起 (to rise; to stand up) + 义 (righteousness). The act of rising against an unjust authority, with 义 marking the moral legitimacy of the act. In Chinese historiography and political vocabulary, 起义 is the standard term for revolts understood as righteous from the inside.

e: the cause; what set something off
d: 起 qǐ (to rise; to start) + 因 yīn (cause). The cause that started a chain of events, the spark that set a matter in motion: 事情的起因 "the origin of the matter."

气 qì + 场 chǎng (field, as in electromagnetic field or a venue). Originally a TCM and qigong term for the field of qi that radiates from a practitioner. Absorbed into popular culture as a way of describing the palpable aura of a charismatic person. 气场强 = powerful aura; 气场弱 = weak presence.

气 qì + 愤 fèn (indignation; righteous anger, from the image of qi pressing against the heart). Slightly stronger and more formal than 生气. Implies that the anger is justified, that you are responding to something genuinely unfair or wrong. Less colloquial, more dignified.

气 qì + 候 hòu (season; to wait; signs). 候 originally referred to the five-day intervals used in classical Chinese to track seasonal changes. 气候 is the patterned behavior of atmospheric qi over time: climate, not weather. Also used metaphorically: 政治气候 (political climate).

气 qì + 色 sè (color; appearance). In TCM, the complexion (the color and quality of the face) is a direct index of the health of one's internal qi. 气色好 (good complexion) = qi is ample and circulating freely; 气色差 (poor complexion) = qi is deficient or blocked. A doctor's first diagnostic tool.

e: momentum; imposing presence; force of spirit
d: 气 qì + 势 shì (power; momentum; force, the potential energy of a situation). The directed force of qi, outward projection of power rather than inner refinement (气质). An army, a waterfall, a master calligrapher's brushstroke, a confident leader entering a room: all can have 气势.

气 qì (air; atmospheric qi) + 温 wēn (warmth; temperature). The temperature of the air, a meteorological and everyday term. Used in weather reports, health advice, and daily conversation about the feel of a day.

气 qì (breath; vital energy) + 韵 yùn (resonance; rhyme; musical tone). The first and supreme of Xie He's Six Principles: 气韵生动 qìyùn shēngdòng, "spirit resonance, life movement." A painting that has 气韵 is alive; one that lacks it is mere skilled craft.

e: spirit resonance and vitality — the supreme aesthetic criterion
d: Spirit resonance, life movement , Xie He first principle of painting, and the supreme criterion by which Chinese paintings are judged. A work with 气韵生动 has a quality of living presence that cannot be reduced to technical competence. It is the highest praise in Chinese art criticism.

气 qì + 质 zhì (substance; essence; nature). The essential quality of a person's qi, their innate temperament and the bearing it produces. In psychological Chinese, it corresponds to personality type. In everyday speech, 有气质 means "has an air about them": elegant, distinctive, refined.

e: through all the ages; eternal; (of the dead) for ever
d: 千 qiān + 古 gǔ (antiquity; old). All the ages of history, time out of mind. 千古名句 is a line famous through the ages; 千古罪人 (a sinner for all time) is someone whose crime history will never forget.

e: a thousand li; a great distance
d: 千 qiān + 里 lǐ (the Chinese mile). Literally a thousand li, but in practice any great distance. 千里迢迢 qiānlǐ tiáotiáo describes a long, arduous journey from far away.

e: from a thousand li away; across a great distance
d: 千里 (a thousand li) + 迢迢 (tiáotiáo, remote, far off , a reduplication conveying long distance and weariness). The compound evokes a journey undertaken across great distance with effort and determination.

e: a connection across a thousand miles; long-distance destined bond
d: 千里 qiānlǐ = a thousand li (the traditional Chinese unit of distance; figuratively: any great distance). The phrase evokes connections that transcend physical separation , the meeting of people from far apart who nonetheless find each other.

e: a journey of a thousand li
a thousand autumns; the ages; eternity
d: 千 qiān + 秋 qiū (autumn, here standing for a year). A thousand years, hence the long span of history and posterity. 千秋万代 (a thousand autumns, ten thousand generations) means for all time, down all future ages. 名垂千秋 is to have one's name endure through the ages.

e: ten million; by all means; absolutely (must / must not)
d: 千 qiān (thousand) + 万 wàn (ten-thousand), literally ten million. But its most common use is adverbial and emphatic, urging or warning with great force: 千万要小心 (you absolutely must be careful), 千万别忘了 (whatever you do, don't forget).
铅 qiān (lead) + 笔 bǐ. The everyday pencil, named for the old idea of a "lead" pencil even though the core is graphite. One of the first writing tools a child learns to name.

e: predecessor; senior; elder in one's field
d: 前 qián (before; preceding) + 辈 bèi (generation; people of the same era). Those of earlier generations who walked the path before you in your field, institution, or family. A term of respect: addressing someone as 前辈 acknowledges their experience and positions you as the newer arrival.

前 qián (former; preceding) + 朝 cháo (dynasty; court; morning). The dynasty that came before the current one , a term of historical reference used constantly in Chinese historical writing, since each dynasty defined itself partly in relation to what it replaced.

e: ahead; the forward direction; the front (military)
d: 前 qián (front) + 方 fāng (direction; area; square). A more formal and often grander term than 前面 , used in military contexts, official broadcasts, and literary or elevated speech. 前方记者 (correspondent at the front) is a journalism term.

e: to advance; to go forward; to march ahead
d: 前 qián (front; forward) + 进 jìn (to advance). To move ahead in space or in cause: 向前进 "advance forward," 勇往直前 the spirit of pressing on. Its opposite is 后退 hòutuì, to fall back.

e: in front; ahead; the front side
d: 前 qián (front) + 面 miàn (face; surface; side). The most common everyday expression for spatial "in front." Works for physical space (前面有个红绿灯 , there is a traffic light ahead) and for sequential position (前面的章节 , the preceding chapter).

前 qián (front) + 排 pái (row; line; rank). The front row of a theater, cinema, classroom, or any seated arrangement. Also used figuratively for first-rank prominence: 前排位置 (front-row position) implies visibility and status in any field.

e: former occupant of a role; the "ex" (ex-partner, ex-boss)
d: 前 qián (former; preceding) + 任 rèn (appointment; term of office; to hold a post). The person who formerly held a given role or position.

e: past life and present life; across lifetimes
d: 前世 qiánshì (previous lifetime; past existence) + 今生 jīnshēng (this present life). A phrase that spans the axis of rebirth, linking the karmic conditions of a previous life to the circumstances of the current one.
前 qián (front; before) + 天 tiān (day; sky). The day that stands two steps "in front of" today.

钱 qián + 包 bāo (bag; to wrap). The wallet, literally the bag for money. In the smartphone era, 钱包 also refers to mobile payment wallets: 电子钱包 diànzǐ qiánbāo = digital wallet. 钱包里没钱 = the wallet is empty (a relatable condition).

e: the money was scammed (colloquial 给 passive)
d: 给 gěi as passive marker: Subject + 给 + Agent + Verb + Result. 给 in this passive function is particularly common in certain regional varieties of Mandarin. The adversarial connotation is strong , money being deceived out of someone is a very 被-appropriate scenario.

e: heaven; pure yang; the creative; hexagram 1 of the Yijing
d: Six solid yang lines: ䷀. The first hexagram represents pure creative force, origination, strength, the father principle, heaven, the ruler. In the Yijing cosmology, 乾 is the generator of all things , it supplies the initiating impulse that 坤 receives and brings to completion.

e: "the great cosmic shift" — a dramatic all-encompassing maneuver; a total reconfiguration
d: 挪移 nuó yí: to move; to shift; to relocate. 乾坤大挪移 names a fictional martial-arts technique in Jin Yong's (金庸) novel "The Smiling Proud Wanderer" (笑傲江湖) and appears in other wuxia fiction as the name for a supreme technique that redirects any force at will.

e: heaven and earth bright and clear; the cosmos in proper order; just governance
d: 朗朗 lǎnglǎng: bright, clear, resounding. Used to describe an era of good governance and moral clarity, where the cosmic and social order is properly maintained. The phrase implies that the right people are in the right positions, justice is upheld, and nothing fundamental is out of place.

腔 qiāng (cavity, the way speech resonates) + 调 diào (pitch, manner). The accent and intonation of a person's speech, often the regional or affected way they talk. 南方腔调 (a southern accent), 装腔作势 (put on airs). The sound that marks where a voice comes from.

e: the foot of a wall; (figurative) one's foundation, one's base of support
d: 墙 qiáng (wall) + 脚. The base of a wall. The figurative idiom 挖墙脚 wā qiángjiǎo "to dig at the foot of the wall" means to undermine someone , poach their staff, steal their partner, erode their support , by attacking the foundation rather than confronting the wall directly.
To snatch the bill , to scramble to pay the check at the end of a meal. The 抢单 is a social performance communicating willingness to host and invest in the relationship.
Bridge, in the formal engineering register (spoken Chinese just says 桥). Used figuratively exactly as in English: a person or institution can be a 桥梁 between two sides.

e: close and dear; intimate; to feel close to
d: 亲 qīn (family; intimate; close , the same phonetic component that appears in 新 as structural filler, but here fully semantic: kin, dear ones) + 近 (near). Closeness that is also warmth , proximity that has become affection.

e: kin and friends: one's close circle
d: 亲 qīn (kin, relatives) + 朋 péng (friends). Relatives and friends taken together, the whole circle of those close to you. Most often heard in the four-character 亲朋好友, the standard phrase for everyone you would invite to a wedding or a feast.

e: family affection; the bond of kinship
d: 亲 qīn (kin; close) + 情 qíng (feeling). The affection that runs between family members, the love of parent and child or among siblings. It completes the trio with 爱情 (love) and 友情 (friendship).
Imperial Observatory / Bureau of Astronomy: the government department responsible for astronomical observation, calendar production, and astrological consultation in imperial China.

e: City God of Shanghai — the official who refused a posting
d: 秦裕伯 (1301–1373) was a Yuan-to-Ming transition official known for his integrity. When Zhu Yuanzhang, the founding Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty, summoned him to court, Qin refused the appointment, pleading age and illness, and retired to Shanghai.

e: the four scholarly arts — qin, chess, calligraphy, painting
d: The canonical curriculum of the 文人 wénrén (literati) tradition. 琴 qín (guqin), 棋 qí (weiqi / go), 书 shū (calligraphy), 画 huà (painting). Proficiency in all four was the mark of an educated person.
青 qīng (green) + 菜 cài (vegetable). A general word for leafy green vegetables, and in the south the name of a specific small green cabbage. 一盘青菜 "a plate of greens."
青 (qīng, green/blue, the color of new growth) + 春 (spring). "Green spring," the years of youth at their freshest. Used for the whole season of being young, often with a note of how briefly it lasts.

e: bronze ritual vessels — the high art of the Shang world
d: 青铜 qīngtóng (bronze: blue-green metal) + 器 qì (vessel; implement). Shang and Zhou bronze vessels were cast using sophisticated piece-mold techniques that produced complex zoomorphic surface decoration; the most iconic motif was the 饕餮纹 tāotiè wén (taotie: a mask-like face of contested meaning, proba…

e: green glutinous rice cakes — the festival food of the Jiangnan region
to treat lightly; to show disrespect through dismissiveness
d: 轻 qīng (light, slight, to make little of) + 慢 màn (dismissive). To treat someone or something as if it barely deserves attention. More literary than 怠慢 or 傲慢. Often appears in classical texts and formal written criticism.

e: to listen attentively; to lean in and hear
d: 倾 qīng (to lean; to incline; to pour out) + 听 (to listen). Listening with the body inclined toward the speaker , attentive, empathetic, fully directed.
倾 qīng (to lean; to tilt) + 向 xiàng (toward). The way a person or thing leans, a tendency or bias: 政治倾向 "political leanings." As a verb, to be inclined toward: 我倾向于同意 "I'm inclined to agree."

清 (clear water) + 楚 (distinct). The clarity of things and statements: 说清楚 (say it clearly), 看清楚 (see it distinctly). Pairs with 明白 across the divide of world and mind: the map is 清楚, the reader is 明白.

Clear and light , the flavor aesthetic of coastal and delta cuisines, particularly Cantonese. Emphasizes the natural flavors of fresh, high-quality ingredients with minimal masking by heavy seasoning. The direct expression of a geography where fresh seafood and produce are excellent and abundant.

e: to check the count: to take stock
to clean up: to sort out

d: Clear and Bright: the solar term around April 4–6, one of the few solar terms that is also a public holiday in China (and Taiwan, Hong Kong). The Tomb-Sweeping Festival (清明节 Qīngmíngjié) falls on or near this term: families visit ancestral graves, sweep them, leave offerings, and burn paper goods.

清明节 (Clear and Bright Festival), falling around April 4–6 of the solar calendar, is the annual day of tomb sweeping (扫墓 sǎomù). Families travel to ancestral graves, clear away weeds, pour libations, burn paper offerings, and share a meal at the grave site.

e: halal food — the most visible face of Hui culture
d: 清真 cuisine is a distinct tradition within Chinese cooking, developed by Hui communities over centuries. Core prohibitions: no pork (猪肉 zhūròu), no blood, no alcohol (in strictly observant contexts), and meat must be slaughtered according to Islamic rite (念清真 niàn qīngzhēn).
情 (feeling, romance) plus 歌 (song). A love song, one of the most productive 歌 compounds in popular music.
情 qíng (circumstance) + 况 kuàng (condition). The standard word for a situation or set of circumstances: 了解情况 "to understand the situation," 紧急情况 "an emergency."

情 qíng (circumstance; feeling) + 形 xíng. The plain, everyday word for a situation or set of circumstances. 实际情形 = the actual situation; 这种情形 = this kind of case. Close to 情况 qíngkuàng and often interchangeable, with 情形 leaning slightly more descriptive.

e: emotion; emotional state; mood (often the volatile side)
d: 情 qíng (feeling) + 绪 xù (threads; strands). The tangled threads of feeling, an emotional state that can run high or low: 控制情绪 "to control one's emotions," 闹情绪 "to be in a mood; to sulk."

h: 晴天 · 雨天 · 阴天
e: sunny day · rainy day · overcast day
d: 天 tiān as suffix: "day of [weather type]." The pattern (weather adjective + 天) is one of the most productive in spoken Chinese. 晴 qíng (clear); 雨 yǔ (rain); 阴 yīn (overcast, shadow-side). Also: 雪天 xuětiān (snowy day), 风天 fēngtiān (windy day), 大热天 dà rètiān (scorching hot day).

e: please look after us; I look forward to working with you
d: The standard closing line of a first introduction, asking the other side's goodwill for the relationship ahead. 初次见面，请多关照 ("meeting for the first time, please look after me") is the full formula. 请多指教 asks for guidance and is slightly humbler.

e: to consult; to ask for advice (politely)
d: 请 qǐng (to request) + 教 jiào (instruction). To respectfully ask someone to teach you, the polite way to seek advice from a senior or an expert: 向您请教 "may I ask your guidance." Here 教 returns to the fourth tone.

e: To treat someone to a meal , to invite and pay
d: To treat someone to a meal , to invite and pay. 请 means "to invite" or "please"; 客 means "guest." 我请客 (wǒ qǐngkè, "I am treating") declares the host role and closes the question of who pays. The person who says this assumes both the financial obligation and the social prestige of hosting.

e: hosting a meal — baijiu is the host's primary tool
to invite a deity's presence; to install a divine figure ritually
d: 请 qǐng (to invite; to request). The ritual act of inviting a deity to be present , either into a statue during a consecration ceremony, into a temporary vessel at a festival, or into a new altar. The statue itself is 神像 shénxiàng; the consecration that animates it with divine presence is the 请神明.

e: may I ask; excuse me (before a question)
d: 请 qǐng (please; to request) + 问 wèn (to ask). The polite opener for putting a question to a stranger, much like English "excuse me, may I ask." One of the first phrases a learner needs for asking directions.
You will be guided to your seat. A modest protest, 您先坐 (nín xiān zuò, "after you"), is polite; then sit where you are put.

p: qióng zé biàn, biàn zé tōng, tōng zé jiǔ
e: when exhausted, change; when changed, break through; when through, endure
d: From the 系辞下传 (Commentary on the Attached Phrases, Part II), one of the Ten Wings. 穷 qióng here means not poverty but exhaustion: having reached a dead end, used up all options, hit the wall. 变 biàn: transform, change the approach. 通 tōng: break through, find passage, flow freely again.
秋 qiū + 千 qiān, written 秋千 or 鞦韆. Here 千 is purely phonetic, lending its sound to a word for a swing that has nothing to do with the number. 荡秋千 dàng qiūqiān is to swing on a swing.

e: rain calling — interceding with sky spirits
d: Rain-calling (求雨 qiú yǔ) bridges shamanic and folk-religion traditions: the shaman performs extended trance-dancing, drumming, and offering to the spirits of rain and sky (天神 tiānshén), petitioning them to release precipitation.
球 (ball) + 队 (team). Any club built around a ball sport: football, basketball, volleyball. Swap the first character for the sport's tool.

The fermentation starter: dried bricks of grain colonized by mold, yeast, and bacteria, used to initiate fermentation. The composition of the qū is proprietary and is the primary differentiator between producers.

Tune pattern , the named melodic templates to which 昆曲 arias are composed. Analogous to the 词牌 of Song dynasty ci poetry, each 曲牌 specifies melodic contour, range, tonal requirements, and emotional register. There are hundreds in the 昆曲 repertoire, each with specific theatrical associations.

The Chǔ minister-poet whose drowning the festival commemorates. Author of 离骚 Lí Sāo (Encountering Sorrow) and associated poems in the 楚辞 Songs of Chu anthology. The first named author in Chinese literary history whose works survive in substantial quantity.

e: to supersede; to replace; to displace
d: 取 qǔ (to take) + 代 dài (the place of). To take over another's place and push it out entirely: 新技术取代了旧技术 "the new technology superseded the old." Stronger and more decisive than 代替, with a sense that the old thing is now gone.
The follow-up question to every 应该 and 尽量: find the condition behind the hedge. Once the condition is named, it can be negotiated.

e: to name; to give a name
d: 取 qǔ (to take; to select; to acquire) + 名 míng (name). The act of choosing a name , for a child, a product, a shop, a poem.

e: go ahead; you may go; off you go
d: 去 qù (to go; to depart) + 吧 ba (softening particle, suggestion or permission). A gentle dismissal or permission to leave. In a parent-child conversation: 去吧，好好玩 (Go on , have fun). In a formal context: 你去吧，我在这等 (Go ahead , I'll wait here).

e: the train to Beijing — clause + 的 + noun
d: 的 can follow entire clauses or verb phrases to mark modification of the following noun. This is Chinese's primary relative clause mechanism , there are no separate relative pronouns. The entire clause precedes 的 which directly precedes the noun being modified.

e: to remove; to eliminate; to get rid of
d: 去 qù (to send away; to remove) + 除 chú (to eliminate; to remove; to divide out). To cause something to go away , to strip out an unwanted element. Used in formal and technical contexts: 去除污染 (remove contamination), 去除杂质 (remove impurities), 去除顾虑 (dispel concerns).

e: to get rid of; to remove; to drop (something)
d: 去 qù (to cause to go) + 掉 diào (resultative complement: dropped away; gone). A colloquial and direct expression for removal. 掉 as a complement emphasizes that the thing has been fully removed and is gone. More informal than 去除; appropriate for everyday speech. 把它去掉！= Get rid of it!

去 qù (to have gone; to have departed) + 年 nián (year). The year that has departed , last year. A vivid temporal use: the year that went away. Contrast: 来年 láinián (the year that is coming , next year; somewhat literary) and 今年 jīnnián (this year).

去 qù (to depart; to leave) + 世 shì (the world; this age; this life). To depart from the world , the standard respectful expression for the death of an adult. Not used for children or animals, and not used for enemies or condemned criminals (for those, more neutral or harsher terms apply).

全 fuses directly onto nouns to mean "the whole": 全家 (the whole family), 全国 (the whole country), 全世界 (the whole world). 整 zhěng insists the unit is complete and uncut: 整个 (the entire), 整天 (all day long), 整整三年 (three full years).
全 quán (whole) + 部 bù (part; section). The complete set of parts, every one included: 全部作品 "the complete works," 全部完成 "all finished." It points at the totality of a definite group of things.
全 quán (entirely) + 都 dōu (all). A reinforced "all," placed before the verb to stress that the whole group is included: 答案全都对 "every answer is right." The two totality words stack for emphasis.
全 quán (whole) + 国 guó (country). The entire nation as one extent: 全国人民 "the whole nation's people," 全国各地 "all parts of the country." A model for 全 + place: 全省 the whole province, 全市 the whole city.

e: the whole family; the entire household
d: 全 quán (whole) + 家 jiā (family; home). The family taken as a complete unit: 全家福 "a whole-family photo," 全家团圆 "the whole family reunited." A warm, everyday use of the whole sense.

e: to rely entirely on; to owe it all to
d: 全 quán (entirely) + 靠 kào (to lean on; to depend). To depend wholly on one person or thing, with nothing else to fall back on: 全靠大家的努力 "thanks entirely to everyone's effort."

e: Full name , surname + given name together
d: Full name , surname + given name together. 请问您贵姓？(qǐngwèn nín guì xìng?) is the polite form of "May I ask your surname?" — literally "May I ask your honorable surname?"

e: all (of a group of people); the entire body
d: 全 quán (whole) + 体 tǐ (body). The entire body of people taken together, used of members, staff, or citizens: 全体学生 "all the students," 全体起立 "everybody stand up." Where 全部 counts things, 全体 gathers people.

e: the eye of a spring; the place where spring water emerges
d: 泉 quán (spring) + 眼. The mouth of a natural spring , the small opening from which water bubbles up. Common in classical Chinese poetry and travel writing.

e: fist; boxing; a school of martial art
d: The character for fist appears in the name of almost every Chinese martial style: 太极拳, 少林拳, 咏春拳 Wing Chun, 螳螂拳 Praying Mantis. 打拳 = to practice boxing; to do martial arts.
To urge someone to drink: the act of pressing a guest or colleague to drink more. Can be warm hospitality or unwanted pressure depending on context and relationship.

缺 quē (to lack) + 德. To be missing virtue. The everyday Chinese accusation for someone whose conduct is not just unkind but morally wrong in a low way , petty cruelty, dishonesty for its own sake, malicious mischief. 太缺德了！ "That's so unscrupulous!" is one of the standard everyday condemnations.

e: to confirm; to be sure; certain
d: 确 què (sure; firm) + 定 dìng (to settle). To pin a thing down as fixed and beyond doubt, or to be sure of it oneself. 我不确定 "I'm not sure," 确定时间 "to fix the time."
The sample the buyer has approved, usually signed and dated. Everything after it is measured against it, so record exactly which version you approved and what you asked to change.

确认 (quèrèn) is the verb of the whole relationship: samples are confirmed, drawings are confirmed, orders are confirmed. 我确认一下 before restating a point; 您确认一下 when handing the other side something to check.

"However" (formal). The more literary cousin of 不过, common in written and formal spoken contexts. In casual conversation it can sound bookish; in lectures, presentations, and considered discussions it fits naturally.

让 is "to yield." 让利 (rànglì) is giving up margin; 降价 (jiàngjià) is simply lowering the price, 涨价 (zhǎngjià) raising it, 还价 (huánjià) making a counteroffer. 底价 (dǐjià) is the floor price a side will not go below.

"Let me think." Direct, slightly more formal than 那个. Appropriate when a question deserves a real answer and you want the listener to wait while you produce one. The reduplicated 想想 softens it, suggesting brief consideration rather than a long pause.
热 (hot) plus 敷 (fū, to apply to the skin): to apply heat, a hot compress. The home remedy for a stiff neck or a sore back, the warm counterpart to 冷敷 (lěngfū), a cold compress.
热 (hot) plus 门 (mén, gate, field): a hot gateway, hence a popular field, trending topic, or in-demand option. The opposite is 冷门 (lěngmén), a cold and obscure one.
热 (hot) plus 闹 (nào, noisy, to make a din): the heat of a busy, crowded, festive scene. Note the neutral tone on 闹 in this word. A market, a holiday street, a full restaurant are all 热闹.
热 rè (hot) + 情 qíng (feeling). Warm feeling, used both as a noun (enthusiasm, passion) and as an adjective for a warm, welcoming person: 他很热情 "he is very warm and friendly."
热 (hot) plus 水 (shuǐ, water). The everyday word for hot water, the staple drink offered to a guest and the cure a Chinese parent prescribes for almost anything.

e: a talented person; talent; capable people
d: 人 rén (person) + 才 cái (talent). A person of real ability, and by extension the pool of skilled people an organization or country can draw on: 培养人才 "to cultivate talent," 人才市场 "the job market for skilled workers."

e: the human realm; the human path of rebirth
d: The human realm is considered the most favorable position for Buddhist practice precisely because of its mixture of suffering and capacity. Humans experience enough pain and impermanence to feel the urgency of liberation, while retaining enough cognitive clarity and agency to pursue the path.

人工 réngōng (man-made; artificial , 人 person + 工 work/craft) + 智能 zhìnéng (intelligent capability , 智 wisdom/intelligence + 能 capability/ability). Abbreviated 人工智能 or simply AI in technical contexts; 智能 alone is used as an adjective: 智能手机 zhìnéng shǒujī (smartphone), 智能家居 zhìnéng jiājū (smart home).

e: a sea of people; a vast crowd
d: 人 rén (person) + 海 hǎi (sea). A crowd so large it reads as an ocean of heads. Famous in the phrase 茫茫人海 "the boundless sea of humanity," the throng in which two people might never meet.

人际 rén jì = between people (人 person + 际 boundary, junction). 人际关系 is the standard term for the full web of interpersonal relationships in Chinese social and professional life. Appears constantly in business advice, psychology, and self-help contexts.

人 rén (person) + 家 jiā (home; family). This single compound has three distinct uses in modern Mandarin: (1) other people in general; (2) someone's specific household; (3) an informal first-person pronoun used primarily by women, expressing mild protest or vulnerability.

e: humanistic Buddhism; Buddhism for the human world
d: The 20th-century reformist movement, associated above all with Master Taixu (太虚, 1890–1947), that repositioned Buddhist practice away from funeral rites and other-worldly concerns toward engagement with society, education, and the relief of present suffering.

e: paradise on earth; heaven in the human world
d: 天堂 (tiāntáng) = paradise; heaven. 人间天堂 collapses the cosmological distance between 人间 and 天界: a place so beautiful it brings the celestial into the human world.

e: the smoke and fire of human life; the warmth of ordinary domestic existence
d: 烟火 (yānhuǒ) = smoke and fire , specifically the smoke of cooking fires and the warmth of a hearth. 人间烟火 refers to the sights, smells, and sounds of ordinary human life: street food stalls, the smell of garlic in a wok, a neighborhood at dusk.

e: "to evaporate from the human world" — to vanish; to go completely off the grid
d: 蒸发 (zhēngfā) = to evaporate; to vaporize. A colorful colloquial expression for someone who has completely disappeared from contact , not answering calls, not posting online, impossible to locate. The humor is cosmological: they have not merely left town, they have vacated 人间 entirely.

人 rén (person) + 口 kǒu (mouth). Population , the number of mouths to feed, the count of human presences. 中国人口约14亿 "China's population is approximately 1.4 billion." 人口众多 rénkǒu zhòngduō = "large population" (a standard description of China).

人 rén + 类 lèi (species; category; kind). Refers to humanity as a biological and civilizational category, the human species in its entirety across all time. Used in philosophical, scientific, and grand-historical registers. Much larger in scope than 人们, and without political coloring.

人 rén + 脉 mài (vein; pulse; artery, the channels through which blood flows). Your social and professional network, imagined as a circulatory system. 脉 is the same character used in 经脉 jīngmài (meridians) in TCM.

人 rén + 们 men (plural suffix for animate nouns). A general, indefinite plural: "people" in the broad social sense, as in "one finds that people…" or "people say…" 们 cannot be combined with numbers; you cannot say ＊三人们. This plural is for social generality, not counting.

人 rén + 民 mín (common people; subjects; citizens). A politically weighted term. In the PRC context, it carries strong ideological resonance: the people as a collective subject and political actor, not merely a demographic count. Appears in major institutional names and slogans.

e: moral character; the quality of a person
d: 人 rén + 品 pǐn (quality; grade; character, three 口 mouths stacked, suggesting the spoken judgments of a community). The overall moral quality of a person as assessed by those around them: moral trustworthiness and reliability in relationships, not talent or intelligence.

e: human feeling; social obligation; the gift economy of favors
d: Human feeling, social obligation , the accumulated weight of favors, gifts, and consideration exchanged between people. To "owe someone rénqíng" is to be in their social debt. Gift-giving is one of the primary means of building and repaying 人情. The concept is inseparable from 关系.
人 rén (person) + 物 wù (thing). A notable person, a "somebody," and also a character in a novel, film, or play: 历史人物 "a historical figure," 主要人物 "the main character."
人 rén + 缘 yuán (fate; karmic bond, a Buddhist term for the predestined connections between people). Literally: one's karmic bond with people. In practice: whether others naturally warm to you.

e: benevolence and love; humanitarian care; genuine concern for others
d: 仁 rén (humaneness) + 爱 ài (love; affection). The compound that captures 仁's essential motion: active, outward-reaching care for others. 仁 without 爱 is a concept; 仁爱 is what it looks like in practice.

仁 rén + 慈 cí (tender care; the warmth of a mother for a child). The quality of someone whose inner humaneness produces visibly tender conduct. Warmer and more personal than 仁爱: 仁爱 can describe a principle, 仁慈 always describes a quality felt by the recipient.

e: humaneness and righteousness; moral conduct; the Confucian ethical pairing
d: 仁 rén (humaneness) + 义 yì (righteousness; moral rightness). The foundational pairing in Confucian ethics: 仁 is the inward quality of genuine care; 义 is the outward expression of doing what is morally right. Together they describe the full ethical person.

e: an army of benevolence and righteousness; a just and humane military force
d: 仁义 (benevolence and righteousness) + 之 (attributive particle) + 师 (army; force; teacher).

e: the humane person; one who possesses 仁 (classical)
d: 仁 rén + 者 zhě (the one who…; nominalizer in classical Chinese). The classical term for a person who has cultivated 仁.

e: to spot, to pick out, to identify (from a group or after a delay)
d: 认 rèn + 出 chū (out; resultative: to come into view). The act of identification , picking someone out of a crowd, recognizing a familiar face after years apart, identifying a body. The 出 marks the moment recognition crystallizes.

e: to admit one's mistake; (also) to mistake one thing for another
d: 认 rèn + 错 cuò (wrong; mistake). Two readings split by context. To acknowledge a mistake: 我向你认错 "I admit my mistake to you." To mistake X for Y: 我认错人了 "I had the wrong person" (lit. "recognized-wrong the person").

e: to recognize, to be able to identify
d: 认 rèn + 得 de (potential complement: be able to). Able to recognize. Slightly more colloquial than 认识 and emphasizes the act of recognition rather than ongoing acquaintance. The negative 不认得 "don't recognize" is very common.

e: to firmly believe; to be certain that; to officially determine
d: 认 rèn + 定 dìng (fixed; settled). Settled recognition. Two registers: personal conviction ("I'm certain that…") and official determination (a court, a regulatory body officially classifying something). Stronger and more committed than 认为.

e: to resign oneself to fate; to accept what is given
d: 认 rèn + 命 mìng (fate; lot; what Heaven decrees). To acknowledge one's fate. The act of accepting what cannot be changed: sometimes wisdom (Confucian 知命), sometimes resignation (giving up the fight). Tone depends on context.

e: to know (a person, a place, a character); knowledge, understanding
d: 认 rèn + 识 shí (to know; to discern). The standard verb for knowing-by-acquaintance: knowing someone, knowing a place, knowing a character. As a noun, it means understanding or grasp of a topic.

e: to concede defeat; to give in
d: 认 rèn + 输 shū (to lose). To acknowledge a loss , in a game, an argument, a contest of will. The negative 不认输 "refuses to give in" is one of the standard ways of praising tenacity.

e: to identify with; to agree with; identification
d: 认 rèn + 同 tóng (same; to be one with). To recognize as one's own: the verb behind identification in the social and psychological sense. 身份认同 shēnfèn rèntóng = identity (in the sense of self-identification with a group).

e: to think; to believe; to consider (one's view)
d: 认 rèn (to recognize; to take as) + 为 wéi (to be; to take as). Literally "to take X as [one's view of the matter]." The most common compound for expressing personal opinion in modern Chinese , 我认为 wǒ rènwéi (I think that...) is the standard opener for stating a perspective in speech or writing.

e: to acknowledge a debt; to own up to a commitment
d: 认 rèn + 账 zhàng (account; bill; debt). To acknowledge the account. Originally and literally a debt; figuratively, any commitment one is held to. The negative 不认账 "to refuse to own up" is the standard accusation against someone who reneges.

e: to get serious about it; to start taking it seriously

d: ISO 9001 is 质量管理体系认证 (the quality management system certificate). 验厂 (yànchǎng) is a factory audit, such as BSCI for social compliance. Check the certificate's 有效期 and that the company name matches the one you are contracting with.

e: to recognize characters; to be literate; to read
d: 认 rèn (to recognize; to identify; to acknowledge) + 字 zì. The act of visually identifying a character and knowing its reading and meaning. Implies the foundational literacy skill. 不认字 = illiterate (cannot read), a stark and socially significant label.
任何 means "any whatsoever" and, true to the system, needs 都 at the verb: 任何人都可以参加 (anyone may take part), 任何问题都欢迎 (any question is welcome).
任 rèn (to entrust; office, post) plus 命. To formally place someone in a role by official decree. The standard verb in government, corporate, and academic contexts for the act of appointment.
仍 réng (still, as before) + 然 rán (so). Marks that a state holds unchanged despite what might have altered it: 仍然 here, the situation is still thus. Close to 还是 háishì but more written.
日 (rì, day) plus 报: a report issued every day. The suffix that names mastheads, as in 《人民日报》 (Rénmín Rìbào, the People's Daily) and 《广州日报》.

日 rì (day) + 常 cháng (constant; ordinary; everyday). The standard adjective for "everyday, routine, daily life." 日常生活 rìcháng shēnghuó = everyday life. 日常用语 rìcháng yòngyǔ = everyday expressions (a category every Chinese textbook includes). 日常工作 = daily work/routine.
日光 (rìguāng, sunlight, daylight) + 灯 (lamp): a fluorescent tube, named for the cool daylight-white glow it gives. The long white strip light common in offices and kitchens.
日 rì (day) + 记 jì (record). A day-by-day record of one's own life and thoughts: 写日记 "to keep a diary." The 日 marks the daily rhythm of the writing.

日 rì (sun; day) + 历 lì (from 曆, the calendar). The everyday word for a calendar as a physical or digital object: the thing on the wall or in your phone that lists the days. This is the 曆 branch of 历, fully about counting and displaying days. For the tear-off page-a-day kind, the same word applies.

e: capacity: how much a container or system can hold
d: 容 róng (to contain, to hold) + 量 liàng (amount). The maximum a vessel, device, or system can take in: a bottle's volume, a battery's charge, a hard drive's storage, a hall's seating. 电池容量 (battery capacity), 硬盘容量 (disk capacity), 存储容量 (storage capacity).

容 róng (face; appearance) + 貌 mào (looks; outward form). A person's facial appearance, slightly literary in tone. Used to describe how someone looks, especially in careful or admiring description. Compare the plainer 长相 zhǎngxiàng used in casual speech.

e: to hold; to accommodate; to seat
d: 容 róng (to hold) + 纳 nà (to take in; to receive). To take something in and have room for it. Used for physical capacity (a stadium holding a crowd) and, by extension, for accommodating ideas or people into a group.

容 róng (to hold) + 器 qì (vessel; implement; utensil). A thing whose whole purpose is to hold. The general noun for any container, from a jar to a software data structure. 器 names a made object with a function; 容器 is the object made for holding.

e: to tolerate; to put up with; to endure
d: 容 róng (to hold) + 忍 rěn (to endure; to bear). To make room for something unwelcome and not act against it. Often carries a sense of restraint under strain: one tolerates because acting out would be worse. The object is typically a behavior, a fault, or a situation rather than a person directly.

e: to permit; to allow; to admit of
d: 容 róng (to allow) + 许 xǔ (to permit; to grant). To leave room for something to happen. Slightly more formal than the everyday 允许 yǔnxǔ, and it often appears in the negative (不容许, does not permit) or with abstract subjects such as time, rules, or circumstances that "do not allow" a thing.

容 róng (ample room) + 易 yì (easy; to change). The most common word built on 容, and a core HSK item. It carries two linked senses: a task is "easy," and an event is "likely" or "apt to happen." The shared idea is low resistance: with room to spare, the thing happens readily.

溶 róng (to melt into liquid) + 解 jiě. To melt and break apart. The scientific verb for a substance dissolving in a solvent: 盐在水里溶解 = salt dissolves in water; 溶解度 = solubility. Here 解 keeps its most literal force, the breaking of a whole into dispersed parts, in the language of chemistry.

融 róng (to melt; to blend; to merge) + 化 huà (to dissolve). The standard verb for a solid melting into a liquid: snow, ice, butter, chocolate. Here 化 supplies its concrete physical sense, the turning of one physical state into another.

e: softness and yielding — the power of the apparently weak
d: 柔 róu (soft, supple) + 弱 ruò (weak). The Daodejing's counterintuitive teaching: the soft overcomes the hard, the yielding overcomes the rigid. Water is soft yet carves rock. The newborn is supremely soft and full of life; the corpse is rigid.
肉 (flesh) + 麻 (má, numb, tingling). The skin-crawling feeling of words too sweet or sentimental, the goosebumps of secondhand embarrassment.
肉 (meat) + 松 (sōng, loose, fluffy). Meat dried and shredded into airy fibers, scattered over porridge or buns.
肉 (flesh) + 体 (tǐ, body). The bodily, corporeal self, set against 精神 (jīngshén, spirit) or 灵魂 (línghún, soul).
肉 (flesh) + 眼 (yǎn, eye). The unaided eye of flesh, as opposed to a telescope or microscope.

e: like this; so; in this way
d: 如 rú (like) + 此 cǐ (this). A literary "like this, so," used both to point back at what was said and to intensify: 如此美丽 "so beautiful." The set phrase 原来如此 means "ah, so that's how it is."

e: as before; unchanged; as it always was
d: 如 (rú, to be like; as if , a woman and a mouth: to speak as the other speaks, to conform to) + 故 (gù, old; former). As before, unchanged since the past. 一切如故 (everything as before) describes a scene that time has not touched.
如 rú (suppose) + 果 guǒ (outcome). The default "if," opening the condition clause and usually answered by 就 jiù in the result: 如果你来，我就很高兴 "if you come, I'll be glad."

e: how; in what way; what about
d: 如 rú (according to) + 何 hé (what). The literary "how," asking by what means or in what manner: 如何解决 "how to solve it." The spoken everyday word is 怎么 zěnme; 如何 belongs to writing and formal speech.

如 rú (like) + 同 tóng (same). A slightly literary way to say one thing is just like another, common in description and writing: 如同白昼 "as bright as day." In speech 好像 hǎoxiàng is the everyday equivalent.
如 rú (according to) + 意 yì (wish; intention). Turning out the way one hoped: 称心如意 "perfectly content." A staple of festive blessings, where 万事如意 wishes that every affair go as desired.

e: Confucianism — the school of ritual and moral cultivation
d: Founded by Confucius (孔子 Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BCE). Core values: 仁 rén (benevolence/humaneness), 礼 lǐ (ritual propriety), 义 yì (righteousness), 忠 zhōng (loyalty), 孝 xiào (filial piety).

e: to get started; to cross the threshold of a subject; a primer
d: 入 rù (to enter) + 门 mén (door). To step across the doorway of a field, to grasp its basics. A book titled 《汉语入门》 is "Chinese: A Primer," a doorway into the language.

e: when in a village, follow its customs — adapt to local ways
d: Lit: enter-village-follow-customs. The essential guide to cross-cultural conduct , observe and adopt local practices rather than imposing your own. Used practically and as a statement of cultural humility. 你到了那里，要入乡随俗 "When you get there, follow local customs."

Hotels must register foreign guests' passports, and not every hotel is licensed to take foreigners, so book one that confirms it does. 押金 (yājīn) is the deposit, 退房 (tuìfáng) checkout. For a company invoice, give the 抬头 (táitóu, the invoice name).

软 ruǎn (soft) + 件 jiàn (a piece). The intangible programs that run on a computer, paired against 硬件 yìngjiàn (hardware), 硬 yìng meaning hard. The soft and hard contrast is a direct calque of the English pair, with 件 supplying the shared unit-of-a-system sense.
Intercalary month, the extra month inserted approximately every 2–3 years (7 times in 19 years) to reconcile the lunar and solar cycles. A year with a 闰月 has 13 months.

e: shamanic dance — the body as ritual instrument
d: Shamanic dance (萨满舞 sàmǎn wǔ) is the physical form of the spirit-journey: the rhythmic movement of the body , spinning, jumping, mimicking animal spirits (bear-stomp, eagle-wing, snake-writhe) , accompanies and intensifies the drum-driven trance.
赛 (sài, to compete) + 跑. The verb-noun for a competitive run. 百米赛跑 (bǎi mǐ sàipǎo, hundred-meter dash) and 长跑赛 (chángpǎo sài, long-distance race) are the standard sports terms.

三 sān + 餐 cān (meal). The three daily meals: breakfast (早餐 zǎocān), lunch (午餐 wǔcān), and dinner (晚餐 wǎncān). The phrase 一日三餐 (three meals a day) is the standard way to refer to daily sustenance, and by extension to reliable, ordinary livelihood.

e: the three poisons that 涅槃 extinguishes

d: The Three Hottest Periods: the three intervals of approximately 10 days each during Major Heat and surrounding terms, traditionally considered the most intensely hot and humid days of the year.

e: the Three Bonds and Five Constants — the Confucian social order
d: The three bonds (三纲): ruler-minister, father-son, husband-wife. The five constants (五常): benevolence (仁), righteousness (义), ritual propriety (礼), wisdom (智), and trustworthiness (信). Systematized in the Han dynasty, this framework defined Confucian social structure for two thousand years.

e: the Three Kingdoms; the era of three rival states
d: 三 sān + 国 guó (kingdom; state; country). The Three Kingdoms period (220–280 CE), when China split into Wei (魏), Shu (蜀), and Wu (吴) after the collapse of the Han dynasty.

三 sān (three) + 角 jiǎo (corner; angle) + 形 xíng. The three-corner shape. 形 is the standard suffix that turns a description into the name of a geometric shape: 正方形 zhèngfāngxíng (square), 圆形 yuánxíng (circle), 长方形 chángfāngxíng (rectangle).

e: three risings three fallings — Junshan Yinzhen's display
Three Pure Ones — the supreme triad of Daoist theology
d: The highest tier of the Daoist theological hierarchy, above even the Jade Emperor.

e: to think carefully; to think three times before acting
d: 三 sān + 思 sī (to think; to reflect). From the Analects: 季文子三思而后行 , "Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting." Confucius's comment was that twice was already sufficient, but the wisdom of pausing before action became proverbial.

Sanxingdui , "Three Star Mounds," the Bronze Age archaeological site near Guanghan. The bronze masks, standing figure, and sacred tree uncovered there belong to a culture with no connection to the contemporaneous Shang dynasty. 堆 means "mound" or "pile."

e: three distances; three modes of spatial recession
d: 三 sān (three) + 远 yuǎn (far; distance). Guo Xi's taxonomy from 林泉高致 (1080s): 高远 gāo yuǎn (high distance -- looking up from base to peak, creates grandeur and vertical drama), 深远 shēn yuǎn (deep distance -- looking through receding layers of mountains and valleys, creates mystery and depth), 平远 píng…

三 sān + 字 zì (character; written word) + 经 jīng (classic; canonical text). A classical primer written in three-character rhyming lines, composed in the Song dynasty and memorized by virtually every literate child in pre-modern China.

The "Sao style" , the poetic tradition derived from Qu Yuan's 离骚, characterized by longer lines, the medial particle 兮 xī, lavish botanical and spiritual imagery, and the theme of exile and unrecognized virtue. One of the two foundational styles of classical Chinese poetry.
您扫我还是我扫您? (Do you scan me or do I scan you?) is the everyday question at a till.

e: tomb sweeping — the annual visit to the graves
d: 扫墓 (lit. "sweep the grave") is the Qingming practice of clearing the tomb of weeds and debris, adding fresh soil, pouring libations of wine, burning paper offerings, and sharing food at the grave site.

p: sè jí shì kōng, kōng jí shì sè
e: form is exactly emptiness; emptiness is exactly form
d: The most quoted line of the Heart Sutra and arguably of any Mahāyāna text. The eight characters fold the entire teaching of emptiness into a single chiastic formula. Quoted across East Asian literature, philosophy, calligraphy, contemporary fiction, and advertising.

Central Asians, Persians, Arabs, Turks, Uighurs, and others. Trusted as financial and commercial intermediaries. Many were Muslim. The term 色目 (lit. "various types of eyes") reflects Mongolian and Chinese perception of Central Asian physical appearance.

h: 僧璨 · 道信 · 弘忍
d: 僧璨 Sengcan (d. 606 CE), the third patriarch, is remembered for the 信心铭 Xìnxīn Míng (Verses on the Faith-Mind), a verse text expressing the Chan teaching that discriminating mind (the tendency to prefer and reject) is the root of suffering.

e: killing the green — the heat-fixing step

d: Once a celestial general, banished to a river as a flesh-eating ogre, then redeemed as the third disciple. Quiet, dutiful, and reliable, he carries the luggage and keeps the peace between the volatile monkey and the wayward pig.
山 shān + 峰 fēng (peak , itself contains 山). The redundancy is expressive emphasis. Used literally (climbing a peak) and figuratively (事业的山峰 "the peak of one's career").

e: Shanhai Pass — eastern terminus of the Ming wall

d: 山 shān (mountain) + 脚. The base of a mountain , where the slope meets the plain, where villages and trailheads sit. Standard geographical vocabulary.

山 shān + 脉 mài (vein; pulse; connected system, the word for pulse in traditional Chinese medicine). A mountain range as a vein of the earth, all peaks connected underground. Same logic as 水脉 (water vein) and 血脉 (bloodline). 秦岭山脉 the Qinling Mountains.

山水 + 风光 (fēngguāng, scenery; views). The standard tourism and travel-writing phrase. 桂林山水甲天下 (Guìlín shānshuǐ jiǎ tiānxià, "the landscape of Guilin is first under heaven") is one of the most-quoted lines in Chinese tourism , a fixed praise-formula, originally a Song-dynasty poem.

e: landscape poetry; the mountain-and-water poem genre
d: 山水 + 诗 (shī, poem). The poetic genre that parallels the painting genre. Founded in the Six Dynasties period by Xie Lingyun (谢灵运, 385–433) and brought to its high point in the Tang by Wang Wei (王维) and Meng Haoran (孟浩然).

e: amid mountains and waters; in the landscape
d: A literary phrase widely used in modern essays, song lyrics, and travel writing. 之间 zhī jiān = between; amid. The phrase carries the Daoist resonance of being in the landscape rather than looking at it. Common in tea-house names, hotel names, and book titles aimed at evoking refinement.
Shandao is the most doctrinally influential of the Chinese Pure Land patriarchs, the figure who gave the tradition its systematic theological foundation.

善 shàn (good) + 恶 è (evil; bad). The paired terms that define the moral axis. In classical Chinese thought, 善 and 恶 are not absolute opposites in a cosmic war but positions on a continuum of conduct , and the line between them runs through every person, which is why cultivation matters.

善 shàn (goodness) + 良 liáng (good; fine; sound). The most common compound in everyday speech for describing a person's character. 善良的人 = a kind-hearted person. 良 reinforces and grounds the abstraction of 善 into lived quality.

善 shàn + 意 yì (intention; meaning). The moral quality of an act before it has been carried out: the intention behind the gesture. 出于善意 chūyú shànyì = "out of goodwill." Often appears in contexts where motives need to be clarified or defended.

e: to be good at; skilled in
d: 善 shàn + 于 yú (at; in; toward , a classical preposition that here marks the domain of competence). The most common modern compound for natural ability or cultivated skill. Takes a verb or activity directly: 善于 + 动词 verb phrase. Implies a degree of mastery, not just familiarity.

伤 shāng (wound; injury) + 心 xīn (heart). Lit. "wounded heart." The heart as a physical organ that can be injured. Used for real losses: a pet dying, a relationship ending, a deeply disappointing outcome. Stronger and more pointed than 难过 nánguò (distressed, upset).

e: the marketplace is a rivers-and-lakes world — X是个江湖 as a productive formula
d: The formula X是个江湖 applies 江湖 logic , its hidden codes, dangers, unwritten rules, and webs of obligation , to any competitive domain.

e: to discuss: to talk something over, to consult
d: 商 shāng (to consult, to confer) + 量 liang (measure, toneless here). To talk a matter over with someone before deciding: to weigh it between two minds.
The deferral. Buys time without saying no, and is the expected answer to any significant new proposal. Name when you will reply so it does not read as a brush-off.

e: Shang Yang's reforms — the Legalist transformation of Qin
d: 商鞅 Shāng Yāng (c. 390–338 BCE), born in Wei, served as the chief minister of Qin under Duke Xiao from 356 BCE.

e: admiring chrysanthemums — the flower of late autumn resilience
d: 赏 shǎng (to appreciate; to admire) + 菊 jú (chrysanthemum). The chrysanthemum (菊花 júhuā) blooms in autumn, long after spring flowers have finished. This timing made it a symbol of resilience, longevity, and the virtuous person who thrives when others have withered.

e: to go to work; to be at work; on duty
d: 上 shàng (to mount; to attend) + 班 bān (shift; work roster; class). To show up for and engage in one's work shift. The most common word for "going to work" in daily speech. Contrast 下班 (to finish work; to get off work): the 上/下 pair governs the entire working day.
上 (to go up onto) + 船 (boat): you step up onto a deck, so boarding is 上, and disembarking is 下船 (xià chuán). The same up/down logic governs 上车 / 下车 for vehicles.

e: to be fooled; to be taken in; to fall for a trick
d: 上 shàng (to go up to) + 当 dàng (the pawnshop). From the image of being shortchanged at the pawnbroker's counter, it now means to be cheated or deceived. 上当受骗 shàngdàng shòupiàn is the common four-character pairing.

e: to visit and offer at the grave

d: 上 shàng (upon; on) + 海 hǎi (sea). China's largest city and busiest port, at the mouth of the Yangtze. The name reads "on the sea," fitting for a town that grew from fishing village to global harbor.

Shanghainese: the Wu Chinese topolect spoken in Shanghai, mutually unintelligible with Mandarin. A marker of local identity increasingly in tension with the spread of Putonghua as the dominant urban language for the younger generation.

e: to get internal heat; to be inflamed; to get irritable
d: 上 shàng (to rise; to ascend) + 火 huǒ (fire). A TCM concept: excess heat (fire) in the body rising upward, causing sore throat, mouth ulcers, red eyes, or irritability. Used medically and colloquially. 吃辣的容易上火 "Eating spicy food easily causes 上火."

上 shàng (upward; advancing) + 进 jìn (to advance; to enter). Moving upward and forward. 上进心 shàngjìnxīn (the drive to improve; ambition) is one of the most positively valenced personal traits in Chinese educational culture: a quality parents want to see in children and teachers in students.

e: high society; the upper class; the social elite
d: 上流 (shàngliú, upper stream; the upper reaches of a river) + 社会. High society, the social elite. The metaphor is of the upper current of a river: those who move at the top of the social flow. Used in both admiring and ironic registers.

e: above; on top; the upper surface
d: 上 shàng (above; up) + 面 miàn (face; side; surface). The upper side of something; the surface on top; the direction above. In spatial description, 上面 is the default way to say "on top of" or "above." In discourse, 上面 can also mean "what was mentioned above" or "the higher authorities."

e: up to mountains, down to countryside (policy)
heaven above; God/fate; to ascend into the sky
d: 上 shàng (above; to ascend) + 天 tiān (heaven). As a noun: the heavens conceived as a moral agent, equivalent to "God" or "fate" in many colloquial contexts. As a verb: to ascend to the sky (a rocket launching; a person dying).

e: to go online; to use the internet
d: 上 shàng (to mount; to get onto) + 网 wǎng (net; network; the internet). To mount the internet. The spatial metaphor is the same as getting on a vehicle or into an institution: you step up onto a platform. Formed in the early 1990s as Chinese internet usage began, and immediately adopted the 上 frame.

e: up and down; approximately; around (a number)
d: 上 shàng (above) + 下 xià (below). The full vertical range , top to bottom , which collapses into an estimate of the middle. When placed after a number, it means "approximately" or "give or take." 三十上下 = around thirty.

e: to go to school; to attend school
d: 上 shàng (to attend; to mount into) + 学 xué (learning; school). To attend school, covering both the daily action (going to school today) and the general state (being a school student). Contrast: 上大学 (to attend university), 上幼儿园 (to go to preschool).

e: to become addicted; to get hooked
d: 上 shàng (to mount into; to be caught by) + 瘾 yǐn (addiction; craving, a disease radical character). To have mounted into the craving, to be in its grip. Works for any powerful habit or compulsion: 游戏上瘾 (game addiction), 咖啡上瘾 (caffeine dependency), 手机上瘾 (phone addiction).

The seat of honor , the seat facing the door, assigned to the most honored guest. The term literally means "upper seat." Understanding the seating logic around 上座 is a practical necessity at any formal Chinese meal. Equivalent: 主位 zhǔwèi.

e: exalting the worthy; meritocracy over hereditary rank
d: Mozi argued that government offices should be filled by those with demonstrable ability and virtue, regardless of birth.

e: to burn incense, to offer joss sticks
d: 烧 (to burn) + 香 (incense). The ritual act of lighting incense at a temple, shrine, or grave. A separable verb-object: 烧了一炷香 (shāo le yí zhù xiāng), burned one stick of incense.

e: burning paper money — offerings for the dead
d: 烧 shāo (burn) + 纸 zhǐ (paper) + 钱 qián (money). Paper replicas of currency, goods, and , in contemporary practice , smartphones, cars, designer bags, and houses, burned so that the smoke carries them to the deceased in the underworld.

From the 少林寺 Shàolín Sì (Shaolin Monastery) on Mount Song 嵩山, Henan. The most internationally recognized style, blending Chan Buddhist meditation with rigorous physical training. Historically credited with the development of northern Chinese external styles.
少 shào (young) + 年 (year; age). A person of young years , typically ages 10–18 in modern usage, though classically it could refer to anyone young.

少 (few) + 数 (number, quantity). A small quantity , the minority. 少数民族 shǎoshù mínzú (ethnic minority , literally "small-number people-clan") is the official Chinese term for China's 55 recognized ethnic minorities (the Han majority plus 55 groups).
机器 (jīqì) is a single machine. Ask whether equipment is owned and how old it is; 进口设备 (imported equipment) is a point of pride.
To design; a design. 设计师 (shèjìshī) covers designers from fashion to industrial. In engineering documents, 设计院 (design institute) is the state-descended firm that produces the drawings.

社会 + 保障 (bǎozhàng, guarantee; protection; safeguard). The welfare system: pensions, unemployment insurance, medical insurance, and other state-provided protections against life's major risks. The compound mirrors the English "social security" almost exactly in logic.

e: social status; social standing; position in society
d: 社会 + 地位 (dìwèi, position; standing; status). One's rank or standing within the social order. Closely related to 面子 , social status is the structural foundation from which face is generated and maintained. Hierarchically sensitive: 地位 implies a vertical ordering.

e: social atmosphere; moral climate; the prevailing spirit of society
d: 社会 + 风气 (fēngqì, prevailing atmosphere; social mores; lit. "wind and air"). The ambient moral climate of a society at a given moment: whether honesty, integrity, and mutual care are in the air, or whether cynicism, materialism, and corruption have taken hold.

社会 + 关系 (guānxi, relationship; connection). One's web of social connections. In Chinese social contexts, 社会关系 encompasses what is often simply called 关系 , the practical network of relationships that enables things to get done.
社会 + 稳定 (wěndìng, stable; stability). A central governing priority. 维护社会稳定 (to maintain social stability) appears throughout official documents, legal texts, and policy announcements.

社会 (society) + 信用 (xìnyòng, credit; trustworthiness) + 体系 (tǐxì, system; framework). A multifaceted platform for tracking trustworthiness and compliance across financial, legal, and behavioral domains.

社会 + 学 (xué, the study of). The academic discipline. The word makes the Meiji translation story visible: 社会学 was coined as the direct Chinese equivalent of sociology (German Soziologie, French sociologie) through the same process that produced 社会. The discipline and its name arrived together.

社会 + 责任 (zérèn, responsibility; obligation; duty). The obligation one has to the broader social world. Used both in the CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) sense , 企业社会责任 (qǐyè shèhuì zérèn) , and in the broader sense of individual duty to society.

社会 + 主义 (zhǔyì, -ism; doctrine; principle). The dominant political compound built on 社会 in the PRC context. 中国特色社会主义 (Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì, Socialism with Chinese Characteristics) is the formal name for the governing ideology.

e: the altars of soil and grain; the state, the realm
d: 社 shè (the soil-god) + 稷 jì (the grain-god). Originally the two altars a ruler maintained, to the powers of the earth and of the harvest. Because land and food are the foundation of any polity, the word came to stand for the state itself: 江山社稷 "the rivers, mountains, and altars," the whole realm.

社 shè (social) + 交 jiāo (to associate, to exchange). The act of mixing with others, the give-and-take of social life: 社交活动 "social activities," 社交能力 "social skills," 社交媒体 "social media." It names the personal practice of meeting and getting along with people.

社 shè (community) + 区 qū (district, zone). A bounded local community: the people of a single neighbourhood, plus the services and administration that serve them. 社区服务 "community services," 社区医院 "a community clinic," 社区活动 "neighbourhood activities." Smaller and more concrete than 社会.

社 shè (association) + 团 tuán (a group, a body). A voluntary organized group bound by a shared interest: 学生社团 "student clubs," 民间社团 "civic associations." The everyday word for the clubs and societies people choose to join, especially at school and university.

谁 (who) fronted before 都 universalizes over all persons. 谁都知道 = "everyone knows," with the implication that no person could be ignorant of this fact. Often carries a mild rhetorical force: the speaker is emphasizing how obvious or widespread something is.

身 (body) + 材 (timber, material): the body as raw material. 身材好 is a compliment on someone's figure; 保持身材 is keeping in shape. Its sibling 身高 (shēngāo) is height, the statistic every basketball conversation begins with.

身 (self) + 份 (share, allotment): one's allotted position. 身份证 (shēnfènzhèng) is the national ID card, the document requested at every train station, hotel, and SIM-card counter, which makes this compound survival vocabulary rather than abstraction.

e: profound and far-reaching (of influence or impact)
d: 深 shēn (deep) + 远 yuǎn (far). The compound stacks vertical depth with horizontal reach. Reserved for influence that is both substantial and long-lasting: 深远影响 shēnyuǎn yǐngxiǎng (profound, far-reaching influence) is a fixed collocation that appears in historical analysis and political commentary.

e: what (thing); what on earth; exclamation of disgust
d: 什么东西 has two registers. As a genuine question, it means "what is this thing?" As an exclamation, it expresses shock, disgust, or contempt , "what the heck is this?" or simply "ugh!" The exclamatory reading is a complete utterance on its own: 什么东西！registers revulsion at something offensive, absurd, o…

什么 fronted before 都 universalizes over all things or all options. 什么都行 literally "anything goes" , no restriction exists. Extremely common in everyday speech for expressing total flexibility or total acceptance.

The question word "when," literally "what time/moment." It sits where the time answer would go, not at the front as in English: 你什么时候走？("When are you leaving?"). One of the core question patterns alongside 哪儿 (where), 谁 (who), 怎么 (how).
Ask about a word, not a person: "这个词是什么意思" is neutral, while a bare 你什么意思？ means "what are you implying?" and sounds hostile. Keep 这个词 in front.

e: the spirit costume — the shaman's armor and identity
d: The spirit costume (神服 shén fú or 萨满服 sàmǎnfú) is a complex ritual garment encoding the shaman's entire cosmological universe.

e: the shaman's drum — vehicle of the spirit-journey
d: The shaman's drum (神鼓 shén gǔ or 萨满鼓 sàmǎn gǔ) is the most essential ritual implement , sometimes called the shaman's horse (萨满的马), for it is the vehicle on which the shaman rides to the spirit world.
神 (gods; divine) + 话 huà (speech; story; words). The modern compound for mythology emerged in the late 19th century as a translation equivalent for the Western academic concept.

e: spirits; supernatural beings (diffuse, including ghosts and nature spirits)
d: 神 (deity; numinous) + 灵 (spirit; soul; efficacious). 神灵 is broader than 神明: it covers any spirit with numinous presence, including ghosts (鬼 guǐ), nature spirits, and ancestral spirits that do not quite reach the status of recognized deities. A 神明 is always a 神灵; a 神灵 is not necessarily a 神明.

e: the bearing of divine clarity; the sage's luminous presence (literary)
d: A Zhuangzi phrase describing the outward appearance of someone whose inner cultivation has reached a state of unconditioned clarity. 容 róng (bearing; countenance; appearance) suggests that 神明 is visible , it shows in how a person carries themselves.

e: divine clarity comes of itself; luminous intelligence arises spontaneously from cultivation
d: From Xunzi's 劝学 (Encouraging Learning): "积善成德，而神明自得，圣心备焉" , accumulate virtue until integrity forms, and divine clarity will arise of itself; the sage-mind will be complete.

神 (numinous; wondrous) + 奇 qí (rare; strange; remarkable). In classical usage, 神奇 described genuine divine wonder. In modern Chinese it has drifted secular: it commonly means simply "remarkable" or "amazing," with no religious connotation.

神 shén (spirit; presence; expression) + 色 sè (appearance). More elevated than 脸色 , captures the whole impression of a person's bearing and expression. 神色慌张 shénsè huāngzhāng "flustered expression" · 神色自若 "composed and calm."
神 (divine; numinous) + 圣 shèng (sage; sagely; sacred). Where 神明 names a being or a quality of intelligence, 神圣 names the quality of sacredness itself , the inviolability of something set apart.

e: immortals; transcendents (Daoist; deities who achieved divinity through cultivation)
d: 神 (divine; deity) + 仙 xiān (immortal; one who has transcended ordinary existence, often depicted living in mountains). 神仙 in the Daoist tradition are achieved immortals: human beings who through alchemical or meditative practice transformed themselves into divine beings. They were not born divine.

审 shěn (to examine; to judge) + 美 měi (beauty). The act of aesthetic discernment , the capacity to evaluate beauty. 审美观 "aesthetic outlook/values" · 审美趣味 "aesthetic taste." Common in design, art, and cultural criticism.

e: going so far as to (emphatic formal)

d: 生 (shēng) means to give rise to or produce, so 生病 is literally "to produce illness," the standard verb for getting sick. It is a separable verb: an object or aspect marker can split the two halves.

生产 (production) + 关系 (relations, relationships). The Marxist term for the social and economic relationships people enter into in the process of production , ownership of means of production, the relationship between capital and labor, the organization of work.

生产 (production) + 力 (force, power). In Marxist theory: the combination of labor power, tools, technology, and organization that determines how much and how efficiently a society can produce. In everyday business usage: productivity in the simpler sense , output per unit of input.

生产 (production) + 线 (line). The physical or process sequence through which materials move to become finished products. 全自动生产线 (fully automated production line), 流水线 (liúshuǐ xiàn, flowing-water line , assembly line).
生 shēng (raw; unfamiliar) + 词 cí (word). A word you have not yet learned, the staple of every textbook vocabulary list. Its opposite is 熟词 shúcí, a word already mastered.
生 shēng + 存 cún (to exist; to preserve). Survival , continuing to exist under difficult conditions. 生存竞争 "survival competition" · 生存危机 "survival crisis." A more pressured, primal register than 生活.

生 shēng (to be born, to grow) + 活 huó (to live). The pairing of two life-words covers both the verb (to live, to make a life) and the noun (life as it is lived day to day). This is the everyday word for "life," distinct from 命 mìng, the life that can be lost.

e: life wisdom; the wisdom of living well
d: 生活 shēnghuó (life; daily living) + 智慧. The wisdom that shows in how a person navigates ordinary life: relationships, hardship, practical decisions, aging, loss. 生活智慧 is the most common everyday compound with 智慧 , found in book titles, popular philosophy, grandparents' advice.

e: life (the abstract concept; the fact of being alive)
d: 生 shēng (to be born; to live) plus 命. The standard modern word for life in the broad sense: biological life, the human life-course, life as a value worth protecting. Distinct from 生活 shēnghuó (daily life, way of living): 生命 is the precious thing you have once, 生活 is what you do with it.

e: to be angry; to get mad (lit. "produce qi")
d: 生 shēng (to produce; to arise) + 气 qì. The most common everyday word for anger, what you reach for when someone cuts in line, when plans fall through, when people are unreasonable. Colloquial, direct, very high frequency.

生 shēng (birth; life) + 日 rì (day). The universal word for birthday. 生日快乐！Shēngrì kuàilè! = "Happy birthday!" (lit. "birth-day joyful"). 生日蛋糕 = birthday cake. 过生日 guò shēngrì = "to celebrate a birthday" (lit. "to pass through the birthday").

e: the birth-and-death cycle; the wheel of life and death
d: 生死 shēngsǐ (birth and death; life and death) + 轮回. Emphasizes the specific axis of birth and death as the visible face of the cycle: the moments of entry and exit that mark each turn of the wheel.
生 shēng (to live) + 物 wù (thing). A living organism, and also the name of the school subject, biology. 微生物 wēishēngwù is a microorganism, a "tiny living thing."

e: to be born in; to be born at
d: 生 shēng (to be born) + 于 yú (at, in). The set formal frame for stating birthplace or birth date, standard in biographies and records: 生于1980年 "born in 1980," 生于江南 "born south of the river."

声 shēng (sound, voice) + 调 diào (pitch pattern). The linguistic tone: the rise and fall of pitch that distinguishes meaning in Mandarin. 第一声 (first tone), 四个声调 (the four tones). Every syllable on this very page carries a 声调.

e: to declare; to state publicly; a statement
d: 声 shēng (to sound out) + 明 míng (to make clear). To state something openly and on the record, or the formal statement itself: 发表声明 "to issue a statement."
声 shēng (sound) + 母 mǔ (mother; base). The consonant that opens a syllable, such as the m in mā. Paired with the 韵母 yùnmǔ, the final that carries the vowel and tone.

声 shēng (voice, repute) + 望 wàng (esteem). The general public regard a person or institution enjoys: 声望很高 "to be held in high esteem." Close to 名望, it leans toward the public, reputational dimension, what people say and think of someone.
声 shēng (name; repute) + 誉 yù (praise; honor). A more formal, weightier word than 名声, leaning toward esteem and public standing: 国际声誉 "international prestige."
圣 shèng (holy; sage) + 经 jīng (scripture). Literally "the holy classic," the standard Chinese name for the Bible. The same pattern names other scriptures: 古兰经 Gǔlánjīng (the Quran).

e: a flourishing age; a golden age; a prosperous era
d: 盛 shèng (flourishing; abundant) + 世 shì (age). An era of peace and prosperity, the high point of a dynasty or a civilization: 太平盛世 "an age of peace and plenty," 康乾盛世 "the High Qing flourishing." The bright opposite of 乱世, an age of chaos.

e: failure is the mother of success
to lose; to be deprived of
d: 失 shī (to lose; to miss; to fail) + 去 qù (to go away). Something that was yours has gone away , loss. 失去 covers losing people (失去亲人 , lose a loved one), opportunities (失去机会), abilities (失去记忆 , lose one's memory), and qualities (失去耐心 , lose patience). A highly emotive verb.

e: to be disappointed; to lose hope
d: The natural counterpart: 失 (to lose) plus 望 (hope), to have one's hope let down. 我对他很失望 ("I'm very disappointed in him"). Stronger still is 绝望 juéwàng ("to despair," hope cut off entirely). Knowing this pair sharpens the warmth of 希望 itself: to hope is to risk 失望.
