围 (surround) + 困 (trap). The concrete, original sense: to ring something so it cannot break out. Used for armies besieging a city and, by extension, for floodwaters or crowds that cut people off.

e: to break the law; to act illegally
d: 违 wéi (to violate; to go against) + 法 fǎ (law). To step over the line the law draws: 违法行为 "an unlawful act." The mirror image of 合法, the foot landing outside the level mark.

A fixed sum payable on breach, such as late delivery. Under Chinese law a court or arbitrator can reduce it if it is far above the actual loss, so set it at a level you can justify. 赔偿 (péicháng) is compensation for actual loss.

唯 wéi (only; alone) + 一. Used before nouns: 唯一的选择 (the only choice), 唯一的儿子 (only son). Stronger than 只有 zhǐyǒu in its emphasis on singularity , the uniqueness is total, not merely circumstantial. In formal or literary contexts: 唯一真神 (the one true God, in religious translation).

The Uyghur people , the Turkic-speaking Muslim majority population of the Tarim Basin oasis cities, one of China's fifty-five recognized ethnic minorities. The word Uyghur (维吾尔) is a transliteration of the Turkic name for the people, meaning roughly "united" or "allied."

e: to hold together; to maintain (a bond)
d: 维 wéi (to tie; to hold) + 系 xì (bind). To keep a relationship or order from coming apart: 维系感情 "to keep a bond alive," 维系和平 "to maintain peace." Two binding words doubled, the threads kept firmly in hand.

伟 wěi (towering, magnificent) + 大 dà. The highest register of greatness, used for great historical figures, great achievements, and (frequently in political contexts) the greatness of the Party or state. In everyday speech it can be slightly ironic if overused.

伪 wěi (false, counterfeit) + 君子. A person who performs the outward markers of virtue without the inward character , the one who speaks of 义 while calculating 利. The word's force comes precisely from the prestige of what it negates.
Drivers confirm the passenger by the last four digits of the phone number: 手机尾号多少? Answer with the digits one by one.

"Tail money." What triggers it is the real negotiation: 出货前 (before shipment), 验货后 (after inspection passes), or 见提单副本 (jiàn tídān fùběn, against a copy of the bill of lading). The later the trigger, the more leverage you keep.
卫生 wèishēng (hygiene) + 间 jiān (room). The polite, standard word for a bathroom in homes and public buildings. A common synonym is 洗手间 xǐshǒujiān.

卫 (guard) + 星: the guard star that attends a planet. Covers the moon, the GPS constellation, and the dish antenna (卫星天线). The Great Leap Forward idiom 放卫星 ("launching a satellite") still means announcing an inflated achievement.

e: for this reason; because of this; to this end
d: 为 wèi (for; on account of) + 此 cǐ (this; the aforementioned). A formal connective linking back to a preceding reason or context and introducing what was done in response. Stronger in register than 因此 yīncǐ (therefore), carrying a sense of specific, deliberate response to the stated situation.

e: in order to; for the sake of; for the purpose of
d: 为 wèi (for; toward) + 了 le (grammatical completion particle; here a suffix to 为). The standard purpose marker in modern Chinese. 为了 introduces the goal or beneficiary of an action and can appear at the start of a sentence or clause.

e: in order to; for the sake of
d: When the real answer is a purpose rather than a cause, use 为了, not 因为. 为了 names the goal the action serves: 为了健康，他每天跑步 ("for the sake of health, he runs every day"). Asking specifically about purpose, you can use 为了什么 ("to what end").

e: to be trapped by emotion; entangled in feeling
to be known by people; to become widely known
to do whatever one pleases; to act without restraint
not necessarily; may not be the case
d: 未 wèi (not yet; not necessarily , the classical negator of something assumed or expected) + 必 bì (certainly). The combination reverses the certainty: what seemed certain is not settled. A courteous, measured way to challenge an assumption without direct contradiction.

e: to be located at; to be situated in
d: 位 wèi (position) + 于 yú (at). The standard verb for stating where a place sits, common in geography and description: 北京位于中国北部 "Beijing is located in the north of China."

e: Cao Wei — the north, the strongest state
d: Founded in 220 when 曹丕 Cao Pi, son of Cao Cao, finally deposed the last Han emperor and took the throne. Wei held the populous, wealthy north China plain, the old heartland, and was the most powerful of the three in territory, population, and armies. Its capital was at 洛阳 Luoyang.

温 (wēn, warm) + 饱 (fed): warm enough and fed enough, the baseline of a decent life. 温饱 names the threshold of basic livelihood in economic and political language, as in 解决温饱问题 (jiějué wēnbǎo wèntí, to solve the subsistence problem).
Temperature, in 度 (degrees Celsius). 气温 is the air temperature of forecasts; 体温 is body temperature, the one measured at clinic doors.

文 wén (writing; letters) + 笔 bǐ (pen). The quality of someone's prose, the line their pen draws across a page: 文笔流畅 "fluent, flowing style." Praise or critique aimed at how a thing is written, not what it says.

The scholar study, the room where the Four Treasures are kept and used. Literally "the room of writing." The aesthetic of the study, quiet, ordered, with good natural light, was itself a moral and aesthetic statement about the conditions necessary for serious intellectual and artistic work.

文化 (cultural) + 大 (great) + 革命 gémìng (revolution). The political campaign launched by Mao Zedong in 1966 to eliminate "bourgeois" and "counterrevolutionary" elements from Chinese society and culture.

文化 (culture) + 交流 jiāoliú (exchange, mutual flow). The official term for cultural diplomacy programs, art exhibitions, study exchanges, and any organized cross-cultural contact. 中美文化交流 (Sino-American cultural exchange) covers everything from touring orchestras to academic partnerships.

文化 (culture) + 遗产 yíchǎn (legacy, inheritance , 遗 left-behind + 产 property/birth). The inherited deposit of past civilization. 世界文化遗产 (World Cultural Heritage, UNESCO designation) is a major category of Chinese public pride.

文化 (culture) + 自信 (self-confidence). Belief in the value of one's own cultural tradition without need for external validation. As a policy concept, 文化自信 frames the assertion of Chinese civilizational values as a counter to what official discourse calls "cultural hegemony" (文化霸权) by Western nations.

文 wén (writing; text) + 件 jiàn (a piece). A written document, an official paper, or a computer file. The word covers both physical paperwork and digital files: on a screen, 文件 is exactly the word for a file, and 文件夹 wénjiànjiā is a folder.

e: literati — the scholarly class who cultivated the guqin
d: 文 wén (culture; writing; civil) + 人 rén (person). The educated class in imperial China: scholars, poets, painters, officials who defined their identity through cultural cultivation rather than martial or commercial pursuits. The guqin was, more than any other object, the emblem of 文人 identity.

文人 wénrén (literatus; cultivated scholar-official) + 画 huà (painting). The tradition of painting as personal cultivation and self-expression rather than as commissioned craft. Theorized by Su Shi 苏轼 and Mi Fu 米芾 in the Northern Song, dominant from the Yuan onward.

Sanskrit Mañjuśrī ("Gentle Glory"). The bodhisattva of wisdom 智慧 zhìhuì, depicted holding a flaming sword (to cut through delusion) and riding a blue lion. Associated with Mount Wutai 五台山 in Shanxi, China's sacred mountain for wisdom, where Mañjuśrī was believed to reside and manifest.

文 wén (writing; culture; pattern) + 学 xué (learning). The discipline of literature , both the creative output (novels, poetry, essays) and the scholarly study of it. 文学家 wénxuéjiā = writer, literary figure. 中国文学 = Chinese literature. 古典文学 = classical literature. 现代文学 = modern literature.

文 wén (writing; written form) + 言 yán (speech; language) + 文 wén (text). The written form of classical spoken Chinese, crystallized in the pre-Han period and used as the literary and official written standard for approximately 2,000 years.

文 wén (writing; culture; pattern; civilization) + 字 zì (character). Broader than 字 alone. 文字 covers the entire written tradition: individual characters, the system, the culture, and the civilization that writing makes possible.
稳 wěn (steady; firm) + 定 dìng (settled). Holding level without swinging, said of prices, jobs, moods, signals, and states. 稳定的工作 "a stable job," 局势稳定 "the situation is stable."

e: to send regards; to greet; to ask after someone
d: 问 wèn (to ask after) + 候 hòu (to wait on; to attend). To inquire warmly after another person, in speech or in writing: 致以亲切的问候 "to extend warm regards."
蜗 (wō, the snail's shell, with the 虫 insect radical) + 牛. The little horns of a snail earned it the ox; the word doubles as a byword for anything slow.

"I don't quite agree." The 不太 ("not too") softens a disagreement into something closer to "I'm not sure about that." Polite, leaves room for further discussion. Common in considered conversations where you want to push back without confrontation.

e: my book — possessive pronoun + 的 + noun
d: 的 marks possession and belonging: pronoun or noun + 的 + noun. This is structurally identical to the adjective pattern , the modifier always comes before 的 which always precedes the noun.
"What I mean is." Used to clarify when you sense you have been misunderstood, or to preface a more careful restatement of your point. Roughly equivalent to English "what I'm trying to say is…"

"Personally, I think." The 个人 (gèrén, "personal") explicitly marks the view as your own and not a claim about consensus. Common in discussions and slightly more formal exchanges. Useful for stating a minority opinion without inviting argument.

"I feel" or "I think." The default opinion frame in spoken Chinese. Softer than 我认为 (wǒ rènwéi, "I hold the view that"), which is the more formal written-register equivalent. 我觉得 carries no special weight; it is the natural way to introduce any personal take.

h: 我来帮你 · 他去买菜
p: wǒ lái bāng nǐ · tā qù mǎi cài
e: I came to help you · he went to buy groceries
d: 来 and 去 can be followed directly by a verb of purpose: "come/go in order to do [V]." This is structurally simple: 来/去 + verb phrase. The motion establishes the direction; the following verb specifies the purpose of the trip. This is one of the most frequent patterns in everyday speech.

e: I understand now; I get it (I have entered a state of understanding)
d: State-change verbs like 明白 (understand), 知道 (know), 懂 (grasp), 累 (tired), 饿 (hungry), 高兴 (happy) pair powerfully with sentence-final 了. The 了 marks the entry into that state , the moment the change occurs. Before: didn't understand. After: understands.

p: wǒ shì zài Běijīng chūshēng de
e: I was born in Beijing (FOCUS: in Beijing, not elsewhere)
d: Place focus with 在 + location between 是 and the verb. The presupposition is that the speaker was born , the focus is the location. This is how Chinese speakers typically answer "Where were you born?" — using 是…的 to frame the location as the focused new information.

e: I want the red one — 的 stands alone as nominal
d: When the noun after 的 is already understood from context, it can be dropped , leaving 的 to function as a standalone noun phrase meaning "the one(s) that are X." This is the nominalizing function of 的, productive across all the adjective and clause patterns above.

e: "I feel the same way" or "I think so too
d: "I feel the same way" or "I think so too." Personal endorsement that aligns your view with the speaker's. Warmer than a simple agreement; signals shared perspective.

p: wǒ yī shuō tā jiù míngbai le
e: I said it once and he immediately understood
d: 一 + Verb + 就 is one of the most important patterns in the language: "as soon as / the moment I did X, immediately Y happened." The 就 marks the near-instant consequence , no delay, no difficulty.

p: wǒ yǒu bù tóng de kànfǎ
e: "I see it differently" or "I have a different view
d: "I see it differently" or "I have a different view." The most direct of the gentle disagreement frames. Acknowledges the other view exists and explicitly marks your own as separate. Useful when you actually want to make the disagreement clear.
卧 (wò, to lie down) plus 房. The room for sleeping. In everyday speech 卧室 (wòshì) is now more common, but 卧房 survives and shows the same logic: the chamber where one lies down.

握 wò (to grasp) + 手 shǒu (hand). To shake hands , the standard formal greeting gesture in modern Chinese business and official contexts. Traditional Chinese greeting was bowing or clasping one's own hands together (拱手 gǒngshǒu) rather than hand-to-hand contact.

e: wet piling — the accelerated post-fermentation process
oolong — also begins with a controlled wither

d: 屋 wū (dwelling) + 顶 dǐng (top; summit; to carry on the head). The roof , the top of a dwelling. 在屋顶上 = on the rooftop. Also used figuratively in the idiom 屋漏偏逢连夜雨.

屋 (wū, room, building) + 里 (interior). The most domestic use of 里 , the interior of the dwelling, the warm and enclosed space against the outdoors. 屋里人 (wūlǐ rén, the person inside the room) was a classical and regional euphemism for one's wife , the person who keeps the interior.

e: room; the inside of a dwelling
d: 屋 wū + 子 zi (nominalization suffix). The colloquial word for a room or the interior of a small house. Warmer and more intimate than 房间. Used in everyday spoken Chinese for the space one actually lives in.

e: without principle; tyrannical; having lost the Way
d: 无 wú (without; lacking) + 道 dào (Way; moral principle). Classical term for a ruler who has abandoned virtue and lost the mandate of heaven, whose governance has become purely arbitrary and cruel. Still used in historical and literary contexts, and occasionally in strong rhetorical condemnation.

e: the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha · ~20,000 characters · Saṅghavarman's 252 CE translation
d: The long Amitabha Sutra. The foundational narrative: the bodhisattva Dharmākara (法藏 Fǎzàng), aeons ago, makes 48 great vows describing the perfect Buddha-land he intends to create; he then accomplishes them, becoming Amitābha, and his Pure Land becomes the destination of those who call his name.
无 wú (without) + 论. A conjunction introducing an exhaustive condition: whatever the case, the main clause still holds. Pairs with 都 or 也 in the second clause. More formal than 不管.

e: to accomplish nothing; to be ineffectual; to do nothing of consequence
d: 无 wú (without) + 所 suǒ (that which; the place of; a nominalizer in classical grammar) + 作为 zuòwéi (accomplishment; what one does; something achieved). A critique: the person who had the position, the time, the resources, and produced nothing.

The serious register negation. 无意义 is used for things that lack weight, purpose, or value at a meaningful level , not just boring (没意思) but genuinely without worth. Common in philosophical, psychological, and social commentary.

e: the use of uselessness; the utility found in apparent absence or emptiness
d: 无用 wúyòng (useless; without direct utility) + 之 zhī (classical possessive/linking particle) + 用 yòng (use; utility; function). Laozi's paradox that the empty space inside the wheel hub, the hollow of the vessel, the opening of the door , these apparent absences are where actual function lives.

e: nirvana without remainder; final liberation at the dissolution of the body
d: 无余 (without remainder) + 涅槃. Sanskrit parinirvāṇa. The death of an awakened being, when the residual karmic body itself dissolves and the cycle of rebirth definitively ends.

e: to have no karmic connection; not fated to be together
d: The absence of karmic connection , not fated to meet, to succeed, or to be together. 无缘 can be used philosophically and without bitterness to accept failure or rejection: 和这份工作无缘 (it was not my fate to have this job) is a graceful way to accept an outcome without assigning blame.

e: Eastern Wu — the southeast, master of the river
d: Founded by 孙权 Sun Quan, who inherited the southeastern domains built by his father and brother and formally took the imperial title in 229. Wu commanded the lower 长江 Yangtze and the southern coast, with its capital at 建业 (modern Nanjing).

e: the Five Constants; the five cardinal virtues of Confucian ethics
d: 仁 rén · 义 yì · 礼 lǐ · 智 zhì · 信 xìn. The five virtues held to be universal moral constants across cultures and times.

五 wǔ + 谷 gǔ (grain). The five staple grains of ancient China, variously listed (commonly rice, two kinds of millet, wheat, and beans). The exact list shifted by region and era, but the number stayed fixed at five.

e: the five facial features; the five senses
d: 五 wǔ + 官 guān (organ; office). The five sense organs of the face: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and (in the common reckoning) the mouth or skin.

e: the Five Classics — the canonical texts of Confucian education
d: 五 wǔ (five) + 经 jīng (classic; canonical text; warp thread of a fabric). The five texts that defined literate education from the Han dynasty through the abolition of the imperial examination system in 1905: 诗经 (Classic of Poetry), 书经 (Classic of Documents), 易经 (Classic of Changes), 礼记 (Record of Rit…

e: the five colors — green-blue, red, yellow, white, black
d: 五 wǔ (five) + 色 sè (color, appearance). The five phase-colors: 青 qīng (green-blue, Wood), 红 hóng (red, Fire), 黄 huáng (yellow, Earth), 白 bái (white, Metal), 黑 hēi (black, Water). These are cosmological categories before they are aesthetic ones.

e: May Fourth (Movement) — context for 她's birth

d: May Fourth Movement: the intellectual and cultural movement sparked by student protests on May 4, 1919, against the terms of the Treaty of Versailles. It catalyzed demands for science and democracy, rejection of Confucian tradition, and the development of a new vernacular literature.

e: the five flavors — sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty
d: 五 wǔ (five) + 味 wèi (flavor, taste). Sour 酸 suān (Wood/Liver), bitter 苦 kǔ (Fire/Heart), sweet 甘 gān (Earth/Spleen), pungent/spicy 辛 xīn (Metal/Lung), salty 咸 xián (Water/Kidney). Each flavor enters and supports its corresponding organ system in moderate amounts; in excess, it taxes it.

e: the Five-Starred Red Flag (flag of the PRC)
d: 五 wǔ + 星 xīng (star) + 红旗 hóngqí (red flag). The national flag of the People's Republic of China: one large star surrounded by four smaller ones on a red field.

e: the five phases; the five agents
d: 五 wǔ + 行 xíng (to move; phase; agent). Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water, understood as five phases of cyclical change rather than fixed substances. The generating cycle (相生) runs Wood feeds Fire, Fire makes Earth (ash), Earth bears Metal, Metal carries Water, Water nourishes Wood.

e: the five yin organ systems — heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney
d: 五 wǔ (five) + 脏 zàng (solid, yin, storing organ). In TCM, 五脏 refers to five functional systems, not five anatomical organs in the Western sense. Heart (心 xīn) , Fire; Liver (肝 gān) , Wood; Spleen (脾 pí) , Earth; Lung (肺 fèi) , Metal; Kidney (肾 shèn) , Water.
Stage combat: the acrobatic fighting sequences of martial opera. Also used colloquially for action-movie fight choreography.

武 wǔ (martial; military) + 功 gōng (skill). Skill in the martial arts, the trained fighting ability central to wuxia fiction and film. 武功高强 = of formidable martial skill. 一身武功 = a whole body of fighting skill. The word also has a classical sense of military accomplishment, the deeds that win wars.

武 wǔ (martial) + 力 lì (force, power). Force exercised through arms, the option of compulsion by military means as opposed to negotiation: 使用武力 "to use force," 武力解决 "to resolve by force." A neutral, often institutional word for the state's capacity to wage war.

e: the martial forest; the community of martial artists
d: 武 wǔ (martial) + 林 lín (forest). The metaphor is ecological: martial arts practitioners form a dense, interconnected ecosystem , as complex and competitive as a forest, with dominant trees, understory growth, and constant struggle for light and resources.

武 wǔ (martial) + 器 qì (implement, tool). The weapon itself, from a single blade to a nation's arsenal: 核武器 "nuclear weapons," 武器装备 "weaponry and equipment." Figuratively, any decisive instrument: 知识是有力的武器 "knowledge is a powerful weapon."

One of the most famous heroes, celebrated for killing a man-eating tiger on Jingyang Ridge with his bare hands, drunk. Upright and ferocious, he later avenges his murdered brother and is driven by repeated injustice into outlawry.

武 wǔ (martial) + 侠 xiá (a chivalrous knight-errant). The genre of stories about wandering martial heroes bound by honour and loyalty: 武侠小说 "martial-arts fiction," 武侠片 "a martial-arts film." A vast and beloved tradition in Chinese popular culture, peopled by swordsmen who right wrongs outside the rea…

武 wǔ (martial) + 勇 yǒng (brave, courageous). Bravery of the martial kind, valour in combat: the courage of a warrior who is both skilled and fearless. A more literary word than the everyday 勇敢, weighting the bravery specifically toward fighting and the battlefield.

武 wǔ (martial) + 装 zhuāng (to equip, to fit out). As a verb, to arm or equip with weapons; as an adjective, armed; as a noun, an armed force: 武装部队 "armed forces," 武装冲突 "armed conflict." Also figurative: 用知识武装头脑 "to arm the mind with knowledge."

e: the transformation of things — all things are in constant change
d: 物 wù (things; beings) + 化 huà (to transform, change). The final concept named in the butterfly dream passage: "Between Zhuang Zhou and the butterfly there must necessarily be a gap, and this is called the transformation of things 物化." All distinctions, including the distinction between self and othe…
物 (goods, things) + 价 (price). The general price level of everyday goods across a market or city. The word that shows up in talk of inflation and the cost of living.
物 wù (thing; matter) + 理 lǐ (principle). Literally "the principles of things," the modern name for physics. A clear case of 理 meaning the lawful pattern running through the physical world.
物 wù (thing) + 品 pǐn (article; kind). The formal word for goods or articles, the kind you see on a shipping label or in a store inventory: 贵重物品 "valuable items," 日用物品 "everyday articles."
物 wù (thing) + 体 tǐ (body). A physical object regarded as a body occupying space, the term used in physics and plain description alike: 不明飞行物 "an unidentified flying object."
物 wù (thing) + 质 zhì (substance). Matter in the scientific sense, and the material as opposed to the spiritual: 化学物质 "a chemical substance," 物质需求 "material needs."
Frames a disagreement as a communication gap rather than bad faith, which lets the other side correct course without losing face. Use it even when you suspect it was no accident.

误 wù (to err; by mistake) + 解 jiě. To take a thing apart wrongly. To read a meaning incorrectly, or the wrong reading itself: 产生误解 = a misunderstanding arises; 消除误解 = clear up a misunderstanding. The 误 marks the comprehension as faulty, the inverse of a clean 理解.

e: to awaken; to realize; to comprehend

d: Smog: fog plus the revived haze character 霾. 今天有雾霾，戴口罩 was the 2010s urban parent's daily instruction; 蓝天 is its cheerful antonym.
夕 xī (dusk; evening) + 阳 yáng (sun). The low sun of late day. By extension 夕阳 marks anything in graceful decline: 夕阳产业 "a sunset industry," the mirror of the 朝阳 sunrise one.

A medial exclamatory or rhythmic particle characteristic of Chu poetry, appearing within lines to create a pause and an emotional breath. It has no precise lexical meaning but gives the 楚辞 style its distinctive incantatory rhythm. Untranslatable; sometimes rendered as "ah" or simply omitted.

西 (western) + 餐 (meal, cuisine). As opposed to 中餐 zhōngcān (Chinese food). In Chinese urban culture, 西餐厅 (Western restaurant) typically means a European-style restaurant with table settings, bread, and fork-and-knife service.

e: the West; western direction; Pure Land (Buddhist)
d: 西 (west) + 方 (direction; region). The context determines which of the three senses is meant: cosmological/Buddhist (the Pure Land), historical-geographic (Western Regions), or modern geopolitical (the liberal West). When paired with 东方, it is almost always the modern cultural/civilizational sense.

e: the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the Pure Land

d: 西 (west) plus 湖 (lake): the storied lake at Hangzhou, ringed by causeways and pagodas, the most painted and most quoted lake in Chinese poetry.

e: Xi Shi, one of the Four Beauties

d: 西 (west) + 游 (journey, travel) + 记 (record, account). The novel by Wú Chéng'ēn (吴承恩, c. 1500–1582) following the monk Xuánzàng, the Monkey King (孙悟空 Sūn Wùkōng), Pig (猪八戒 Zhū Bājiè), and Sandy (沙僧 Shā Sēng) on their journey to India to retrieve Buddhist scriptures.

e: rinsing the tea — the first discard infusion

d: 洗 (to wash) + 脸 (face). The first ritual of the morning. A verb-object pair, so you can split it: 洗个脸 (xǐ ge liǎn), to give the face a quick wash.

e: to love; to be fond of; to favor
d: 喜 xǐ (to delight in) + 爱 ài (to love). A warmer, more literary cousin of 喜欢, often used of things admired or cherished: 深受喜爱 "deeply loved (by the public)," 喜爱的作家 "a favorite author."

e: a liking; a preference; to be keen on
d: 喜 xǐ (to like) + 好 hào (to be fond of, 4th tone). Both a verb and a noun for a settled preference or taste: 个人喜好 "personal preferences," 喜好读书 "fond of reading." Note 好 here is hào, not hǎo.

e: a festive air; an atmosphere of joy
d: 喜 xǐ (joy) + 气 qì (air, mood). The bright, celebratory atmosphere of a happy occasion, the feeling in a room hung with red: 满屋喜气 "the whole house full of festive joy."

e: happy money — cash gifts at joyous occasions

d: Auspicious, festive: the quality of being celebratory and lucky. Red is described as 喜庆 by default; white and black are explicitly not 喜庆 in gift or festive contexts.

A "joyful funeral": the death of a person who lived to old age and left many descendants. Treated as cause for celebration alongside mourning, and marked with comparatively festive elements: the music may be more exuberant, the occasion more public.

e: a happy occasion; a joyous event; (esp.) a wedding
d: 喜 xǐ (joy) + 事 shì (matter, affair). Any auspicious event, and by default a wedding. Its standing opposite is 丧事 sāngshì, a funeral, the unhappy event.
喜 xǐ (joy) + 悦 yuè (pleased). A literary, slightly elevated word for inner gladness, the quiet glow of a good thing: 丰收的喜悦 "the joy of a good harvest," 内心的喜悦 "the delight within."
Opera fan, literally "theatre-obsessive." The devoted fan who can sing along from memory, knows every role's vocal style, and has opinions about every major performer.

系 xì (string together) + 列 liè (row; to arrange). A run of related items strung in a row: 系列产品 "a product series," 一系列问题 "a whole series of problems." The connecting 系 makes the separate items read as one ordered set.
系 xì (connection) + 统 tǒng (to unify). An ordered whole of interworking parts: 操作系统 "operating system," 神经系统 "nervous system." As an adjective it means systematic: 系统地学习 "to study systematically."
Cell: fine wrap. 干细胞 (gànxìbāo) is a stem cell, and 细胞分裂 is cell division, vocabulary every 生物课 student recites before exams.

e: to finish work; to get off work; end of shift
d: 下 xià (to descend; to leave the higher platform) + 班 bān (shift; work roster). To come down from the work platform , to leave one's post at the end of the day. The indispensable pair of 上班. 下班后 (after work) is the default framing for evening activities in Chinese urban conversation.

e: to put in the work; to make a serious effort; to buckle down
d: 下 xià (to place; to put down) + 功夫 (effort/work). The verb phrase for serious, sustained investment of effort. The directional 下 is crucial: you are depositing effort into something, like placing a foundation. Not a momentary burst of energy but a committed, extended investment.

e: class is over; end of class; to dismiss class
d: 下 xià (to end; to come down from) + 课 kè (lesson; class). Class has descended from its height, releasing students and teacher. The verb pair 上课/下课 (class begins/class ends) is the daily rhythm of Chinese school life. 下课了！is the joyful announcement that class is over.

e: come down; slow to a stop
below; underneath; the lower surface; the following
d: 下 xià (below; under) + 面 miàn (face; side; surface). The underside; what is below. Used for physical position (床下面 = under the bed) and for discourse organization (下面请看 = please see the following).

下 xià (to come down; to fall) + 雪 xuě (snow). The standard way to say "it is snowing," built on the same 下 used for 下雨 (to rain). Chinese treats weather that falls from the sky as something the sky "sends down," so snow, rain, and frost all take 下.

下 xià (to descend; to fall from above) + 雨 yǔ (rain). Rain descending from the sky. The 下 construction extends to all precipitation: 下雪 (to snow), 下冰雹 (to hail). Notably, 下 is the standard verb for precipitation in Mandarin , not "fall" or "pour" but "descend." The sky issues weather downward.

e: it's raining now; it has started to rain
d: The canonical example of sentence-final 了 announcing a new situation. There is no past tense here , the rain is starting now, and the 了 signals a change of state has occurred or is occurring. This 了 carries the meaning: "now things are different from before."
To download: carry down. Paired with 上传 (upload). 载 also reads zǎi meaning "year" in classical texts, a polyphone trap for advanced readers.

下 xià (next; the following) + 周 zhōu (week). The temporal use of 下: what descends next into the present from the future. Consistent across all time units: 下周 (next week), 下个月 (next month), 下年 / 明年 (next year).

e: to scare away; to frighten off
d: 吓 (xià, to frighten) + 跑. A V+跑 resultative: the action of frightening produces the result of running off. Highly productive pattern: 赶跑 gǎnpǎo (chase off), 撵跑 niǎnpǎo (drive off), 骂跑 màpǎo (scold off). The construction packages cause and escape into one verb.

e: let some get rich first — permission for inequality as a stage
d: 先 (first, beforehand) + 富 (wealthy, to become rich) + 起来 (resultative complement indicating a process coming into effect). The condensed form of Deng's proposition: 让一部分人先富起来 (ràng yī bùfen rén xiān fù qǐlai, let some people get rich first).

先 xiān (first; ahead; earlier) + 生 shēng (one born; person). "One born earlier" , originally a teacher or Confucian master; now the standard polite term for "Mr." and also "husband" in formal contexts (我先生 "my husband"). A word whose meaning has drifted beautifully from teacher → gentleman → Mr.
鲜 xiān (fresh) + 花 huā (flower). Living, fresh-cut blossoms, the flowers you buy and give: 一束鲜花 "a bouquet of fresh flowers." Distinct from 假花 jiǎhuā, artificial flowers.

鲜 xiān (fresh; vivid , the "umami" character, fish + sheep 鱼+羊) + 美 měi (beautiful; delicious). The compound for food that is both fresh and deeply flavorful. Note: 鲜 also contains the sheep radical 羊, linking back to 美's own etymology. Used for broths, seafood, and fresh ingredients.
显 xiǎn (visible, to show) + 然 rán (-ly). States that something is plain to see: 显然 he was lying. Often opens a sentence as a comment on the whole: 显然，这是个错误 "clearly, this is a mistake."
县 xiàn (county) + 城 chéng (walled town). The administrative town at the center of a county, historically walled, the seat of the local magistrate.
现 xiàn (present) + 场 chǎng (site; field). The very place where something is happening: 案发现场 "the scene of a crime," 现场直播 "a live broadcast."

e: ready-made; off the shelf; already prepared
d: 现 xiàn (on hand) + 成 chéng (completed). Already finished and available, needing no further making: 现成的答案 "a ready-made answer," 现成的衣服 "off-the-rack clothing."

现代 xiàndài (modern; the modern era) + 化 huà (the -ize suffix). The textbook example of the 化 suffix at work: "to make modern." 现代化 is one of the central words of twentieth-century Chinese politics, most famously in 四个现代化 (the Four Modernizations: agriculture, industry, defense, science and technolog…

现 xiàn (present; to appear) + 金 jīn (gold; money). Cash in hand, as opposed to digital payments, credit, or promises. 付现金 "to pay in cash." In a society where 微信支付 and 支付宝 (WeChat Pay and Alipay) dominate, 现金 is increasingly rare.

e: reality; actual; (of a person) realistic, practical
d: 现 xiàn (present) + 实 shí (real; solid). What is actually the case here and now, set against 理想 lǐxiǎng (the ideal). As an adjective for a person it can mean clear-eyed, or pointedly materialistic.
Filling: the stuffing inside the wrapper. The -r suffix is a Beijing-dialect feature that appears frequently in food vocabulary.

e: homesickness; nostalgia for one native place
d: 乡 xiāng (native place; hometown; rural area) + 愁 chóu (sorrow; melancholy; anxiety). The specific emotional register of Double Ninth as a festival: not grief for the dead (清明节), not fear of wandering spirits (中元节), but the longing of those separated from home by distance.
Zodiac conflict: signs that are diametrically opposite in the twelve-year cycle and considered incompatible. The Rat-Horse conflict, the Tiger-Monkey conflict, etc.

e: to get along; to spend time together
d: 相 xiāng (each other) + 处 chǔ (to dwell; to be with). To live alongside or get along with others: 容易相处 "easy to get along with," 相处了很多年 "spent many years together."

相 xiāng (mutual) + 克 kè (to conquer, to regulate, to check). In the Five Phases context, 克 means disciplined control rather than destruction , the river bank that contains the flood, not the dam that annihilates the water.

e: to be linked; to be connected to each other
d: 相 xiāng (mutually; each other) + 连 lián (to link). To be mutually joined, used when two or more things are connected to one another rather than one connecting the other. Common in describing geography, anatomy, and abstract relations: lands that border each other, ideas that are bound together.
相 xiàng (appearance) + 片 piàn (a flat slice; sheet). The printed photograph as an object. Its everyday synonym 照片 zhàopiàn is equally common; both name the picture you hold or hang.

e: to meet a prospective marriage partner; a matchmaking meeting
d: 相 xiàng (to examine) + 亲 qīn (marriage; relative). The arranged meeting where two people look each other over with marriage in mind, often set up by family or a matchmaker. Note: this 相 keeps a level tone for many speakers, but the sense is the inspecting one.

相 xiāng (mutual, reciprocal) + 生 shēng (to give birth, to generate, to produce). Each phase nourishes and gives rise to the next; each is simultaneously "mother" to the phase it generates and "child" to the phase that generates it.
相 xiāng (mutually; each other) + 思 sī (to miss; to long for). The classical word for romantic yearning. 相思 is not a modern word , it carries centuries of weight from classical poetry.
相 xiāng (mutually) + 同 tóng (same). Two or more things being the same as each other: 完全相同 "exactly the same." More formal and written than the everyday 一样 yīyàng.
相 xiāng (mutual) + 信 xìn (trust). To place trust in someone or to believe a thing is so: 我相信你 "I trust you," 相信科学 "to believe in science." One of the most common verbs built on the mutual reading.

Fragrant herbs and beautiful women: the conventional shorthand for the allegorical system of the 楚辞, in which fragrant plants represent virtuous ministers and women represent the king who should (but does not) receive them.
香 (fragrant) + 水 (water). Literally fragrant water, the modern word for bottled perfume. Measured with 瓶 (píng, bottle) or 滴 (dī, drop).
香 (fragrant) + 甜 (sweet). Of food, fragrant and sweet at once. By extension, of sleep, deep and contented, the way you sleep after a good meal.
香 (fragrant) + 味 (smell, flavor). The scent something gives off, especially of food or flowers. The everyday word for a good aroma.
香 (fragrant) + 烟 (smoke). The everyday word for a cigarette, named for the scented smoke it gives off. Counted with 支 (zhī, stick) or 包 (bāo, pack).

e: the Xiang Army — Zeng Guofan's force
to respond to; to answer (a call); response
d: 响 xiǎng (to sound, to echo) + 应 yìng (to respond). To answer a call or appeal, often a collective one: 响应号召 (respond to a call), 积极响应 (respond actively). The image is of an echo answering a sound.

e: to think of; to occur to; to realize
d: 想 xiǎng (to think; to consider) + 到 dào (arrive). Thinking that arrived at an idea: the thought reached its destination. 想到 implies the idea arrived in mind, often unexpectedly or after searching.

想 xiǎng (to think) + 法 fǎ (method; approach; way). The product of thinking: what thinking produces when it runs long enough. Used freely for ideas, opinions, views, and intentions. 你有什么想法？ is one of the most common ways to ask for someone's opinion in meetings and conversations.

e: to be homesick; to miss home
d: 想 xiǎng (to miss) + 家 jiā (home; family; household). The heart facing home from a distance. A verb in Chinese where English uses an adjective ("homesick").

e: to miss someone; to long for; to think of fondly
d: 想 xiǎng (to think of; to miss) + 念 niàn (to think of; to recite; to hold in mind). Two overlapping words for mental attending-to, doubled for emphasis: 念 carries the connotation of something repeated, recurring, kept alive by repetition, the way a prayer or a name is recited.

e: to recall; to call to mind

d: 想 xiǎng (to think) + 象 xiàng (image; likeness; elephant , 象 was borrowed for "image" because of its visual suggestiveness: the elephant is the largest thing you picture). Think-image: to form mental images of things not present. Used as both a verb (to imagine) and a noun (imagination).

想 xiǎng (want; think) + 要 yào (want; need; will). The two wanting words stacked for explicitness or emphasis. Where 想 alone can be tentative (I'd like to; I'm thinking of), 想要 is more direct and pointed. Used when desire is clear and conscious rather than a vague inclination.

e: always (up to now); from the start; hitherto
d: 向 xiàng (facing back along) + 来 lái (coming up to now). A close synonym of 一向, slightly more literary: 他向来诚实 "he has always been honest." Frames a quality as having held from the beginning to the present.
向 xiàng (toward) + 前 qián (front). Directed at the space ahead: 向前走 "walk forward," 向前看 "look ahead," both literally and in the sense of looking to the future rather than dwelling on the past.

e: to yearn for; to long for; to look forward to
d: 向 xiàng (toward) + 往 wǎng (to go toward). The heart facing a place or life it longs for: 向往自由 "to yearn for freedom," 向往美好的生活 "to long for a good life." Warmer and more aspirational than plain "to want."

e: facing the sun; sunny (of an aspect)
d: 向 xiàng (toward; facing) + 阳 yáng (sun). Oriented toward the sun, said of a room, window, or slope that gets good light. A 向阳的房间 is a sought-after sunny room.

向 (toward; in the direction of) + 右 (right). The standard directional command for turning right: 向右转 (turn right), 向右走 (go right). As with its mirror pair 向左, used in navigation, military drill, physical education, and any instruction involving directional movement.

向 (toward; in the direction of) + 左 (left). The standard instruction for turning or moving left: 向左转 (turn left), 向左走 (go left, walk left). Used in navigation, traffic directions, dance instruction, and any context requiring directional movement.

e: to resemble; to be like; such as
d: A verb meaning "to resemble, to be like." The basic frame is A 像 B ("A is like B"), asserting likeness rather than identity. It powers similes in the frame A 像 B 一样 + Adj/Verb ("A is just like B"). 像 also introduces examples, "such as / like" (像…这样的, "things like…").

e: to digest; to absorb (food, or by extension, information)
d: 消 xiāo (to dissolve; to dissipate; to consume) + 化 huà (to transform). The verb for digestion: food broken down and turned into something the body can absorb. 化 again names the physical turning of one substance into another.

e: Theravada — the Lesser Vehicle (pejorative Mahayana term)

d: Small cleverness: the shortcut-finding wit that games the rule and misses the point. 耍小聪明 (deploying petty cleverness) is what teachers accuse corner-cutting students of; its grown-up antonym is 大智慧, great wisdom.

e: this humble younger brother (self-deprecating first person)
d: Used by a male speaker to refer to himself deferentially, regardless of birth order. The formula downsizes the speaker relative to the listener. Also used literally for a younger brother. In gangster/triad contexts, 小弟 means a low-ranking follower , the hierarchy is explicit.
小 (xiǎo, small) + 狗. The everyday word for a puppy or any small dog. 小狗 is warm and affectionate, the term a child reaches for first.

小 xiǎo (small) + 孩 hái (child). The standard neutral word for a child. Related: 小朋友 xiǎopéngyou (young friend , the standard address for children, used by teachers and adults), 小孩子 xiǎoháizi (a slightly more affectionate variant with the diminutive 子).
小 (xiǎo, small) + 鸡 (chicken). The fluffy yellow chick just out of the shell, a favorite in children's songs and picture books.

小 (small, young) plus 姐 is the classic polite title for a young, unmarried woman, like English "Miss." Register matters: in some mainland contexts a bare 小姐 can sound off, so service settings often prefer 美女 (měinǚ) or a surname plus 姐.

Short lyric form: tune patterns of 58 characters or fewer. The most concentrated 词 form, requiring the greatest compression. Contrasted with 长调 chángdiào or 慢词 màncí, the extended long forms of 91 characters or more.

Childhood nickname , a pet name used within the family, often deliberately humble or silly to avoid attracting bad luck to the child. 狗蛋 (Gǒudàn, "Dog Egg") or 二毛 (Èrmáo, "Second Fuzz") are classic examples.

A father's way of referring to his daughter when speaking to someone of higher status. The 小 does not mean the daughter is young or small , it encodes the father's self-positioning as lesser. Compare 犬子 quǎnzǐ (my unworthy son , lit. "dog son"), the parallel self-deprecating term for sons.
Small qi: a constricted spirit, tight with money and with grace. The direct opposite is 大方 (dàfang, generous, poised). Milder than 小人; a friend can be teased as 小气 and remain a friend.

e: quiet; softly; in a low voice
d: 小 xiǎo (small) + 声 shēng (voice). A small voice, the opposite of 大声: 小声说 "to speak quietly," often so others do not overhear.

小 xiǎo (small) + 时 shí (time; hour). A small slice of time: one hour. The compound reflects a traditional view of time's granularity , the hour as the smallest standard unit. Contrast 小时候 xiǎoshíhou (childhood, "when one was small"), where 小时 carries the older sense of "young age."

"When little," a fixed expression for one's childhood. 我小时候 = "when I was a child." Compare 那时候 (back then, at that time) and 到时候 (when the time comes). Note: 小时 (without 候) means "an hour," a different word, so the 候 matters.

小 xiǎo (small; minor) + 说 shuō (speech; theory). Literally "minor talk" , the genre of fiction was long considered a lower form of literature compared to history and philosophy. The term was coined to contrast with 大道 "the Great Way" of classical learning.

e: small room; cabin; cottage; little shelter
d: 小 xiǎo (small) + 屋 wū. A small dwelling , intimate, often cozy or rustic. In fiction and poetry, 小屋 carries warmth: a retreat, a nest, a place apart. In real estate, sometimes used lightly for a studio flat.

小 xiǎo (small) + 心 xīn (heart; mind). A small heart is one drawn in, watchful, attentive to fine detail. The literal image captures the bodily experience of caution: the heart pulling back, contracting, alert to what is delicate or dangerous.
Small heart-aperture: a mind with a narrow gate, through which slights enter easily and never leave. The grudge-keeping cousin of 小气, aimed at temperament rather than wallet.

e: a small token; "it's nothing"; the understated gift
d: The standard self-deprecating framing when presenting a gift. Used across all gift-giving contexts , bringing something to a dinner host, giving a business contact a present, sending something to a teacher.

e: small seal script — the Qin standardized writing form
d: Lesser Seal Script , standardized by the Qin minister Li Si as part of the First Emperor's unification project. Characterized by even-weight strokes, systematic construction, and balanced proportions.

e: to imitate, to follow the example of

d: 校 xiào (school) + 长 zhǎng (elder; head; chief). The head of a school at any level, from primary school principal to university president. The pattern [institution] + 长 = head of that institution is extraordinarily productive: 院长 (dean), 部长 (minister), 市长 (mayor), 省长 (governor), 班长 (class monitor).

笑 xiào (laugh) + 话 huà (speech; words). Laugh-words: a joke, a funny story. As a verb it flips to "to laugh at, to make a fool of." 讲笑话 = to tell a joke; 闹笑话 = to make an embarrassing blunder that others laugh at.

e: smiling face; a smile worn for others
d: 笑 (laugh, smile) + 脸 (face). A face shaped into a smile, especially the welcoming one you put on for guests or customers. The opposite expression is 板着脸 (bǎnzhe liǎn), to hold the face stiff and stern.

笑 xiào (to smile; to laugh) + 容 róng (facial expression). The smile as a look worn on the face, treated as a noun: something one has, shows, or loses. Where 笑 is the act of smiling, 笑容 is the expression itself, the way the face holds a smile.

e: said with a smile; said, smiling
d: The canonical attendant circumstance: 笑着 (smiling) + 说 (to say). The 着 links the two actions , the smiling frames and accompanies the speaking. This construction is the default way to describe facial expression or gesture accompanying speech in Chinese narrative.

e: to rest one's feet (during a journey); to take a break en route
d: 歇 xiē (to rest) + 脚. The classic verb for stopping during a long walk or trip , at a tea-house, an inn, a roadside pavilion. Carries the texture of pre-modern travel; still used for any pause on a long journey.
Near-homophone, sound-alike , the phonetic mechanism underlying most Chinese number symbolism. 谐音 relationships exist wherever two syllables sound similar enough that one can evoke the other.

e: method of writing a character; stroke order

d: For technical terms and every figure. Hand over your notebook or phone. Pinyin input is fine; most people will type the characters for you.

e: impressionist; expressive — capturing spirit over likeness
a portrayal; a true reflection of reality

d: 写 xiě (to write; to depict) + 真. To depict the real. Originally a classical term for a lifelike portrait painting; in modern usage, a posed portrait photo (especially of a model or celebrity). In Japanese, the same word 写真 shashin simply means "photograph."

e: to write characters; to write by hand
d: 写 xiě (to write) + 字 zì (character). The fundamental literacy act: hand meeting surface, character taking form. Specifically implies handwriting rather than typing or printing. In Chinese civilization, handwriting is never merely functional.

e: to write; to compose — literary register
insight from experience; what one gained

d: Wang Yangming's direct challenge to Zhu Xi. Principle 理 is not located in external things requiring investigation; it is not separate from the moral mind. The mind is itself the site of 理.

e: the Heart Sutra · 260 characters · Xuanzang's 649 CE translation
d: The shortest and most chanted Buddhist scripture in East Asia. The condensed essence of the Prajñāpāramitā literature: emptiness applied to every Buddhist category in turn, then the closing mantra. Memorized by every Chan novice; recited daily across China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam.

e: in one's heart; in one's mind; emotionally
d: 心 (heart, mind) + 里 (interior). Functions as a locative: something is in the heart, occurs in the heart. Covers both cognitive interior (I understand in my mind) and emotional interior (I feel in my heart). More intimate and less clinical than 内心 nèixīn (inner heart , a literary register).

e: sincere words; what one truly means
d: 心里 (inside the heart) + 话 (speech, words). The words that come from the interior rather than from performance. Sharing 心里话 is an act of trust and intimacy , it signals that the speaker is not managing their presentation but revealing what is actually held inside.

e: to have a clear grasp; to know what's what
d: 心里 (inside the heart) + 有 (to have) + 数 (numbers, a count). To hold the numbers privately in one's interior , to have a clear reckoning of a situation that one carries internally.
心 xīn (heart) + 理 lǐ (logic; principle; grain of wood). "The logic of the heart." Used both as the general term for one's psychological state and as the root of 心理学 (psychology as a discipline).

心 xīn (heart) + 情 qíng (emotion; situation). The weather of the inner world. Where 情 alone is broad, covering emotion, circumstance, and romantic feeling, 心情 focuses it: the specific emotional atmosphere a person inhabits right now. It fluctuates by the hour.

e: thoughts; mental energy; what the mind is occupied with
d: 心 xīn (heart) + 思 sī (to think; thought). What the heart is currently thinking about, or whether it has the mental space to think about something at all.
From passage 7. 挂碍 guà ài means hindrance or obstruction in the literal sense of something snagging or hooking. 心无挂碍 describes the mind that, having seen emptiness, has nothing left to snag on.

e: School of Mind; Wang Yangming's Neo-Confucian tradition
d: The Neo-Confucian tradition associated with Wang Yangming. Holds that 理 is not separate from the mind; the moral faculty 良知 is the ground of both knowledge and action.

e: wits; smarts; (also) intent, motive of the heart
d: 心 xīn (heart) + 眼. The eye of the heart , the inner faculty of judgment and quick-wittedness. 心眼多 xīnyǎn duō "to have many wits" (clever, calculating, or scheming, depending on tone). 心眼好 xīnyǎn hǎo "to have a good heart-eye" (kind-hearted, well-intentioned).

e: intention; goodwill; the feeling behind a gesture
d: 心 xīn (heart) + 意 yì (intention; meaning). The feeling or thought behind an action: the sincerity and warmth that a gift, gesture, or visit carries. Often used when downplaying the material value of what you have brought: 这只是一点心意 ("this is just a small token of my regard").

心 xīn + 脏 zàng (internal organ, the biological sense; same character used in 器官, organs of the body). In modern Chinese, 心 alone almost never refers to the biological organ; that role belongs entirely to 心脏. The standalone 心 is always the conceptual, emotional, and cognitive heart.

e: the 1911 Revolution that ended the Qing
hard, toilsome; thanks for your trouble
d: 辛 (xīn), pungent or laborious, pairs with 苦 (kǔ), bitter, to name effort that wears you down. As a set phrase it doubles as warm thanks: telling someone 辛苦了 acknowledges the toil they just put in for you.

Acknowledges effort someone made for you: picking you up at the station, preparing samples, staying late. Factory staff hear it constantly from managers and appreciate it from a buyer. Answer with 不辛苦 or 应该的 (yīnggāi de, "it's what I should do").

新华 Xīnhuá (New China, the name of the official news agency and many state institutions) + 字典. The most widely-sold book in Chinese history and the standard reference for mainland Chinese students since its first edition in 1953. Simple, portable, and comprehensive for modern literacy needs.

新 (new) + 婚 (hūn, marriage). Newly married , in the fresh state of the new relationship. 新婚快乐 (congratulations on the marriage , Happy Newlywed); 新婚夫妇 (newlywed couple); 新郎 xīnláng (groom , new-man) and 新娘 xīnniáng (bride , new-woman) are the standard terms for a wedding couple.

e: the new replacing the old; transition between old and new
d: 新 (new) + 旧 (old) + 交替 (jiāotì, to alternate; to replace one another in succession). The pairing of 新 and 旧 as a compound unit , 新旧 , appears constantly in Chinese: 新旧对比 (contrast between old and new), 新旧交融 (old and new blending together), 新旧矛盾 (conflict between old and new).

新 (new) + 年 (year). The new year , the most basic New Year compound, usable for both the Gregorian New Year (January 1) and the Chinese Lunar New Year. 新年快乐 (Happy New Year) and 新年好 (New Year greetings) are the standard phrases.

e: Happy New Year , literally "new year happy
d: Happy New Year , literally "new year happy." The standard greeting for the solar New Year (January 1). For Lunar New Year, 新春快乐 (xīnchūn kuàilè) or 恭喜发财 (gōngxǐ fācái, "congratulations and may you prosper") are more appropriate.

新 (new) + 鲜 (xiān, fresh , especially of food; vivid; rare). Fresh in the sensory sense: 新鲜蔬菜 (fresh vegetables), 新鲜空气 (fresh air). Also used for novel experiences: 对我来说这是个新鲜事物 (this is something new to me). 鲜 alone means fresh-vivid; 新鲜 combines freshness with newness.
信 (xìn, letter) plus 封 (the sealing/wrapper): the paper sleeve that closes around a letter. The most common everyday word built on 封.

信 xìn (trustworthy communication; word) + 号 hào (sign; designation; mark; sound used as a signal). A signal is a word that has been stripped of language and reduced to a reliable mark: it carries only its presence or absence, its strength or weakness, rather than semantic content.

信 xìn (letter; trust) + 件 jiàn (a piece). A collective, somewhat formal term for letters and written correspondence. A single letter is 一封信 (using 封 fēng); 信件 names the whole category of correspondence, the kind of word a post office or office form would use.

e: trust; to trust; to have confidence in
d: 信 xìn (trustworthiness; to trust) + 任 rèn (to appoint; to entrust; to allow , 任 carries the sense of delegating responsibility to someone). To trust is to appoint a person as worthy of reliance. 信任危机 xìnrèn wéijī = a crisis of trust (institutional or personal). 建立信任 jiànlì xìnrèn = to build trust.

信 xìn (trustworthy word; communication) + 息 xī (breath; rest; news , 息 contains 自 zì, nose, over 心 xīn, heart: breath as the sign of life; by extension, news and tidings). A word that travels and carries meaning , information as a form of 信. 信息时代 xìnxī shídài = the information age.

e: creditworthiness; credit; trustworthiness in financial conduct
d: 信 xìn (trustworthiness) + 用 yòng (use; to use; practical application). Trustworthiness made actionable , the record of a person or institution reliably standing by its commitments. 信用卡 xìnyòng kǎ = credit card. 信用评级 xìnyòng píngjí = credit rating.
星 (star) + 期 (period): the star period, from the seven-luminary week. Days attach numbers: 星期三 is Wednesday. Asking the day is 今天星期几? , one of the few questions where 几 needs no measure word.

Star, in the affectionate reduplicated form used in speech and songs. Single 星 does the compounding work: 星空 (starry sky), 星系 (galaxy, "star system"), 星座 (constellation, and the zodiac sign small talk runs on).

星 + 座 (seat): the seats of the stars. In young urban small talk it means the Western zodiac sign: 你是什么星座的? has largely displaced asking one's Chinese zodiac animal among the under-forty, an ironic import given the antiquity of native Chinese astral lore.

行 xíng + 动 dòng (to move). The general word for action , both as a verb (to take action) and as a noun (an action, an operation). Used in everything from personal life (我们应该立刻行动 "we should act at once") to police and military operations (军事行动 "military operation").

e: market quotation; the going rate; market conditions
d: 行 háng + 情 qíng (situation; circumstances). The state of the trade. The going prices, the market mood, the supply-and-demand conditions in a particular industry. 股市行情 = stock market quotes; 看行情 = "to watch the market"; 行情看涨 = "the market is bullish."

e: to do good deeds; to practice virtue
d: 行 xíng (to practice; to carry out) + 善 shàn (goodness). Goodness made active , not merely possessed as a quality but enacted as conduct. Appears equally in Confucian moral discourse and Buddhist merit accumulation.

行 xíng + 为 wéi (to do; to act). What one does, framed as observable behavior. The clinical/formal noun used in psychology, law, and ethics , 行为艺术 "performance art," 犯罪行为 "criminal behavior," 不文明行为 "uncivilized behavior."

行 háng + 业 yè (occupation; enterprise). The trade as a category. Used for entire industries: 教育行业 the education sector; 服务行业 the service industry; 各行各业 "every trade, every profession" (the standard phrase for "all walks of life").

e: walking, standing, sitting, lying down — enlightenment in every posture
d: The four bodily postures covering all of waking life. Chan's radical claim: enlightenment is not a special state achieved in meditation and then lost in ordinary life , it is the natural condition of mind, available in every action.

e: to form; to take shape; to come into being
d: 形 xíng + 成 chéng (to become; to complete). To shape-into-being. The all-purpose verb for something forming through a process: 形成习惯 form a habit; 形成共识 reach (form) a consensus; 逐渐形成 gradually take shape. Used constantly in writing about how systems, opinions, and conditions arise.

e: to describe; to characterize in words
d: 形 xíng + 容 róng (appearance; countenance). To give a thing its look in words. The verb for describing, especially feelings and impressions that resist plain statement. 难以形容 = hard to describe; 无法形容的美 = indescribable beauty.

e: form; format: the outward shape, as opposed to content
d: 形 xíng + 式 shì (pattern; format). The form or format of something, set against its 内容 nèiróng (content). 各种形式 = various forms; 形式上 = in form only, nominally. 形式主义 = formalism, prizing appearance over substance. Do not confuse with 形势 (the situation): see the 辨析 section above.

e: the situation; the lay of forces; circumstances
d: 形 xíng + 势 shì (momentum; force). The configuration of forces at a given moment, weightier than 情形. Used for politics, war, economy, and any contest of momentum: 国际形势 the international situation; 形势严峻 the situation is grim; 看清形势 read the situation clearly. Do not confuse with 形式 (form vs. content).

形 xíng + 体 tǐ (body). The body as form: the physical figure of a person, often in contexts of posture, dance, and bearing. 形体训练 = physical/figure training; 形体优美 = a graceful figure. This is the bodily branch of 形, where shape means the shape of a living body.

e: garment structure; the form category of a historical garment
shape: the outward form of a thing
d: 形 xíng + 状 zhuàng (state; appearance). The everyday word for the shape of a physical object: what outline it has, what it looks like. 奇怪的形状 = a strange shape; 各种形状 = all kinds of shapes. This is the first 形-word a learner meets.

Evocative image: the poetic mode in which a natural scene opens a poem and resonates emotionally with the human subject to follow without being a direct comparison. The most distinctively Chinese of the three classical poetic modes.

兴 (aroused spirit, the xìng reading) + 趣 (inclination, delight). 对…感兴趣 ("to feel interest toward") is the essential pattern: 我对中国历史很感兴趣. 兴趣班 are the after-school enrichment classes filling Chinese childhood weekends.

杏 xìng (apricot) + 仁 (kernel). The seed inside the apricot pit , the everyday Chinese word also used for almonds in modern usage (e.g. 杏仁奶 "almond milk"). In Chinese medicine, 苦杏仁 is a classical herb used to "moisten the lung and stop coughing."

姓 xìng (surname) + 名 míng (given name). The formal term for a full name. Note: Chinese names are surname-first, given-name-second, the reverse of Western convention. 你叫什么名字？= "What is your name?" (informal, just the name). 请问您的姓名？= "May I ask your full name?" (formal).

幸 xìng (fortunate; lucky; to survive) + 福 fú (blessing). The compound for subjective happiness and well-being , what you feel when life is going right. 幸福感 = sense of well-being. 幸福生活 = a happy life. One of the most searched Chinese words globally.
Formal "fortunate meeting," said with the handshake on first contact. Pairs naturally with 久仰 (jiǔyǎng, "I've long admired you") when you know the person by reputation. Plain 很高兴认识您 is never wrong.

性 xìng (sex) + 别 bié (distinction, category). The category of male or female: 性别平等 "gender equality," the 性别 field on an application form. The standard, neutral word in both everyday and formal contexts for the sex or gender of a person.

e: human nature is bad — innately insufficient for morality without cultivation
d: Xunzi's foundational claim: 人之性恶，其善者伪也, "Human nature is bad; what is good in humans is their deliberately cultivated achievement." 性 xìng: what one is born with. 恶 è: bad, harmful, insufficient. 伪 wèi: artificial, deliberately made (not fake). Goodness is real but must be built, not grown.

性 xìng (nature) + 格 gé (standard, frame). The settled set of traits that make up who a person is: 性格开朗 "an open, cheerful character," 性格内向 "an introverted personality." The standard word for someone's overall character, often the answer to "what kind of person are they."

性 xìng (property) + 能 néng (capability). The functional properties of a machine, device, or material: 性能稳定 "stable performance," 高性能 "high-performance." How well a thing does what it is built to do, the practical measure of its inherent quality.

性 xìng (nature) + 情 qíng (feeling). Temperament considered through the lens of mood and emotional reaction: 性情温和 "of a gentle temperament," 性情大变 "a sharp change in temperament." Warmer and more feeling-laden than the neutral 性格, closer to the heart's weather than its frame.

e: elder and younger sibling — fraternal respect
d: 悌 tì , fraternal respect , is the virtue governing sibling relations. The elder brother owes kindness and example; the younger owes deference and respect.

e: "heaven and earth in the breast" — a person of sweeping strategic vision and depth
d: 胸 xiōng (chest; breast; the seat of mind and intention in classical Chinese thought) + 有 (to have; to hold) + 乾坤. A grand classical expression of praise for someone who holds the entire world in mind: a strategist, a statesman, a general, a writer who sees at the largest possible scale.

e: to revise, to amend, to edit
d: 修 (mend, trim) + 改 (alter). To go back over a text, plan, or law and revise it. The standard word for editing a document or amending a draft.

e: to build/repair the Great Wall; (slang) to play mahjong
d: 修 (xiū) means to build, repair, or construct. 修长城 in its literal sense describes the labour of wall-building. In colloquial slang, 修长城 is a playful way to say "playing mahjong": the rows of mahjong tiles arranged on the table look like sections of wall.

e: the heart of shame and dislike — sprout of 义 righteousness
d: 羞 xiū: shame (about one's own moral failures). 恶 wù: dislike, aversion (to moral failure in others). Together: the capacity to feel shame about one's own wrong actions and moral distaste for wrongdoing in general.

e: the lowest examination degree; a local scholar
d: The degree produced by the local examination (童试), the entry point of the examination ladder. A 秀才 had cleared the first hurdle and earned a recognized scholarly identity, but stood far from power.

e: open-minded; receptive; humble in one's willingness to learn
d: 虚 xū (empty; hollow; receptive , the vessel with space in it) + 心 xīn (heart; the seat of thought and feeling in Chinese understanding). An empty heart , a mind that has not pre-filled itself with conclusions and so can genuinely receive what it encounters.

e: to study with an open mind; to learn receptively
d: A fixed phrase in educational and developmental discourse. The combination of 虚心 (open-minded) + 学习 (to study; to learn) makes the stance toward learning explicit: approach the subject without assuming you already know, without defending existing positions, with the mind empty enough to receive new…

e: to need; to require (necessity, not merely desire)
d: 需 xū (to need; to require, a more formal or objective necessity) + 要. 需要 focuses on objective need rather than personal desire. 我需要帮助 (I need help , genuinely require it) vs. 我要帮助 (I want help , requesting it).

e: to publicize; to promote; publicity; propaganda
d: 宣 xuān (to proclaim) + 传 chuán (to spread). To put out a message deliberately so it reaches the public: 宣传海报 "a promotional poster," 宣传活动 "a publicity campaign." Carries a sense of organized, purposeful spreading, and in political contexts the meaning of propaganda.

e: to read out formally (a statement, verdict, decree)
d: 宣 xuān (to announce; to proclaim) + 读. To read aloud in a formal setting , a court verdict, a wedding vow, an official document at a ceremony. The 宣 marks the public, declarative force.

e: Xuan paper, made in Jingxian, Anhui province
d: Xuan paper, made in Jingxian, Anhui province. The standard for Chinese calligraphy and painting. Made from wingceltis bark and rice straw. Comes in raw (生宣, highly absorbent) and sized (熟宣, controlled absorbency) varieties. Archival: properly stored examples survive over a thousand years.

e: the monk who walked to India — Tang Buddhism's greatest figure
d: The monk 玄奘 Xuánzàng (602–664 CE) traveled overland to India in 629 CE , without imperial authorization, defying a travel ban , spent sixteen years there studying at Nalanda and other Buddhist centers, and returned to Chang'an in 645 CE carrying 657 Sanskrit texts.

Suspended river , a river whose bed has been raised by sediment deposition above the level of the surrounding plain, contained only by embankments. The lower Yellow River is the world's most extreme example, running up to 10 meters above the adjacent farmland.

e: to choose; to elect; to select
ballot: a ballot paper; a vote (as a counted unit)
d: 选 xuǎn (to choose; to elect) + 票 piào (slip; ballot). The physical ballot paper you mark and cast, and by extension a vote as a unit to be counted. The tally of votes is 票数 piàoshù, and to win is to gather the most 选票. Here 票 is the slip that carries a single person's choice.

Acupoint , a specific location on a channel where qi gathers close to the surface and is most accessible to needling or moxa stimulation. Also called 腧穴 shùxué in classical texts. The body has 361 standard points on the 14 main channels.

e: to pick up bad habits, to be led astray
d: 学 (to learn) + 坏 (bad). To learn the wrong things, the classic parental worry that good company makes good children and bad company corrupts them. 坏 here works as a result complement: the learning turns out badly.
Study + acquire-the-skill. 学了三年 states duration; 学会了 states victory. The complement 会 restricts itself to learnable skills, which is a nice grammatical definition of what a skill is.

了 with a duration complement signals an action sustained for a period of time and treated as a completed, bounded episode. This construction is essential for talking about study, work, residence, and sustained experience. The duration frames the action as a finished chunk of time.

学 xué (to study; to learn) + 生 shēng (one who is still "green"; a junior person). The student as someone still growing, not yet ripe. One of the most common nouns in Chinese , every school context relies on it.

学 xué (to study) + 问 wèn (to ask). Knowledge built by studying and asking, the deep, earned kind. 很有学问 "highly learned." The word itself teaches that real knowledge grows from questions, not answers alone.

学 xué (to learn) + 习 xí (to practice; to review; to get accustomed to). The compound captures the Confucian dual process: 学 (receiving new knowledge) + 习 (practicing and consolidating it). Not just acquisition but repeated reinforcement. The most common word for "to study" in general.
学 xué (to learn) + 业 yè (course of work). One's studies taken as a whole: 完成学业 "to complete one's studies," 学业成绩 "academic results." The general term for the body of work a student carries.

学 (to study) + 者. The standard modern word for a scholar or academic researcher. This compound has been in continuous use since at least the Han dynasty. A 学者 is someone whose work consists of systematic study , the word appears in book reviews, conference programs, and academic citations alike.

雪 xuě (snow) + 白 bái (white). The brightest, purest white, with snow as the standard of comparison, exactly parallel to English "snow-white." This is a productive pattern in Chinese: a vivid object plus a color word yields an intensified shade.

雪 xuě (snow) + 花 huā (flower). A snowflake, the snow seen as a falling blossom. The flower metaphor is old and pervasive in Chinese: snow falling is 雪花飘 (snow-flowers drifting), and the six-petaled structure of a real snow crystal was noticed early, with classical texts remarking that snow flowers h…

Snow Land: a poetic name for Tibet, used in both Chinese and Tibetan contexts. Refers to the snowcapped mountains and high plateau character of the Tibetan landscape and appears in poetry, song, and political rhetoric from multiple perspectives.

e: to inquire; to ask about; to seek information
d: 询 xún (to inquire) + 问 wèn (to ask). A formal verb for asking in order to gather information, common in writing and service contexts: 询问情况 "to inquire about the situation," 向某人询问 "to make inquiries of someone."
训 (to instruct, to discipline) + 练 (to drill). Organized, directed training: athletes, soldiers, dogs, new staff. Heavier and more institutional than 练习.

压 yā (to press down) + 力 lì (force). The force pressing from outside. In physics it is pressure on a surface; in daily life it is the weight of stress: 工作压力 "work stress," 压力很大 "under a lot of pressure."

e: lucky money for children at New Year
d: New Year's money, given in red envelopes; literally "money that suppresses the year-beast." The year-beast (岁 suì) was a mythological monster; the money and noise were protective against it.

押 yā (to detain; to hold) + 解 jiè. The clearest home of the second reading jiè. To escort a prisoner or valuables under guard from one place to another: 押解犯人 = escort a prisoner; the related 解送 jièsòng = send under escort.
鸭 (yā, duck) + 蛋: a duck egg, larger and richer than a hen's. Among students it means a score of zero, since the round 0 on a test paper looks like an egg sitting there.

e: Battle of Yamen, final Song defeat
pulling up seedlings to help them grow
fireworks; smoke and fire; the warmth of lived life
d: 烟 yān (smoke) + 火 huǒ (fire). Literally: fireworks. Poetically: 人间烟火 rénjiān yānhuǒ , "the smoke and fire of the human world" , the warmth and vitality of ordinary life.
Say plainly how serious it is; understatement is heard as "not urgent." 影响很大 (the impact is large) and 不能接受 (bù néng jiēshòu, cannot be accepted) are firm without being rude.

言 yán (speech; words) + 语 yǔ (language; speech). The near-synonym of 语言, but with the elements reversed and the emphasis shifted: where 语言 is language as system, 言语 is the specific words someone uses , their speech acts, their chosen phrasing, what came out of their mouth in a particular moment.

e: rock rhyme — the mineral terroir of Wuyi

d: The standard academic term for one's research focus. Appears on every Chinese CV, every graduate-school admission form, and every department web page. 你的研究方向是什么? — "What's your research direction?" — is the second question Chinese academics ask each other after the name.

e: King Yama — judge of the underworld
d: The ruler of the underworld and its ten courts of judgment, borrowed from Buddhist cosmology and fully integrated into Chinese folk religion by the Tang dynasty. Every soul that died passed through Yama's courts for a comprehensive moral accounting.

颜 yán (color; face , the face radical) + 色 sè. The standard compound for "color." 什么颜色？"What color?" Also used figuratively: 给你点颜色看看 gěi nǐ diǎn yánsè kànkan = "I'll show you what I'm capable of" (lit. "let you see some color" , a threat or challenge to someone who has been underestimating you).

红 hóng (red) , the color of luck, celebration, life force. Worn at weddings, hung at new year, placed in red envelopes (红包 hóngbāo). 白 bái (white) , the color of mourning; worn at funerals, avoided at celebrations.

e: Yan Zhenqing — Tang 楷书 master
vision; taste; judgment; the discerning eye
d: 眼 yǎn + 光 guāng (light). Literally eye-light. The kind of seeing a person has , their taste in art, their judgment in business, their ability to spot a good investment or a good partner. 有眼光 yǒu yǎnguāng "to have a good eye"; 没眼光 "to have poor judgment"; 长远的眼光 "long-term vision."

e: to have blurred vision; to be dazzled
d: 眼 yǎn (eye) + 花 huā (blurred). Eyes swimming or dazzled, unable to focus, from too much to look at or from dizziness: 看得我眼花 "it left my eyes swimming." 头晕眼花 is "dizzy and bleary."

e: horizon (of experience); breadth of one's outlook
d: 眼 yǎn + 界 jiè (boundary; realm). The boundary of what one's eye has taken in , how widely one has seen, traveled, read, lived. 开阔眼界 kāikuò yǎnjiè "to broaden one's horizons" is one of the standard reasons given in Chinese for travel, study abroad, and reading widely.

眼 yǎn + 睛 jīng (eyeball; pupil). The standard everyday word for "eyes" in spoken Chinese. Single 眼 alone almost never serves this role; for "her eyes are beautiful" you say 她的眼睛很美 not 她的眼很美. The 睛 is light and unstressed in pronunciation.
眼 yǎn + 泪 lèi (tear). Standard word for tears. 流眼泪 liú yǎnlèi "to shed tears"; 擦眼泪 cā yǎnlèi "to wipe away tears." The classical/literary equivalent is just 泪 alone or 泪水 lèishuǐ.

眼 yǎn + 力 lì (strength). The strength of one's seeing , both literally (sharpness of vision) and figuratively (judgment, ability to spot quality or fakery). The skilled antique-dealer is praised for 眼力 in detecting forgeries.

眼 yǎn + 皮 pí (skin). Eyelid. The colloquial idiom 眼皮底下 yǎnpí dǐxià "right under one's eyelids" means "right in front of one, in plain sight" , usually used to describe something missed or stolen despite being right there.

e: the look in one's eyes; gaze; expression
d: 眼 yǎn + 神 shén (spirit; expression). Not the eyes themselves but the spirit visible in them , the look one gives, the expression of feeling that the eyes carry. A high-frequency word in fiction and dialogue: 他的眼神很温柔 "the look in his eyes was very gentle"; 用眼神告诉我 "tell me with your eyes."

e: to act; to perform; to develop

d: 演 yǎn (to perform) + 唱 chàng (to sing). To sing before an audience as a performance. 演唱会 yǎnchànghuì is a concert, the standard word for a pop or vocal live show.

Inspection before shipment, by your own staff or a 第三方 (dì-sān fāng, third party). 抽检 (chōujiǎn) is sampling inspection, usually by AQL level; 全检 (quánjiǎn) is 100% inspection. 来料检验 checks incoming materials.
羊 (yáng, sheep/goat) + 肉 (meat). The meat of choice in the northwest, central to hotpot and skewers.

e: sunlight; sunshine; (of a person) sunny, positive, and open
d: 阳 yáng (yang; sun) + 光 guāng (light; radiance). Literal sunlight, and by extension a personality quality: someone who is 阳光 is warm, open, optimistic , they bring light into the room. The metaphor is exact: they embody yang qualities in their social presence.

阳 yáng (the sun; the yang principle) + 历 lì (calendar). The sun-based calendar, in modern usage the Gregorian calendar used for official and international dates. Also called 公历 gōnglì (the "common," that is internationally standard, calendar).

e: Yangming Cave; the retreat for which he was named
yang energy: warm, active vital force
d: 阳 yáng (active; bright) + 气 qì (vital energy). The warm, rising, animating energy of the body in traditional medicine, set against 阴气 yīnqì. A person low on 阳气 is thought to feel cold and sluggish.
阳 yáng (sun) + 台 tái (platform; stage). The sun-platform: the balcony or open terrace of a home, valued precisely because it catches the light and is where laundry is hung to dry.
阳 yáng (the active; the positive pole) + 性 xìng (nature; gender). In medicine, a positive test result; in grammar, the masculine gender. Its pair is 阴性 yīnxìng (negative; feminine).

e: yang deficiency — the yang warmth is insufficient; cold dominates
d: Classic 阳虚 symptoms: aversion to cold (怕冷 pà lěng), cold hands and feet, pale complexion, fatigue and low energy, frequent clear urination, low libido, loose stools.

e: yang dwelling = home for the living

d: Oxygen (as breathable gas): the nourishing 氧 plus 气. 缺氧 (quēyǎng) is oxygen deprivation, used literally at altitude and figuratively for stuffy rooms and dull meetings.
样 yàng (sample) + 品 pǐn (article, product). One specimen held up to represent a whole batch: a free sample, a trade-show display, a test piece sent to a buyer.

e: appearance; look; manner; the way it seems
d: 样 yàng (appearance) + 子 zi (noun-suffix). The look or manner of a person or thing. The idiom 看样子 kàn yàngzi means "from the looks of it." For the toneless suffix 子, see the 子 entry.

e: remote; very far away; vast distance
d: 遥 yáo (far off; distant; also a walk-movement compound) + 远 yuǎn (far). Both components carry the meaning of distance, making 遥远 the intensified form: not just far, but vertiginously far. Used for cosmic distances, ancient history, or inaccessible places. Primarily literary and written.
Medicine. 吃药 is taking it, 开药 is prescribing it, 中药 is the herbal kind, and 药店 the pharmacy. The grass radical 艹 on top remembers that medicine began as herbs.

e: food and medicine share an origin
intention and plan: what someone is going to do
d: 要 before a verb marks intention or imminence: 我要回家 (I'm going home / I want to go home; context decides). 打算 dǎsuàn (to plan) and 准备 zhǔnbèi (to prepare, to be about to) make the plan explicit: 我打算明年去中国 (I plan to go to China next year).
要 (yào, to want, to need) + 紧 (tight). What is held tight is what matters. Most common in the negative 不要紧 (bùyàojǐn), meaning never mind, it doesn't matter, often said to reassure.
要紧 (crucial) + 关头 (guāntóu, the pivotal point). The hinge of a situation, where the outcome is decided and there is no room to hesitate.

要 (want/will) + 是 shì (be/this). A colloquial conditional meaning "if; supposing that." Slightly warmer and more personally invested than the neutral 如果 rúguǒ. Implies the speaker has some stake in the condition. Typically paired with 就 jiù in the consequence clause.

e: 也: one more added to an existing set
d: 也 always implies that the predicate has already been established for another entity. The sentence using 也 adds one more item. This requires a prior context (explicit or implicit) in which the predicate was already true of someone or something else. 也 cannot start a discourse out of nowhere.

e: that works too; either way is fine
"In other words" or "what I mean is
d: "In other words" or "what I mean is." The restatement marker. Used to reframe something you just said in clearer or simpler terms. Indispensable when you sense the listener has not quite caught your point.

e: that is also true; that's fair

d: "Maybe so." Noncommittal acknowledgment that signals you are not convinced but are not interested in arguing the point. The 吧 keeps it soft. Functionally close to English "I guess" or "could be."

e: outdoor stage performances — theatre for an audience of spirits
d: 野 yě (outdoor; wild) + 台 tái (stage) + 戏 xì (theatre; opera). Temporary wooden stages erected in public spaces for Ghost Month performances , 歌仔戏 (Taiwanese opera), puppet theatre (布袋戏 bùdài xì), and traditional opera forms.

e: a palm's worth of sweat — anxious, breaking out in a sweat
d: 把 can measure abstract quantities that could theoretically fill a cupped hand , a handful of something. 一把汗 (a palm of sweat) is an idiom for being anxious or nervous to the point of sweating. 一把泪 (a handful of tears) appears in literary contexts for weeping.

e: getting on in age; a certain age (often with mild reproach)
